The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.

p.seg: 1.1 The Book of Rites says:
Be reverent in all things,
composed as in deep thought,
and settled in speech.
Thus the people will be at peace!
1.2 Arrogance should not be indulged,
desires should not be followed,
ambitions should not be satisfied,
pleasures should not be taken to extremes.
1.3 For the worthy: be intimate yet respectful,
awed yet loving.
Love others while knowing their faults,
hate others while knowing their merits.
Accumulate wealth yet be able to disperse it,
settle in comfort yet be able to move when needed.
Faced with wealth, do not acquire it improperly;
faced with difficulty, do not avoid it improperly.
Do not seek victory in disputes,
do not seek more than your share.
Do not insist on certainty in doubtful matters,
be straightforward but do not claim possession of truth.
1.4 As for bearing: sit like a corpse (in solemnity),
stand like one in sacrifice.
Rites follow what is appropriate,
missions follow local customs.
1.5 Rites serve to
determine intimacy and distance,
resolve doubts and suspicions,
distinguish similarities and differences,
and clarify right and wrong.
In rites,
do not frivolously please others,
do not use excessive words.
In rites,
do not overstep boundaries,
do not insult or bully,
do not indulge in undue familiarity.
Cultivate oneself and fulfill one's words—
this is called good conduct.
When conduct is cultivated and speech follows the Way,
that is the substance of rites.
It is said that rites are learned from others,
not that rites are used to acquire others.
It is said that one comes to learn rites,
not that rites go to teach.
1.6 For the Way, virtue, benevolence, and righteousness,
without rites they cannot be accomplished;
for teaching, instruction, correcting customs,
without rites they are not complete.
In settling disputes and litigation,
without rites they cannot be decided.
For ruler and minister, superior and inferior, father and son, elder and younger brother,
without rites their roles are not fixed.
For officials and students serving teachers,
without rites there is no closeness.
In arranging court and governing the army,
in overseeing offices and enforcing laws,
without rites authority and dignity cannot be exercised.
In prayers, offerings, and sacrifices,
in serving ghosts and spirits,
without rites there is no sincerity or solemnity.
Therefore, the gentleman is reverent,
respectful, restrained,
moderate, yielding,
and deferential to illuminate rites.
A parrot can speak,
yet it remains a flying bird.
A gorilla can speak,
yet it remains a wild beast.
If a person has no rites,
even if they can speak,
are they not of the heart of beasts?
Only beasts have no rites,
hence father and son share a mate.
Thus the sages created
rites to teach people,
so that people, having rites,
know to distinguish themselves from beasts.
1.7 The highest values virtue,
the next emphasizes giving and repayment.
Rites value reciprocity:
if one gives but receives nothing in return,
it is contrary to rites;
if one receives but gives nothing in return,
it is also contrary to rites.
With rites, one is secure;
without rites, one is in peril.
Hence it is said,
rites must be studied.
Rites involve
humbling oneself and honoring others.
Even a peddler
must have respect,
how much more the wealthy and noble?
If the wealthy and noble know to value rites,
they will not be arrogant or dissolute;
if the poor and lowly know to value rites,
their hearts will not be timid.
1.8 At ten, one is called young
and learns.
At twenty, one is called weak
and is capped.
At thirty, one is called strong
and has a household.
At forty, one is called firm
and serves in office.
At fifty, one is called ài
and administers government duties.
At sixty, one is called qí
and directs others.
At seventy, one is called old
and passes on responsibilities.
At eighty or ninety, one is called mào;
at seven, one is called dào.
For dào and mào,
even if they commit crimes,
punishment is not applied.
At a hundred, one is called qī, cared for.
A senior official retires at seventy.
If he cannot decline,
he must be given a stool and staff,
and attended by women on missions.
When traveling to other states,
he rides in a comfort carriage.
He calls himself "old man,"
but in his own state uses his name;
if asked by another state,
he must inform them of its regulations.
1.9 When consulting an elder,
one must carry a stool and staff for him.
If an elder asks a question,
to answer without deferring
is contrary to rites.
1.10 The rites for being a child:
warm in winter and cool in summer,
settle at night and inquire in the morning,
and among peers
or equals, do not contend.
1.11 For a child,
even three gifts do not include carriages or horses.
Thus the districts and villages praise his filial piety,
brothers and relatives praise his kindness,
colleagues praise his fraternal duty,
close friends praise his benevolence,
and companions praise his trustworthiness.
When meeting his father's friends,
he does not advance unless told to advance,
does not retreat unless told to retreat;
if not asked,
he does not dare to answer.
This is the conduct of a filial child.
1.12 For a child:
when going out, he must inform;
when returning, he must show his face;
his travels must have regular places,
his studies must have set subjects.
He never calls himself old.
For one twice his age, he serves as a father;
for one ten years older, he serves as an elder brother;
for one five years older, he walks shoulder-to-shoulder.
When five sit together,
the elder must have a separate mat.
1.13 A child
does not occupy the main corner,
sit in the center of the mat,
walk in the middle of the path,
or stand in the middle of the gate.
He does not set limits in feasts,
nor act as the corpse in sacrifices.
He listens to the unsaid,
sees the unseen.
He does not climb heights,
nor approach depths.
He does not criticize lightly,
nor laugh lightly.
A filial child does not serve in darkness,
nor climb to dangerous places,
fearing to disgrace his parents.
While parents live,
he does not pledge his life to friends,
nor have private wealth.
1.14 For a child:
while parents live,
his cap and clothes are not pure white.
An orphan in charge of the household
wears cap and clothes not purely colored.
1.15 A young child should often be shown no deception;
a youth does not wear furs or skirts.
He stands squarely.
He does not eavesdrop.
If an elder leads him by the hand,
he holds the elder's hand with both hands.
If the elder bends to speak in his ear, he covers his mouth to reply.
1.16 When following a teacher,
do not cross the road to speak with others.
Meeting the teacher on the road,
hurry forward,
stand straight with hands clasped.
If the teacher speaks, answer;
if not, quickly withdraw.
When following an elder up a hill,
one must face the direction the elder is looking.
Do not point while ascending the city wall,
nor shout on the wall.
When about to enter a residence,
seek nothing from it.
When approaching the hall,
one's voice must be raised.
If there are two pairs of shoes outside the door,
enter only if conversation is heard;
if not, do not enter.
Before entering the door,
lower your gaze.
Upon entering, hold the door latch respectfully,
and do not look around;
if the door was open, leave it open;
if closed, close it again;
if someone enters after you,
close it gently without slamming.
Do not step on shoes,
nor stride over mats;
gather your robe and move quickly to a corner.
Be cautious in your responses.
When officials enter or leave the ruler's gate,
they pass to the right of the threshold stone,
and do not step on the threshold.
1.17 When entering with a guest,
yield to the guest at every gate.
When the guest reaches the chamber door,
the host requests to enter and prepare the mat,
then comes out to welcome the guest.
The guest firmly declines,
and the host respectfully ushers the guest in.
The host enters and turns right,
the guest enters and turns left.
The host approaches the eastern steps,
the guest the western steps.
If the guest is of lower status,
they approach the host's steps.
The host firmly declines,
after which the guest returns to the western steps.
Host and guest yield in ascending,
the host ascends first,
the guest follows,
stepping on each step with both feet together,
moving steadily upward.
On the eastern steps, lead with the right foot;
on the western steps,
lead with the left foot.
1.18 Do not hasten outside curtains or screens,
nor in the hall,
nor when holding jade.
In the hall, take small steps;
below the hall, walk normally.
Do not swing arms in the room,
nor stretch elbows when sitting side by side.
When giving something to someone standing, do not kneel;
when giving to someone seated, do not stand.
1.19 In the ritual of cleaning for an elder,
place the broom on the dustpan,
use sleeves to sweep and retreat,
ensuring dust does not reach the elder,
and hold the dustpan facing oneself.
Carry a mat like a balanced beam.
Ask which direction the mat should face;
ask where the pillow should point.
For mats:
if facing north or south,
the west is the honored position;
if facing east or west,
the south is honored.
For non-dining guests,
spread mats
with a zhang (about ten feet) between them.
The host kneels to adjust the mat,
the guest kneels to smooth it and decline.
If the guest removes extra mats,
the host firmly objects.
The guest steps on the mat,
then sits.
The host does not speak first unless asked,
nor does the guest initiate conversation.
When about to sit,
maintain a composed expression.
Hold the robe with both hands,
keeping it a foot from the ground.
Do not let the robe flap,
nor stumble with the feet.
If the teacher's books, zither, or lute are in front,
move them while seated,
being careful not to step over them.
Sit fully back when not eating,
and fully forward when dining.
Sit steadily,
maintaining a calm demeanor.
If the elder has not mentioned a topic,
do not interrupt.
Keep your expression proper,
and listen respectfully.
Do not plagiarize others' words,
nor echo mindlessly.
Base speech on ancient examples,
citing former kings.
When attending a teacher seated:
if the teacher asks,
answer after they finish.
Rise to request instruction,
and rise to ask for further explanation.
Respond promptly to a father's call,
and to a teacher's call,
rising with a respectful "yes."
When sitting with a respected person,
do not leave extra space.
Do not rise for peers.
Rise when a candle arrives,
when food comes,
and when an honored guest appears.
Do not let the candle burn to the stub.
Do not scold a dog in front of a respected guest.
Do not spit when declining food.
1.20 When attending a superior seated,
if they yawn or stretch,
gather their staff and shoes,
or check the time,
the attendant should ask to leave.
When attending a superior seated,
if they change the topic,
rise to respond.
When attending a superior seated,
if someone announces,
"In a moment,
I wish to report,"
step aside and wait.
1.21 Do not eavesdrop,
do not answer shrilly,
do not gaze wildly,
do not be idle or sloppy.
Do not be arrogant when walking,
do not stand unevenly,
do not sit with legs spread,
do not sleep prone.
Tie hair neatly without extensions,
do not remove your cap,
do not bare yourself when working,
do not lift robes in heat.
1.22 When sitting with an elder,
do not wear shoes in the hall,
nor remove them facing the steps.
To put on shoes,
kneel to pick them up,
and retreat to the side.
Face the elder while donning shoes;
kneel to move them,
and bend to put them on.
1.23 If two people are sitting or standing apart,
do not join them.
For those standing apart,
do not pass between them.
1.24 Men and women do not sit together,
share clothes racks,
towels or combs,
nor hand items directly.
Brothers- and sisters-in-law do not exchange inquiries,
and stepmothers do not wash trousers.
Outside matters not discussed inside the threshold,
inside matters not discussed outside.
A girl engaged to marry
wears a tassel;
without serious reason,
no man enters her door.
Aunts, sisters, and daughters
who return after marriage
should not sit on the same mat
nor eat from the same dish as their brothers.
Father and son do not share a mat.
Without a matchmaker,
men and women do not know each other's names.
Without betrothal gifts,
they do not interact or become intimate.
Thus, the date is reported to the ruler,
purification and fasting to the spirits,
and wine and food shared with community and friends,
to emphasize the separation.
Do not marry someone of the same surname.
If buying a concubine of unknown surname,
divine it.
Do not befriend a widow's son
unless he shows exceptional qualities.
1.25 To congratulate a bridegroom,
say:
"So-and-so sent me,
hearing you have guests,
to offer a gift."
1.26 The poor need not use wealth for rituals,
the old need not use physical effort for rituals.
1.27 When naming a child, one should not use the name of a state,
nor use the names of sun or moon,
nor use the name of a hidden ailment,
nor use the names of mountains or rivers.
1.28 Boys and girls are ranked separately.
When a man reaches twenty,
he is capped and given a courtesy name.
In the presence of his father,
a son is called by his given name;
in the presence of the ruler,
a minister is called by his given name.
When a girl is betrothed,
she is given a hairpin and a courtesy name.
1.29 In the ritual of serving food,
sliced meat is placed on the left and whole meat on the right,
cooked grains are placed to the left of the person,
and soup to the right.
Minced and roasted meats are placed farther out,
vinegar and sauces farther in,
scallions and steamed vegetables at the end,
and wine and beverages on the right.
When dried meat is set out,
the bent part is on the left and the end on the right.
If a guest is of lower rank,
he should take the food, rise, and decline;
the host rises to decline the guest's gesture,
after which the guest sits.
The host invites the guest to offer a sacrifice:
sacrifice to the food,
starting with what was served first.
For the order of meats,
sacrifice to each in turn.
After three mouthfuls of rice,
the host invites the guest to eat the whole meat,
then the guest may taste all the meats.
If the host has not finished,
the guest should not rinse his mouth.
When attending an elder at a meal,
if the host personally serves the food,
one should bow and then eat.
If the host does not personally serve,
then one does not bow before eating.
When eating together, do not eat to fullness; when sharing rice, do not wipe hands on it.
Do not form rice into balls,
do not return rice to the bowl,
do noisily gulp down soup,
do not make noises while eating,
do not gnaw on bones,
do not return fish or meat to the dish,
do not throw bones to dogs.
Do not insist on getting a particular dish,
do not fan the rice to cool it.
Do not eat millet with chopsticks.
Do not swallow soup whole,
do not add seasoning to the soup,
do not pick teeth,
do not drink the sauce.
If a guest adds seasoning to the soup,
the host apologizes for not cooking it well;
if a guest drinks the sauce,
the host apologizes for being poor.
Tender meat is bitten off,
dried meat is not bitten with teeth.
Do not gobble roasted meat.
When the meal ends,
the guest kneels forward,
clears away the rice and dishes, and hands them to the attendant;
the host rises to decline the guest's help,
after which the guest sits.
When attending an elder with drink,
if wine is offered, one rises,
and bows to receive it at the place of the vessel.
If the elder declines,
the younger returns to the mat and drinks.
If the elder raises
the cup but has not finished,
the younger does not dare drink.
If an elder gives a gift,
the younger or inferior does not dare decline.
If given fruit in the ruler's presence,
those with pits should carry the pits in their bosom.
When serving food to the ruler,
if the ruler offers leftovers,
if the vessel is washable, one does not transfer the food;
otherwise, transfer all.
Leftovers are not offered in sacrifice.
A father does not sacrifice to his son,
a husband does not sacrifice to his wife.
When attending an elder in the same way,
even if served doubly, one does not decline,
nor when sitting as a companion.
For soup with vegetables, use chopsticks;
for soup without vegetables, do not use chopsticks.
For the Son of Heaven, pare a melon and cut it into segments,
covering it with fine linen.
For a feudal lord, split it,
covering it with coarse linen.
For a senior official, leave it whole,
for a scholar, break it,
for a commoner, bite it.
When parents are ill,
the capped one does not comb hair,
does not swing arms when walking,
does not speak idly,
does not play the zither,
eats meat but not to the point of changing taste,
drinks wine but not to the point of changing complexion,
laughs but not to baring teeth,
is angry but not to cursing.
When the illness ceases, resume normal behavior.
Those in worry sit on a single mat,
those in mourning sit on a lone mat.
1.30 When floods descend,
do not offer fish or turtles;
those offering birds should cover their heads,
but those offering domesticated birds need not.
Those offering carriages or horses hold the whip and mounting cord,
those offering armor hold the helmet,
those offering a staff hold the end.
Those offering captives grasp their right sleeve.
Those offering millet hold the right tally,
those offering rice hold the measure.
Those offering cooked food hold the sauce and pickles.
Those offering fields or houses hold the title deed.
When presenting a bow to someone:
for a strung bow, keep the string up;
for an unstrung bow, keep the back up.
Hold the tip with the right hand,
support the grip with the left.
Regardless of rank, let the girdle pendants hang.
If the host bows,
the guest steps aside,
avoiding the bow.
If the host receives it himself,
he goes to the guest's left,
takes it under and supports the grip;
facing the guest side by side,
then receives it.
When presenting a sword, point the hilt left.
When presenting a dagger-axe, point the butt forward,
the blade backward.
When presenting a spear or halberd, point the butt forward.
When presenting a stool or staff, dust it.
When presenting a horse or sheep, lead it with the right hand;
when presenting a dog, lead it with the left.
When holding fowl, point the head left.
Adorn lambs and geese with embroidered cloth.
Receive pearls or jade with cupped hands.
Receive a bow or sword with sleeves.
One who drinks from a jade cup does not shake it.
When presenting a bow, sword, bundle, or basket to someone,
hold it as if receiving orders,
with the demeanor of an envoy.
1.31 When acting as the ruler's envoy,
having received orders,
the ruler's words do not linger overnight at home.
When the ruler's message arrives,
the host comes out and bows to honor the message;
when the envoy returns,
he must be seen off with a bow outside the gate.
If sending someone to the ruler,
one must order him in court dress;
when the envoy returns,
one must descend the hall to receive the report.
1.32 Vast in learning and strong in memory, yet humble,
diligent in good deeds and never idle,
such a one is called a gentleman.
A gentleman does not exhaust others' joy,
nor drain others' loyalty,
thus preserving friendships.
The Rites say:
"A gentleman holds his grandson, not his son."
This means a grandson can act as the impersonator of the deceased grandfather,
but a son cannot act as the impersonator of his father.
For the impersonator of the ruler,
when ministers and officials see him,
they dismount.
If the ruler knows he is the impersonator,
he dismounts himself,
and the impersonator must bow from the carriage.
He must mount using a stool.
Those in abstinence do not enjoy music nor offer condolences.
1.33 In the rites of mourning,
do not become emaciated to the point of deformity,
and do not let sight and hearing decline.
Do not use the eastern steps to ascend or descend,
do not pass through the central gate path.
1.34 In the rites of mourning,
if the head has a sore, wash it;
if the body has a sore, bathe it;
if ill, drink wine and eat meat,
and resume the initial practice when the illness ceases.
If one cannot bear the mourning,
it is compared to being unfilial and unkind.
At fifty, do not extreme emaciation;
at sixty, do not emaciate;
at seventy, just wear mourning clothes,
drink wine and eat meat,
and stay indoors.
Life is concerned with the days to come,
death with the days past.
Those who knew the deceased in life offer condolences,
those who knew them in death express grief.
If one knew them in life but not in death,
offer condolences without grief;
if one knew them in death but not in life,
express grief without condolences.
If unable to contribute financially at a funeral,
do not ask about the expenses.
If unable to send gifts to the sick,
do not inquire what they desire.
If unable to host a visitor,
do not ask where they will stay.
When giving, one does not say
"Come and take it."
When giving to others, do not ask what they want.
1.35 When approaching a grave, do not climb the mound;
when assisting in a burial, one must hold the funeral cords.
Do not laugh in the presence of mourning.
When bowing to someone, one must move from one's position.
Do not sing when seeing a coffin.
Do not pace freely when entering a mourning scene.
Do not sigh during meals.
If a neighbor has a funeral,
do not chant while pounding grain.
If there is a burial in the village,
do not sing in the lanes.
Do not sing when approaching a grave.
Do not sing on the day of weeping.
Do not take shortcuts when accompanying a funeral procession,
nor avoid muddy roads during a burial.
In mourning, one must show a sorrowful expression;
when holding the funeral cords, do not laugh;
in joyful settings, do not sigh;
in armor
one must have an inviolable demeanor.
Thus, the noble person is cautious and vigilant,
never losing composure before others.
When the ruler touches the handrail of his carriage,
the senior officials dismount.
When a senior official touches the handrail,
the lower officials dismount.
Rituals do not extend to commoners,
punishments do not apply to senior officials.
Convicted persons should not be near the ruler.
1.36 Military carriages do not require dismounting salutes.
War chariots have streaming banners,
virtue chariots have furled banners.
1.37 Historians carry writing tools,
officials carry documents.
If water lies ahead,
a blue banner is raised.
If dust is ahead,
a calling kite banner is raised.
If chariots and cavalry are ahead,
a wild goose banner is raised.
If troops are ahead,
a tiger skin is displayed.
If fierce beasts are ahead,
a pixiu banner is raised.
On the march:
the Vermilion Bird ahead
and the Black Tortoise behind,
the Azure Dragon to the left and the White Tiger to the right.
The banner of Yao waves above,
strengthening the resolve in urgency.
Advance and retreat have their measures,
left and right have their divisions,
each managing their own duties.
1.38 For a father's enemy,
one cannot share the same sky.
For a brother's enemy
one never returns weapons unused.
For a friend's enemy
one does not share the same state.
1.39 If the suburbs are full of fortifications,
it is a disgrace for the ministers and senior officials.
If the land is vast,
but left wild and untended,
it is also a disgrace for the officials.
1.40 Do not be negligent during sacrifices.
Worn sacrificial garments should be burned,
worn sacrificial vessels buried,
worn turtle shells and stalks buried,
and dead sacrificial animals buried.
Those who sacrifice for the state
must clear away their own sacrificial stands.
1.41 After the cessation of weeping, naming taboos begin.
By ritual, homophonic names are not avoided.
Two-character names need not both be avoided.
If one served one's parents,
then avoid the names of grandparents;
if one did not serve one's parents,
then do not avoid grandparents' names.
In the ruler's presence, no private taboos apply,
but in a senior official's presence, public taboos are observed.
In poetry and books, no taboos;
in writing, no taboos.
In the temple, no taboos.
The taboos of the ruler's wife,
even when speaking directly to the ruler,
are not observed by officials;
women's taboos do not leave the household.
No taboos for distant mourning grades.
Upon entering a territory, inquire about prohibitions;
upon entering a state, inquire about customs;
upon entering a house, inquire about taboos.
1.42 External affairs use strong days,
internal affairs use soft days.
For divining dates:
beyond ten days is called "a distant certain day",
within ten days "a near certain day".
Mourning affairs prefer the distant day,
auspicious affairs the near day.
Say:
"For the day,
we borrow your great turtle's constancy,
we borrow your great stalks' constancy."
Do not divine more than three times,
and do not mix turtle and stalk divination.
Turtle shells are for bu divination,
stalks for shi divination.
Divination
is how the ancient sage kings made people trust timing,
revere spirits,
and fear laws;
how they helped people resolve doubts,
and settle hesitations.
Thus it is said:
"If in doubt, divine,
and none will fault it;
once a day is set for action,
it must be carried out."
1.43 When the ruler's carriage is about to be harnessed,
the driver stands before the horses with a whip.
Once harnessed,
the driver checks the carriage and reports it ready,
shakes his sleeves and ascends from the right,
takes the secondary rein,
kneels to mount,
holds the whip and divides the reins,
drives five steps and halts.
When the ruler approaches the carriage,
the driver gathers the reins and offers the handhold.
Those on left and right step aside,
and the carriage moves with outriders.
Upon reaching the main gate,
the ruler presses the driver's hand, looks back,
and orders the guard to mount;
at gates, bridges, and ditches
the guard must walk.
In all driver etiquette,
one must offer the handhold.
If the driver is of lower rank,
accept it;
otherwise,
decline.
If the driver is of lower rank,
press his hand;
otherwise,
reach for it from below.
Guest carriages do not enter the main gate.
Women do not stand in carriages.
Dogs and horses are not brought into the hall.
Thus, the noble person salutes the elderly,
dismounts at ministers' positions;
in the capital, do not gallop;
entering a village, always salute.
If summoned by the ruler,
even if by a lowly person,
officials must personally receive them.
Armed men do not bow,
for their bow is a simulated bow.
The funeral carriage keeps the left seat empty;
when riding the ruler's carriage,
one dare not leave the left empty;
on the left, one must salute.
When driving for a woman,
place the left hand forward,
right hand behind;
when driving for the ruler,
place the right hand forward,
left hand behind, and bow.
The ruler does not ride irregular carriages.
In a carriage, do not cough loudly,
nor point recklessly.
Standing, look five wheel-hubs ahead;
saluting, look at the horse's tail;
turning, do not look past the wheel hub.
In the capital, use a whip to groom the horse
without urging speed.
Dust should not leave the wheel tracks.
When a ruler passes by a sacrificial ox,
he should bow to it from his carriage.
When officials and scholars pass by the gate of the ducal palace,
they should bow to the ruler's carriage horse.
When riding the ruler's carriage horse,
one must wear court attire,
carry a whip,
dare not accept the mounting strap,
and bow from the left side.
When walking the ruler's carriage horse,
one must stay in the middle of the road.
Kicking the fodder of the ruler's carriage horse
is punishable.
Estimating the age of the ruler's carriage horse
is punishable.
2.1 When holding an object, position it at heart level;
when carrying an object, position it at belt level.
For holding the Son of Heaven's vessels, raise them above the heart;
for a feudal lord's, hold them level with the heart;
for a senior official's, lower them slightly;
for a scholar's, carry them at belt level.
When holding the ruler's vessel,
treat even light objects as if they were too heavy to bear.
When holding the ruler's vessel,
or handling ceremonial silks, jade tablets, or discs,
keep the left hand higher,
walk without lifting the feet,
dragging the heels like a cart's wheels.
When standing, bend like a chime stone and let the pendant hang.
If the ruler's pendant rests against him,
the minister's should hang down.
If the ruler's pendant hangs down,
the minister's should droop low.
When holding jade,
if it has a backing, bare the inner garment;
if not, keep the outer garment on.
2.2 A ruler does not address senior ministers and palace ladies by name;
a senior official does not address veteran ministers, nieces, or younger sisters-in-law by name;
a scholar does not address the household steward or senior concubine by name.
The son of a ruler or senior official
dare not refer to himself as "this unworthy youth";
the son of a senior official or scholar
dare not refer to himself as "the heir so-and-so",
and dare not share the same name as the crown prince.
2.3 If a ruler orders a scholar to participate in archery
and he is unable,
he should decline on grounds of illness,
saying:
"I have the worry of carrying firewood."
When attending a superior,
answering without looking around
is contrary to ritual.
2.4 A gentleman practicing rituals
does not seek to change customs.
The rituals of sacrifice,
the garments of mourning,
the positions for weeping—
all should follow the traditions of his state,
carefully adhering to its rules
and practicing them conscientiously.
If three generations have passed since leaving the state,
but rank and stipend are still listed at court,
and comings and goings are reported to the state,
and if brothers and clan members still remain,
then one should report back to the clan successor;
if three generations have passed since leaving the state,
and rank and stipend are no longer listed at court,
and comings and goings are not reported to the state,
then only upon rising to office
does one follow the laws of the new state.
2.5 A gentleman does not change his name after being orphaned.
If orphaned and suddenly ennobled,
he does not create a posthumous title for his father.
During mourning,
before burial,
study funeral rites;
after burial,
study sacrificial rites;
when mourning ends and normal life resumes,
study music.
During mourning, do not speak of music;
during sacrifices, do not speak of inauspicious matters;
in the court, do not speak of women.
2.6 Shaking or straightening documents before the ruler
is punishable.
Reversing or tilting divination stalks or turtle shells before the ruler
is punishable.
Divination stalks and turtle shells,
small tables and staffs,
mats and canopies,
plain white clothing,
fine or coarse hemp garments—
these should not enter the ducal gate.
Straw sandals,
tucked lapels,
flattened mourning caps—
these should not enter the ducal gate.
Written funeral plans,
mourning garments, funeral objects—
unless reported,
should not enter the ducal gate.
Public affairs should not be discussed privately.
2.7 When a gentleman plans to build residences:
the ancestral temple comes first,
stables and storerooms next,
living quarters last.
2.8 For household provisions:
sacrificial vessels come first,
animal offerings next,
utensils for daily use last.
Those without land stipends
do not prepare sacrificial vessels;
those with land stipends
first make sacrificial robes.
A gentleman, though poor,
does not sell sacrificial vessels;
though cold,
does not wear sacrificial robes;
when building residences,
does not cut trees from grave mounds.
When senior officials or scholars leave their state,
they do not take sacrificial vessels beyond the border.
A senior official entrusts his sacrificial vessels to another senior official,
a scholar to another scholar.
When senior officials or scholars leave their state:
crossing the border,
they set up an altar facing their state and weep.
Wearing plain upper garments,
plain lower garments,
plain caps,
removing all trim,
wearing thin leather shoes,
plain bamboo hats,
riding unadorned horses,
not cutting nails or hair,
not offering food in sacrifice,
not telling others of their innocence;
women do not serve.
After three months, they resume normal dress.
When senior officials or scholars are received by the ruler,
if the ruler consoles them,
they step aside,
bow twice, and kowtow.
If the ruler bows in welcome,
they step aside,
not daring to return the bow.
When senior officials and scholars meet each other,
even if their status differs,
if the host respects the guest,
he bows first to the guest;
if the guest respects the host,
he bows first to the host.
Except when condoling
or meeting the ruler,
all bows should be returned.
When a senior official is received by the ruler,
the ruler bows to acknowledge his humble visit.
When a scholar is received by a senior official,
the senior official bows to acknowledge his humble visit.
When meeting for the first time in the same state,
the host bows to acknowledge the guest's humble visit.
The ruler, to a scholar,
does not return a bow;
if the scholar is not his subject,
then he does return it.
A senior official, to his own subjects,
even if lowly,
must return their bows.
Men and women bow to each other in return.
2.9 In spring hunting, the ruler does not surround marshes;
senior officials do not take whole herds,
scholars do not take fawns or eggs.
2.10 In years of famine,
when grain harvests fail,
the ruler's meals omit the lung offering,
horses are not fed grain,
the imperial road is not cleared,
and sacrifices lack hanging bells.
Senior officials do not eat fine grain,
scholars drink without music.
Unless for a reason,
the ruler does not remove his jade;
unless for a reason,
senior officials do not remove their bells;
scholars, unless for a reason, do not remove their lutes and zithers.
If a scholar presents something to the ruler,
and later
the ruler asks him:
"Where did you get that?"
he should bow twice, kowtow, and then answer.
When a senior official travels privately beyond the borders,
he must seek permission.
Upon returning,
he must present something.
When a shì (scholar-official) travels privately beyond the borders,
he must request permission.
Upon returning,
he must report.
If the ruler shows him concern,
he bows;
if asked about his journey,
he bows before responding.
2.11 When a ruler of a state leaves his country,
he is admonished with the words:
"How can you abandon the altars of soil and grain!"
For a dàfū (high minister),
it is said:
"How can you abandon the ancestral temple!"
For a shì,
it is said:
"How can you abandon the graves [of your ancestors]!"
A ruler should die for his altars of soil and grain,
a dàfū should die with the masses,
and a shì should die for the regulations.
2.12 One who rules over the world
is called "Tiānzǐ" (Son of Heaven).
When receiving feudal lords in audience,
assigning duties, administering governance, and appointing to merit,
he calls himself "yǔ yī rén" (I, the one man).
Ascending the throne and presiding over sacrifices:
for domestic affairs, he is called "Xiào Wáng mǒu" (the Filial King So-and-so);
for external affairs, he is called "Sì Wáng mǒu" (the Successor King So-and-so).
When visiting the feudal lords,
and communicating with spirits and deities,
he is called "Yǒu tiān wáng mǒu fǔ" (There is the Heavenly King So-and-so, of such a name).
Upon his death,
it is announced as "Tiānwáng bēng" (The Heavenly King has fallen).
The recall of his soul is called
"Tiānzǐ fù" (The Son of Heaven returns).
Announcing the mourning,
it is said "Tiānwáng dēng xiá" (The Heavenly King has ascended afar).
When placed in the temple,
and a tablet is erected for him,
he is called "Dì" (Thearch).
Before the Son of Heaven has completed the mourning period,
he calls himself "yǔ xiǎozi" (I, the humble child).
He is called thus while alive,
and also thus after death.
2.13 The Son of Heaven has a Hòu (queen),
Fūrén (consorts),
Shìfù (ladies of the household),
Pín (court ladies),
Qī (wives),
and Qiè (concubines).
The Son of Heaven establishes the celestial offices:
first are the Six Dà (Great Offices),
namely Dàzǎi (Grand Steward),
Dàzōng (Grand Ancestral Priest),
Dàshǐ (Grand Historian),
Dàzhù (Grand Invocator),
Dàshì (Grand Officer),
and Dàbǔ (Grand Diviner),
who oversee the six regulations.
The Five Offices of the Son of Heaven:
are Sītú (Minister of Land),
Sīmǎ (Minister of War),
Sīkōng (Minister of Works),
Sīshì (Minister of Officials),
and Sīkòu (Minister of Justice),
who oversee the five categories of people.
The Six Treasuries of the Son of Heaven:
are Sītǔ (Keeper of Land),
Sīmù (Keeper of Wood),
Sīshuǐ (Keeper of Water),
Sīcǎo (Keeper of Grasslands),
Sīqì (Keeper of Implements),
and Sīhuò (Keeper of Goods),
who oversee the six functions.
The Six Artisans of the Son of Heaven:
are Tǔgōng (Earthenware Artisans),
Jīngōng (Metalworkers),
Shígōng (Stoneworkers),
Mùgōng (Woodworkers),
Shòugōng (Hide/Animal Workers),
and Cǎogōng (Straw/Vegetable-fiber Workers),
who control the six materials.
When the five offices present tribute,
it is called xiǎng (offering).
2.14 The heads of the five offices
are called Bó (Earls):
they are in charge of regions.
When introduced to the Son of Heaven,
they are called "Tiānzǐ zhī lì" (Officers of the Son of Heaven).
If of the same surname as the Son of Heaven,
they are called "Bófù" (Paternal Uncle);
if of different surname, they are called "Bójiù" (Maternal Uncle).
They refer to themselves before feudal lords
as "Tiānzǐ zhī lǎo" (The Elder of the Son of Heaven);
abroad, they are called "Gōng" (Duke);
in their own state, they are called "Jūn" (Ruler).
The chiefs of the Nine Provinces,
when entering the domain of the Son of Heaven, are called "Mù" (Shepherds).
If of the same surname as the Son of Heaven,
they are called "Shūfù" (Younger Uncle),
if of different surname, they are called "Shūjiù" (Younger Maternal Uncle),
abroad they are called "Hóu" (Marquis),
in their own state they are called
"Jūn" (Ruler).
Those among the Eastern Yí, Northern Dí, Western Róng, and Southern Mán,
even if large, are called "Zǐ" (Viscount).
Domestically, they refer to themselves as "bù gǔ" (the inept one);
abroad, they refer to themselves as "wáng lǎo" (the king's elder).
The minor lords of various regions,
when entering the domain of the Son of Heaven, are called "mǒu rén" (So-and-so),
abroad they are called "Zǐ" (Viscount),
and they refer to themselves as
"gū" (the orphan).
The Son of Heaven stands before the screen.
Feudal lords face north to see the Son of Heaven,
which is called jìn (audience).
The Son of Heaven stands at the níng (gate screen);
the dukes face east,
the feudal lords face west,
which is called cháo (court assembly).
2.15 When feudal lords meet before the scheduled time, it is called yù (encounter);
meeting in a border area is called huì (meeting).
When feudal lords send a dàfū to inquire of another feudal lord, it is called pìn (embassy);
setting a covenant is called shì (oath);
overseeing the sacrificial animal is called méng (covenant).
2.16 A feudal lord appearing before the Son of Heaven says "Chén mǒu hóu mǒu" (Your servant, Marquis So-and-so);
when speaking with the people,
he refers to himself as
"guǎrén" (the morally deficient one).
When in mourning garments,
he is called "dí zǐ gū" (the orphaned rightful heir).
Presiding over sacrifices,
for domestic affairs he is called "Xiàozǐ mǒu hóu mǒu" (Filial Son, Marquis So-and-so);
for external affairs, he is called "Zēngsūn mǒu hóu mǒu" (Great-Grandson, Marquis So-and-so).
His death is called "hōng" (demise);
the recall of his soul is called "mǒu fǔ fù yǐ" (So-and-so, of such a name, returns).
After burial,
his appearance before the Son of Heaven is called lèi jiàn (appearance by proxy).
Discussing his posthumous title is called lèi.
When a feudal lord sends an envoy to another feudal lord,
the envoy refers to himself as
"guǎ jūn zhī lǎo" (the elder of my deficient lord).
The Son of Heaven is dignified and profound;
feudal lords are majestic and grand;
dàfū are orderly and composed;
shì are respectful and proper;
common people are hurried and anxious.
The consort of the Son of Heaven is called Hòu (Queen);
that of a feudal lord is called Fūrén (Lady);
that of a dàfū is called Rúrén (Consort);
that of a shì is called Fùrén (Woman);
that of a commoner is called Qī (Wife).
Dukes and marquises have Fūrén,
Shìfù,
Qī,
and Qiè.
A Fūrén refers to herself before the Son of Heaven
as
"lǎo fù" (old woman);
before feudal lords
she says
"guǎ xiǎo jūn" (the deficient small ruler);
before her own lord
she says
"xiǎo tóng" (little child).
From Shìfù downwards,
they refer to themselves as "bì zǐ" (handmaid).
A child, before parents, uses his personal name.
Dàfū from various states,
when entering the domain of the Son of Heaven,
are called "mǒu shì" (So-and-so, a shì),
and refer to themselves as "péi chén mǒu" (subordinate minister So-and-so).
Abroad, they are called "Zǐ" (Viscount),
in their own state, they are called "guǎ jūn zhī lǎo" (the elder of our deficient lord).
As envoys, they refer to themselves as
"mǒu" (So-and-so).
2.17 The Son of Heaven is not said to 'flee';
feudal lords are not named while alive.
A nobleman does not associate with evil;
if a feudal lord loses his territory,
he is named;
if he extinguishes a state of the same surname,
he is named.
The ritual for a minister:
do not remonstrate openly.
If after three remonstrations he is not heeded,
then he flees.
For a son serving his parents:
if after three remonstrations they are not heeded,
then he follows them weeping and wailing.
2.18 When the ruler is ill,
and takes medicine,
the minister tastes it first.
When a parent is ill,
and takes medicine,
the son tastes it first.
If a physician is not from three generations of doctors,
do not take his medicine.
When comparing people, one must do so within their own category.
2.19 When asked about the age of the Son of Heaven,
the reply should be:
"I have heard that
he has begun to wear garments of a certain length."
When asked about the age of a feudal lord:
if he is grown, say, "He is able to oversee the affairs of the ancestral temple and the altars of soil and grain";
if he is young,
say,
"He is not yet able to oversee the affairs of the ancestral temple and the altars of soil and grain."
When asked about the son of a senior official:
if he is grown, say,
"He is able to drive a carriage";
if he is young, say,
"He is not yet able to drive a carriage."
When asked about the son of a scholar:
if he is grown, say,
"He is able to manage receptions";
if he is young, say,
"He is not yet able to manage receptions."
When asked about the son of a commoner:
if he is grown, say,
"He is able to carry firewood";
if he is young, say,
"He is not yet able to carry firewood."
2.20 When asked about the wealth of a feudal lord,
respond by enumerating his lands,
and the produce from his mountains and marshes.
When asked about the wealth of a senior official,
say, "He has a steward to manage his resources,
and his sacrificial vessels and robes are not borrowed."
When asked about the wealth of a scholar,
respond with the number of his carriages.
When asked about the wealth of a commoner,
respond by counting his livestock.
2.21 The Son of Heaven sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
to the Four Directions,
to the mountains and rivers,
and to the Five Household Deities,
completing the cycle annually.
Feudal lords sacrifice within their own domains.
They sacrifice to the mountains and rivers,
and to the Five Household Deities,
completing the cycle annually.
Senior officials sacrifice to the Five Household Deities,
completing the cycle annually.
Scholars sacrifice to their ancestors.
2.22 In all sacrifices,
if a rite has been abolished, none dare revive it;
if it has been established, none dare abolish it.
To sacrifice to those to whom one should not sacrifice
is called excessive sacrifice.
Excessive sacrifice brings no blessing.
2.23 The Son of Heaven uses a pure-colored ox,
feudal lords use a fattened ox,
senior officials use a selected ox,
scholars use a sheep or pig.
A collateral son does not perform sacrifices;
if he must sacrifice, he must inform the principal son.
2.24 In the rites of sacrificing in the ancestral temple:
an ox is called "the great unitary warrior",
a pig "the stiff-bristled",
a suckling pig "the plump",
a sheep "the soft-furred",
a chicken "the long-crowing",
a dog "the broth-offering",
a pheasant "the wide-stepping",
a rabbit "the bright-eyed",
dried meat "the governor's offering",
dried fish "the merchant's offering",
fresh fish "the straight offering",
water "the clear cleanser",
wine "the clear drink",
millet "the fragrant union",
fine millet "the fragrant stalks",
common millet "the bright grains",
rice "the excellent vegetables",
leeks "the abundant roots",
salt "the salty brine",
jade "the excellent jade",
silk "the measured silk".
2.25 The death of the Son of Heaven is called
"collapse",
that of a feudal lord
"demise",
that of a senior official
"end",
that of a scholar
"no more salary",
that of a commoner
"death".
When on the bed, it is called a corpse;
when in the coffin, it is called a coffin.
The death of a feathered bird is called "descent",
that of a four-legged animal "soaking".
Dying at the hands of an enemy is called "falling in battle".
In sacrifice, a grandfather is called "illustrious ancestor",
a grandmother "illustrious ancestress".
A father is called "illustrious father",
a mother "illustrious mother".
A husband is called "illustrious spouse".
In life, they are called father, mother, wife;
in death, they are called departed father, departed mother, honored consort.
Dying at an old age is called "end",
dying young is called "no more salary".
2.26 For the Son of Heaven,
one's gaze should not rise above the collar seam
nor fall below the girdle;
for a feudal lord,
one's gaze should follow the flow of his sash;
for a senior official,
one's gaze should be level;
for a scholar,
one may gaze within five paces.
In all gazing:
above the face indicates arrogance,
below the girdle indicates sorrow,
and a sidelong glance indicates cunning.
2.27 When the ruler issues commands,
senior officials and scholars practice them.
In the office, speak of office matters;
in the treasury, speak of treasury matters;
in the storehouse, speak of storehouse matters;
in the court, speak of court matters.
In court, do not speak of dogs or horses.
To look around after court is dismissed
indicates either unusual matters
or unusual thoughts.
Therefore, to look around after court is dismissed,
the gentleman considers rude.
In court, speak according to ritual,
ask according to ritual,
and reply according to ritual.
At the great feast, do not consult the oracle,
and do not seek excessive richness.
2.28 Regarding ceremonial gifts:
the Son of Heaven gives fragrant wine,
feudal lords give jade tablets,
high ministers give lambs,
senior officials give geese,
scholars give pheasants,
commoners give a pair of ducks;
a child presents his gift and withdraws.
In the野外 or army where there is no gift,
a cap tassel,
armguard,
or arrow
may suffice.
A woman's gifts are
jujubes, hazelnuts,
dried meat, seasoned meat,
dates, and chestnuts.
2.29 Presenting a woman to the Son of Heaven
is called "completing the hundred surnames";
to a feudal lord,
it is called "preparing the wine and sauces";
to a senior official,
it is called
"preparing the sweeping and sprinkling".
3.1 At the mourning for Gōngyí Zhòngzǐ,
Tángōng appeared with his head uncovered.
Zhòngzǐ had passed over his grandson and set up his son instead,
and Tángōng said:
"What is this?
I have not heard of such a thing before."
He hurried to the right of the gate where Zǐfú Bózǐ was,
and said:
"Zhòngzǐ passed over his grandson and set up his son instead;
why is this?"
Bózǐ said:
"Zhòngzǐ was also following the way of antiquity.
In former times, King Wén passed over Bó Yìkǎo and set up King Wǔ;
Wēizǐ passed over his grandson Tú and set up Yǎn instead;
so Zhòngzǐ was also following the way of antiquity."
Zǐyóu asked Confucius about this,
and Confucius said:
"No!
Set up the grandson."
3.2 In serving one's parents, one should conceal their faults but not offend them;
attend to them in every way without fixed rules;
serve them diligently until death,
and observe the full three years of mourning.
In serving one's ruler, one should remonstrate without concealing;
attend to him with fixed rules;
serve him diligently until death,
and observe a three-year mourning akin to that for parents.
In serving one's teacher, one should neither offend nor conceal;
attend to him in every way without fixed rules;
serve him diligently until death,
and observe three years of mourning in heart.
3.3 Jì Wǔzǐ built a residence,
and the burial of the Dù family was below the western steps.
He requested to have them reburied together,
and this was permitted.
When entering the palace, they did not dare to weep.
Wǔzǐ said:
"Joint burial is not an ancient practice,
yet since the Duke of Zhōu,
it has remained unchanged.
I permit the major aspects but not the minor ones,
why is that?"
He ordered them to weep.
3.4 Zǐshàng's mother died but he did not observe mourning.
A disciple asked Zǐsī:
"Did your late father
mourn for his divorced mother?"
He replied:
"Yes."
"You do not allow Bái to mourn for her.
Why?"
Zǐsī said:
"My late father never deviated from the Dào;
when the Dào was elevated, he followed its elevation,
when the Dào was degraded, he followed its degradation.
How can Jí do the same?
She who was Jí's wife
is Bái's mother;
she who is not Jí's wife
is not Bái's mother."
Thus, the Kǒng family's practice of not mourning for divorced mothers
began with Zǐsī.
3.5 Confucius said:
"Bowing first and then touching the forehead to the ground
shows proper sequence;
touching the forehead to the ground first and then bowing
shows utmost sincerity.
For the three-year mourning,
I follow the most sincere way."
3.6 After Confucius had jointly buried his parents at Fáng,
he said:
"I have heard that
in ancient times, graves had no mounds;
but now I, Qiū,
am a man who travels east, west, south, and north,
so I cannot leave it unmarked."
Thereupon, he raised a mound
four feet high.
Confucius returned first,
his disciples later.
It rained heavily,
and when they arrived,
Confucius asked them,
saying:
"Why are you so late?"
They replied:
"The tomb at Fáng collapsed."
Confucius did not respond.
Three times.
Then, with tears streaming down, he said:
"I have heard:
the ancients did not repair tombs."
3.7 Confucius wept for Zǐlù in the central courtyard.
When someone came to offer condolences,
the Master bowed to them.
After weeping,
he approached the messenger and asked for details.
The messenger said:
"He was minced into paste."
Thereupon, he ordered the meat paste to be discarded.
3.8 Zēngzǐ said:
"When a friend's grave
has grass grown over it through a season, one does not weep for them."
3.9 Zǐsī said:
"Three days after death, the body is encoffined;
everything that touches the body
must be sincere and trustworthy,
so that there is no regret.
After three months, it is buried;
everything that accompanies the coffin
must be sincere and trustworthy,
so that there is no regret.
Mourning for three years is the extreme,
but even after it ends, it is not forgotten.
Thus, a noble person has lifelong sorrow,
but not a single day's distress.
Therefore, on the anniversary of a death, one does not enjoy music."
3.10 Confucius was orphaned young,
and did not know his father's grave.
The body was placed in the street of Wǔfù.
Those who saw it
all thought it was a burial.
It was done cautiously,
as it was actually a temporary placement.
After inquiring of the mother of Zōu Mànfū,
he was able to jointly bury them at Fáng.
3.11 When a neighbor has a funeral,
one does not sing while pounding grain;
when there is a coffin in the village,
one does not sing in the lanes.
The mourning cap has no tassels.
3.12 The Yǒuyúshì used earthenware coffins,
the Xiàhòushì used brick enclosures,
the Yīnrén used inner and outer coffins,
the Zhōurén used ornamental screens.
The Zhōurén used the Yīnrén's inner and outer coffins
to bury those who died at age 16-19,
used the Xiàhòushì's brick enclosures to bury
those who died at age 12-15 and 8-11,
and used the Yǒuyúshì's earthenware coffins
to bury those who died under age 8 without mourning attire.
3.13 The Xiàhòushì esteemed black;
for great affairs, encoffining was at dusk,
for military affairs, they rode black horses,
and used black animals for sacrifice.
The Yīnrén esteemed white:
for great affairs, encoffining was at noon,
for military affairs, they rode white horses,
and used white animals for sacrifice.
The Zhōurén esteemed red;
for great affairs, encoffining was at sunrise,
for military affairs, they rode red horses.
and used red animals for sacrifice.
3.14 When the mother of Duke Mù died,
he sent someone to ask Zēngzǐ:
"What should be done?"
He replied:
"Shēn has heard from Shēn's father:
the grief of weeping,
the emotions of even and hemmed mourning clothes,
the food of congee,
apply from the Son of Heaven down.
Cloth canopy,
is from Wèi;
silk canopy,
is from Lǔ."
3.15 When Duke Xiàn of Jìn was about to kill his heir, Shēnshēng,
Prince Chóng'ěr said to him:
"Why not tell the duke your intentions?"
The heir said:
"No,
the lord is content with Lí Jī,
this would hurt the lord's heart."
He said:
"Then why not leave?"
The heir said:
"No,
the lord would say I wish to murder him,
is there any state under heaven without a father?
Where could I go?"
He sent a message to Hú Tū, saying:
"Shēnshēng is guilty,
for not heeding Bóshì's words,
leading to death,
Shēnshēng does not dare cling to life,
however,
our lord is old,
his sons are young,
the state faces many troubles,
if Bóshì does not come out to assist our lord,
but if Bóshì would come out and assist our lord,
Shēnshēng would receive favor and die content."
He bowed twice, touching his head to the ground,
and then died.
Thus, he was called the Reverent Heir.
3.16 A man from Lǔ, having performed the xiáng sacrifice in the morning, sang in the evening,
and Zǐlù laughed at him.
The Master said:
"Yóu,
you criticize others,
will it never end?
The three-year mourning
is indeed long enough."
After Zǐlù left,
the Master said:
"How much longer should it be?
Another month would have been better."
3.17 Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ fought with the people of Sòng at Shèngqiū.
Xiàn Bēnfǔ drove the chariot,
Bǔ Guó was the right-hand guard.
The horses startled,
the battle was lost,
and the duke fell.
The auxiliary chariot handed him the mounting cord.
The duke said:
"It was not divined properly."
Xiàn Bēnfǔ said:
"On other days we did not lose,
but today we lost,
this shows lack of courage."
Thereupon, he died in battle.
When the groom was bathing the horses,
he found a stray arrow in their flesh.
The duke said:
"It was not their fault."
Then he composed a eulogy for them.
For officers to have eulogies,
began from this.
3.18 Zēngzǐ lay ill in bed,
seriously ill.
Yuèzhèng Zǐchūn sat below the bed,
Zēng Yuán and Zēng Shēn sat at his feet,
a youth sat in the corner holding a candle.
The youth said:
"So splendid and smooth,
is this a grandee's mat?"
Zǐchūn said:
"Stop!"
Zēngzǐ heard this,
startled,
and said:
"Ah!"
He said:
"That ornate and glossy mat,
is it a senior official's mat?"
Zēngzǐ said:
"Yes,
it was a gift from Jìsūn,
and I haven't been able to change it.
Yuán,
help me up to change the mat."
Zēngyuán said:
"Your illness is critical, father,
you cannot be moved.
If we're fortunate enough to last until morning,
we'll respectfully change it then."
Zēngzǐ said:
"Your love for me is not as good as his;
a gentleman loves others with virtue,
a petty person loves others with indulgence.
What more do I seek?
To die having rectified myself is enough."
They lifted him and changed the mat.
Before he could settle back on the mat comfortably, he passed away.
3.19 At the moment of death,
the bereaved feel constrained as if at a dead end;
after the encoffining,
they look anxious as if seeking something not found;
after the burial,
they appear restless as if expecting someone who doesn't arrive.
At the first anniversary, they sigh with emotion;
at the second anniversary, they feel empty and detached.
3.20 The people of Zhūlóu used arrows in the funeral recall ritual,
which began after the battle at Shēngxíng.
The women of Lǔ wearing the casual hairstyle 'zhuā' to offer condolences
started after the defeat at Táitái.
3.21 When the mother-in-law of Nángōng Tāo's wife passed away,
the Master instructed her on the 'zhuā' hairstyle, saying:
"Don't make it too high,
nor too broad.
Use hazel wood for the hairpin,
one foot long,
with the hair knot eight inches."
3.22 After Mèngxiànzǐ's dàn sacrifice,
and though it was time to resume marital relations, he did not enter.
The Master said:
"Xiànzǐ surpasses others by one degree!"
3.23 After Confucius completed the xiáng sacrifice,
for five days he played the qin without achieving harmony,
but after ten days he could play the shēng and sing.
3.24 Yǒuzǐ, it seems, after the xiáng sacrifice,
wore silk shoes
and a ribboned cap.
3.25 There are three types of deaths for which one does not offer condolences:
those from fear, from being crushed,
and from drowning.
Zǐlù had observed mourning for his sister;
it was time to end it,
but he hadn't.
Confucius asked:
"Why haven't you ended it?"
Zǐlù said:
"I have few brothers and cannot bear to."
Confucius said:
"The ancient kings established rituals,
considering that those who practice the Way
all find it hard to bear."
Zǐlù heard this
and then ended the mourning.
3.26 Tàigōng was enfeoffed at Yíngqiū,
yet for five generations,
all were returned to be buried in Zhōu.
A gentleman remarked:
"Music brings joy to its origins,
ritual does not forget its roots.
The ancients had a saying:
'When a fox dies, it faces its mound,'
which is humanity."
3.27 When Bóyú's mother died,
after the one-year mourning he was still crying.
The Master heard and asked:
"Who is that crying?"
A disciple replied:
"It's Lǐ."
The Master said:
"Alas!
That is excessive."
Bóyú heard this
and then stopped.
3.28 Shùn was buried in the wilds of Cāngwú,
and it seems his three consorts were not buried with him.
Jìwǔzǐ said:
"The Duke of Zhōu was probably buried together."
At Zēngzǐ's funeral,
the washing was done in the kitchen.
3.29 During the dàgōng mourning, one suspends studies.
Some say:
"During dàgōng,
reciting is permissible."
3.30 Zǐzhāng fell ill,
summoned Shēnxiáng and told him:
"A gentleman says 'end,'
a petty person says 'die';
might I be close today?"
3.31 Zēngzǐ said:
"The offerings at death,
are they from the leftover shelves?"
Zēngzǐ said:
"Not having a position for xiǎogōng mourning
is the etiquette of back alleys.
Zǐsī wept for his sister-in-law in position,
with the women leading the leaps;
Shēnxiáng's mourning for Yánsī was the same."
3.32 In ancient times,
caps were sewn vertically,
but now
they are sewn horizontally;
thus the mourning cap's reversal for auspicious occasions
is not ancient.
Zēngzǐ said to Zǐsī:
"Jí,
when I observed mourning for my parent,
I took no water or gruel for seven days."
Zǐsī said:
"The ancient kings established rituals
so that those who exceed would bend to comply,
and those who fall short
would stretch to reach.
Thus a gentleman observing parental mourning
takes no water or gruel for three days,
and can rise only with a staff."
3.33 Zēngzǐ said:
"If there's no mourning for xiǎogōng beyond the territory,
then distant brothers would ultimately have no mourning,
is that acceptable?"
3.34 At Bógāo's funeral,
before the messenger from the Kǒng family arrived,
Rǎnzǐ prepared a bundle of silk
and a team of horses
to present.
Confucius said:
"How inappropriate!
This merely makes my ritual to Bógāo insincere."
When Bógāo died in Wèi,
the news reached Confucius,
who said:
"Where should I mourn him?
For a brother,
I mourn in the ancestral temple;
for my father's friend,
outside the temple gate;
for a teacher,
in the main room;
for a friend,
outside the main room's door;
for an acquaintance,
in the fields.
To mourn in the fields
would be too distant;
in the main room
too intimate.
Since he came to know me through Cì,
I'll mourn at Cì's place."
So he instructed Zǐgòng to host,
saying:
"For those who come mourning for you,
bow to them;
for those who come knowing Bógāo,
do not bow."
3.35 Zēngzǐ said:
"If ill during mourning,
one may eat meat and drink wine,
necessarily with the flavor of plants and trees,
meaning ginger and cinnamon."
3.36 Zǐxià lost his son and then his eyesight.
Zēngzǐ condoled, saying:
"I have heard:
when a friend loses sight, one weeps for him."
Zēngzǐ wept,
Zǐxià also wept,
saying:
"Heaven!
I am without fault."
Zēngzǐ angrily said:
"Shāng,
how can you say you're without fault?
You and I served the Master between the Zhū and Sì rivers,
then you retired to grow old west of the Yellow River,
making the people there
compare you to the Master—
that is your first fault;"
When you lost your parent,
you did so without the people hearing of it,
which is your second offense;
when you lost your child,
you lost your eyesight,
which is your third offense.
And yet you say, 'What offense have I committed?'"
Zǐxià threw down his staff and bowed, saying:
"I was wrong!
I was wrong!
I have left the flock and lived in seclusion
for too long already."
3.37 If one stays indoors during the day,
it is acceptable to inquire about his illness;
if one stays outdoors at night,
it is acceptable to offer condolences.
Therefore, a gentleman, unless for a major reason,
does not stay overnight outdoors;
unless for fasting in preparation for sacrifice,
or due to illness,
does not stay indoors day and night.
3.38 When Gāo Zìgāo was observing the mourning for his parent,
he wept tears of blood for three years,
never showing his teeth in a smile,
and the gentleman considered this difficult to achieve.
3.39 As for mourning garments,
if they are not appropriate to the occasion,
it is better to have no mourning garments at all.
In wearing the zīcuī,
one should not sit casually;
in wearing the dàgōng,
one should not perform laborious tasks.
3.40 When Confucius went to Wèi,
he encountered the funeral of his former hostel keeper,
and entered to weep for him sorrowfully.
Upon exiting,
he had Zǐgòng take off a side horse to contribute to the funeral.
Zǐgòng said:
"For the funeral of a disciple,
you have never taken off a side horse;
to take one off for a former hostel keeper,
is that not excessive?"
The Master said:
"When I entered just now and wept for him,
I met with a moment of grief and shed tears.
I detest that my tears had no follow-through.
My disciples, carry this out."
3.41 When Confucius was in Wèi,
there was a funeral procession,
and the Master observed it,
saying:
"How excellent is this conduct of the funeral!
It is sufficient to be taken as a model.
Disciples, remember it."
Zǐgòng said:
"Master, what do you find excellent about it?"
He said:
"Their going is like longing,
their return is like hesitation."
Zǐgòng said:
"Wouldn't it be better to return quickly for the yú sacrifice?"
The Master said:
"Disciples, remember this,
I have not been able to practice it."
3.42 At the funeral of Yán Yuān,
when the auspicious meat was offered,
Confucius went out to receive it;
upon entering,
he played the qín and then ate it.
3.43 Confucius was standing with his disciples,
holding his hands with the right over the left,
and the disciples all also placed the right over the left.
Confucius said:
"You disciples are fond of learning,
but in my case, it is because I am in mourning for my elder sister."
Then the disciples all placed the left over the right.
3.44 Confucius rose early,
with hands behind his back, dragging his staff,
strolling leisurely at the gate,
singing:
"The Tài Shān is crumbling,
the beam is breaking,
the philosopher is withering."
After singing, he entered
and sat facing the door.
Zǐgòng heard this and said:
"If the Tài Shān crumbles,
on what shall I gaze?
If the beam breaks,
the philosopher withers,
on whom shall I rely?
The Master is likely to fall ill."
He hurried in.
The Master said:
"Cì!
Why have you come so late?
The Xiàhòu clan laid the coffin on the eastern steps,
which is like the host's position;
the Yīn people laid it between the two pillars,
which is between host and guest;
the Zhōu people laid it on the western steps,
which is like the guest's position.
And I, Qiū, am a man of Yīn.
Last night,
I dreamed I was sitting with offerings between the two pillars.
Since no enlightened king arises,
who in the world can honor me?
I am about to die."
He lay ill for seven days and passed away.
At Confucius's funeral,
the disciples were uncertain about the mourning attire.
Zǐgòng said:
"When the Master mourned for Yán Yuān,
it was as for a son
but without the specific garments;
so it was for Zǐlù.
Let us mourn for the Master
as for a father but without the specific garments."
3.45 At Confucius's funeral,
Gōngxī Chì arranged the details:
decorating the coffin,
setting up the shà screens and the pī cords,
was the Zhōu way;
setting up the banners,
was the Yīn way;
using the silk and streamers,
was the Xià way.
3.46 At Zǐzhāng's funeral,
Gōngmíng Yí arranged the details.
A red curtain,
with ant-like knots at the four corners,
in the manner of a Yīn officer.
3.47 Zǐxià asked Confucius:
"How should one deal with the enemy of one's parents?"
The Master said:
"Sleep on straw and pillow on a shield, do not take office,
do not share the world with them;
if met in the market or court,
fight without returning for a weapon."
He asked:
"May I ask how to deal with the enemy of one's brothers?"
He said:
"Do not share the state with them in office;
if on a mission by the ruler's command,
even if met, do not fight."
He asked:
"May I ask how to deal with the enemy of one's paternal cousins?"
He said:
"Do not take the lead;
if the principal avenger is capable,
then follow behind with weapons."
3.48 At Confucius's funeral,
the disciples all wore the dié mourning band when going out.
In group residence, they wore it;
when going out, they did not.
3.49 Altering graves
is not ancient practice.
3.50 Zǐlù said:
"I heard from the Master:
'In funeral rites,
if grief is insufficient but ritual is abundant,
it is better that ritual be insufficient but grief abundant.
In sacrificial rites,
if reverence is insufficient but ritual is abundant,
it is better that ritual be insufficient but reverence abundant.'"
3.51 Zēngzǐ went to offer condolences at Fùxià,
where the host had already performed the 'zǔ' ceremony,
filled the pond,
and pushed the coffin back,
having the women descend before performing the rites.
A follower asked:
"Is this according to ritual?"
Zēngzǐ said:
"The 'zǔ' is provisional;
provisional—
why can it not be returned and stayed overnight?"
The follower also asked Zǐyóu:
"Is this according to ritual?"
Zǐyóu said:
"The rice is placed under the window,
the minor dressing inside the door,
the major dressing on the eastern steps,
the encoffining in the guest's position,
the 'zǔ' in the courtyard,
burial at the tomb,
all to signify the departure.
Thus, in funeral matters, there is advance without retreat."
Zēngzǐ heard this and said:
"How much more
do I know about the 'zǔ' ceremony!"
3.52 Zēngzǐ wore an unlined fur robe to offer condolences,
while Zǐyóu wore a lined one.
Zēngzǐ pointed at Zǐyóu and said to others:
"That man,
considered well-versed in ritual,
how can he wear a lined fur robe to offer condolences?"
After the master had been dressed in the burial attire,
the family bared their shoulders and tied up their hair;
Zǐyóu hurried out,
then returned wearing a fur robe, a sash, and a mourning headband.
Zēngzǐ said:
"I was mistaken,
I was mistaken,
this gentleman is correct."
3.53 Zǐxià, having removed his mourning garments, came for an audience.
He was given a qín,
but when he tried to tune it, it wouldn't harmonize,
and when he played it, it produced no proper melody.
He rose and said:
"My grief is not yet forgotten.
The ancient kings established the rites,
and I dare not exceed them."
Zǐzhāng, having removed his mourning garments, came for an audience.
He was given a qín,
and when he tuned it, it harmonized,
and when he played it, it produced a proper melody.
He rose and said:
"The ancient kings established the rites,
and I dare not fail to fulfill them."
3.54 At the funeral of Minister of Justice Huìzǐ,
Zǐyóu wore hempen mourning clothes and a headband of male hemp.
Wénzǐ declined, saying:
"You have condescended to befriend Mímóu's younger brother,
and now you further condescend to wear mourning for him;
I dare to decline this honor."
Zǐyóu said:
"It is according to ritual."
Wénzǐ withdrew and returned to his weeping.
Zǐyóu hurried to take his place among the ministers.
Wénzǐ again declined, saying:
"You have condescended to befriend Mímóu's younger brother,
and now you further condescend to wear mourning for him,
and also to attend his funeral;
I dare to decline this honor."
Zǐyóu said:
"I insist on my request."
Wénzǐ withdrew,
then supported the rightful heir to face south and stand, saying:
"You have condescended to befriend Mímóu's younger brother,
and now you further condescend to wear mourning for him,
and also to attend his funeral;
how dare Hǔ not return to his proper position?"
Zǐyóu then hurried to take his place among the guests.
3.55 At the funeral of General Wénzǐ,
after the mourning period had been concluded,
people from Yuè came to offer condolences.
The host, wearing a deep robe
and a cap of cooked silk,
waited in the ancestral temple,
with tears and snivel flowing.
Zǐyóu observed this and said:
"The son of General Wén is indeed nearly perfect!
This is the ritual beyond the ritual,
his actions hit the mark."
3.56 To give a name in childhood,
a style name at capping,
and to use the titles Bó or Zhòng at fifty,
with a posthumous title at death—
this is the way of Zhōu.
The mourning headband signifies substance.
To dig a hole in the central room for bathing the corpse,
and to break down the stove to support the feet;
at the burial,
to break through the temple wall and tread over the offerings,
exiting through the main gate—
this is the way of Yīn.
Scholars practice these.
3.57 When Zǐliǔ's mother died,
Zǐshuò requested to make preparations.
Zǐliǔ said:
"With what means?"
Zǐshuò said:
"I propose to sell our commoner brother's mother."
Zǐliǔ said:
"How can we sell another's mother to bury our own mother?
It cannot be done."
After the burial,
Zǐshuò wished to use the leftover condolence gifts to purchase sacrificial vessels.
Zǐliǔ said:
"It cannot be done.
I have heard that
a gentleman does not enrich his household through mourning.
Let us distribute it among our impoverished brothers."
3.58 The gentleman says:
"He who plans for another's army,
if it is defeated, should die for it;
he who plans for another's state or city,
if it is endangered, should flee from it."
3.59 Gōngshū Wénzǐ ascended Xiáqiū hill,
with Qú Bóyù following.
Wénzǐ said:
"How delightful is this hill!
When I die, I wish to be buried here."
Qú Bóyù said:
"If you, sir, find delight in it,
then Yuàn requests to go first."
3.60 A man of Biàn had his mother die,
and he wept like a child.
Confucius said:
"He grieves indeed,
but it is hard to sustain.
As for ritual,
it is meant to be transmitted,
and to be sustained.
Therefore, weeping and leaping have their measures."
3.61 When the mother of Shūsūn Wǔshū died,
after the dressing of the corpse,
the bearers carried it out the door,
and upon exiting, they bared their shoulders,
threw off their caps, and tied up their hair.
Zǐyóu said:
"They know the rites."
3.62 In supporting the ruler,
the diviner supports the right,
the archer supports the left;
when the ruler passes away, they lift him thus.
3.63 For the husband of one's maternal aunt,
or the wife of one's maternal uncle,
some say these two should mourn for each other,
but the gentleman has never spoken of it.
Some say: If they shared the same hearth, they should wear the sī mourning.
3.64 In mourning affairs,
one desires them to be hurried;
in auspicious affairs,
one desires them to be leisurely.
Thus, though mourning affairs are urgent,
they do not overstep the proper measures;
though auspicious affairs are calm,
they are not neglected.
Therefore, to be too hasty is rustic,
to be too leisurely is petty.
The gentleman should be appropriately measured.
3.65 As for mourning implements,
the gentleman is ashamed to have them prepared in advance;
those that can be made in one or two days,
the gentleman does not prepare beforehand.
3.66 In mourning garments,
the son of a brother is treated as one's own son,
drawing him closer;
for a sister-in-law or brother-in-law, there is no mourning,
pushing them further away;
the light mourning for a paternal aunt or sister
is because there is someone who receives them and mourns them deeply.
3.67 When eating beside someone in mourning,
one should never eat one's fill.
3.68 Zēngzǐ was standing by the gate with a guest,
when his disciple hurried out.
Zēngzǐ said:
"Where are you going?"
He replied:
"My father has died,
and I am going out to weep in the alley."
Zēngzǐ said:
"Return,
and weep in your own room."
Zēngzǐ then faced north to offer condolences.
3.69 Confucius said:
"To treat the dead as completely dead
is inhumane and cannot be done;
to treat the dead as still living
is unwise and cannot be done.
Therefore,
bamboo vessels are not finished for use,
earthenware vessels are not glazed,
wooden vessels are not carved,
lutes and zithers are strung but not tuned,
reed pipes and mouth organs are complete but not harmonious,
there are bells and chime stones but no stands;
these are called spirit vessels,
for they are meant for the spirits."
3.70 Yǒuzǐ asked Zēngzǐ:
"Have you inquired about mourning from the Master?"
He replied:
"I have heard it said:
When losing office, one should quickly become poor;
when dying, one should quickly decay."
Yǒuzǐ said:
"These are not the words of a gentleman."
Zēngzǐ said:
"I, Shēn, heard this from the Master."
Yǒuzǐ said again:
"These are not the words of a gentleman."
Zēngzǐ said:
"I, Shēn, heard it along with Zǐyóu."
Yǒuzǐ said:
"Indeed,
then the Master must have had a reason for saying it."
Zēngzǐ reported these words to Zǐyóu.
Zǐyóu said:
"How remarkable!
Yǒuzǐ's words resemble the Master's.
Once when the Master was living in Sòng,
he saw Minister Huán having a stone outer coffin made for himself,
which after three years was still not completed.
The Master said:
'If it is to be so extravagant,
it would be better to rot away quickly after death.'
The wish to rot away quickly after death
was spoken with reference to Minister Huán Sīmǎ.
When Nángōng Jìngshū returned,
he would invariably bring his treasures and present himself at court.
The Master said:
'If it is to be so acquisitive,
it would be better to become poor quickly after losing office.'
The wish to become poor quickly after losing office
was spoken with reference to Jìngshū.'
Zēngzǐ reported Zǐyóu's words to Yǒuzǐ,
and Yǒuzǐ said:
"Indeed,
I always said
that was not the Master's saying."
Zēngzǐ said:
"How did you know?"
Yǒuzǐ said:
"The Master regulated in Zhōngdū
that the inner coffin should be four inches thick
and the outer one five inches thick.
From this I know he did not wish to rot away quickly.
Formerly, when the Master lost his position as Minister of Crime in Lǔ
and was about to go to Jīng,
he sent Zǐxià first,
and then repeated the mission with Rǎn Yǒu.
From this I know he did not wish to become poor quickly."
3.71 When Chén Zhuāngzǐ died,
the news was sent to Lǔ.
The people of Lǔ wished not to wail for him,
but Duke Mù called Xiànzǐ and asked about it.
Xiànzǐ said:
"In ancient times, a great officer
did not go beyond the borders even to present a gift of dried meat.
Even if one wished to wail for him,
how could one do so?
Nowadays, great officers
conduct government affairs throughout the central states.
Even if one wishes not to wail for him,
how can one avoid it?
Moreover, I have heard
that there are two reasons for wailing:
one wails out of affection,
and one wails out of fear."
The duke said:
"True,
but then what should be done?"
Xiànzǐ said:
"I beg to wail for him in the temple of a different surname."
Thereupon they wailed for him at Xiàn's temple.
3.72 Zhòng Xiàn said to Zēngzǐ:
"The Xià dynasty used spirit vessels
to show the people that the dead have no consciousness;
the Yīn people used sacrificial vessels
to show the people that the dead have consciousness;
the Zhōu people used both,
to show the people that they are in doubt."
Zēngzǐ said:
"Surely that is not so!
Surely that is not so!
Spirit vessels
are for the ghosts;
sacrificial vessels
are for the living.
Why would the ancients
treat their parents as dead?"
3.73 When Gōngshū Mù had a brother of the same mother but different father who died,
he asked Zǐyóu about it.
Zǐyóu said:
"Should it be the nine months' mourning?"
When Dí Yí had a brother of the same mother but different father who died,
he asked Zǐxià about it,
and Zǐxià said:
"I have not heard of this before;
but the people of Lǔ wear the plain hemmed sackcloth for it."
Dí Yí accordingly wore the plain hemmed sackcloth.
The present practice of wearing plain hemmed sackcloth
stems from Dí Yí's question.
3.74 When Zǐsī's mother died in Wèi,
Liǔ Ruò said to Zǐsī:
"You,
being a descendant of a sage,
are observed by all quarters for your propriety.
You should be careful in this matter."
Zǐsī said:
"Why should I be careful?
I have heard that
if one has the proper rites
but not the means,
a gentleman does not perform them;
if one has the proper rites
and the means,
but not the proper time,
a gentleman does not perform them.
Why should I be careful?"
3.75 Xiànzǐ Suǒ said:
"I have heard that
in ancient times there was no reduction in mourning,
high and low each mourned for their relatives accordingly.
Téng Bówén wore the plain hemmed sackcloth for Mèng Hǔ,
who was his uncle;
and he wore the plain hemmed sackcloth for Mèng Pí,
who was his uncle."
3.76 Hòu Mù said:
"Regarding mourning,
I heard from Xiànzǐ that
mourning
must be deeply and long pondered.
When buying a coffin, examine it inside and out thoroughly.
When I die, it should be done likewise."
3.77 Zēngzǐ said:
"Before the corpse is adorned,
the hall is screened;
after the slight dressing, the screen is removed."
Zhòng Liángzǐ said:
"While husband and wife are in confusion,
the hall is screened;
after the slight dressing, the screen is removed."
3.78 Regarding the offering at the slight dressing,
Zǐyóu said:
"It should be placed in the east."
Zēngzǐ said:
"It should be placed in the west,
and the mat is then laid."
Placing the offering at the slight dressing in the west
was an error in the later Lǔ rites.
3.79 Xiànzǐ said:
"Coarse hemp for the upper garment and fine hemp for the lower garment
are not ancient practices."
3.80 When Zǐ Pú died,
the mourners cried out 'Miè'.
Zǐgāo
said:
"This is so rustic."
The mourners then changed their cry.
3.81 At the mourning for Dù Qiáo's mother,
there was no director in the house,
which was considered too casual.
3.82 The Master said:
"At the moment of death,
those wearing lamb fur and dark caps
should change them."
Lamb fur and dark caps
were not worn by the Master when making condolence visits.
3.83 Zǐyóu asked about funeral implements,
and the Master said:
"They should correspond to the family's means."
Zǐyóu said:
