"How should one regulate according to means?"
The Master said:
"If one has means,
do not exceed the rites;
if one has no means,
wrap the head and feet to preserve the shape,
bury immediately,
and lower the coffin with ropes.
Who would criticize such a person?"
3.84 Sīshì Bēn informed Zǐyóu, saying:
"I request to dress the corpse on the bed."
Zǐyóu said:
"Very well."
Xiànzǐ heard of this
and said:
"How excessive, Shūshì,
to so readily approve others in matters of ritual!"
3.85 When Duke Xiāng of Sòng buried his wife,
he included a hundred jars of pickles and sauces.
Zēngzǐ said:
"Since they are called spirit vessels,
why fill them with real things?"
3.86 At the mourning for Mèng Xiànzǐ,
the minister of revenues returned the remaining contributions from the four quarters.
The Master said:
"This was acceptable."
3.87 When the list of funeral gifts was read,
Zēngzǐ said:
"This is not an ancient practice;
it is a second announcement."
3.88 When Chéngzǐ Gāo was ill in bed,
Qìng Yí entered
and requested,
saying:"Your illness is critical.
If it should come to the great illness,
what should be done?"
Zǐgāo said:
"I have heard that
one should live to benefit others,
and not harm others by one's death.
Though I may have lived without benefiting others,
can I harm others by my death?
When I die,
choose an infertile piece of land to bury me."
3.89 Zǐxià asked the Master, saying:
"When mourning for the ruler's mother or wife,"
"one's dwelling, speech, and diet remain composed."
3.90 When a guest arrived
with no lodging place,
the Master said:
"While alive, lodge with me;
when dead, let me handle your funeral."
3.91 Guǒzǐgāo said:
"Burial means
concealment;
concealment means
wishing people cannot see it.
Therefore,
garments suffice to adorn the body,
the inner coffin encloses the garments,
the outer coffin encloses the inner coffin,
and earth encloses the outer coffin.
Why return to mound-building and tree-planting?"
3.92 At Confucius's funeral,
someone came from Yān to observe,
staying at Zǐxià's house.
Zǐxià said:
"Is it the sage burying others?
Or others burying the sage.
What are you observing?
Formerly the Master said:
'I have seen graves shaped like halls,
some like dikes,
some like inverted summer houses,
some like hatchets.
I follow the hatchet-shaped ones.'
This is called the horse-mane mound.
Now in one day we cut boards thrice,
and complete the burial.
Are we still following the Master's wish?"
3.93 Women do not wear hempen girdles.
3.94 When offering fresh harvest,
it is like the new moon sacrifice.
3.95 After burial,
each removes mourning garments according to their relationship.
3.96 The pond [on the bier] resembles the double eaves.
3.97 When the ruler ascends the throne, he makes his inner coffin,
lacquering it once a year,
and stores it away.
3.98 The recalling of the soul,
propping open the teeth,
binding the feet,
placing rice in the mouth,
arranging the ornaments,
and setting up the hall screen all occur together.
The father and elder brothers appoint the messenger.
3.99 For the ruler's soul-recalling,
it is done in the small resting place, great resting place,
small ancestral temple, great ancestral temple,
treasury gate, and four suburbs.
3.100 In mourning, not exposing
refers to offerings?
Or sacrificial meat?
After the encoffining,
after ten days distribute wood and burial objects.
Morning offerings at sunrise,
evening offerings before sunset.
For parents' mourning,
weeping has no fixed time,
but when sent on missions, they must report their return.
3.101 During the lesser silk mourning,
wear silk robes with yellow lining,
and light red edges,
hempen girdle and headband,
rope sandals without hooks,
horn earplugs,
deerskin fur coat with even-length cuffs,
which may be worn uncovered.
3.102 If there is a funeral at home,
and one hears of a distant brother's death,
even if only slight mourning, one must go;
if not a brother,
even if a neighbor, one does not go.
For acquaintances,
all their non-cohabiting brothers should be condoled.
3.103 The Son of Heaven's coffin has four layers:
water-buffalo and rhinoceros hide coffins covering it,
three inches thick,
one catalpa coffin,
two lacquer coffins,
all four enclosing.
Coffin bindings: two vertical, three horizontal,
with one wooden wedge per binding.
Cypress outer coffin six feet long at the ends.
3.104 When the Son of Heaven mourns feudal lords,
he wears dark cap with mourning headband and robe;
some say:
he has officials mourn for them,
and does not eat with music.
3.105 The Son of Heaven's encoffining:
embankment coating with dragon-painted bier as outer coffin,
adding axe-patterned canopy over the coffin,
completely coating it like a house,
this is the Son of Heaven's ritual.
3.106 Only for the Son of Heaven's funeral
do different clans weep separately.
3.107 Lǚ Āigōng eulogized Kǒngqiū, saying:
"Heaven leaves us no elder,
none to assist my position,
Alas, sorrowful!
Nìfù!"
3.108 When the state loses major cities,
dukes, ministers, great officers, and officers all wear mourning caps,
weeping in the grand temple
for three days,
the ruler does not hold celebrations.
Some say:
the ruler holds celebrations but weeps to the earth god.
3.109 Confucius disliked wild mourning.
3.110 Those not in office
dare not give gifts to others;
if giving gifts,
they do so in the name of father or elder brother.
3.111 After all officers have entered, then morning and evening weeping with jumps occurs.
3.112 After the greater sacrifice, wear plain silk;
in the same month, perform the removal sacrifice;
in the following month, resume music.
3.113 The ruler may give a canopy to an officer.
4.1 For the ruler's legitimate eldest son dying between 16-19,
three chariots;
for a duke's non-legitimate eldest son dying between 16-19,
one chariot;
for a great officer's legitimate eldest son dying between 16-19,
one chariot.
4.2 For a duke's funeral,
all senior officials
use staffs.
4.3 When the ruler deals with a great officer's funeral,
before burial,
he condoles at the home;
when the coffin emerges,
he orders pulling it,
stopping after three steps,
repeating this thrice,
then the ruler withdraws;
similarly at court audience,
and similarly at the mourning station.
4.4 Those over fifty without carriages
do not cross borders to condole others.
4.5 Jì Wǔzǐ lay ill,
when Jiǎo Gù entered to see him without removing his hempen mourning,
saying:
"This principle
is about to be lost;
officers only remove hempen mourning at the duke's gate."
Wǔzǐ said:
"Is this not excellent?
The nobleman manifests subtleties."
At his funeral,
Zēng Diǎn leaned against his gate and sang.
4.6 When a great officer condoles,
"if arriving during funeral affairs,
then decline him.
When condoling others,
one does not enjoy music that day.
Women do not cross borders to condole others.
On the day of condoling
one does not drink alcohol or eat meat.
When condoling at a burial, one must pull the hearse;
if following the coffin to the grave,
all hold the cords.
4.7 During mourning,
if the ruler condoles,
there must be someone bowing in response,
even if just friends, neighbors, or householders.
The condolence says:
"Our humble ruler shares your duties."
The host says:
"We are honored by your presence."
If the ruler encounters a coffin on the road,
he must send someone to condole.
For a great officer's funeral,
the illegitimate son does not receive condolences.
4.8 When the wife's brother who inherits his father dies,
mourn him in the main room,
with the son as chief mourner,
baring shoulders, wearing the mourning band, weeping and jumping,
the husband entering to the right,
having someone stand outside the gate informing arrivals,
if intimate then entering to weep;
if the father lives,
mourn in the wife's room;
for non-inheriting brothers,
mourn in a different room.
4.9 If there is a funeral at home,
and one hears of a distant brother's death,
weep in the side room;
if no side room,
weep inside the gate to the right;
if in the same state,
then go to weep for him.
4.10 When Zǐzhāng died,
Zēngzǐ, who was in mourning for his mother,
went to weep for him in his hemmed sackcloth.
Someone said:
"One should not pay condolences in hemmed sackcloth."
Zēngzǐ said:
"Am I there to offer condolences?"
4.11 At the funeral of Yǒuruò,
Duke Dào offered condolences,
with Zǐyóu acting as usher,
moving from the left.
4.12 At the funeral of the royal princess of Qígǔ,
Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ wore the great功 mourning for her.
Some said:
"Because she was married from Lǔ,
he wore mourning as for a sister";
others said:
"She was his maternal grandmother,
hence he wore mourning for her."
4.13 During the mourning for Duke Xiàn of Jìn,
Duke Mù of Qín sent a messenger to offer condolences to Prince Chóng'ěr,
saying:
"I have heard that
the loss of a state often occurs at such a time,
and the gaining of a state often occurs at such a time.
Although you, sir, are solemnly in the midst of mourning garments,
mourning cannot last forever,
and the opportunity should not be missed.
Young man, consider this."
Chóng'ěr informed Jiùfàn,
who said:
"Young man, you should decline;
an exile has no treasures,
but considers benevolence and familial affection as treasures.
What does the death of one's father mean?
To use it for personal gain,
who in the world would approve of that?
Young man, you should decline."
Prince Chóng'ěr replied to the envoy:
"The ruler graciously condoles with this exiled minister Chóng'ěr.
In exile and bereaved of my father,
I cannot partake in the sorrow of weeping,
causing the ruler concern.
What does the death of one's father mean?
How dare I entertain other ambitions,
thus disgracing the ruler's righteousness?"
He knocked his head to the ground but did not bow,
wept and then rose,
rose without private words.
Zǐ Xiǎn reported this to Duke Mù.
Duke Mù said:
"How benevolent is Prince Chóng'ěr!
Knocking his head without bowing
shows he has not become the heir,
hence he did not complete the bow.
Weeping and then rising
shows love for his father;
rising without private words
shows he distances himself from profit."
4.14 Enshrouding the coffin with curtains
was not an ancient practice;
it began with Jìng Jiāng weeping for Mù Bó.
4.15 Mourning rites
express the height of grief.
Moderating grief
accords with the change;
the gentleman remembers the one who gave him life.
The calling back of the soul
is the way to express full love,
with the heart of prayer;
looking to return from the darkness,
seeking the way of the spirits and gods;
facing north,
signifies seeking in the darkness.
Bowing and knocking the head
is the depth of grief's expression;
knocking the head
is its utmost intensity.
Using rice and shells to fill the mouth
shows unwillingness to leave it empty;
not using the way of food,
but employing beauty instead.
The inscription
is a clear banner,
as the deceased can no longer be distinguished,
hence his flag is used to identify him.
Loving him,
thus recording him;
respecting him,
thus fulfilling the way to the utmost.
The tablet stand
represents the way of the spirit tablet;
in the Yīn dynasty, the tablet was attached to the stand;
in the Zhōu, the stand was removed after the tablet was made.
Offerings in plain vessels
reflect the mourners' sorrowful simplicity;
only in sacrificial rites
does the host exert himself fully;
how can one know what the spirits enjoy?
It also depends on the host's reverent heart.
Beating the breast and jumping
express extreme grief;
they are counted,
to regulate and formalize them.
Baring the shoulder and binding the hair
signify change;
distress,
is a change in grief.
Removing ornaments
means abandoning beauty;
baring the shoulder and binding the hair
are the extreme of removing ornaments.
Sometimes bared, sometimes covered,
shows the moderation of grief.
Wearing a mourning cap with hemp and burying in a leather cap
is the way to interact with the spirits,
showing a respectful heart.
The Zhōu people buried in leather caps,
the Yīn in Xǔ caps.
The host, hostess, and steward drink gruel,
because they are ill with grief,
and the ruler orders them to eat.
Returning to weep in the hall
is returning to where the deceased performed rites;
the hostess entering the chamber
is returning to where she cared for him.
The condolences upon returning to weep
come at the height of grief;
once returned and he is gone,
the loss is felt,
and it is most intense then.
The Yīn condoled after the burial,
the Zhōu after returning to weep.
Confucius said:
"The Yīn were sincere,
but I follow the Zhōu."
Burying in the north, with the head north,
was the universal rite of the three dynasties,
oriented towards the darkness.
After the burial,
the host presents the grave goods,
and the inviter prepares the Yú sacrifice's impersonator.
After returning to weep,
the host and officers inspect the Yú sacrifice animals;
the officers set out mats and offer sacrifices to the left of the tomb,
then return,
and at midday perform the Yú.
The Yú on the burial day
shows unwillingness to be apart even for a day.
In that month,
the Yú replaces the奠 offering.
The cessation of weeping is called 'completion';
on that day,
the sacrificial rite changes from mourning to auspicious,
and the next day,
the spirit is joined to that of the grandfather.
The change to auspicious sacrifice
until the joining
must connect on that day,
unwilling to leave it unaffiliated for even a day.
The Yīn joined after the练 sacrifice,
the Zhōu after cessation of weeping.
Confucius approved of the Yīn.
4.16 When a ruler attends a minister's funeral,
he is accompanied by shamans, invokers, peachwood, brooms, and spear-bearers,
to ward off evil;
this distinguishes it from when the minister was alive.
4.17 In mourning, there is a way of death.
This is what the former kings found hard to speak of.
4.18 The farewell in mourning
complies with the filial heart of the deceased,
whose sorrow is to leave his home,
hence he goes to the temple of ancestors before departure.
The Yīn bid farewell and encoffined in the ancestral temple,
the Zhōu bid farewell and then buried.
4.19 Confucius said:
Those who make spirit vessels
understand the way of mourning,
preparing objects but not for use.
Alas!
Using the living's utensils for the dead
is close to using human sacrifices.
Calling them spirit vessels
treats them as divine.
Clay chariots and straw figures
have existed since antiquity,
embodying the way of spirit vessels.
Confucius said those who make straw figures do well,
but those who make tomb figurines are inhuman,
is it not close to using humans?
4.20 Duke Mù asked Zǐsī:
"Is it ancient to wear mourning for a former ruler?"
Zǐsī said:
"The ancient gentlemen
advanced others with ritual,
and dismissed them with ritual,
hence there was the rite of wearing mourning for a former ruler."
The gentlemen of today,
when promoting a man, act as if they would set him on their knees,
but when dismissing a man, as if they would plunge him into an abyss.
If one refrains from being the chief instigator of conflict,
is that not good enough?
Why must there be a return to the old ways?"
4.21 During the mourning for Duke Dào,
Jì Zhāozi asked Mèng Jìngzǐ,
"What should one eat for the ruler?"
Jìngzǐ replied,
"Eating congee
is the universal rite of the world.
That we three ministers cannot maintain the ducal house
is known everywhere.
If I forced myself to become emaciated, I could do it,
but would that not make people suspect that I was not genuinely maintaining emaciation?
Therefore, I will eat regular food."
4.22 When Sītú Jìngzǐ of Wèi died,
Zǐxià went to offer condolences.
Before the master of the house had performed the minor dressing,
he went wearing his mourning headband.
Zǐyóu also went to offer condolences.
After the master had performed the minor dressing,
Zǐyóu went out, put on his mourning headband, and returned to wail.
Zǐxià asked,
"Did you hear about this?"
He replied,
"I heard it from the Master:
'When the master of the house has not changed his clothes, one does not wear the mourning headband.'"
4.23 Zēngzǐ said,
"Yànzǐ can be said
to have known the rites indeed,
for he possessed reverence and respect."
Yǒuruò said,
"Yànzǐ wore one fox-fur robe for thirty years,
had only one hearse,
and returned upon reaching the tomb.
For a ruler of a state, there are seven sacrificial victims,
and seven hearses;
for a senior official, five sacrificial victims,
and five hearses.
How could Yànzǐ know the rites?"
Zēngzǐ said,
"When the state is without the Way,
a gentleman considers full ritual observance shameful.
If the state is extravagant,
he demonstrates frugality;
if the state is frugal,
he demonstrates the rites."
4.24 When the mother of Guó Zhāozǐ died,
he asked Zǐzhāng,
"At the burial when reaching the tomb,
where should men and women take their positions?"
Zǐzhāng said,
"At the funeral of Sītú Jìngzǐ,
the Master directed the ceremony:
men faced west,
and women faced east."
He said,
"Alas!
No."
He continued,
"At my funeral, it will be widespread.
You take charge of it:
let guests be as guests,
hosts as hosts,
—women following the men all face west."
4.25 At the funeral of Mù Bó,
Jìng Jiāng wailed during the day;
at the funeral of Wén Bó,
she wailed day and night.
Confucius said,
"She knows the rites."
At the funeral of Wén Bó,
Jìng Jiāng leaned on his bed and did not wail,
saying,
"In the past, I had this son,
and I thought he would be a worthy man,
so I never went to the ducal court with him;
now that he has died,
none of his friends or various ministers have shed tears,
yet all the women of the household have wailed until they lost their voices.
This son
must have often neglected the rites!"
4.26 When the mother of Jì Kāngzǐ died,
intimate garments were displayed.
Jìng Jiāng said,
"A woman who is not properly attired
dares not appear before her parents-in-law.
Since guests from all directions will come,
why are intimate garments displayed here?"
She ordered them removed.
4.27 Yǒuzǐ and Zǐyóu were standing together
when they saw a child yearning for its parents.
Yǒuzǐ said to Zǐyóu,
"I have never understood the leaping in mourning.
I have long wished to abolish it.
True feeling lies here;
is this not right?"
Zǐyóu said,
"In the rites:
some moderate emotions,
some use external things to arouse feelings;
to follow emotions directly and act straightforwardly
is the way of the Róng and Dí barbarians.
The way of the rites is not so.
When people are happy, they are content;
content, they sing;
singing, they sway;
swaying, they dance;
dancing leads to displeasure;
displeasure leads to sorrow;
sorrow leads to sighing;
sighing leads to beating the breast;
beating the breast leads to leaping.
To grade and regulate this
is what is called the rites.
When a person dies,
others dislike it;
being incapable,
they turn away from it.
Therefore,
shrouds and coverlets are made,
biers and fans are set up,
to make people not dislike it.
At the beginning of death,
there are offerings of dried meat and pickles;
when about to depart,
there are farewell offerings sent off;
after burial, there are sacrifices;
no one has ever seen the deceased enjoy them;
yet from ancient times onward,
none have abandoned these practices,
to make people not turn away.
Thus, what you criticize in the rites
is not a fault of the rites."
4.28 When Wú invaded Chén,
they cut down sacrificial trees and killed the plague-stricken.
As the army was returning and leaving the border,
the Grand Steward Pǐ of Chén was sent to the army.
Fūchāi said to the Diplomat Yí,
"This man talks a lot;
why not ask him:
'An army must have a name;
what do people call this army?'"
The Grand Steward Pǐ said,
"In ancient times, those who invaded
did not cut down sacrificial trees,
did not kill the plague-stricken,
and did not capture those with gray hair;
now this army
has killed the plague-stricken—
should it not be called the army that kills the plague-stricken?"
He said,
"If we return your land
and give back your children,
what would you call it?"
He replied,
"If our king punishes the crimes of our humble state
and then pities and pardons us,
what army
would lack a name?"
4.29 Yán Dīng was good at observing mourning.
At the beginning of death,
he was anxious as if seeking something he could not find;
at the encoffining,
he gazed expectantly as if following but could not reach;
after burial,
he was sorrowful as if he could not return and rest.
4.30 Zǐzhāng asked,
"The Book of Documents says:
'King Gāozōng did not speak for three years;
when he spoke, there was joy.'
Is this true?"
Zhòngní said,
"How could it be otherwise?
In ancient times, when the Son of Heaven died,
the crown prince listened to the prime minister for three years."
4.31 When Zhì Dàozǐ died,
before he was buried,
Duke Píng was drinking,
with Shī Kuàng
and Lǐ Tiáo in attendance,
and bells were being played.
Dù Kuài came from outside,
heard the bell sounds,
and asked,
"Where is this?"
They said,
"In the chamber."
Dù Kuài entered the chamber,
ascended the steps in succession,
poured a cup,
and said,
"Kuàng, drink this."
He poured another cup
and said,
"Tiáo, drink this."
He poured another cup,
and facing north in the hall, sat down to drink it.
Then he descended,
hurriedly exiting.
Duke Píng called him back in,
saying:
"Dù Kuì,
earlier your mind might have enlightened me,
hence I did not speak with you;
why did you make Kuàng drink?"
He replied:
"On zǐ and mǎo days, there is no music;
with Zhī Dàozǐ in the temple,
this is even more significant than zǐ and mǎo days.
Kuàng is the Grand Maestro,
yet he did not advise against it,
so I made him drink."
"Why did you make Diào drink?"
He said:
"Diào is a close attendant of the ruler,
for the sake of a single drink or meal,
he neglects the ruler's faults,
so I made him drink."
"Why did you drink yourself?"
He said:
"I, Kuì, am a steward,
not only failing in my duties with knife and spoon,
but daring to involve myself in matters of prevention,
so I drank myself."
Duke Píng said:
"I too have faults,
pour and make me drink."
Dù Kuì washed the zhì cup and raised it high.
The duke said to his attendants:
"If I die,
you must never abandon this cup."
To this day,
after the offering is completed,
this raising of the zhì
is called the "Dù Raise."
4.32 When Gōngshū Wénzǐ passed away,
his son Wù requested a posthumous title from the ruler,
saying:
"The date is set,
and he is to be buried soon.
Please grant a name to replace his own."
The ruler said:
"In the past, when Wèi suffered famine,
the Master made congee for the starving people of the state—
was this not benevolent?
In the past, when Wèi faced calamity,
the Master risked his life to protect me—
was this not faithful?
When the Master administered the governance of Wèi,
he reformed the ranks and systems,
and in dealings with the four neighboring states,
Wèi's altars of soil and grain were not dishonored—
was this not cultured?
Therefore, let the Master be called Zhēnhuìwénzǐ."
4.33 Shí Táizhòng passed away,
having no legitimate son,
but six sons by concubines.
They divined to determine the successor.
The oracle said:
"He who bathes and wears jade will receive the auspicious sign."
Five of them bathed and wore jade;
Shí Qízi said:
"How can one
bathe and wear jade while in mourning for a parent?"
He did not bathe or wear jade.
Shí Qízi received the auspicious sign.
The people of Wèi believed the turtle shell to be wise.
4.34 Chén Zǐchē died in Wèi,
his wife and the family steward plotted to bury people with him,
having decided
when Chén Zǐgāng arrived.
They informed him, saying:
"The Master is ill
and has no one to care for him in the underworld,
we request to bury people with him."
Zǐgāng said:
"Burying people with the dead
is against ritual;
even so,
if someone must care for his illness,
who is better than his wife and steward?
If it can be stopped,
I wish to stop it;
if it cannot,
then I would have you two serve that purpose."
Thus, it was not carried out.
4.35 Zǐlù said:
"How pitiful is poverty!
In life, one cannot provide for parents;
in death, one cannot perform the rites."
Confucius said:
"Feeding them beans and water, yet bringing them joy—
this is called filial piety;
wrapping the body,
burying without an outer coffin,
according to one's means—
this is called ritual."
4.36 When Duke Xiàn of Wèi was exiled,
he returned to Wèi,
and upon reaching the outskirts,
planned to distribute fiefs to his followers before entering.
Liǔ Zhuāng said:
"If all had guarded the altars of soil and grain,
then who would have held the reins and followed?
If all had followed,
then who would have guarded the altars?
For the ruler to return to his state and show favoritism—
is that not improper?"
Thus, he did not distribute the fiefs.
4.37 Wèi had a Grand Historian named Liǔ Zhuāng,
who fell gravely ill.
The duke said:
"If his condition worsens,
even during a sacrifice, you must inform me."
The duke bowed twice and kowtowed, requesting of the impersonator:
"There is a minister, Liǔ Zhuāng,
who is not just my minister,
but a minister of the altars of soil and grain.
Hearing of his death,
I request to go."
He went without changing his sacrificial robes
and presented burial garments.
He bestowed upon him the lands of Qiúshì and the district of Pānshì,
wrote it down, and placed it in the coffin,
saying:
"For generations upon generations, for ten thousand子孙
let this remain unchanged."
4.38 Chén Qiānxī lay ill,
entrusted his brothers,
and commanded his son Zūnjǐ, saying:
"If I die,
you must make a large coffin for me,
and have my two maids lie beside me."
When Chén Qiānxī died,
his son said:
"Burying people with the dead
is against ritual,
let alone in the same coffin?"
Thus, he did not kill them.
4.39 Zhòng Suì died in Chuí;
on rénwǔ day, they still held the yì sacrifice,
with the Wàn dance performed but the Yuè removed.
Confucius said:
"This is against ritual;
when a minister dies, the yì should not be held."
4.40 When Jì Kāngzǐ's mother died,
Gōngshū Ruò was still young,
and during the encoffining,
Bān requested to use a mechanical device for sealing the tomb.
As they were about to agree,
Gōngjiān Jiǎ said:
"No!
Lǔ has its traditions:
the ducal house uses fēngbēi,
the three families use huányíng.
Bān,
you would experiment with someone's mother—
could you not avoid it?
Must you experiment?
Would that not be deplorable?
Alas!"
Thus, they did not proceed.
4.41 During the battle at Láng,
Gōngshū Yùrén came upon a man leaning on his staff, entering the fort to rest,
and said:
"Though the conscription is harsh,
and the burdens heavy,
if the noblemen cannot devise strategies,
and the officers cannot die for the state,
it is unacceptable!
I have spoken."
He went with his neighbor's child Wāng Qí,
and both died there.
The people of Lǔ considered not burying Wāng Qí as a child,
and asked Confucius.
Confucius said:
"He could bear arms to defend the altars of soil and grain;
even if you wish not to bury him as a child,
is that not acceptable?"
4.42 When Zǐlù was leaving Lǔ,
he said to Yán Yuān:
"What parting words do you have for me?"
Yán Yuān said:
"I have heard:
when leaving one's state,
one weeps at the ancestral graves before departing;
upon returning to one's state,
one does not weep,
but visits the graves before entering."
He then asked Zǐlù:
"How should I conduct myself?"
Zǐlù said:
"I have heard:
when passing a tomb, one bows from the chariot;
when passing a shrine, one descends."
4.43 Gōng Yǐn Shāng Yáng and Chén Qìjí pursued the army of Wú,
and caught up with them.
Chén Qìjí said to Gōng Yǐn Shāng Yáng:
"This is the king's business,
you may take up your bow."
He took up his bow.
"You should shoot them."
He shot,
and killed one man,
then put his bow back in its case.
When they caught up again,
he was urged,
and killed two more men.
For each man killed,
he covered his eyes.
He stopped his charioteer, saying:
"At court I do not sit in the presence of the ruler,
at banquets I do not partake,
having killed three men,
it is enough to report back."
Confucius said:
"Even in killing men,
there is ritual propriety."
4.44 When the feudal lords attacked Qín,
Duke Huán of Cáo died at the meeting.
The feudal lords requested to perform the 'hán' ceremony,
and had him enshrouded.
4.45 When Duke Xiāng went to pay court to Jīng,
King Kāng died.
The people of Jīng said:
"You must request to perform the enshrouding."
The people of Lǔ said:
"This is not according to ritual."
The people of Jīng pressed them.
The shaman first brushed the coffin.
The people of Jīng regretted it.
4.46 At the funeral of Duke Chéng of Téng,
Zǐ Shū Jìng Shū was sent to offer condolences,
and present the written message,
with Zǐfú Huì Bó as his assistant.
When they reached the outskirts,
because of the anniversary of Yì Bó's death
they did not enter.
Huì Bó said:
"This is government business,
we cannot because of private matters concerning our uncle
fail to carry out public duties."
So they entered.
4.47 Duke Āi sent someone to offer condolences to Kuì Shàng,
and met him on the road.
He made way by the roadside,
drew a temporary palace on the ground and received condolences there.
Zēngzǐ said:
"Kuì Shàng was not as knowledgeable about ritual as the wife of Qǐ Liáng.
When Duke Zhuāng of Qí attacked Jǔ at Duó,
Qǐ Liáng died there.
His wife met his coffin on the road and wept mournfully.
Duke Zhuāng sent someone to offer condolences.
She replied:
'If your servant has not escaped crime,
he should be exposed in the marketplace or court,
and his wives and concubines seized;
if your servant has escaped crime,
then there are the humble dwellings of his ancestors.
The ruler need not demean his command.'"
4.48 At the funeral of Rúzǐ Tún,
Duke Āi wanted to set up the funeral drapery,
and asked Yǒu Ruò,
Yǒu Ruò said:
"It can be done,
even your three ministers have it."
Yán Liǔ said:
"The Son of Heaven has a dragon-decorated hearse and coffin covering,
feudal lords have a hearse and set up a covering,
- because of the elm-wood sinking they set up the drapery;
the three ministers abandoned the hearse and set up the drapery,
this is an improper use of ritual,
so why should the ruler learn from them?"
4.49 When the mother of Duke Dào died,
Duke Āi wore mourning for her of the zīcuī grade.
Yǒu Ruò said:
"Wearing zīcuī mourning for a concubine,
is this according to ritual?"
The duke said:
"Could I avoid it?
The people of Lǔ made her my wife."
4.50 Jì Zǐgāo buried his wife,
and damaged people's grain,
Shēn Xiáng told him about it,
saying:
"Please compensate them."
Zǐgāo said:
"The Mèng clan does not blame me for this,
my friends do not abandon me for this,
because I am the district chief here,
if I buy the way to bury,
it will be hard for successors to follow."
4.51 An officer who has not yet received a salary,
if the ruler gives him a gift it is called 'presenting';
if sent on a mission he says 'our humble ruler';
if he leaves and the ruler dies,
he does not wear mourning.
4.52 At the yú sacrifice, they set up a representative of the dead,
with a small table and mat.
After the 'end of weeping' sacrifice, they avoid the name,
for the service to the living ends and the service to the ghost begins.
After the 'end of weeping',
the steward holds a wooden bell and announces in the palace:
"Discard the old taboos and avoid the new."
From the inner gate to the outer gate.
4.53 With two-character names, both need not be avoided together,
the mother of the Master was named Zhēng Zài;
when saying 'Zài' they did not mention 'Zhēng',
when saying 'Zhēng' they did not mention 'Zài'.
4.54 If the army suffers a defeat,
they wear plain clothes and weep outside the arsenal gate,
the reporting chariot does not carry its arrow and bow cases.
4.55 If someone's ancestral temple is burned down,
they weep for three days.
Hence it is said:
"When the new palace burned,
they also wept for three days."
4.56 Confucius was passing by the side of Mount Tài,
and there was a woman weeping mournfully at a grave.
The Master leaned on his carriage rail and listened.
He sent Zǐgòng to ask her, saying:
"Your weeping,
seems like you have repeated sorrows."
And she said:
"Yes,
formerly my father-in-law died by a tiger,
my husband also died so,
and now my son has died so too."
The Master said:
"Why don't you leave?"
She said:
"There is no oppressive government here."
The Master said:
"Remember this, my disciples,
oppressive government is fiercer than a tiger
4.57 There was a man from Lǔ named Zhōu Fēng,
Duke Āi took a gift and requested to see him.
But he said "It cannot be."
The duke said:
"Then I shall give up."
He sent someone to ask him,
saying:
"The Yǒu Yú clan did not impose trust on the people yet the people trusted them,
the Xià Hòu clan did not impose respect on the people yet the people respected them,
what must be done to gain this from the people?"
He replied:
"Among the ruins of graves and tombs,
though no sorrow is imposed on the people, they feel sorrow;
in the altars of soil and grain and ancestral temples,
though no respect is imposed on the people, they feel respect.
The Yīn people made oaths and the people began to rebel,
the Zhōu people held assemblies and the people began to doubt.
If without ritual righteousness,
loyalty, trustworthiness, sincere and honest hearts to govern them,
even if firmly bound,
would the people not break away?"
4.58 In mourning, one should not impair one's dwelling,
in grief, one should not endanger one's life.
In mourning, one should not impair one's dwelling,
because there should be no loss of the temple;
in grief, one should not endanger one's life,
because there should be no loss of descendants.
4.59 Yánlíng Jìzǐ went to Qí,
on his return journey,
his eldest son died,
and was buried between Yíng and Bó.
Confucius said:
"Yánlíng Jìzǐ
is one well-versed in the rites of Wú."
He went to observe the burial.
The grave pit was not dug deep enough to reach the water spring,
and he was buried in his everyday clothes.
After burial, the mound was raised,
covering the pit in breadth and length,
its height such that one could bend and touch it.
After the mound was raised,
he bared his left arm,
circled the mound to the right three times while wailing,
saying:
"Flesh and bones return to the earth,
this is fate.
But the soul and spirit go everywhere,
go everywhere."
And then he departed.
Confucius said:
"Yánlíng Jìzǐ's practice of the rites,
is indeed appropriate."
4.60 At the funeral of Zhūlóu Kǎogōng,
the lord of Xú sent Róng Jū to offer condolences and present jade for the mouth.
He said:
"My humble lord has sent me, Róng Jū, to kneel and present the jade for the mouth, offering jade to the marquis.
He has dispatched me, Róng Jū, to perform the mouth-filling."
The officials said:
"When lords come to our humble state,
for those of equal rank, we treat them as equals;
for superiors, we treat them as superiors.
Mixing the two has never been done."
Róng Jū replied:
In serving one's lord, one must not forget his lord,
nor dare neglect his ancestors.
Long ago, my ancestor Lord Jūwáng campaigned west across the river,
and never failed to use these words.
I, Róng Jū,
am a man of Lǔ,
and dare not forget my ancestors."
When Zǐsī's mother died in Wèi,
the news was sent to Zǐsī,
who wept in the ancestral temple.
A disciple came and said:
"When the mother of the Shù family dies,
why weep in the temple of the Kǒng family?"
Zǐsī said:
"I was wrong,
I was wrong."
Then he wept in another room.
4.61 When the Son of Heaven passes away,
after three days, the prayer officials don mourning;
after five days, the officials and chiefs;
after seven days, all men and women in the capital;
after three months, all under heaven.
The foresters supply wood from the hundred shrines,
cutting down trees suitable for inner and outer coffins.
Those who fail to deliver
have their sacrifices abolished,
and the person is executed.
4.62 During a great famine in Qí,
Qián Áo set up food by the roadside,
waiting to feed the starving.
A starving man came, covering his face with his sleeve and dragging his shoes,
walking unsteadily.
Qián Áo held food with his left hand,
drink with his right,
and said:
"Hey! Come eat."
The starving man raised his eyes and looked at him,
saying:
"It is precisely because I refuse to eat 'hey-come-eat' food
that I have come to this state."
Though Qián Áo then apologized,
the man ultimately did not eat and died.
Zēngzǐ heard of this,
and said:
"Wasn't this excessive?
When he said 'hey,' one could leave;
when he apologized, one could eat."
4.63 During the time of Zhūlóu Dìnggōng,
there was one who murdered his father.
The officials reported it,
and the duke, startled, fell from his mat, saying:
"This is my fault."
He said:
"I have studied how to judge such cases:
When a minister kills his lord,
all officials shall execute him without pardon;
when a son kills his father,
all in the household shall execute him without pardon.
Kill the person,
destroy his house,
and turn it into a pond.
The lord should wait over a month before raising a cup."
4.64 When Jìn Xiànwénzǐ completed his house,
the great officers of Jìn went to present gifts.
Zhāng Lǎo said:
"How magnificent its grandeur!
How splendid its beauty!
Here you may sing,
here you may weep,
here you may gather the state and clan."
Wénzǐ said:
"If I, Wǔ, can sing here,
weep here,
and gather the state and clan here,
then I can preserve my head and spine to follow the former great officers at Jiǔjīng."
He faced north and bowed twice, touching his head to the ground.
The gentleman said they excelled in praise and prayer.
4.65 When Confucius's pet dog died,
he had Zǐgòng bury it,
saying:
"I have heard
that one does not discard a worn-out curtain,
using it to bury a horse;
one does not discard a worn-out canopy,
using it to bury a dog.
I, Qiū, am poor,
and have no canopy;
when you inter it,
give it a mat,
so its head does not touch the dirt."
When a road horse died,
it was buried with a curtain.
4.66 When Jìsūn's mother died,
Duke Āi came to offer condolences,
and Zēngzǐ and Zǐgòng also came.
The gatekeeper, because the lord was inside,
did not admit them.
Zēngzǐ and Zǐgòng entered the stable to tidy their appearance.
Zǐgòng entered first,
and the gatekeeper said:
"I have already announced you."
Zēngzǐ entered after,
and the gatekeeper stepped aside for him.
When they reached the inner eaves,
the ministers all moved from their positions,
and the duke descended one step to greet them.
The gentleman commented:
"The way of perfect grooming
ensures one's travels are far."
4.67 When the guard of the Yángmén gate died,
Sīchéng Zǐhǎn entered and wept for him sorrowfully.
A Jìn spy observing Sòng
returned and reported to the marquis of Jìn:
"The guard of Yángmén died,
and Zǐhǎn wept for him sorrowfully,
and the people are pleased.
It may be unwise to attack."
Confucius heard of this and said:
"Excellent was this spying on the state!
The Book of Songs says:
'Whenever people suffer misfortune,
rush to their aid.'
Even without Jìn,
who in all under heaven could withstand them?"
4.68 At the funeral of Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ,
after the burial,
the mourning sash was not brought inside the treasury gate.
After the officers and great officers concluded the wailing,
the hempen garments were not worn inside.
4.69 Confucius had an old friend named Yuán Rǎng.
When his mother died,
the Master helped him prepare the outer coffin.
Yuán Rǎng climbed onto the wood and said:
"Long has it been since I expressed myself in song!"
He sang:
"Like the patterned head of a lynx,
holding your hand so soft and curled."
The Master acted as if he did not hear and passed by.
A follower said:
"Can you not break with him?"
The Master said:
"I have heard:
With kin, do not lose kinship;
with old friends, do not lose old friendship."
4.70 Zhào Wénzǐ and Shū Yù toured Jiǔyuán.
Wénzǐ said:
"If the dead could rise,
with whom would I associate?"
Shū Yù said:
"Perhaps with Yáng Chùfǔ?"
Wénzǐ said:
"He wielded power in Jìn,
yet did not die a natural death;
his wisdom is not commendable."
"Then with Jiù Fàn?"
Wénzǐ said:
"Seeing profit, he disregarded his lord;
his benevolence is not commendable.
I would follow Suí Wǔzǐ,
who benefited his lord without forgetting himself,
and planned for himself without abandoning his friends."
The people of Jìn said Wénzǐ understood men.
Wénzǐ was retiring as if unable to bear his clothes;
his speech was halting as if words hardly left his mouth.
Yet those he recommended in Jìn for minor posts
numbered over seventy families.
In life, he did not seek profit;
in death, he did not entrust his sons.
4.71 Shūzhòng Pí studied with Zǐliǔ.
When Shūzhòng Pí died,
his wife, a woman of Lǔ,
wore mourning with a hempen sash tied at the neck.
Shūzhòng Yǎn reported this,
requesting fine hemp and a round sash,
saying:
"In the past, when I mourned my aunts and sisters, it was like this,
and no one forbade me."
He withdrew,
and had his wife wear fine hemp with a round sash.
4.72 A man of Chéng had an elder brother die but did not wear mourning.
Hearing that Zǐgāo would become governor of Chéng,
he then wore mourning.
The people of Chéng said:
"The silkworm spins, yet the crab has a basket;
the wasp has a cap, yet the cicada has a tassel;
the elder brother dies, yet Zǐgāo makes him wear mourning."
4.73 When Yuèzhèng Zǐchūn's mother died,
he did not eat for five days.
He said:
"I regret it;
since even with my own mother I could not maintain my true feelings,
where then should I employ my true feelings?"
4.74 During a drought,
Duke Mù summoned Xiànzǐ and asked him about it,
saying:
"Heaven has not rained for a long time;
I wish to expose the hunchback - what would that be like?"
Xiànzǐ replied:
"Heaven has not rained for a long time,
yet to expose someone's sick child,
is cruel;
would that not be improper?"
"Then I wish to expose the shaman - what would that be like?"
He said:
"If Heaven will not rain,
and you place hopes on a foolish woman,
by this to seek rain,
would that not be too far-fetched?"
"What about moving the market?"
He said:
"When the Son of Heaven dies,
markets are held in alleys for seven days;
when a feudal lord dies,
markets are held in alleys for three days.
To move the market for this purpose,
would that not be acceptable?"
4.75 Confucius said:
"The people of Wèi place the accompanying burial separate;
they keep them apart;
the people of Lǔ place them together,
they join them,
and this is good."
5.1 The system of ranks and emoluments of the king:
Duke, Marquis, Earl, Viscount, Baron,
making five grades in all.
For the feudal lords: High Ministers and Ministers of State,
Lower Ministers,
Upper Servicemen, Middle Servicemen, Lower Servicemen,
making five grades in all.
The Son of Heaven's fields extend a thousand lǐ square,
those of Dukes and Marquises a hundred lǐ square,
those of Earls seventy lǐ,
those of Viscounts and Barons fifty lǐ.
Those unable to reach fifty lǐ,
do not associate directly with the Son of Heaven,
but attach to the feudal lords,
and are called Attached Territories.
The fields of the Three Dukes of the Son of Heaven are equivalent to those of Dukes and Marquises,
the Ministers of the Son of Heaven equivalent to Earls,
the Great Officers of the Son of Heaven equivalent to Viscounts and Barons,
the Principal Servicemen of the Son of Heaven equivalent to Attached Territories.
5.2 Regulations:
agricultural land is one hundred mǔ per farmer.
The distribution from one hundred mǔ:
the best farmer feeds nine people,
the next feeds eight,
the next feeds seven,
the next feeds six;
the poorest farmer feeds five.
Commoners in official positions,
their emoluments are graded accordingly.
The Lower Servicemen of feudal lords are equivalent to the best farmer.
Their emolument is sufficient to replace their farming.
Middle Servicemen double that of Lower Servicemen,
Upper Servicemen double that of Middle Servicemen,
Lower Ministers double that of Upper Servicemen;
Ministers of State,
have four times the emolument of a Great Officer;
the Ruler,
has ten times that of a Minister.
In a secondary state, the Minister,
has three times the emolument of a Great Officer;
the Ruler,
has ten times that of a Minister.
In a small state, the Minister,
doubles the emolument of a Great Officer,
the Ruler, has ten times that of a Minister.
5.3 In a secondary state, the High Minister,
holds a position equivalent to the Middle Minister of a great state,
the Middle Minister equivalent to its Lower Minister,
the Lower Minister equivalent to its Upper Great Officer.
In a small state, the High Minister,
holds a position equivalent to the Lower Minister of a great state,
the Middle Minister equivalent to its Upper Great Officer,
the Lower Minister equivalent to its Lower Great Officer,
and where there are Middle and Lower Servicemen,
their numbers are each three-tenths of those above them.
5.4 Within the Four Seas, there are nine provinces,
each province a thousand lǐ square.
In a province,
thirty states of a hundred lǐ are established,
sixty states of seventy lǐ,
one hundred and twenty states of fifty lǐ,
making two hundred and ten states in all;
famous mountains and great marshes are not enfeoffed,
the remainder becomes Attached Territories and interstitial land.
In eight provinces,
each has two hundred and ten states.
5.5 Within the domain of the Son of Heaven,
nine states of a hundred lǐ square,
twenty-one states of seventy lǐ,
sixty-three states of fifty lǐ,
making ninety-three states in all;
famous mountains and great marshes are not distributed,
the remainder is used for emoluments of servicemen,
and as interstitial land.
5.6 Throughout the nine provinces,
there are one thousand seven hundred and seventy-three states.
The Principal Servicemen of the Son of Heaven,
and the Attached Territories of feudal lords are not included.
5.7 Within a hundred lǐ of the Son of Heaven, revenue supplies the officials,
within a thousand lǐ, it serves the imperial needs.
5.8 Beyond a thousand lǐ,
Regional Chiefs are established.
Five states form a Shǔ,
each Shǔ has a leader.
Ten states form a Lián,
each Lián has a commander.
Thirty states form a Zú,
each Zú has a director.
Two hundred and ten states form a province,
each province has a Chief.
Eight provinces have eight Chiefs,
fifty-six directors,
one hundred and sixty-eight commanders,
three hundred and thirty-six leaders.
The eight Chiefs each with their subordinates
belong to the two Elders of the Son of Heaven,
dividing the world into left and right,
called the Two Chiefs.
5.9 Within a thousand lǐ is called the Royal Domain,
beyond a thousand lǐ
is called the Tributary Region,
and the Remote Region.
5.10 The Son of Heaven has:
Three Dukes,
Nine Ministers,
twenty-seven Great Officers,
eighty-one Principal Servicemen.
5.11 A great state has:
three Ministers;
all appointed by the Son of Heaven;
five Lower Great Officers,
twenty-seven Upper Servicemen.
5.12 A secondary state has:
three Ministers;
two appointed by the Son of Heaven,
one appointed by its own ruler;
five Lower Great Officers,
twenty-seven Upper Servicemen.
5.13 A small state has:
two Ministers;
both appointed by its own ruler;
five Lower Great Officers,
twenty-seven Upper Servicemen.
5.14 The Son of Heaven sends his Great Officers as Three Supervisors,
supervising in the states of the Regional Chiefs,
three per state.
The feudal lords within the Son of Heaven's domain,
receive emoluments;
5.15 external feudal lords,
inherit.
5.16 Regulations:
for the Three Dukes,
one ceremonial robe at first appointment;
if there are additions,
they are by special grant.
They do not exceed nine appointments.
The ruler of a secondary state,
does not exceed seven appointments;
the ruler of a small state,
does not exceed five appointments.
5.17 The Minister of a great state,
does not exceed three appointments;
a Lower Minister has two appointments,
the Minister of a small state
and a Lower Great Officer have one appointment.
5.18 In appointing talented people from among the populace,
one must first evaluate them.
After evaluation and discernment, then employ them,
after entrusting them with responsibilities, then rank them,
after their position is fixed, then emolument them.
5.19 Ennoble people at court,
sharing it with the servicemen.
Execute people in the market,
abandoning them with the multitude.
Therefore, the public does not keep convicts,
Great Officers do not support them,
servicemen meeting them on the road do not speak with them;
they are banished to the four quarters,
going only where they are sent,
not involved in governance,
nor are they desired to live.
5.20 The feudal lords in relation to the Son of Heaven:
every year, a minor embassy;
every three years, a major embassy;
every five years, a personal court visit.
5.21 The Son of Heaven tours the domains every five years:
5.22 In the second month of the year,
he tours eastward, reaching Dàizōng,
where he burns wood and gazes in sacrifice to the mountains and rivers;
receives the feudal lords in audience;
inquires about those who are a hundred years old and goes to visit them.
He orders the Grand Music Master to present the odes
to observe the customs of the people,
commands the markets to report prices
to observe what the people like and dislike.
If their inclinations are excessive, their preferences are depraved.
He orders the Director of Ceremonies to examine the seasons and months,
fix the days,
unify the pitch-pipes,
and correct the rituals, music, institutions, measures, and clothing.
For the mountains, rivers, and spirits,
if any are neglected in sacrifice,
it is deemed disrespect;
for those who are disrespectful,
the ruler reduces their territory.
For the ancestral temples,
if there is any impropriety,
it is deemed unfilial;
for those who are unfilial,
the ruler strips them of their rank.
Those who alter rituals and change music
are deemed disobedient;
for those who are disobedient,
the ruler exiles them.
Those who change institutions and clothing
are deemed rebellious;
for the rebellious, the ruler punishes them.
Those who have merit and virtue among the people
are granted additional land and advanced in rank.
In the fifth month,
he tours southward, reaching the Southern Peak,
following the same rituals as the eastern tour.
In the eighth month,
he tours westward, reaching the Western Peak,
following the same rituals as the southern tour.
In the eleventh month,
he tours northward, reaching the Northern Peak,
following the same rituals as the western tour.
Upon returning,
he reports to the ancestors and father's temple,
using a single beast.
5.23 When the Son of Heaven is about to depart,
he offers the Lèi sacrifice to the Supreme Deity,
the Yí sacrifice to the Earth God,
and the Zào sacrifice to his father's temple;
when a feudal lord is about to depart,
he offers the Yí sacrifice to the Earth God,
and the Zào sacrifice to his father's temple.
5.24 When the Son of Heaven, without specific affairs, meets with the feudal lords, it is called a court assembly;
they examine rituals, correct punishments, and unify virtue,
to show respect to the Son of Heaven.
When the Son of Heaven bestows music upon a feudal lord,
it is presented with a zhù;
when bestowing music upon a bó, zǐ, or nán,
it is presented with a táo.
5.25 A feudal lord,
only after being bestowed with bow and arrows
may he launch a campaign;
only after being bestowed with the axe of authority
may he execute;
only after being bestowed with a jade libation cup
may he prepare aromatic liquor.
If not bestowed with the jade cup,
he obtains the aromatic liquor from the Son of Heaven.
5.26 Only after the Son of Heaven commands education
is a school established.
The elementary school is to the south and left of the ducal palace,
the university is in the suburbs.
The Son of Heaven's is called the Pìyōng,
the feudal lords' is called the Pàngōng.
5.27 When the Son of Heaven is about to campaign,
he offers the Lèi sacrifice to the Supreme Deity,
the Yí sacrifice to the Earth God,
the Zào sacrifice to his father's temple,
and the Mà sacrifice at the land of campaign.
He receives the mandate at the ancestral temple,
and receives the finalized plans at the school.
On campaign,
he captures the guilty,
returns,
and offers a sacrifice at the school,
reporting the captives and severed ears.
5.28 The Son of Heaven and feudal lords,
without state affairs,
hunt three times a year.
The first is for dried offerings,
the second for guests,
the third to supply the ruler's kitchen.
Not hunting when without affairs
is called disrespect;
hunting not in accordance with ritual
is called wasting nature's bounty.
The Son of Heaven does not surround completely,
feudal lords do not surprise entire herds.
When the Son of Heaven kills, the large banner is lowered;
when a feudal lord kills, the small banner is lowered;
when a minister kills, the auxiliary chariots stop.
When the auxiliary chariots stop,
the common people may hunt.
After the otter offers fish,
then the foresters enter marshes and weirs.
After the jackal offers game,
then hunting begins.
After the dove transforms into the hawk,
then nets are set.
After plants and trees wither and fall,
then they enter the mountains and forests.
Before insects hibernate,
no firing of fields is allowed.
Do not take fawns,
do not take eggs,
do not kill the pregnant,
do not slaughter the young,
do not overturn nests.
5.29 The Grand Steward regulates the state's expenditures,
necessarily at the year's end,
after all five grains are harvested
then he regulates the state's expenditures.
According to the size of the land,
he considers the year's abundance or scarcity.
Based on a thirty-year average, he regulates state expenditures,
measuring income to determine outlay.
For sacrifices, use one-tenth of the revenue.
During mourning,
for three years, no sacrifices are held,
except for sacrifices to Heaven, Earth, and the Land and Grain,
which are performed overriding the funeral rites.
For mourning, use three years' tenth of revenue.
For mourning and sacrifices,
insufficiency is called wastefulness,
excess is called extravagance.
In sacrifices,
in abundant years, do not be lavish;
in lean years, do not be frugal.
If the state lacks nine years' reserves
it is called insufficiency;
if it lacks six years' reserves
it is called urgency;
if it lacks three years' reserves
it is called a state no longer its own.
With three years of farming,
there must be one year's food;
with nine years of farming,
there must be three years' food.
With a thirty-year average,
even with calamities, drought, or floods,
the people will have no hungry looks,
and then the Son of Heaven may eat
daily with music.
The Son of Heaven is encoffined after seven days,
buried after seven months.
Feudal lords are encoffined after five days,
buried after five months.
Ministers,
officers,
and commoners
are encoffined after three days,
buried after three months.
The three-year mourning,
from the Son of Heaven down to
commoners, the coffin is suspended and sealed;
burial does not stop for rain;
no mound is raised, no trees planted;
during mourning, no secondary affairs are undertaken;
this applies from the Son of Heaven down to commoners.
Mourning follows the deceased,
sacrifices follow the living.
Branch sons do not offer sacrifices.
5.30 The Son of Heaven has seven temples:
three zhāo and three mù,
together with the great ancestor's temple, making seven.
Feudal lords have five temples:
two zhāo and two mù,
together with the great ancestor's temple, making five.
Ministers have three temples:
one zhāo and one mù,
together with the great ancestor's temple, making three.
Officers have one temple,
commoners sacrifice in their living quarters.
5.31 The sacrifices in the ancestral temples of the Son of Heaven and feudal lords:
in spring, called yuè;
in summer, called dì;
in autumn, called cháng;
in winter, called zhēng.
The Son of Heaven sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
the feudal lords sacrifice to the gods of soil and grain,
and the great officers sacrifice to the five household gods.
The Son of Heaven sacrifices to the famous mountains and great rivers throughout the land:
the Five Peaks are treated with the rank of the Three Dukes,
and the Four Rivers are treated with the rank of feudal lords.
Feudal lords sacrifice to the famous mountains and great rivers located within their territories.
5.32 The Son of Heaven and feudal lords sacrifice to the states that formerly existed in their territories but now have no rulers or descendants.
5.33 The Son of Heaven offers a special sacrifice in spring,
a combined sacrifice in summer,
a combined sacrifice in autumn,
and a combined sacrifice in winter.
For feudal lords, if they offer the spring sacrifice, they do not offer the summer sacrifice;
if they offer the summer sacrifice, they do not offer the autumn sacrifice;
if they offer the autumn sacrifice, they do not offer the winter sacrifice;
if they offer the winter sacrifice, they do not offer the spring sacrifice.
For feudal lords, the spring sacrifice
is special;
the summer sacrifice
alternates between one special and one combined;
the autumn sacrifice
is combined;
the winter sacrifice
is combined.
5.34 For the Son of Heaven, sacrifices to the gods of soil and grain both use the great offering (a bull, a sheep, and a pig);
for feudal lords, sacrifices to the gods of soil and grain both use the lesser offering (a sheep and a pig).
For great officers and scholars, the sacrifices in the ancestral temple
are performed if they have land,
but if they have no land, they only present offerings.
Common people present leeks in spring,
wheat in summer,
millet in autumn,
and rice in winter.
With leeks, eggs are offered;
with wheat, fish;
with millet, a suckling pig;
with rice, a wild goose.
The ox for sacrificing to Heaven and Earth
has horns the size of a silkworm cocoon or a chestnut;
the ox for the ancestral temple
has horns a handful long;
the ox for guests
has horns a foot long.
Feudal lords do not kill oxen without reason,
great officers do not kill sheep without reason,
scholars do not kill dogs or pigs without reason,
and common people do not eat delicacies without reason.
5.35 Common delicacies should not exceed the sacrificial animal in quality,
casual clothing should not surpass sacrificial robes,
and living quarters should not exceed the ancestral temple in grandeur.
5.36 In ancient times:
on the public fields,
people cultivated them without paying tax.
In the markets,
stalls were provided without tax.
inspection was conducted without levying duties.
For forests, hills, rivers, and marshes,
people entered according to the season without prohibition.
The fields for official salaries were not taxed.
5.37 In employing the labor of the people,
it should not exceed three days per year.
5.38 Farmland should not be sold,
and gravesites should not be requested.
5.39 The Minister of Works holds the measures
to survey the land,
settling people in mountains, rivers, marshes, and wetlands,
according to the four seasons.
He measures the distance of the land,
and initiates projects according to the labor force.
In all cases of employing the people:
assign them the tasks of the elderly,
but feed them the food of the strong.
5.40 In settling people and developing their talents,
it must be in accordance with the natural conditions of
cold and warmth, dryness and humidity,
with different systems for broad valleys and great rivers.
The customs of the people living among them vary:
in firmness and softness, lightness and heaviness, slowness and speed, they differ in adjustment;
the five flavors are blended differently;
tools and vessels are made differently;
clothing is appropriate differently.
Cultivate their education,
but do not change their customs;
unify their governance,
but do not change what is suitable for them.
The central states and the Róng and Yí tribes,
the peoples of the five regions,
all have their own natures,
which cannot be shifted.
Those in the east are called Yí,
with unbound hair and tattooed bodies,
and some do not eat cooked food.
Those in the south are called Mán,
with tattooed foreheads and crossed toes,
and some do not eat cooked food.
Those in the west are called Róng,
with unbound hair and wearing skins,
and some do not eat grains.
Those in the north are called Dí,
wearing feathers and fur and living in caves,
and some do not eat grains.
The central states,
Yí, Mán, Róng, and Dí,
all have peaceful dwellings,
harmonious flavors,
suitable clothing,
useful implements,
and complete tools.
The peoples of the five regions,
though their languages are not mutually intelligible,
and their desires differ,
convey their intentions
and communicate their desires:
in the east, it is called Jì;
in the south, Xiàng;
in the west, Dídī;
in the north, Yì.
5.41 In all cases of settling people,
measure the land to establish settlements,
and survey the land to settle the people.
Land, settlements, and dwellings
must be in harmonious proportion.
There should be no wasted land,
no idle people,
food should be regulated and work timed,
all people should be content in their dwellings,
enjoy their work and encourage achievement,
honor the ruler and cherish their superiors,
and only then should education be promoted.
5.42 The Minister of Education cultivates the six rites to regulate the nature of the people,
clarifies the seven teachings to promote their virtue,
unifies the eight administrative measures to prevent excess,
harmonizes the Way and virtue to unify customs,
supports the elderly to encourage filial piety,
cares for the orphaned and solitary to assist the insufficient,
honors the worthy to exalt virtue,
and selects the unworthy to reject the wicked.
He orders the districts
to report those who do not follow the teachings.
The elders all assemble at the school,
on the first day,
practice archery with emphasis on merit,
practice district ceremonies with emphasis on age,
and the Grand Minister of Education leads the talented scholars of the state
to participate in the activities.
If they do not change,
he orders the right district of the state
to move those who do not follow the teachings to the left,
and orders the left district of the state
to move those who do not follow the teachings to the right,
following the initial ceremony.
If they do not change,
move them to the suburbs,
following the initial ceremony.
If they do not change,
move them to the remote areas,
following the initial ceremony.
If they do not change,
banish them to distant regions,
and they shall never be recognized for life.
He orders the districts
to evaluate the outstanding scholars,
promote them to the Minister of Education,
calling them Xuǎnshì (selected scholars).
The Minister of Education evaluates the outstanding among the Xuǎnshì and promotes them to the academy,
calling them Jùnshì (talented scholars).
Those promoted to the Minister of Education
are not subject to district labor;
those promoted to the academy
are not subject to the Minister of Education's labor,
and are called Zàoshì (accomplished scholars).
The Director of Music honors the four arts,
establishes the four teachings,
and follows the former kings' "Odes," "Documents," "Rites," and "Music" to cultivate scholars.
In spring and autumn, he teaches "Rites" and "Music,"
in winter and summer, "Odes" and "Documents."
The crown prince, the king's sons,
the crown princes of the various lords,
the legitimate sons of dukes, ministers, and senior officers,
and the talented selections of the state,
all are cultivated there.
All enter school according to age.
When about to leave school,
the minor and major music officers,
and the minor music director
report those who do not follow the teachings
to the grand music director.
The grand music director reports to the king.
The king orders the Three Dukes,
the Nine Ministers, officers, and senior officers all to enter the school.
If they do not change,
the king personally inspects the school.
If they do not change,
the king refrains from feasting for three days,
and banishes them to distant regions.
Those in the west are called Jí,
those in the east are called Jì,
and they shall never be recognized for life.
The Grand Director of Music evaluates the outstanding scholars among the cultivated men
and reports them to the king,
elevating them to the Minister of War,
calling them presented scholars.
The Minister of War discerns and discusses official talents,
assessing the virtuous among the presented scholars
to report to the king,
thus finalizing their evaluation.
Once the evaluation is settled, they are then appointed to office;
after being entrusted with office, they are then enfeoffed with rank;
once their position is determined, they then receive their emoluments.
If a senior official neglects his duties,
he shall not hold office for life,
and upon death, he is buried with the rites of a scholar.
When there is a mobilization,
the Grand Minister of Education is ordered to instruct the scholars in chariots and armor.
All those who practice skills and contend in strength,
going to the four directions,
baring their limbs,
compete in archery and charioteering.
All those who practice skills to serve their superiors include:
invocators, scribes, archers, charioteers, physicians, diviners, and various artisans.
All those who practice skills to serve their superiors:
do not engage in secondary tasks,
do not change their official duties,
and when leaving their community, do not rank alongside scholars.
Those who serve in noble households,
when leaving their community, do not rank alongside scholars.
5.43 The Minister of Justice corrects punishments
and clarifies laws to adjudicate legal cases.
There must be three inquiries.
If there is intent but no evidence, it is not heard.
In applying laws, follow the lighter;
in granting pardons, follow the heavier.
5.44 In all cases of determining the five punishments,
one must align with the principles of Heaven,
ensuring that penalties correspond to the facts.
In all hearings of cases involving the five punishments,
one must consider the bond between father and son,
and establish the righteousness between ruler and minister to weigh them.
Deliberate on the sequence of severity,
carefully measure the depth of circumstances to distinguish them.
Exert one's intelligence,
and apply one's loyalty and compassion to the fullest.
In doubtful cases,
broadly consult with the multitude;
if the multitude is doubtful,
pardon them.
One must examine comparisons of minor and major cases to reach a decision.
Once the verdict is formed,
the clerk reports the completed case to the corrector,
who reviews it.
The corrector reports the completed case to the Grand Minister of Justice,
who reviews it under the jujube tree.
The Grand Minister of Justice reports the completed case to the king,
who orders the three ducal ministers to jointly review it.
The three ducal ministers report the completed case to the king,
the king grants three pardons,
and only then is punishment decreed.
In all enactments of punishments and penalties,
even light ones are not pardoned.
Punishment is about shaping;
shaping means finalizing,
once finalized, it cannot be changed,
hence the nobleman devotes his full attention to it.
Those who split hairs to break laws,
confuse names and alter institutions,
and uphold heretical ways to disrupt governance,
are executed.
Those who create licentious music, strange clothing, bizarre skills,
and curious devices to mislead the multitude,
are executed.
Those whose conduct is deceitful yet firm,
whose speech is false yet eloquent,
whose learning is erroneous yet broad,
and who follow wrongs with smoothness to mislead the multitude,
are executed.
Those who deceive with ghosts and spirits,
auspicious days, and divination to mislead the multitude,
are executed.
These four categories of execution
are not subject to hearing.
All who enforce prohibitions to regulate the multitude,
do not pardon offenses.
Jade scepters, bi disks, gold, and zhang tablets
are not sold in the market.
Court robes and carriages
are not sold in the market.
Vessels of the ancestral temples
are not sold in the market.
Sacrificial animals are not sold in the market.
Weapons are not sold in the market.
Utensils that do not meet standards
are not sold in the market.
Chariots of war that do not meet standards
are not sold in the market.
Cloth and silk, whether fine or coarse, not meeting the required measures,
or with widths not meeting the standard,
are not sold in the market.
Colors that are deceptive and confuse the proper hues
are not sold in the market.
Brocades, pearls, and jade formed into vessels
are not sold in the market.
Clothing and food
are not sold in the market.
The five grains not in season,
fruits not yet ripe,
are not sold in the market.
Wood not fit for felling
is not sold in the market;
birds, beasts, fish, and turtles not fit for killing
are not sold in the market.
At the passes, prohibitions are enforced with inspections,
banning unusual clothing,
and identifying strange speech.
5.45 The Grand Historian oversees rituals,
holds the bamboo records,
and presents the taboos and inauspicious matters.
5.46 The Son of Heaven fasts and receives admonitions.
The Minister of Revenues, with the annual achievements,
presents them to the Son of Heaven for verification,
while the Prime Minister fasts and receives the verification.
The Grand Director of Music,
the Grand Minister of Justice,
and the Market official,
these three officers with their achievements
follow in presenting to the Son of Heaven for verification.
The Grand Minister of Education,
the Grand Minister of War,
and the Grand Minister of Works fast and receive verification,
while all officials each with their achievements
present to the three officers for verification.
The Grand Minister of Education,
the Grand Minister of War,
and the Grand Minister of Works, with the achievements of all officials,
present to the Son of Heaven for verification,
and all officials fast and receive verification.
After this,
the elderly are honored and farmers are rewarded,
the year's affairs are concluded,
and the state's expenditures are regulated.
5.47 In all cases of caring for the elderly:
the Yǒuyú clan used the banquet rites,
the Xiàhòu clan used the feast rites,
the Yīn people used the food rites,
and the Zhōu people refined and combined them all.
At fifty, one is cared for in the local community;
at sixty, in the state;
at seventy, in the academy,
extending to the feudal lords.
5.48 At eighty, one receives the ruler's commands with a bow,
kneeling once and touching the ground twice,
and the blind are treated similarly.
At ninety, someone is sent to receive on their behalf.
At fifty, one has different grains;
at sixty, meat is kept overnight;
at seventy, a second meal is provided;
at eighty, delicacies are constant;
at ninety,
food and drink are never away from the bedside,
and meals and drinks follow them even on outings.
At sixty, funeral preparations are made yearly;
at seventy, seasonally;
at eighty, monthly;
at ninety, daily maintenance is done,
only the shroud, coverings, quilt, and burial cloths
are made after death.
At fifty, one begins to decline,
at sixty, one is not satisfied without meat,
at seventy, not warm without silk,
at eighty, not warm without another person,
at ninety,
even with someone, one is not warm.
At fifty, one uses a staff at home;
at sixty, in the community;
at seventy, in the state;
at eighty, at court;
for those ninety,
if the Son of Heaven wishes to consult them,
he goes to their residence,
bringing delicacies along.
At seventy, one does not wait at court;
at eighty, one is visited monthly to check on well-being;
at ninety, daily provisions are provided.
At fifty, one is exempt from labor services;
at sixty, from military duties;
at seventy, from entertaining guests;
at eighty, one is not involved in mourning rites.
At fifty, one may receive rank;
at sixty, one does not attend studies in person;
at seventy, one retires from governance.
Only the mourning garments of hemp are worn for bereavement.
5.49 The Yǒuyú clan supported the state elders at the Upper School,
and supported the common elders at the Lower School.
The Xiàhòu clan supported the state elders at the Eastern Academy,
and supported the common elders at the Western Academy.
The Yīn people supported the state elders at the Right School,
and supported the common elders at the Left School.
The Zhōu people supported the state elders at the Eastern Jiāo,
and supported the common elders at the Yúxiáng:
the Yúxiáng was located in the western suburbs of the capital.
The Yǒuyú clan wore the huáng headdress for sacrifices,
and deep robes for supporting the elderly.
The Xiàhòu clan wore the shōu headdress for sacrifices,
and informal robes for supporting the elderly.
The Yīn people wore the xǔ headdress for sacrifices,
and plain white robes for supporting the elderly.
The Zhōu people wore the miǎn crown for sacrifices,
and black robes for supporting the elderly.
In all three dynasties, the support of the elderly was based on age.
For those eighty years old, one son was exempt from government service;
for those ninety years old, their entire household was exempt from government service;
for the disabled who could not be cared for without assistance,
one person was exempt from government service.
For the mourning of parents,
three years were exempt from government service.
For the mourning of zīcuī and dàgōng,
three months were exempt from government service.
When moving to another feudal state,
three months were exempt from government service.
When moving from another feudal state to one's home,
one year was exempt from government service.
5.50 Those who are young and fatherless are called orphans,
those who are old and childless are called the solitary,
those who are old and wifeless are called the widowers,
those who are old and husbandless are called the widows.
These four types of people
are the destitute and helpless among the people of heaven,
and all receive regular provisions.
5.51 The mute, deaf, lame,
crippled, amputated, dwarfs, and various artisans,
are each provided for according to their abilities.
5.52 On the roads:
men keep to the right,
women keep to the left,
and carriages travel in the center.
When walking with one's father's peers, follow behind;
when walking with one's elder brothers' peers, walk in a V-formation;
friends do not overtake each other.
Light burdens are shared,
heavy burdens are divided,
the gray-haired do not carry loads.
Noble elders do not walk on foot,
common elders do not eat without meat.
5.53 Great officers do not borrow sacrificial vessels.
If sacrificial vessels are not yet completed,
they do not make vessels for daily use.
5.54 An area of one lǐ square yields nine hundred mǔ of farmland.
An area of ten lǐ square,
is equivalent to one hundred areas of one lǐ square,
yielding ninety thousand mǔ of farmland.
An area of one hundred lǐ square,
is equivalent to one hundred areas of ten lǐ square,
yielding nine hundred million mǔ of farmland.
An area of one thousand lǐ square,
is equivalent to one hundred areas of one hundred lǐ square,
yielding nine trillion mǔ of farmland.
5.55 From Héngshān to the Southern River,
it is nearly a thousand lǐ.
From the Southern River to the Jiāng,
it is nearly a thousand lǐ.
From the Jiāng to Héngshān,
it is over a thousand lǐ.
From the Eastern River to the Eastern Sea,
it is over a thousand lǐ.
From the Eastern River to the Western River,
it is nearly a thousand lǐ,
from the Western River to the Liúshā,
it is over a thousand lǐ.
To the west, it does not extend beyond the Liúshā,
to the south, it does not extend beyond Héngshān,
to the east, it does not reach the Eastern Sea,
to the north, it does not extend beyond Héngshān,
within the Four Seas altogether,
taking the longer and shorter distances and making them even,
it is three thousand lǐ square,
yielding eight hundred and one trillion mǔ of farmland.
An area of one hundred lǐ square,
yields nine hundred million mǔ:
deducting mountains, forests,
rivers, marshes, ditches,
city walls, palaces, roads, and lanes,
one-third is removed,
leaving six hundred million mǔ.
5.56 In ancient times, a step was eight Zhōu chǐ,
now a step is six Zhōu chǐ and four cùn.
Ancient one hundred mǔ,
is equivalent to one hundred forty-six mǔ and thirty steps of present eastern fields.
Ancient one hundred lǐ,
is equivalent to one hundred twenty-one lǐ, sixty steps, four chǐ, and two cùn and two fēn of today.
5.57 An area of one thousand lǐ square,
is equivalent to one hundred areas of one hundred lǐ square.
Enfeoff thirty states of one hundred lǐ square,
the remainder is seventy areas of one hundred lǐ square.
Also enfeoff sixty states of seventy lǐ square,
-- equivalent to twenty-nine areas of one hundred lǐ square,
and forty areas of ten lǐ square.
The remainder is forty areas of one hundred lǐ square,
and sixty areas of ten lǐ square;
also enfeoff one hundred twenty states of fifty lǐ square,
-- equivalent to thirty areas of one hundred lǐ square,
-- the remainder,
is ten areas of one hundred lǐ square,
and sixty areas of ten lǐ square.
Famous mountains and great marshes are not enfeoffed,
the remainder becomes attached territories and vacant land.
Feudal lords who have merit,
take from the vacant land for their stipends;
those whose lands are reduced,
return them to the vacant land.
Within the Son of Heaven's domain:
an area of one thousand lǐ square is equivalent to one hundred areas of one hundred lǐ square.
Enfeoff nine areas of one hundred lǐ square,
the remainder is ninety-one areas of one hundred lǐ square.
Also enfeoff twenty-one areas of seventy lǐ square,
-- equivalent to ten areas of one hundred lǐ square,
and twenty-nine areas of ten lǐ square,
-- the remainder,
is eighty areas of one hundred lǐ square,
and seventy-one areas of ten lǐ square.
Also enfeoff sixty-three areas of fifty lǐ square,
-- equivalent to fifteen areas of one hundred lǐ square,
and seventy-five areas of ten lǐ square,
-- the remainder
is sixty-four areas of one hundred lǐ square,
and ninety-six areas of ten lǐ square.
5.58 The lower-ranking officers of feudal lords have stipends supporting nine people,
middle-ranking officers support eighteen people,
upper-ranking officers support thirty-six people.
Lower grand masters support seventy-two people,
ministers support two hundred eighty-eight people.
The ruler supports two thousand eight hundred eighty people.
The ministers of secondary states support two hundred sixteen people,
the ruler supports two thousand one hundred sixty people.
The ministers of small states support one hundred forty-four people,
the ruler supports one thousand four hundred forty people.
The ministers of secondary states,
appointed by their ruler,
are like the ministers of small states.
The grand masters of the Son of Heaven who serve as three supervisors,
supervising the states of feudal lords,
their stipends are equivalent to the ministers of feudal lords,
their rank is equivalent to the rulers of secondary states,
their stipends are taken from the lands of the regional chiefs.
The regional chiefs, when attending court to see the Son of Heaven,
all have bath towns within the Son of Heaven's domain,
equivalent to the primary officers.
The heirs of feudal lords inherit the state,
grand masters do not inherit rank.
Appointments are made based on virtue,
ranks are conferred based on merit,
if not yet granted a rank,
they are treated as the primary officers of the Son of Heaven,
to rule their state.
The grand masters of feudal lords,
do not inherit rank and stipend.
5.59 The six rites:
capping, wedding, mourning, sacrifice, district, and mutual visits.
The seven teachings:
father and son, elder and younger brothers,
husband and wife, ruler and minister,
elder and younger, friends, and host and guest.
The eight administrative affairs:
food and drink, clothing,
work and crafts, distinctions and differences,
standards, capacities, numbers, and regulations.
6.1 In the first month of spring,
the sun is in the constellation Yíngshì,
