at dusk the constellation Shēn is in the meridian,
at dawn the constellation Wěi is in the meridian.
Its days are Jiǎ and Yǐ.
Its emperor is Dàhào,
its spirit is Gōumáng.
Its creatures are the scaly.
Its musical note is Jué.
The pitch pipe is Dàcù.
Its number is eight.
Its flavor is sour,
its odor is pungent.
Its sacrifice is to the household deity,
offering the spleen first.
6.2 The east wind thaws the ice,
hibernating insects begin to stir,
fish rise to the ice,
otters offer fish,
wild geese arrive.
6.3 The Son of Heaven resides in the left chamber of Qīngyáng.
He rides in a carriage with bells,
drawn by azure dragons,
bearing a blue banner,
dressed in blue robes,
and wearing azure jade.
He eats wheat and mutton,
and his vessels are open and well-ventilated.
6.4 In this month,
the Beginning of Spring is established.
Three days before the Beginning of Spring,
the Grand Historian reports to the Son of Heaven, saying:
"On such-and-such a day, the Beginning of Spring arrives,
and the abundant virtue resides in wood."
The Son of Heaven then fasts.
On the day of the Beginning of Spring,
the Son of Heaven personally leads the Three Dukes, Nine Ministers, feudal lords, and high officials
to welcome spring in the eastern suburbs.
Upon returning,
he rewards the dukes, ministers, feudal lords, and high officials at court.
6.5 He orders the prime minister to promulgate virtuous decrees and harmonize ordinances,
to distribute blessings and bestow favors,
reaching down to the myriad people.
Rewards and gifts are thus carried out,
with nothing inappropriate.
6.6 He then orders the Grand Historian to uphold the statutes and uphold the laws,
overseeing the movements of the heavens, sun, moon, and stars,
ensuring that the lodgings and separations are not neglected,
and not losing the regular order,
taking the beginning as the constant standard.
6.7 In this month,
the Son of Heaven, on the first day, prays for grain to the Supreme Deity.
He then selects an auspicious day,
personally loads the plow and share,
places them among the attendants and guards,
leads the Three Dukes, Nine Ministers, feudal lords, and high officials,
and personally plows the imperial field.
The Son of Heaven pushes the plow three times,
the dukes five times,
and the ministers and feudal lords nine times.
Upon returning,
he holds a cup in the great chamber,
with the Three Dukes, Nine Ministers, feudal lords, and high officials all in attendance,
and it is called the "feast of toil."
6.8 In this month,
the heavenly qi descends,
the earthly qi rises,
heaven and earth harmonize and unite,
and plants and trees begin to sprout.
The king orders the dissemination of agricultural affairs,
commanding the field officers to reside in the eastern suburbs,
all to repair the boundaries,
and carefully align the paths and waterways.
They should carefully observe the hills and mounds,
slopes and dangerous places, plains and lowlands,
to determine what the land is suitable for,
and what grains should be planted,
in order to instruct and guide the people,
and must do so personally.
Once the field affairs are put in order,
and standards and straightness are first established,
the farmers will not be confused.
6.9 In this month,
the Director of Music is ordered to enter the school to teach dancing.
The sacrificial codes are then revised.
Sacrifices are ordered to the mountains, forests, rivers, and marshes,
and female animals are not to be used as offerings.
6.10 The cutting of trees is prohibited.
Nests should not be overturned,
and infant insects,
fetuses, young animals, or flying birds should not be killed.
Fawns and eggs should not be taken.
Large crowds should not be gathered,
and city walls should not be built.
Bones and carcasses should be buried.
6.11 In this month,
armies should not be raised,
for raising armies will surely bring heavenly calamity.
Let no armed conflict arise,
and certainly not begin from us.
Do not alter the way of heaven,
do not disrupt the principles of earth,
and do not confuse the order of humanity.
6.12 If the ordinances of summer are carried out in the first month of spring,
then wind and rain will be untimely,
plants and trees will wither early,
and the state will frequently experience fear.
If the ordinances of autumn are carried out, then the people will suffer great epidemics,
violent winds and heavy rains will arrive together,
and weeds like lí, yǒu, péng, and hāo will flourish together.
If the ordinances of winter are carried out, then floods will cause damage,
frost and snow will be severe,
and the first plantings will not yield.
6.13 In the second month of spring,
the sun is in the constellation Kuí,
at dusk the constellation Hú is in the center,
and at dawn the constellation Jiàn is in the center.
Its days are Jiǎ and Yǐ,
its emperor is Tàihào,
its spirit is Gōumáng.
Its creatures are the scaly.
Its musical note is Jué,
and the pitch pipe is Jiázhōng.
Its number is eight.
Its flavor is sour,
its odor is rank,
its sacrifice is to the door,
and the spleen is offered first.
6.14 The rains begin,
peach trees begin to bloom,
the golden oriole sings,
and eagles transform into doves.
6.15 The Son of Heaven resides in the great hall of Qīngyáng,
rides in a carriage with bells,
drawn by azure dragons,
bearing a blue banner,
dressed in blue robes,
and wearing azure jade.
He eats wheat and mutton.
His vessels are open and well-ventilated.
In this month,
sprouts are nurtured,
the young are cared for,
and orphans are supported.
An auspicious day is chosen,
and the people are ordered to perform the shè sacrifice.
Officials are ordered to inspect the prisons,
remove fetters and handcuffs,
cease floggings,
and halt lawsuits.
6.16 In this month,
the dark birds arrive.
On the day of their arrival,
a great sacrifice is offered to the Gāoméi with a tàiláo.
The Son of Heaven goes in person,
and the empress leads the nine concubines to attend.
Then, the women favored by the Son of Heaven are honored,
adorned with bow covers,
and presented with bows and arrows,
before the Gāoméi.
6.17 In this month,
day and night are equal.
Thunder then begins to sound,
lightning first appears,
hibernating insects all stir,
and they open their burrows to emerge.
Three days before the thunder,
bells are shaken to warn the myriad people, saying:
"Thunder is about to sound;
those who do not guard their behavior
will give birth to children with defects,
and there will surely be misfortune and disaster."
When day and night are equal,
measures and volumes are standardized,
steelyards and weights are balanced,
pecks and bushels are calibrated,
and scales and measures are corrected.
6.18 In this month,
farmers take a brief rest.
Then, doors and gates are repaired,
and the ancestral temples are fully prepared.
No major undertakings should be initiated
to interfere with agricultural work.
In this month,
rivers and marshes should not be drained,
ponds and pools should not be dried up,
and mountains and forests should not be burned.
6.19 The Son of Heaven then offers a lamb and opens the ice,
first presenting it in the ancestral temple.
6.20 On the first Dīng day,
the Director of Music is ordered to practice dancing,
and vegetable offerings are presented.
The Son of Heaven then leads the Three Dukes, Nine Ministers, feudal lords, and high officials to personally observe it.
On the second Dīng day,
the Director of Music is again ordered to enter the school to practice music.
6.21 In this month,
sacrifices do not use live animals,
but use jade tablets and discs,
and substitute hides and silks.
6.22 If the ordinances of autumn are carried out in the second month of spring,
then the state will suffer great floods,
cold air will arrive in full force,
and enemy troops will come to attack.
If the ordinances of winter are carried out,
then the yang energy will not prevail,
the wheat will not ripen,
and the people will frequently plunder each other.
If the ordinances of summer are carried out,
then the state will suffer great drought,
warm air will arrive early,
and insects and pests will cause harm.
6.23 In the third month of spring,
the sun is in the constellation Wèi,
at dusk the Seven Stars are at the zenith,
at dawn the Oxherd is at the zenith.
Its days are Jiǎ and Yǐ.
Its emperor is Dà Hào,
its deity is Gōu Máng.
Its creatures are scaly.
Its musical note is Jué,
the pitch-pipe is Gū Xiǎn.
Its number is eight.
Its flavor is sour,
its odor is rank.
Its sacrifice is to the door,
and the spleen is offered first.
6.24 The paulownia begins to bloom,
field mice transform into quails,
rainbows begin to appear,
duckweed begins to grow.
6.25 The Son of Heaven resides in the right chamber of the Qīng Yáng Hall,
rides in a carriage with bells,
drives a blue dragon,
carries a blue banner,
wears blue robes,
and adorns himself with blue jade.
He eats wheat and mutton.
His vessels are open and penetrating.
6.26 In this month,
the Son of Heaven offers the Jú Yī garment to the former emperors.
He orders the boat master to inspect the boats,
five inspections and five reports.
Only when it is reported that "the boats are fully prepared" to the Son of Heaven,
does the Son of Heaven begin to ride in a boat.
He offers sturgeon in the ancestral temple,
and then prays for the grain of the wheat.
6.27 In this month,
the vital energy is at its peak,
the yang energy is dispersing,
all that is bent emerges,
all that is sprouting reaches forth.
One should not restrain it.
The Son of Heaven spreads virtue and bestows kindness,
orders the officials to open the granaries,
give to the poor,
relieve the destitute,
open the treasuries,
bring out silks and cloth,
and aid all under heaven.
He encourages the feudal lords,
invites famous scholars,
and honors the worthy.
6.28 In this month,
he orders the Minister of Works:
"The seasonal rains are about to fall,
water below will rise upward,
tour the cities and towns,
inspect the fields and plains all around,
repair and strengthen the dikes and defenses,
clear and open the ditches and canals,
open up the roads,
so that there are no obstructions.
For hunting, traps, nets,
snares, poisoned baits for animals,
must not be taken out of the nine gates."
6.29 In this month,
order the field officials not to cut down mulberry or paper mulberry trees.
The turtledove shakes its feathers,
the hoopoe descends upon the mulberry trees.
Prepare the frames, stands, mats, and baskets.
The queen and consorts fast,
personally face east and tend to the mulberry trees.
Forbid women from adorning themselves,
reduce their duties to encourage sericulture.
When the silkworm work is completed,
divide the cocoons, weigh the silk, and assess the work,
to supply garments for the suburban and ancestral temples,
and none dare be lazy.
In this month,
order the master craftsmen to command the various artisans to inspect the stores of the five warehouses:
metals and iron,
hides, sinews,
horns and teeth,
feathers, arrows, and shafts,
fats, glues, cinnabar, and lacquer,
so that none are of poor quality.
6.30 All artisans are to be managed,
supervisors daily give orders;
do not go against the season,
do not create extravagant crafts to confuse the ruler's mind.
6.31 At the end of this month,
choose an auspicious day,
for a grand concert,
the Son of Heaven leads the Three Dukes, Nine Ministers, feudal lords, and high officials to personally attend it.
6.32 In this month,
bring together the breeding oxen and stallions,
and release the females to pasture.
For sacrificial animals,
foals and calves,
record them,
and write down their numbers.
6.33 Order the exorcism in the state,
dismember sacrifices at the nine gates to ward off evil,
to end the spring energy.
6.34 If in the third month of spring, the commands of winter are carried out,
then cold energy will frequently arise,
plants and trees will wither,
and the state will experience great fear.
If the commands of summer are carried out,
then the people will suffer many diseases and epidemics,
timely rains will not fall,
and the mountains and forests will yield no harvest.
If the commands of autumn are carried out,
then the sky will often be overcast,
excessive rains will fall early,
and weapons and armor will arise together.
6.35 In the first month of summer,
the sun is in the constellation Bì,
at dusk the Wings are at the zenith,
at dawn the Weaving Maiden is at the zenith.
Its days are Bǐng and Dīng.
Its emperor is Yán Dì,
its deity is Zhù Róng.
Its creatures are feathered.
Its musical note is Zhǐ,
the pitch-pipe is Zhōng Lǚ.
Its number is seven.
Its flavor is bitter,
its odor is scorched.
Its sacrifice is to the stove,
and the lung is offered first.
The mole crickets and frogs croak,
earthworms emerge,
the royal melon grows,
and the bitter vegetable blooms.
6.36 The Son of Heaven resides in the left chamber of the Ming Táng,
rides in a red carriage,
drives a red horse,
carries a red banner,
wears red robes,
and adorns himself with red jade.
He eats beans and chicken.
His vessels are tall and coarse.
6.37 In this month,
summer begins.
Three days before the beginning of summer,
the Grand Historian reports to the Son of Heaven:
"On such a day summer begins,
the abundant virtue is in fire."
The Son of Heaven then fasts.
On the day of the beginning of summer,
the Son of Heaven personally leads the Three Dukes, Nine Ministers, and high officials
to welcome summer in the southern suburb.
Upon returning,
he bestows rewards,
enfeoffs feudal lords.
Congratulations and gifts are then distributed,
and all are joyful.
6.38 Then he orders the music master
to practice and harmonize rituals and music.
Orders the Grand Commandant
to recommend the outstanding and talented,
promote the virtuous and good,
elevate the tall and strong,
confer ranks and distribute emoluments,
ensuring they match their positions.
In this month,
as growth continues and height increases,
do not allow any destruction,
do not start earthworks,
do not mobilize the masses,
do not cut down large trees.
In this month,
the Son of Heaven begins to wear fine linen.
Order the field officials to go out to the fields and plains,
to encourage the farmers and urge the people on behalf of the Son of Heaven,
so that none miss the season.
6.39 Order the Minister of Education to tour the counties and borders,
command the farmers to work diligently,
and not to rest in the capital.
In this month,
drive away beasts to prevent harm to the five grains,
and do not engage in large-scale hunting.
The farmers then present the wheat,
the Son of Heaven tastes the wheat with pork,
first offering it in the ancestral temple.
In this month,
gather and store all kinds of medicines.
The delicate grasses die,
the wheat harvest arrives.
Settle light penalties,
decide minor offenses,
and release those in light detention.
After the silkworm affairs are concluded,
the queen and consorts present the cocoons.
Then the cocoon tax is collected,
based on the mulberry trees as a standard,
uniform for noble and commoner, young and old alike,
to supply robes for suburban and ancestral temple ceremonies.
6.40 In this month,
the Son of Heaven partakes of the fermented spring wine,
with ritual music.
6.41 If autumn ordinances are practiced in early summer,
bitter rains will frequently come,
the five grains will not flourish,
and people from the four borders will retreat into fortresses.
If winter ordinances are practiced,
plants and trees will wither early,
followed by great floods,
damaging the city walls.
If spring ordinances are practiced,
locusts will cause disasters,
violent winds will arrive,
and flowering grasses will not bear fruit.
6.42 In the mid-summer month,
the sun is in Jǐng (Well constellation),
at dusk the Kàng constellation is centered,
at dawn the Wēi constellation is centered.
Its days are Bǐng-Dīng.
Its emperor is Yándì,
its spirit is Zhùróng.
Its creatures are the feathered,
its musical note is Zhǐ,
the pitch pipe is Ruíbīn.
Its number is seven.
Its flavor is bitter,
its odor is scorched,
its sacrifice is to the hearth,
offering the lungs first.
6.43 Slight heat arrives,
praying mantises are born.
The shrike begins to sing,
the mockingbird becomes silent.
6.44 The Son of Heaven resides in the Grand Chamber of the Bright Hall,
rides in a vermilion carriage,
driven by chestnut-red horses,
bearing vermilion banners,
dressed in vermilion robes,
adorned with red jade,
eating beans and chicken.
His vessels are tall and coarse.
He nurtures the strong and robust.
6.45 In this month,
the music masters are ordered to repair the táo, pí, and drums,
tune the qín, sè, guǎn, and xiāo,
prepare the shields, battle-axes, dagger-axes, and feathers,
adjust the yú, shēng, chí, and huáng,
and set the bells, qìng, zhù, and yǔ in order.
6.46 Officials are ordered to pray and sacrifice to the mountains, rivers, and all sources for the people,
perform the great rain sacrifice to the emperor,
using grand music.
Then all districts are ordered
to conduct rain sacrifices to the hundred rulers and ministers who benefited the people,
to pray for grain harvest.
6.47 Farmers present the millet.
In this month,
the Son of Heaven tastes the millet with young chicken,
accompanied by cherries,
first offering them in the ancestral temple.
6.48 People are ordered not to cut indigo for dyeing,
not to burn ashes,
not to sun cloth.
City gates and village gates are not to be closed,
passes and markets are not to be searched.
Prisoners in heavy chains are relieved,
and their food is increased.
6.49 Mares in pasture are separated from the herd,
then stallions are tethered,
and horse administration is proclaimed.
6.50 In this month,
the day reaches its longest,
yīn and yáng contend,
death and life divide.
The gentleman fasts and abstains,
must cover his body when staying indoors,
and not be agitated.
He stops music and beauty,
and none should be presented to him.
He lightens his flavors,
not seeking harmony.
He moderates his desires,
stabilizes his heart and energy,
all officials attend quietly to affairs without punishments,
to settle what the calm yīn accomplishes.
6.51 Deer antlers shed,
cicadas begin to sing.
Pinellia grows,
hibiscus blooms.
6.52 In this month,
do not use fire in the southern direction.
One may reside in high, bright places,
may gaze into the distance,
may ascend hills and mounds,
may stay in towers and pavilions.
6.53 If winter ordinances are practiced in mid-summer,
hail and frost will damage the grains,
roads will become impassable,
and violent soldiers will arrive.
If spring ordinances are practiced,
the five grains will ripen late,
hundred caterpillars will rise in season,
and the state will suffer famine.
If autumn ordinances are practiced,
plants and trees will wither and fall,
fruits will mature early,
and the people will suffer from epidemics.
6.54 In the late summer month,
the sun is in Liǔ,
at dusk the Huǒ constellation is centered,
at dawn the Kuí constellation is centered.
Its days are Bǐng-Dīng.
Its emperor is Yándì,
its spirit is Zhùróng.
Its creatures are the feathered.
Its musical note is Zhǐ,
the pitch pipe is Línzhōng.
Its number is seven.
Its flavor is bitter,
its odor is scorched.
Its sacrifice is to the hearth,
offering the lungs first.
Warm winds begin to arrive,
crickets dwell in the walls,
young eagles learn to fly,
and rotten grass turns into fireflies.
6.55 The Son of Heaven resides in the right chamber of the Bright Hall,
rides in a vermilion carriage,
driven by chestnut-red horses,
bearing vermilion banners,
dressed in vermilion robes,
adorned with red jade.
He eats beans and chicken,
his vessels are tall and coarse.
6.56 Fishing masters are ordered to hunt jiaolong and capture tuó,
present turtles and capture yuán.
Marsh men are ordered to deliver timber and reeds.
6.57 In this month,
the four inspectors are ordered to gather the designated fodder from all districts,
to nourish the sacrificial animals.
The people are ordered to all exert their strength,
to supply the spirits of August Heaven, Supreme Deity, famous mountains, great rivers, and the four directions,
to sacrifice to the spirits of the ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain,
thereby seeking blessings for the people.
6.58 In this month,
the women officials are ordered to dye the silks,
the embroidered patterns and designs
must follow the ancient regulations,
without any error or deviation.
Black, yellow, green, and red
all must be of genuine quality,
none daring to be deceitful or false,
to supply robes for suburban and ancestral temple sacrifices,
to make banners and insignia,
to distinguish the measures of rank and supply for noble and commoner.
6.59 In this month,
as trees are at their peak of growth,
the forest keepers are ordered to inspect the mountains and trees,
with no felling allowed.
Earthworks should not be initiated,
feudal lords should not be assembled,
troops and masses should not be mobilized,
major undertakings should not be launched,
so as not to disturb the nurturing energy.
Do not issue orders and wait,
thereby hindering the affairs of Shénnóng.
Floodwaters are abundant and flourishing,
Shénnóng is about to achieve his work,
launching major undertakings will bring heavenly calamities.
6.60 In this month,
the soil is moist and the heat is oppressive,
heavy rains fall seasonally,
burning weeds and applying water,
beneficial for killing grasses,
as if with hot water.
It can be used to manure the fields,
to improve the soil strength.
6.61 If spring ordinances are practiced in late summer,
grain kernels will fall prematurely,
the state will have much wind-induced coughing,
and the people will migrate.
If autumn ordinances are practiced,
hills and marshes will flood,
crops will not ripen,
and there will be many childbirth disasters.
If winter ordinances are practiced,
wind and cold will be untimely,
hawks and falcons will turn fierce early,
and people from the four borders will retreat into fortresses.
6.62 The center belongs to earth.
Its days are Wù-Jǐ,
its emperor is Huángdì,
its spirit is Hòutǔ.
Its creatures are the naked ones,
its musical note is gōng,
the pitch-pipe is that of Huángzhōng's gōng.
Its number is five.
Its flavor is sweet,
its odor is fragrant.
Its sacrifice is to the center of the house,
offering the heart first.
The Son of Heaven resides in the great hall's great chamber.
He rides in the great carriage,
drives yellow-maned horses,
bears a yellow banner,
wears yellow robes,
and adorns himself with yellow jade.
He eats millet and beef.
His vessels are round and capacious.
6.63 In the first month of autumn,
the sun is in Yì,
at dusk Jiànxīng is in the center,
at dawn Bì is in the center.
Its days are Gēng and Xīn.
Its emperor is Shàohào,
its deity is Rùshōu.
Its creatures are the hairy ones.
Its musical note is shāng,
the pitch-pipe is Yízé.
Its number is nine.
Its flavor is pungent,
its odor is rank.
Its sacrifice is to the door,
offering the liver first.
6.64 Cool winds arrive,
white dew descends,
cold cicadas chirp.
Eagles then sacrifice birds,
and executions begin.
6.65 The Son of Heaven resides in the left apartment of Zǒngzhāng,
rides in the war carriage,
drives white-maned horses,
bears a white banner,
wears white robes,
and adorns himself with white jade.
He eats hemp and dog meat,
his vessels are angular and deep.
6.66 In this month,
autumn is established.
Three days before the establishment of autumn,
the Grand Historian informs the Son of Heaven, saying:
"On such a day, autumn is established,
the abundant virtue is in metal."
The Son of Heaven then fasts.
On the day of establishing autumn,
the Son of Heaven personally leads the Three Dukes, Nine Ministers, feudal lords, and high officials
to welcome autumn in the western suburb.
Upon returning,
he rewards military commanders and warriors at court.
The Son of Heaven then orders the generals
to select soldiers, sharpen weapons,
train the brave and talented,
appoint exclusively those with merit,
to punish the unrighteous.
He interrogates and executes the violent and arrogant,
to clarify likes and dislikes,
and pacify those distant regions.
In this month,
officials are ordered to revise laws and institutions,
repair prisons,
prepare fetters and handcuffs,
prohibit villainy,
be cautious of crimes and evils,
and strive to capture and detain.
Order the jailers to inspect wounds,
examine injuries,
observe fractures,
and review verdicts.
In adjudicating lawsuits,
they must be just and fair.
Execute the guilty,
and strictly enforce punishments.
Heaven and Earth begin to turn severe,
and one must not be indulgent.
In this month,
farmers present their grain.
The Son of Heaven tastes the new harvest,
first offering it in the ancestral temple.
He orders all officials
to begin gathering,
complete dikes and embankments,
carefully block up leaks,
to prepare for floods.
Repair palaces and houses,
mend walls and enclosures,
and fortify city walls.
In this month,
do not enfeoff feudal lords,
or appoint high officials.
Do not grant lands,
send great envoys,
or distribute large sums of money.
6.67 If in the first month of autumn the ordinances of winter are practiced,
then Yin energy will greatly prevail,
armored insects will damage the grain,
and soldiers will come.
If the ordinances of spring are practiced,
then the state will suffer drought,
Yang energy will return,
and the five grains will not bear fruit.
If the ordinances of summer are practiced,
then the state will have many fires.
Cold and heat will be unregulated,
and the people will suffer from malaria.
6.68 In the second month of autumn,
the sun is in Jiǎo,
at dusk Qiānniú is in the center,
at dawn Zīxī is in the center.
Its days are Gēng and Xīn,
its emperor is Shàohào,
its deity is Rùshōu.
Its creatures are the hairy ones.
Its musical note is shāng,
the pitch-pipe is Nánlǚ.
Its number is nine.
Its flavor is pungent,
its odor is rank.
Its sacrifice is to the door,
offering the liver first.
6.69 Fierce winds arrive,
wild geese come,
swallows return.
Flocks of birds store food.
6.70 The Son of Heaven resides in the great hall of Zǒngzhāng,
rides in the war carriage,
drives white-maned horses,
bears a white banner,
wears white robes,
and adorns himself with white jade.
He eats hemp and dog meat.
His vessels are angular and deep.
6.71 In this month,
care for the aged and decrepit,
provide them with stools and canes,
and distribute congee and food.
6.72 Then order the director of garments
to prepare all robes and gowns,
with constant patterns and embroideries,
regulations for large and small,
measures for short and long.
Clothing has its measures,
must follow the old ways,
caps and sashes have their constants.
6.73 Then order the officials
to strictly enforce all punishments,
executions must be appropriate,
with no injustice or bending.
Injustice and bending are inappropriate,
and one will suffer retribution.
6.74 In this month,
order the stewards and invocators
to inspect the sacrificial animals,
check their completeness,
examine their feed,
observe their fatness or leanness,
and scrutinize their colors.
They must compare types,
measure sizes,
check lengths,
all meeting the standard.
When these five are fully appropriate,
the Supreme Deity will enjoy them.
6.75 The Son of Heaven then performs the exorcism,
to express the autumn energy.
6.76 With dogs, he tastes the hemp,
first offering it in the ancestral temple.
6.77 In this month,
one may build city walls,
establish capitals and towns,
dig cellars and pits,
and repair granaries.
6.78 Then order the officials
to urge the people to gather,
strive to store vegetables,
and accumulate much.
Encourage the planting of wheat,
do not miss the season.
Those who miss the season,
will be punished without doubt.
6.79 In this month,
day and night are equal,
thunder begins to cease.
Hibernating insects seal their burrows,
the killing energy gradually strengthens,
Yang energy daily declines,
and water begins to dry up.
6.80 When day and night are equal,
then standardize measures and volumes,
balance scales and weights,
correct dàn and shí,
and regulate dǒu and yǒng.
In this month,
the tariffs at passes and markets are lightened,
merchants and travelers are attracted,
goods and valuables are collected,
to facilitate the people's affairs.
People from all directions gather,
even from distant villages all arrive,
then wealth is not scarce,
the superiors have no lack of supplies,
and all affairs are accomplished.
6.81 In all major undertakings,
do not go against the numbers of heaven,
but must follow its seasons,
carefully aligning with their categories.
6.82 If in mid-autumn the ordinances of spring are practiced,
then autumn rains do not fall,
plants and trees flourish and bloom,
and the state will have fears.
If summer ordinances are practiced,
then the state will suffer drought,
hibernating insects do not hide,
and the five grains grow again.
If winter ordinances are practiced,
then wind disasters frequently arise,
thunder ceases early,
and plants and trees die prematurely.
6.83 In the month of late autumn,
the sun is in the constellation Fáng,
at dusk the constellation Xū is at the zenith,
at dawn the constellation Liǔ is at the zenith.
Its days are Gēng and Xīn.
Its emperor is Shàohào,
its deity is Rùshōu.
Its animals are the hairy ones,
its musical note is Shāng,
the pitch-pipe is Wúyì.
Its number is nine.
Its flavor is pungent,
its odor is fishy.
Its sacrifice is at the gate,
offering the liver first.
6.84 The wild geese arrive as guests.
Sparrows enter the great waters and become clams.
Chrysanthemums have yellow flowers,
jackals sacrifice beasts and kill birds.
6.85 The Son of Heaven resides in the right chamber of the Zǒngzhāng Hall,
rides in a war chariot,
drives white-maned horses,
carries white banners,
wears white clothes,
and adorns himself with white jade.
He eats hemp and dog meat,
his vessels are angular and deep.
6.86 In this month,
orders and commands are strictly enforced.
All officials, high and low, are commanded to focus on internal affairs,
to align with the storage of heaven and earth,
with nothing unnecessarily expended.
6.87 Then the chief minister is ordered,
to record the essentials of the five grains,
storing the harvest from the imperial fields in the divine granaries,
with reverence and diligence.
In this month,
frost begins to descend,
and all artisans rest.
6.88 The officials are then commanded:
"The cold air is arriving altogether,
the people's strength cannot endure it,
let them all enter their homes."
6.89 On the first Dīng day,
the music master is ordered to enter the school to practice wind instruments.
6.90 In this month,
the great sacrifice to the emperor is performed, and the tasting sacrifice,
reporting the readiness of the sacrificial animals to the Son of Heaven.
6.91 Feudal lords are assembled,
all districts are regulated,
to receive the calendar for the coming year,
along with the laws on the轻重 of taxes levied by the feudal lords on the people,
the amounts of tributes,
based on distance and the suitability of the land,
to supply the affairs of the suburban and ancestral temples,
with no partiality.
6.92 In this month,
the Son of Heaven instructs in hunting,
to practice the five weapons,
and promulgates horse administration.
The charioteers and seven grooms are all commanded to harness the chariots,
bearing banners and flags,
assigning vehicles according to rank,
arranged in order outside the screen.
The Minister of Education, with his baton inserted,
faces north to administer the oath.
The Son of Heaven, in stern attire,
grasps his bow and arrows to hunt,
ordering the chief priest to sacrifice the game to the four directions.
6.93 In this month,
plants and trees turn yellow and fall,
and firewood is cut to make charcoal.
6.94 Hibernating insects all crouch in their burrows,
sealing their entrances.
Then lawsuits and punishments are expedited,
with no guilty left unaddressed.
Emoluments and ranks that are inappropriate,
and provisions that are unsuitable, are withdrawn.
6.95 In this month,
the Son of Heaven tastes the new rice with dog meat,
first offering it in the ancestral temple.
6.96 If in late autumn summer ordinances are practiced,
then the state will have great floods,
winter stores will spoil and fail,
and the people will mostly suffer from nasal congestion and sneezing.
If winter ordinances are practiced,
then the state will have many robbers and thieves,
the borders will be unsettled,
and the land will be divided.
If spring ordinances are practiced,
then warm winds will arrive,
the people's energy will become lax,
and military campaigns will not cease.
6.97 In the month of early winter,
the sun is in the constellation Wěi,
at dusk the constellation Wēi is at the zenith,
at dawn the constellation Qīxīng is at the zenith.
Its days are Rén and Guǐ.
Its emperor is Zhuānxū,
its deity is Xuánmíng.
Its animals are the shelled ones.
Its musical note is Yǔ,
the pitch-pipe is Yìngzhōng.
Its number is six.
Its flavor is salty,
its odor is rotten.
Its sacrifice is at the road,
offering the kidneys first.
6.98 Water begins to freeze,
the ground begins to harden.
Pheasants enter the great waters and become giant clams.
Rainbows hide and are not seen.
6.99 The Son of Heaven resides in the left chamber of the Xuántáng Hall,
rides in a black chariot,
drives iron-black horses,
carries black banners,
wears black clothes,
and adorns himself with dark jade.
He eats millet and pork.
His vessels are large and covered.
6.100 In this month,
winter begins.
Three days before the beginning of winter,
the Grand Historian informs the Son of Heaven, saying:
"On such a day winter begins,
the abundant virtue is in water."
The Son of Heaven then fasts.
On the day of the beginning of winter,
the Son of Heaven personally leads the three ducal ministers, nine high officials, and other officers
to welcome winter at the northern suburb,
upon returning,
rewards those who died in service,
and comforts the orphans and widows.
6.101 In this month,
the Grand Historian is ordered to anoint the tortoise shells and yarrow stalks,
interpret the cracks and signs, examine the omens for good or ill,
to detect any favoritism or cliques,
so that crimes are not concealed.
6.102 In this month,
the Son of Heaven begins to wear fur.
6.103 The officials are commanded:
"The qi of heaven ascends,
the qi of earth descends,
heaven and earth do not communicate,
closing and blocking to form winter."
All officials are ordered to carefully cover and store.
The Minister of Education is ordered to inspect the accumulations,
ensuring nothing is left uncollected.
Repair the city walls,
guard the gates and wards,
mend the bolts and locks,
carefully manage the keys,
secure the seals,
prepare the borders,
strengthen the fortresses,
guard the passes and bridges,
block the bypaths.
6.104 Regulate the mourning rites,
distinguish the burial garments,
examine the thickness of the inner and outer coffins,
the size, height, and depth
of the grave mounds and tombs,
according to the ranks of nobility and commonality.
6.105 In this month,
the master craftsmen are ordered to present their work,
display the sacrificial vessels,
and check against standards and measurements.
Do not create overly clever items that might unsettle the ruler's mind.
Solid workmanship must be the priority.
Artifacts bear the names of their craftsmen,
to verify their integrity.
If the work is not proper,
punishment must be enforced,
to thoroughly investigate the circumstances.
6.106 In this month,
grand drinking ceremonies and sacrificial offerings are held.
6.107 The Son of Heaven prays to the celestial deities for the coming year,
and conducts major sacrifices at the public altars and city gates.
He offers sacrifices to ancestors and the five household gods,
and rewards the farmers with rest.
6.108 The Son of Heaven orders generals and commanders to drill in martial arts,
practicing archery, charioteering, and wrestling.
6.109 In this month,
he commands the water officials and fishing masters
to collect taxes from ponds, springs, and marshes.
None should dare to exploit or oppress the masses,
lest the Son of Heaven incur resentment from below.
If any act in this manner,
they shall be punished without pardon.
6.110 If in early winter the ordinances of spring are practiced,
then the freeze will not be solid,
earthly vapors will rise and escape,
and many people will become refugees.
If summer ordinances are practiced,
the state will suffer frequent storms,
and in the heart of winter, it will not be cold,
with hibernating insects reappearing.
If autumn ordinances are practiced,
then snow and frost will fall untimely,
minor military conflicts will arise frequently,
and territories will be encroached upon.
6.111 In the midwinter month,
the sun is in Dǒu,
at dusk the eastern wall is centered,
at dawn Zhěn is centered.
Its days are Rén and Guǐ.
Its emperor is Zhuānxū,
its deity is Xuánmíng.
Its creatures are the shelled.
Its musical note is Yǔ,
the pitch pipe is Huángzhōng.
Its number is six.
Its flavor is salty,
its odor is putrid.
Its sacrifice is to the wayfarer,
offering the kidneys first.
6.112 Ice grows thicker,
the earth begins to split.
The hé dàn ceases to crow,
tigers begin to mate.
6.113 The Son of Heaven resides in the grand chamber of the dark hall,
rides in a black carriage,
driven by iron-black horses,
bearing dark banners,
dressed in black robes,
and wearing dark jade.
He eats millet and pork,
his vessels are large and covered.
6.114 He attends to matters of death.
He commands the officials:
"Do not undertake earthworks,
carefully avoid uncovering shelters,
do not open houses
or mobilize large crowds,
to secure and close up.
If earthly vapors are released,
it is called opening the chambers of heaven and earth,
then all hibernating creatures will die,
the people will surely suffer plagues,
followed by calamity.
Name this the month of abundance."
6.115 In this month,
he orders the eunuch director
to reiterate palace regulations,
inspect the gates and alleys,
secure the rooms and chambers,
ensuring they are tightly closed.
Reduce women's tasks, prevent extravagance,
even among the noble relatives and close attendants,
none are exempt from these restrictions.
6.116 He then commands the chief brewer,
that glutinous rice must be uniform,
yeast and malt must be timely,
soaking and heating must be clean,
water and springs must be fragrant,
pottery vessels must be excellent,
the fire's intensity must be right,
combining these six elements.
The chief brewer supervises this,
allowing no errors or negligence.
6.117 The Son of Heaven orders officials
to pray and sacrifice to the four seas, great rivers, famous sources, deep marshes, wells, and springs.
6.118 In this month,
if farmers have not stored their harvests,
or if horses, cattle, and livestock are left wandering,
they may be taken without inquiry.
In mountains, forests, marshes, and wetlands,
those who can gather wild vegetables
or hunt game,
the field officials shall guide them.
If there are disputes or seizures,
they shall be punished without pardon.
In this month,
the day is at its shortest.
Yin and Yang contend,
all living things stir.
The noble person fasts and abstains,
staying indoors and covering the body.
The body should be calm,
avoiding music and beauty,
restraining desires.
Pacify the form and nature,
affairs should be tranquil,
awaiting the stabilization of Yin and Yang.
6.119 The yún grass begins to grow,
lì tǐng emerges,
earthworms coil,
elk antlers shed,
springs begin to move.
6.120 When the day is shortest,
then cut trees,
and gather bamboo arrows.
In this month,
one may dismiss officials with no duties
and discard useless utensils.
6.121 Plaster the palace gates and city gates,
build prisons,
this is to aid heaven and earth in closing and storing.
6.122 If in midwinter summer ordinances are practiced,
then the state will suffer drought,
with dense fog and gloom,
and thunder will sound.
If autumn ordinances are practiced,
then the weather will bring rainy sleet,
melons and gourds will not ripen,
and the state will face major military conflicts.
If spring ordinances are practiced,
then locusts will cause damage,
springs and streams will all dry up,
and the people will suffer many skin diseases and plagues.
6.123 In the late winter month,
the sun is in Wùnǚ,
at dusk Lóu is centered,
at dawn Dī is centered.
Its days are Rén and Guǐ.
Its emperor is Zhuānxū,
its deity is Xuánmíng.
Its creatures are the shelled.
Its musical note is Yǔ,
the pitch pipe is Dàlǚ.
Its number is six.
Its flavor is salty,
its odor is putrid.
Its sacrifice is to the wayfarer,
offering the kidneys first.
6.124 Wild geese head north,
magpies begin to nest.
Pheasants call,
hens brood.
6.125 The Son of Heaven resides in the right chamber of the dark hall.
He rides in a black carriage,
driven by iron-black horses,
bearing dark banners,
dressed in black robes,
and wearing dark jade.
He eats millet and pork,
his vessels are large and covered.
6.126 He orders officials to conduct the great exorcism,
with dismemberment sacrifices on all sides,
and the presentation of an earthen ox,
to send off the cold air.
6.127 Birds of prey become fierce and swift.
Then complete the sacrifices to the mountains and rivers,
and to the great ministers of the emperor,
and the celestial deities.
6.128 In this month,
he commands the fishing masters to begin fishing,
the Son of Heaven personally goes,
and tastes the fish,
first offering it in the ancestral temple.
6.129 Ice is at its peak,
waters and marshes are solidly frozen.
Order the collection of ice,
and store it indoors.
Instruct the people
to bring out the five grains.
Order farmers to plan for paired plowing,
repair plows and shares,
and prepare field tools.
6.130 Command the music master to hold a grand wind instrument concert and then cease.
6.131 Then order the four inspectors to collect firewood according to rank,
to supply for suburban, temple, and various sacrifices' bonfires.
In this month,
the sun completes its cycle,
the moon finishes its course,
and the stars revolve across the heavens.
The count is nearing its end,
and the year is about to renew.
Focus on the farmers,
and do not assign them any tasks.
6.132 The Son of Heaven, along with the dukes, ministers, and officials,
reviews the state's statutes,
discusses the seasonal ordinances,
to prepare for the appropriateness of the coming year.
6.133 He then orders the Grand Historian to rank the feudal lords,
collect sacrificial animals from them,
to offer to the August Heaven, the Supreme Deity, and the gods of the land and grain.
He commands the states of the same surname
to contribute the animals for the sacrifices at the ancestral temples.
He orders the steward to record the landholdings of the ministers, officials, and common people,
and collect sacrificial animals,
to offer in sacrifices to the mountains, forests, and famous rivers.
All the people within the nine provinces under heaven
must contribute their efforts,
to provide for the sacrifices to the August Heaven, the Supreme Deity, the gods of the land and grain, the ancestral temples, the mountains, forests, and famous rivers.
6.134 If in the last month of winter the ordinances of autumn are carried out,
then white dew will fall early,
armored insects will cause calamities,
and people from the four borders will retreat into fortresses.
If the ordinances of spring are carried out,
then many fetuses and young will be harmed,
the state will have many chronic illnesses,
and it is called a rebellion.
If the ordinances of summer are carried out,
then floods will damage the state,
timely snow will not fall,
and ice will melt away.
7.1 Zēngzǐ asked:
"If the ruler passes away and the heir is born,
what should be done?"
Confucius said:
"The ministers, officials, and scholars follow the regent
to face north
at the south of the western steps.
The Grand Invocator, in ceremonial attire and crown,
holds a bundle of silk,
ascends from the western steps, reaches the top step,
but does not enter the hall,
and orders that there be no weeping.
The Invocator calls out three times,
and announces:
'A son of so-and-so has been born,
I dare to announce.'
He ascends,
places the silk on the table east of the coffin,
weeps,
and descends.
The other masters, ministers, officials, and scholars,
and those in the inner chambers
all weep but do not leap.
After expressing their grief fully,
they return to their positions.
Then the morning offering is made.
The minor steward ascends to remove the silk.
After three days,
the other masters, ministers, officials, and scholars
take their positions as before,
facing north.
The Grand Steward, the Grand Patriarch, and the Grand Invocator all wear ceremonial attire and crowns.
The junior tutor carries the child in mourning clothes;
the Invocator leads,
the child follows,
and the steward and the ritualist follow.
They enter the gate,
and the weepers stop,
the child ascends from the western steps.
He stands before the coffin facing north.
The Invocator stands at the southeastern corner of the coffin.
The Invocator calls out three times,
and says:
'The son of so-and-so, named so-and-so,
following the officers,
dares to present himself.'
The child bows and touches his head to the ground,
and weeps.
The Invocator, steward, ritualist, other masters,
ministers, officials, and scholars
weep and leap three times in sets of three,
then descend,
return to their positions in the east,
all baring their shoulders,
the child leaps,
and those in the inner chambers also leap
three times in sets of three.
They then put on the mourning clothes,
take up the staff,
and also leave.
The Grand Steward orders the Invocator and the historian
to announce the name to the five household gods and the mountains and rivers."
7.2 Zēngzǐ asked:
"If the heir is born after the burial,
then what should be done?"
Confucius said:
"The Grand Steward and the Grand Patriarch follow the Grand Invocator to announce to the father's spirit.
After three months,
the name is announced at the father's shrine,
and the name is announced to the gods of the land and grain, the ancestral temples, and the mountains and rivers."
7.3 Confucius said:
"When a feudal lord goes to the Son of Heaven,
he must announce it at the ancestral temple,
and make an offering at the father's shrine.
He dons his crown and holds court,
orders the Invocator and historian to announce it to the ancestral temples and mountains and rivers.
Then he orders the five officials of the state and then departs,
performing the road-offering as he leaves.
The announcements
must be completed within five days;
beyond that
is against ritual.
All announcements
use animals and silk.
Upon return,
it is the same.
When feudal lords meet each other,
they must announce it at the father's shrine,
don court attire and hold court.
They order the Invocator and historian to announce it to the five temples and
the mountains and rivers they pass.
They also order the five officials of the state,
and perform the road-offering as they leave.
Upon return,
they must personally announce it at the ancestral and father's temples.
Then they order the Invocator and historian to announce it to those previously informed,
and only then do they hold court and enter."
7.4 Zēngzǐ asked:
"If there are two mournings at the same time,
what should be done?
Which comes first and which later?"
Confucius said:
"For burials,
the lighter precedes and the heavier follows;
for offerings,
the heavier precedes and the lighter follows; this is ritual.
From the opening of the coffin to the burial,
no offerings are made,
and during the burial procession, they do not stop at the mourning station;
upon return, the burial offering is made,
and then they report at the coffin,
and proceed with the burial matters.
For the post-burial sacrifice,
the heavier precedes and the lighter follows,
this is ritual."
7.5 Confucius said:
"Even if the clan head is seventy,
he must not be without a main wife;
if not the clan head,
it is acceptable to be without a main wife."
7.6 Zēngzǐ asked:
"When about to cap a son,
and the cappers have arrived,
after exchanging courtesies and entering,
if news of a mourning in the close or heavy mourning category is heard,
what should be done?"
Confucius said:
"If it is an internal mourning, it is canceled;
if external, the capping proceeds but without the sweet wine ceremony,
the offerings are cleared and the area swept,
and they take their positions and weep.
If the cappers have not arrived,
it is canceled.
If about to cap a son but before the scheduled day,
there is mourning in the close, heavy, or lighter categories,
then the capping is performed in mourning clothes."
"After the mourning period, is the capping not redone?"
Confucius said:
"When the Son of Heaven bestows caps and robes upon feudal lords or officials at the great temple,
upon return, they set up an offering,
wear the bestowed robes,
and in this case, there is a capping with libation,
but not the sweet wine ceremony.
If the father has died and then capping occurs,
after the capping,
the ground is swept
and an offering is made at the father's shrine;
after the offering,
they meet the uncles,
and then feast the cappers."
7.7 Zēngzǐ asked:
"In sacrifices, under what circumstances
is the reciprocal toasting not performed?"
Confucius said:
"I have heard that,
in the minor auspicious ceremony,
the host performs the plain sacrifice but does not conduct the toasting,
though he offers a toast to the guest,
the guest does not raise his cup;
this is ritual."
In the past,
Duke Zhāo of Lǔ offered toasts to travelers while wearing the one-year mourning attire,
which was against ritual propriety;
Duke Xiào, after the two-year mourning period,
did not offer toasts during the libation ceremony,
which was also against ritual propriety."
7.8 Zēngzǐ asked:
"Can one participate in the funeral offerings while wearing the nine-month mourning attire?"
Confucius said:
"Not just the nine-month mourning!
From the three-year mourning attire down, all may participate;
this is in accordance with ritual."
Zēngzǐ said:
"Is it not to treat lightly the mourning attire and heavily the mutual assistance?"
Confucius said:
"That is not what I mean.
For the mourning of the Son of Heaven and feudal lords,
those in three-year mourning make the offerings;
for high officials,
those in one-year mourning make the offerings;
for lower officials,
then friends make the offerings;
if insufficient,
then select from those in nine-month mourning or below;
if still insufficient,
then reverse the order."
Zēngzǐ asked:
"Can one in five-month mourning participate in the sacrifices?"
Confucius said:
"Why only five-month mourning!
From three-year mourning down, all participate in sacrifices;
this is ritual."
Zēngzǐ said:
"Is it not to treat lightly the mourning and heavily the sacrifice?"
Confucius said:
"For the sacrificial mourning of the Son of Heaven and feudal lords,
those not in three-year mourning do not participate;
for high officials,
those in one-year mourning participate;
for lower officials,
if insufficient for the sacrifice,
then select from brothers in nine-month mourning or below."
7.9 Zēngzǐ asked:
"If acquainted,
can one wearing mourning attire participate in the sacrifice?"
Confucius said:
"One in three-month mourning does not sacrifice,
how much less assist others."
7.10 Zēngzǐ asked:
"After laying aside mourning attire,
can one participate in the funeral offerings?"
Confucius said:
"To remove mourning attire and then make offerings
is against ritual;
but to act as an usher is permissible."
7.11 Zēngzǐ asked:
"After the betrothal gifts have been presented in the wedding ceremony,
and an auspicious day set,
if the bride's parents die,
what should be done?"
Confucius said:
"The groom sends someone to offer condolences.
If the groom's parents die,
then the bride's family also sends someone to offer condolences.
In case of the father's death, the father is named;
in case of the mother's death, the mother is named.
If parents are not present,
then the paternal uncle and aunt are named.
The groom,
after the burial,
has his paternal uncle convey a message to the woman's family saying:
'So-and-so's son has the mourning of his parents,
and cannot continue as your kinsman,
so I am sent to deliver this message.'
The woman's family consents,
but does not dare marry her to another;
this is ritual.
The groom,
after the mourning period,
is requested by the woman's parents;
if the groom does not marry her,
then she may marry another;
this is ritual.
If the bride's parents die,
the groom does likewise."
7.12 Zēngzǐ asked:
"During the groom's procession to fetch the bride,
if the bride is on the road,
and the groom's parents die,
what should be done?"
Confucius said:
"The bride changes into plain deep robes,
with a white silk headband, and hastens to the mourning.
If the bride is on the road,
and her parents die,
then she returns."
"If the groom has gone to fetch the bride,
and she has not yet arrived,
when mourning for one-year
or nine-month attire occurs,
what should be done?"
Confucius said:
"The groom does not enter,
but changes clothes in the outer chamber;
the bride enters,
changes clothes in the inner chamber;
then they take their positions and wail."
Zēngzǐ asked:
"After the mourning is removed, is the wedding not resumed?"
Confucius said:
"For sacrifices,
if the time passes, they are not performed;
this is ritual;
how much more so for returning to the initial state?"
7.13 Confucius said:
"The family marrying off a daughter
does not extinguish candles for three nights,
thinking of the separation.
The family taking a wife
does not make music for three days,
thinking of continuing the family line.
After three months, she is presented in the ancestral temple,
and called 'the newly come wife.'
On a chosen day, she sacrifices at the father's temple,
thus completing the wife's duty."
7.14 Zēngzǐ asked:
"If the wife dies before being presented in the temple,
what should be done?"
Confucius said:
"She is not moved to the ancestral grave,
nor associated with the husband's grandmother;
the husband does not use the staff, wear mourning shoes, or dwell apart;
she is buried in her own family's graveyard,
showing she had not become a wife."
7.15 Zēngzǐ asked:
"If the bride
dies after an auspicious day is set,
what should be done?"
Confucius said:
"The groom mourns in one-year attire and offers condolences,
and removes it after burial.
If the husband dies, it is the same."
Zēngzǐ asked:
"Having two chief mourners in a funeral,
and two spirit tablets in a temple,
is this ritual?"
Confucius said:
"Heaven has no two suns,
earth no two kings;
in the seasonal, great, suburban, and earth sacrifices,
there is no dual supremacy.
I do not know this to be ritual.
In the past, Duke Huán of Qí frequently raised armies,
and made a duplicate tablet to take along.
Upon return,
he stored it in the ancestral temple.
Having two tablets in a temple
began with Duke Huán.
As for two chief mourners in a funeral,
when Duke Líng of Wèi went to Lǔ,
he encountered the mourning for Jì Huánzǐ.
The ruler of Wèi requested to offer condolences,
but Duke Āi declined;
unable to refuse the request,
the duke acted as host,
and the guest entered to offer condolences.
Kǎngzǐ stood at the right of the gate,
facing north;
the duke bowed and yielded, ascending by the eastern steps,
facing west;
the guest ascended by the western steps to offer condolences.
The duke bowed,
rose,
and wailed;
Kǎngzǐ bowed and knocked his head at his position,
and the officers did not correct it.
The present practice of two chief mourners
originated from Jì Kǎngzǐ's error."
7.16 Zēngzǐ asked:
"In ancient times, when armies marched,
did they necessarily take the removed temple tablet along?"
Confucius said:
"When the Son of Heaven toured the domains,
he took the removed temple tablet along,
carried in the fasting carriage,
meaning there must be reverence.
Nowadays,
taking the tablets of the seven temples to travel
is a mistake.
In the seven or five temples, there should be no empty place for the tablet;
an empty place for the tablet
occurs only when the Son of Heaven dies,
a feudal lord dies or leaves his state,
or during the combined sacrifice to the ancestors,
when there is no tablet present."
I have heard from Lǎodān that:
'When the Son of Heaven passes away,
or a feudal lord dies,
the prayer official takes the ancestral tablets from all the temples and stores them in the ancestral temple,
which is according to ritual.
After the wailing is completed and matters are settled,
the tablets each return to their own temples.
When a lord leaves his state,
the grand steward takes the tablets from all the temples to follow him,
which is according to ritual.
For the xiá sacrifice at the ancestral temple,
the prayer official welcomes the tablets from the four temples.
When the tablets
leave or enter the temple, the path must be cleared.'
So said Lǎodān."
7.17 Zēngzǐ asked:
"In ancient times, when the army marched
and there was no moving ancestral tablet,
then what was used as the tablet?"
Confucius said:
"The command tablet."
He asked:
"What does that mean?"
Confucius said:
"When the Son of Heaven or feudal lords are about to depart,
they must use silk, cloth, hides, and jade tablets to report to the ancestors and father,
then respectfully take them out,
carrying them on the fasting carriage when traveling.
At each stop,
they make offerings before going to their quarters.
Upon return, they must report,
set up offerings, and when finished,
collect the silk and jade,
storing them between the two steps,
before leaving.
This honors the command."
7.18 Zǐyóu asked:
"Mourning for a caring mother as for one's own mother,
is this according to ritual?"
Confucius said:
"It is not according to ritual.
In ancient times,
men had tutors outside
and caring mothers inside,
appointed by the lord's command to educate the children,
so why should there be mourning attire?
In the past,
Duke Zhāo of Lǔ lost his mother when young,
and had a good caring mother.
When she died,
the duke could not bear it
and wanted to mourn her.
The officials reported,
saying:
'According to ancient ritual,
there is no mourning for a caring mother.
Now if you, lord, mourn her,
this would violate ancient ritual and disrupt state law;
if you proceed with it,
the officials will record it to leave for later generations.
Would this not be improper?'
The duke said:
'In ancient times, the Son of Heaven wore plain caps while at leisure.'
The duke could not bear it,
so he wore a plain cap to mourn his caring mother.
Mourning for a caring mother
began with Duke Zhāo of Lǔ."
7.19 Zēngzǐ asked:
"When feudal lords assemble to see the Son of Heaven,
after entering the gate
but unable to complete the ceremony,
how many situations cause its cancellation?"
Confucius said:
"Four."
He asked about them.
He said:
"The great temple catching fire,
a solar eclipse,
the death of the queen,
rain soaking robes and disheveling appearance—
then it is canceled.
If all feudal lords are present and a solar eclipse occurs,
they follow the Son of Heaven to rescue the sun,
each with their directional color and weapons.
If the great temple catches fire,
they follow the Son of Heaven to fight the fire,
not using directional colors or weapons."
7.20 Zēngzǐ asked:
"When feudal lords meet each other,
after bowing and yielding to enter the gate,
but unable to complete the ceremony,
how many situations cause its cancellation?"
Confucius said:
"Six."
He asked about them.
He said:
"The Son of Heaven's death,
the great temple catching fire,
a solar eclipse,
the death of the queen or lady,
rain soaking robes and disheveling appearance—
then it is canceled."
7.21 Zēngzǐ asked:
"For the Son of Heaven's seasonal, ancestral, suburban, earth, and five sacrifices,
when the grain vessels are already set out,
if the Son of Heaven dies,
or the queen dies,
what should be done?"
Confucius said:
"Cancel it."
7.22 Zēngzǐ asked:
"If during a sacrifice a solar eclipse occurs,
or the great temple catches fire,
how should the sacrifice proceed?"
Confucius said:
"Conclude it quickly.
If the sacrificial animal has arrived
but not been killed,
then cancel it."
7.23 When the Son of Heaven dies,
before encoffining,
the five sacrifices are not performed;
after encoffining, when sacrificing,
in such sacrifice,
the impersonator enters,
takes three mouthfuls without urging,
rinses without toasting in return, that is all.
From opening the coffin to returning crying,
the five sacrifices are not performed;
after burial, when sacrificing,
the prayer official completes the offering, that is all.
7.24 Zēngzǐ asked:
"When feudal lords sacrifice to earth and grain,
with sacrificial vessels already set out,
upon hearing of the Son of Heaven's death,
the queen's death,
their lord's death,
or their lady's death,
what should be done?"
Confucius said:
"Cancel it.
From death until encoffining,
from opening the coffin to returning crying,
follow the Son of Heaven's example."
7.25 Zēngzǐ asked:
"For a great officer's sacrifice,
with tripods and stands already set out,
bamboo and wooden vessels already arranged,
but unable to complete the ritual,
how many situations cause its cancellation?"
Confucius said:
"Nine."
He asked about them.
He said:
"The Son of Heaven's death,
the queen's death,
the lord's death,
the lady's death,
the lord's great temple catching fire,
a solar eclipse,
the three-year mourning,
the zīcuī mourning,
the dàgōng mourning—
all cancel it.
External mourning
from zīcuī downward
may proceed.
For sacrifices during zīcuī mourning,
the impersonator enters,
takes three mouthfuls without urging,
rinses without toasting in return, that is all;
for dàgōng, toasting in return, that is all;
for xiǎogōng and sī,
only the chamber matters, that is all.
What differs for officers is that
during sī mourning, they do not sacrifice;
if sacrificing, for the deceased without mourning attire, then sacrifice."
Zēngzǐ asked:
"During three-year mourning,
should one offer condolences?"
Confucius said:
"During three-year mourning,
even at the plain ceremony, one should not stand in groups,
nor travel together.
The gentleman uses ritual to adorn feelings;
during three-year mourning to condole and wail,
would that not be insincere?"
Zēngzǐ asked:
"If officers and great officers have private mourning,
which they could end,
but also have lord's mourning attire,
how should they end it?"
Confucius said:
"With the lord's mourning attire on one's person,
one dare not wear private mourning attire,
so how end it?
Thus there are cases where it is not ended at the proper time.
For the lord's mourning,
after the mourning attire is removed, then perform the yīn sacrifice,
which is according to ritual."
7.26 Zēngzǐ asked, saying:
"In the mourning for parents,
may one not put it aside?"
Confucius said:
"The ancient kings established the rules of ceremony,
and when the time had passed, they did not carry them out.
This was according to those rules.
It was not that they could not have kept them up without setting them aside,
but they were afraid lest they should go beyond the rules.
Therefore the superior man, when the time has passed, does not offer the sacrifice;
this is in accordance with the rules."
7.27 Zēngzǐ asked, saying:
"When a ruler has died,
and the coffin has been placed in the court,
if it happen that a minister has the mourning rites for a parent to observe,
what should he do?"
Confucius said:
"He should go home and remain there,
and when there is an occasion of special service to the ruler,
he should go to the ruler's palace,
but not for the regular morning and evening duties."
Zēngzǐ said:
"When the ruler's coffin has been taken from the court to be buried,
if it happen that a minister has the mourning rites for a parent to observe,
what should he do?"
Confucius said:
"He should go home and wail, and then return to escort the ruler to the grave."
Zēngzǐ said:
"If the ruler have not been coffined,
and a minister has the mourning rites for a parent to observe,
what should he do?"
Confucius said:
"He should go home and have the coffin placed in the court,
and then return to the ruler's palace.
On occasions of special service he should go home,
but not for the regular morning and evening duties.
In the case of a Great officer,
his house-steward will discharge his duties for him;
in that of an ordinary officer,
his sons and grandsons will do so.
The wife of a Great officer,
on occasions of special service,
will also go to the ruler's palace,
but not for the regular morning and evening duties."
7.28 The poor should not pronounce the eulogy of the rich;
the young should not pronounce that of the old:
this was the rule.
Only for the Son of Heaven
is it said that Heaven pronounces his eulogy.
For the feudal lords to pronounce eulogies of one another
was contrary to rule.
7.29 Zēngzǐ asked, saying:
"When a ruler goes out of his state,
he takes with him every preparation for death for three years,
and the inner coffin follows him.
If he die abroad,
how is he brought home?"
Confucius said:
"The ruler's servants provide the grave-clothes;
the ruler's son, with a hempen band round his hair,
a cap with its string of ties,
untrimmed mourning,
and straw sandals,
leaning on a staff.
They enter by the gap in the wall,
and ascend by the steps on the west.
If the ruler have been encoffined in a small coffin,
then the son, with his head bandaged, follows the hearse,
entering by the great gate,
and ascending by the steps on the east.
In this there is the same rule for the ruler, the Great officer, and the ordinary officer."
Zēngzǐ asked, saying:
"When the ruler's coffin is on its way to the grave,
and a minister hears of the mourning for a parent,
what should he do?"
Confucius said:
"He should proceed.
When the coffin has been let down into the grave, he returns,
and does not wait for the son."
Zēngzǐ asked, saying:
"When the coffin of a parent is on its way to the grave,
and on the road
one hears of the death of the ruler,
what should he do?"
Confucius said:
"He should proceed.
When the coffin has been let down into the grave,
he changes his dress and goes to the court."
7.30 Zēngzǐ asked, saying:
"The head of the clan is only an ordinary officer,
while a son by a concubine is a Great officer:
how will the latter sacrifice?"
Confucius said:
"He will sacrifice with the victim of a Great officer in the temple of the head of the clan,
and the officer of prayer will say:
'Filial So-and-so presents the constant offerings for So-and-so, the second son.'
If the head of the clan be living in another state,
having been obliged to leave his own,
and a son by a concubine is a Great officer,
when he sacrifices,
the officer of prayer will say:
'Filial So-and-so charges So-and-so, the second son, to undertake the constant services.'
But the substitute for the chief sacrificer will not give the 'repletion' sacrifice;
he will not take his place at the end of the row of stands;
he will not address the representative of the departed;
he will not present the offering of the silk;
and he will not take the place of his father.
He will set forth the offerings before the guests;
the guests will set them aside, and not raise them:
he will not give the portions of flesh to the visitors.
His words to them will be:
'Our honoured cousin, our honoured brother, the head of the clan, is in another state,
and has charged me So-and-so to make this announcement.'"
7.31 Zēngzǐ asked, saying:
"The head of the clan having gone and is in another state,
while a son by a concubine, who has no rank, remains at home,
can he sacrifice?"
Confucius said:
"He should sacrifice."
Zēngzǐ asked further,
"How should he sacrifice?"
Confucius said:
"He should raise a mound looking towards the grave of the ancestor,
and sacrifice to him at the proper season.
If the head of the clan die, he will announce his death at the grave, and afterwards sacrifice in his own house.
When the head of the clan is dead, he will be designated by his name, and not called 'the Filial one',
and so till his own death.
Among the disciples of Zǐyóu,
there were those who were sons by concubines and sacrificed in this way,
and this
is the right practice.
Those who sacrifice now,
do not take this as their first principle,
and therefore they err in sacrificing."
7.32 Zēngzǐ asked, saying:
"In sacrificing must there be the representative of the dead?
Or can the sacrifice without such be accepted?"
Confucius said:
"In sacrificing to a grown-up person, there must be such a representative.
That representative must be a grandson.
If the grandson be young,
some one carries him in his arms.
If there be no grandson,
one of the same surname may be chosen.
In sacrificing to one who has died prematurely, there must be the representativeless sacrifice,
because such a one is not considered grown-up.
To sacrifice to a grown-up person without a representative
is to treat him as if he had died prematurely."
Confucius said:
"There is the 'repletion' sacrifice in the dark,
and the 'repletion' sacrifice in the light."
Zēngzǐ asked:
"In sacrificing to one who has died prematurely, there is no accompanying sacrifice:
what do you mean by the 'repletion' sacrifice in the dark and that in the light?"
Confucius said:
"When the son of the chief wife dies prematurely,
and a son by a concubine becomes the successor,
at the auspicious sacrifice for the former,
a single victim is used.
In sacrificing to one who has died prematurely, the lungs are not set forth;
there is no stand for the offering of the spleen;
there is no clear water;
there is no announcement that the nourishing portion has been presented:
this is what is called the 'repletion' sacrifice in the dark.
In all sacrifices to those who have died prematurely,
and to those who have left no posterity,
the sacrifice is in the temple of the head of the clan.
The place for it is the clear space in the apartment,
with the vase in the eastern chamber:
this is what is called the 'repletion' sacrifice in the light."
7.33 Zēngzǐ asked, saying:
"When the coffin has been taken to the grave,
and there is an eclipse of the sun,
are there any changes made?
Or is the ceremony proceeded with?"
Confucius said:
"Formerly,
when I was with Lǎodān, assisting at a funeral in Xiàngdǎng,
when we had got to the path leading to the grave,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
Lǎodān said to me:
'Qiū,
let the bier be stopped,
and set on the right of the road,
and let all wailing cease, till the change passes.'
When it was light again, we proceeded.
He said:
'That was according to the rule.'
When we had returned and completed the burial,
I said to him:
'In the progress of the bier, it ought not to return.
When there is an eclipse of the sun,
we do not know whether it will pass quickly or slowly:
would it not have been better to proceed?'"
Lǎo Dān said:
'When feudal lords go to court to see the Son of Heaven,
they set off at sunrise
and stop at sunset
to make offerings;
when grand officers are on missions,
they set off at sunrise
and stop at sunset.
The coffin should not leave too early,
nor lodge overnight.
Those who travel by starlight—
are they not only criminals and those rushing to their parents' funerals?
If there is a solar eclipse,
how can one be sure not to see stars?
Moreover, when gentlemen perform rituals,
they do not bring distress upon others' parents.'
I heard this from Lǎo Dān."
7.34 Zēngzǐ asked:
"If one dies in his lodging while on a mission for his lord,
the rites say:
'There is a recalling of the soul at a public lodge,
but not at a private lodge.'
Now, in any state to which one is sent,
the lodging provided by the officials
is considered a public lodge;
what then is meant by 'no recalling at a private lodge'?"
Confucius said:
"An excellent question!
The homes of ministers, grand officers, and officers
are called private lodges;
public lodges and those provided by the state
are called public lodges.
'Recalling at a public lodge' refers to this."
7.35 Zēngzǐ asked:
"For a child who dies between eight and eleven:
they are buried in an earthen enclosure in the garden,
and taken there on a wheeled bier,
because the way is near.
Now if the tomb is far,
how should the burial be conducted?"
Confucius said:
"I heard from Lǎo Dān:
'Once Shǐ Yì had a son who died,
a child between eight and eleven.
The tomb was far.'
Shào Gōng said to him:
'Why not encoffin him in the palace?'
Shǐ Yì said:
'Would I dare?'
Shào Gōng spoke to Zhōu Gōng,
and Zhōu Gōng said:
'Why not?'
Shǐ Yì then did it."
Using a coffin and shroud for a child who dies between eight and eleven
began with Shǐ Yì."
7.36 Zēngzǐ asked:
"If a minister or grand officer is to serve as the impersonator of the dead for the lord,
and has already received the notice to fast,
but then has a domestic mourning of the lowest grade,
what should be done?"
Confucius said:
"He goes out
and lodges at a public lodge to await the ceremony,
as is proper."
Confucius said:
"The impersonator, wearing his cap, goes out,
and ministers, grand officers, and officers all descend;
the impersonator must bow to the crossbar,
and there must be a vanguard."
7.37 Zǐxià asked:
"After the cessation of wailing in the three-year mourning,
if one does not avoid military service,
is this proper?
Or was it initially an official's duty?"
Confucius said:
"Under the Xià, during the three-year mourning,
one resigned office after the encoffining;
under the Yīn, after the burial.
The Record says:
'A gentleman does not deprive others of their kinship duties,
nor should he be deprived of his own.'
Does it not refer to this?"
Zǐxià said:
"Not avoiding military service—
is it not improper?"
Confucius said:
"I heard from Lǎo Dān:
'In the past, Lǔ's Bó Qín had a reason for doing so;
but now, to pursue profit
during the three-year mourning—
I do not understand it!'"
8.1 When King Wén was heir apparent,
he attended upon his father Jìlì
three times a day.
At the first crow of the cock, he dressed
and went to the outer door of the bedchamber,
asking the attending inner page:
"How is he today?"
The inner page said:
"Well."
Then King Wén was pleased.
At midday,
he came again,
and did the same.
In the evening,
he came again,
and did the same.
If there was any discomfort,
the inner page would inform King Wén,
who would look worried
and walk unsteadily.
When Jìlì resumed his meals,
then King Wén also returned to normal.
When food was served,
he was always present,
checking its temperature;
when it was taken away,
he asked what was eaten;
and ordered the cook:
"Do not serve leftovers!"
The reply was:
"Yes,"
and then he withdrew.
King Wǔ followed this example,
not daring to exceed it.
When King Wén was ill,
King Wǔ attended him without removing his cap or sash.
If King Wén ate one meal,
he ate one;
if King Wén ate two,
he ate two.
After twelve days, King Wén recovered.
King Wén asked King Wǔ:
"What did you dream?"
King Wǔ replied:
"I dreamed the Lord gave me nine ling."
King Wén said:
"What do you think it means?"
King Wǔ said:
"There are nine states in the west;
will you, lord, eventually pacify them?"
King Wén said:
"No.
In ancient times, ling meant years;
age is also called ling.
I have a hundred, you have ninety;
I will give you three."
King Wén died at ninety-seven,
and King Wǔ at ninety-three.
King Chéng was young
and could not ascend the throne;
so Zhōu Gōng acted as regent,
governing in his stead.
He applied the Heir Apparent's Rules to Bó Qín,
wishing King Chéng to understand the ways of father and son, ruler and minister, elder and younger;
if King Chéng erred,
he would whip Bó Qín,
thus showing King Chéng the way of an heir apparent.
This was King Wén as heir apparent.
8.2 In teaching the heir apparent and officers,
timing is essential.
In spring and summer, they learn shield and spear;
in autumn and winter, feather and flute;
all at the Eastern Hall.
The Minor Music Master teaches the shield,
assisted by the Grand Coordinator.
The Flute Master teaches the spear,
assisted by the Flute Master's deputy.
The Coordinator drums the "South."
In spring, they recite; in summer, they play strings—
the Grand Master instructs them.
In autumn at the Blind Musicians' Hall, they study the Rites,
instructed by the Rites Master;
in winter, they read the Documents,
instructed by the Documents Master.
The Rites are at the Blind Musicians' Hall,
the Documents at the Upper School.
8.3 For all ceremonies, caring for the elderly,
seeking their words,
and the ritual of shared conversation,
the Minor Music Master instructs at the Eastern Hall.
The Grand Music Master teaches dance with shield and axe,
discourse,
and the request for words;
all are taught the methods by the Grand Music Master,
with the Grand Tutor discussing and explaining at the Eastern Hall.
8.4 Those attending the Grand Tutor in session
should sit three mats away,
and may then ask questions.
At the end, they lean against the wall;
if matters are not fully presented,
they do not ask.
8.5 In all schools,
in spring the officials perform the Diǎnmò sacrifice to their former teachers,
and similarly in autumn and winter.
Whenever a school is first established,
a Diǎnmò sacrifice must be performed to the ancient sages
and former teachers,
and when conducting these affairs,
silk must be used.
All Diǎnmò sacrifices
must involve a gathering of music,
unless there is a state mourning.
8.6 Whenever there is a grand musical gathering,
it must be followed by the ceremony of honoring the elderly.
All those who are discussed in the suburban schools
must be selected for their virtue and gathered for their talents.
Some are advanced for their virtue,
some are recommended for their service,
some are elevated for their speech.
Those skilled in minor arts are all instructed,
awaiting further discussion.
If one possesses even one of these three qualities,
they are promoted in rank,
according to their order,
and are called Jiāo rén.
They are kept distant from the main academy,
yet may still receive a cup from the superior vessels.
8.7 When a school is first established,
after the vessels have been set up and silk offered,
then the Shìcài ceremony is performed,
without dancing and without handing out instruments,
before retiring.
Guests are received in the eastern hall,
with one offering of wine,
and it is acceptable to have no assistant or conversation.
(This is for) educating the crown prince.
8.8 The three dynastic kings always educated the crown prince with rites and music.
Music
is used to cultivate the inner self;
rites
are used to cultivate the outer conduct.
Rites and music interact within,
and manifest outwardly,
thus their completion brings joy,
reverence and gentle refinement.
Grand tutors and junior tutors are appointed to nurture him,
desiring him to understand the way of father and son, ruler and minister.
The grand tutor examines the way of father and son, ruler and minister to show him,
while the junior tutor attends the crown prince,
observing the grand tutor's virtuous conduct and carefully instructing him.
The grand tutor is in front,
the junior tutor behind;
when entering there is a guardian,
when exiting there is a teacher—
thus through teaching and understanding, virtue is achieved.
The teacher
instructs through affairs and elucidates various virtues;
the guardian
cautions his person to assist and guide him toward the Way.
The Record says:
"Yú, Xià, Shāng, and Zhōu
had teachers and guardians,
doubt-resolvers and assistants,
establishing four supports and three dukes.
They need not all be filled,
only the right persons."
This speaks to employing the capable.
The noble man speaks of virtue:
virtue achieved then teaching is revered,
teaching revered then officials are upright,
officials upright then the state is well-governed—
this refers to the ruler.
Zhòngní said:
"Formerly, the Duke of Zhōu acted as regent,
ascended the throne and governed,
applying the 'Crown Prince Laws' to Bó Qín,
in order to perfect King Chéng.
I have heard it said:
'As a minister,
