if killing oneself benefits the ruler, one should do it.'
How much more so by embodying it to perfect one's ruler?
The Duke of Zhōu excelled at this!"
Therefore, knowing how to be a good son,
one can then be a father;
knowing how to be a good minister,
one can then be a ruler;
knowing how to serve others,
one can then employ others.
King Chéng was young,
unable to ascend the throne,
and as crown prince,
had nothing to do;
therefore, the 'Crown Prince Laws' were applied to Bó Qín,
making him reside with King Chéng,
wanting King Chéng to understand
the principles of father and son, ruler and minister, and elder and younger.
The ruler towards the crown prince—
in intimacy is a father,
in honor is a ruler.
Having a father's intimacy,
and a ruler's honor,
then one can unite and possess all under heaven.
Therefore,
nurturing the crown prince must not be careless.
One act that yields three goods—
only the crown prince achieves this,
referring to his ordering by age in school.
Thus the crown prince is ordered by age in school,
and the people see it, saying:
"He who will rule me
yields to me by age—why?"
The answer:
"While his father lives, ritual requires it."
Thus the masses understand the way of father and son.
The second says:
"He who will rule me yields to me by age,
why?"
The answer:
"While the ruler lives, ritual requires it."
Thus the masses grasp the duty of ruler and minister.
The third says:
"He who will rule me yields to me by age,
why?"
The answer:
"To honor elders."
Thus the masses understand the precedence of elder and younger.
Therefore, with father present, one is a son;
with ruler present, one is called a minister;
maintaining the roles of son and minister
is how to honor the ruler and cherish kin.
Thus, learn to be father and son,
learn to be ruler and minister,
learn to be elder and younger;
when the ways of father and son,
ruler and minister,
and elder and younger are attained,
the state is well-governed.
It is said:
"The music master oversees learning,
the father-teacher oversees completion;
once there is great goodness,
all states are rectified."
This refers to the crown prince.
The Duke of Zhōu ascended the throne.
The official in charge of the ducal clan among the sons of concubines
teaches them filial piety, fraternal duty, harmony, friendship, and parental love,
clarifying the principles of father and son,
and the order of elder and younger.
Their attendance at the ducal court:
in the inner court,
they face east with the north as superior;
among ministers who are nobles,
order is by age.
In the outer court,
order is by office,
managed by the director of officials.
In the ancestral temple,
positions are as in the outer court.
The temple director assigns duties
by rank and office.
For ascending to offer leftovers, presenting offerings, and receiving cups,
the eldest son of the primary wife takes precedence.
The director of secondary sons manages this;
even with the three highest ranks,
one does not surpass fathers and elder brothers.
In ducal great affairs,
order is by the fineness or coarseness of mourning garments.
Even for funerals of the ducal clan it is similar,
ordering after the host.
If the duke feasts with the clan,
then those of different surnames act as guests,
the steward acts as host,
and the duke is ordered by age with fathers and elder brothers.
At clan meals, each generation is one grade lower.
8.9 In the army,
they guard the ducal mobile ancestral shrine.
If the duke has affairs beyond the borders,
the director of secondary sons has the unoccupied members of the ducal clan guard the ducal palace,
the primary-line sons guard the great temple,
uncles guard the noble palaces and rooms,
and other sons and grandsons guard the lower palaces and rooms.
8.10 The descendants of the five temples,
whose ancestral temple is not yet abolished,
even if commoners,
at capping,
taking a wife,
must report;
at death,
must announce;
at the liàn and xiáng sacrifices, report.
Among the clan, mutual obligations—
if due condolences are not given,
or due mourning bands not worn,
the officials penalize them.
As for funeral gifts
and contributions, bearing
and mouth pearls,
all have regulations.
When a member of the ducal clan commits a capital crime,
they are executed by hanging at the Diànrén's place.
For corporal punishments,
they are either beheaded or cut in two,
also reported to the Diànrén.
Members of the ducal clan are exempt from castration.
Once the case is concluded,
the officials report it to the duke.
For a capital crime,
they say, "So-and-so's crime warrants the death penalty";
for corporal punishment,
they say, "So-and-so's crime warrants corporal punishment."
The duke says,
"Pardon him."
The officials respond,
"It is according to the law."
The duke says again,
"Pardon him."
The officials respond again,
"It is according to the law."
After three pardons,
they do not reply,
but leave,
carrying out the punishment at the Diànrén's place.
The duke then sends someone to pursue them, saying,
"Even so,
you must spare him."
The officials reply,
"It is too late!"
They return to report to the duke,
who dons plain garments and refrains from music,
altering his demeanor,
as if mourning a relative of the same rank.
He does not wear mourning clothes,
but personally weeps for him.
8.11 Members of the ducal clan attend court in the inner court,
to maintain closeness among relatives.
Even those of high rank are ordered by age,
emphasizing the father-son relationship.
In the outer court, they are ordered by office,
to distinguish those of different surnames.
In the ancestral temple,
positions are determined by rank,
honoring virtue.
The Zōngrén assigns duties by office,
respecting the worthy.
The eldest descendant offers sacrifices and receives the cup,
honoring the way of the ancestors.
In mourning ceremonies, order is based on the degree of mourning garments,
so as not to disrupt familial bonds.
When the duke feasts with his clan, order is by age,
and the way of filial piety and fraternal duty is upheld.
In clan feasts, each generation is seated one level lower,
showing the gradations of kinship.
In war, they guard the duke's mobile ancestral shrine,
demonstrating deep filial love.
The main lineage guards the great temple,
honoring the ancestral line,
and the way of ruler and minister is made clear.
Uncles and elder brothers guard the noble chambers,
younger members guard the lower chambers,
and the way of deference is upheld.
8.12 Descendants of the five temples,
whose ancestral temple has not been dismantled,
even if they become commoners, must report for capping,
marriage,
and report deaths,
not forgetting kinship.
If kinship is not severed but they are listed as commoners,
it is because they are deemed incapable.
Respectfully offering condolences, attending funerals, and giving gifts
is the way of maintaining friendly relations.
In ancient times,
when the office of the Shùzǐ was well managed,
the state had order.
When the state had order,
the people followed the right path.
For crimes of the ducal clan,
even if they are relatives, they do not interfere with the officials'
proper administration,
thus embodying care for the common people.
Punishments are carried out in private,
so as not to involve the people in worrying about their brothers.
They do not mourn them,
nor wear mourning garments,
but weep in the temple of a different surname,
keeping them distant as a disgrace to the ancestors.
They wear plain garments and stay outside,
not listening to music,
privately mourning them,
for the bond of flesh and blood is never severed.
The ducal clan is exempt from castration,
to not cut off their lineage.
8.13 When the Son of Heaven inspects the school,
drums are beaten at dawn to summon,
alerting the crowd.
After the crowd arrives,
the Son of Heaven arrives.
He then orders the officials to perform the rites.
They follow the proper order,
sacrificing to the former teachers
and sages.
When the officials finish,
they report back.
Then the nurturing begins:
He goes to the eastern hall,
offers libations to the former elders,
and sets up seats for the Three Elders,
Five Seniors,
and other elders.
He inspects the offerings and wine,
ensuring the delicacies for the elders
are complete;
then songs are sung,
and they retire to cultivate filial nurturing.
Upon returning,
they sing the "Qīng Miào" hymn,
and after singing, they converse,
to complete the ceremony.
They speak of the ways of father and son,
ruler and minister,
elder and younger,
combining the essence of virtuous sounds,
which is a great ritual.
Below, the "Xiàng" is played,
and the "Dà Wǔ" dance is performed.
The multitude gathers for the event,
connecting with the divine,
and promoting virtue.
The positions of ruler and minister are rectified,
and the distinctions between noble and humble are clear,
so the principles of high and low are practiced.
When the officials announce the end of the music,
the king orders the dukes,
marquises, earls,
barons, viscounts, and all officials, saying:
"Return
to nurture the old and young in the eastern hall."
This concludes with benevolence.
8.14 Therefore,
when sages record events,
they consider the greater good,
cherish with respect,
act with ritual,
cultivate with filial nurturing,
record with righteousness,
and conclude with benevolence.
8.15 Thus, in ancient times, whenever someone undertook an action,
all would know their virtue was complete.
The noble persons of old,
when undertaking great affairs,
were careful from start to finish,
so how could the people not understand?
The "Yuè Mìng" says:
"Always think of learning from beginning to end."
The "Record of the Heir Apparent" says:
Morning and evening, he goes outside the door of the great chamber,
and asks the inner attendant:
"How is he today?"
The inner attendant says:
"He is well today."
The heir apparent then shows a happy expression.
If there is any discomfort,
the inner attendant reports it to the heir apparent,
who then looks worried and somber.
When the inner attendant says "recovered,"
then he returns to normal.
When meals are served morning and evening,
the heir apparent must be present
to check the temperature.
After the meal is taken away,
he asks what was served.
He must know what was presented,
instruct the cook,
and then retire.
If the inner attendant says "ill,"
then the heir personally fasts, wears dark clothes, and tends to him.
The food prepared by the cook
must be carefully inspected.
Medicine for the illness
must be tasted personally.
If the food tastes good,
the heir can also eat;
if the food is poor,
the heir also cannot eat his fill;
until recovery,
then he returns to normal.
9.1 Once, Zhòngní participated as a guest at the year-end sacrifice,
and after the ceremony,
he went out and wandered on the tower,
sighing deeply.
Zhòngní's sigh
was likely sighing over Lǔ.
Yán Yǎn was by his side and said:
"Why is the gentleman sighing?"
Confucius said:
"When the Great Way was practiced,
and the eminent rulers of the Three Dynasties,
I, Qiū, did not live to see it,
yet I have aspirations for it.
When the Great Way was practiced,
the world was shared by all.
The worthy and able were selected,
sincerity was cultivated and harmony was promoted.
Thus, people did not only love their own parents,
nor did they only care for their own children.
The elderly were provided for until their death,
the able-bodied were employed,
the young were nurtured to maturity,
and the widowed, orphaned, childless, disabled, and ill
were all cared for.
Men had their roles,
women had their homes.
Goods were disliked if left discarded on the ground,
but not necessarily hoarded for oneself;
effort was disliked if not exerted from oneself,
but not necessarily for one's own benefit.
Therefore,
scheming was suppressed and did not flourish,
theft, rebellion, and banditry did not arise.
Thus, outer doors were left unbolted.
This is called the Great Unity.
Now the Great Way has become hidden,
the world is owned by families.
Each loves only their own parents,
each cares only for their own children.
Goods and labor are for oneself.
Rulers pass down their positions as a ritual.
Walls, moats, and trenches are built for defense,
and rites and righteousness are used as guidelines:
to rectify the relationship between ruler and subject,
to deepen the bond between father and son,
to harmonize brothers,
to unite husband and wife,
to establish institutions,
to organize fields and villages,
to honor the brave and wise,
and to achieve merit for oneself.
Thus, scheming arises from this,
and warfare emerges from this.
Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, Wǔ, King Chéng, and the Duke of Zhōu
were the select ones of this era.
These six gentlemen
were all meticulous in their observance of the rites.
They used them to manifest righteousness,
to test sincerity,
to expose errors,
to exemplify humanity and promote deference,
and to show the people a constant standard.
If anyone did not follow this,
those in power were removed,
and the people considered them a calamity.
This is called the Small Tranquility."
9.2 Yán Yǎn asked again:
"Is the rite so urgent as this?"
Confucius said:
"The rite
was used by the former kings to follow the Way of Heaven
and to govern human emotions.
Thus, those who lose it perish,
those who attain it survive.
The 'Book of Songs' says:
'Look at the rat, it has a body;
if a person has no rites,
if a person has no rites,
why not quickly die!'
Therefore, the rite
must be rooted in Heaven,
modeled on Earth,
arranged with the spirits,
and applied to mourning, sacrifice,
archery, charioteering, capping, marriage,
court audiences, and diplomatic visits.
Thus, the sages use the rite to guide the people,
so that the world, states, and families can be properly ordered."
9.3 Yán Yǎn asked again:
"Master, you speak of the rite in the highest terms;
may I hear about it?"
Confucius said:
"I wished to study the Way of the Xià,
so I went to Qǐ,
but found insufficient evidence;
I obtained the 'Xià Calendar.'
I wished to study the Way of the Yīn,
so I went to Sòng,
but found insufficient evidence;
I obtained the 'Kūn Qián.'
The principles of the 'Kūn Qián,'
and the gradations of the 'Xià Calendar,'
I use to study them.
9.4 "The beginning of the rite
started with food and drink.
They roasted millet and split pork,
dug pits for wine and drank from their hands,
made drums from earthen frames and beat them with clods,
yet they could still express reverence to the spirits.
When someone died,
they climbed the roof and called out,
saying:
'Hear!
So-and-so, return!'
Then they placed raw rice in the mouth and wrapped the body with grass.
Thus, they looked to Heaven and buried in the Earth,
for the body descends,
while the conscious energy rises.
Therefore, the dead are laid with heads to the north,
and the living face south,
all following the ancient ways.
9.5 "In the past, the former kings
had no palaces;
in winter, they lived in caves,
in summer, in nests.
They had not yet learned to use fire;
they ate the fruits of plants and trees,
the meat of birds and beasts,
drank their blood,
and swallowed the fur.
They had no hemp or silk;
they clothed themselves in feathers and hides.
9.6 "Later, when sages arose,
they utilized the benefits of fire,
molded metals, mixed clay,
to build towers, houses, windows, and doors;
they roasted, grilled,
boiled, and barbecued,
making sweet wines and cheeses;
they processed hemp and silk
to make cloth and silk,
to support the living and send off the dead,
and to serve the spirits and God.
All followed these beginnings.
9.7 "Thus, plain water was placed in the inner room,
sweet wine and clear wine at the door,
millet wine in the hall,
and clear wine below.
They displayed the sacrificial animals,
prepared the tripods and stands,
arranged the zithers, lutes, pipes, stone chimes, bells, and drums,
perfected the prayers and blessings,
to invoke the high gods and their ancestors.
They used this to rectify ruler and subject,
to deepen father and son,
to harmonize brothers,
to align superior and inferior,
and to establish roles for husband and wife.
This is called receiving the blessings of Heaven.
9.8 "They formulated the prayers and names,
used plain water in sacrifice,
presented the blood and hair,
offered raw meat on the stands,
cooked the dishes,
with mats of rushes,
coarse cloth for covers,
robes of undyed silk,
sweet and clear wines for offerings,
presented the roasted and grilled meats,
the ruler and his wife alternating in offerings,
to please the souls and spirits.
This is called union with the ethereal.
9.9 "Then they retired to cook everything together,
divided the dogs, pigs, oxen, and sheep,
filled the grain vessels, baskets, bamboo dishes, and soup bowls.
The prayer announced filial piety,
the blessing conveyed kindness.
This is called great auspiciousness.
This is the completion of the rite.
9.10 Confucius said:
"Alas, how lamentable!
I observe the Way of Zhōu,
damaged by Yōu and Lì,
where can I turn if not to Lǔ!
The suburban and ancestral sacrifices of Lǔ
are not in accordance with the rites;
the Duke of Zhōu's practices have declined!
Qǐ's suburban sacrifice is for Yǔ;
Sòng's suburban sacrifice is for Xiè.
These are the duties preserved by the Son of Heaven.
Thus, the Son of Heaven sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
the feudal lords sacrifice to the gods of soil and grain.
9.11 "The prayers and blessings dare not change their ancient forms;
this is called great borrowing.
9.12 "The words of the prayers and blessings
are stored by the temple officers, prayer masters, shamans, and scribes;
this is not in accordance with the rites,
this is called a dark state.
Using certain wine cups and impersonating the ruler in sacrifices
is not in accordance with the rites,
this is called a usurping ruler.
9.13 "To store royal caps, ceremonial headdresses, weapons, and armor in private households
is contrary to ritual,
and this is called coercing the ruler.
9.14 "For a minister to maintain a full set of officials,
not borrow sacrificial vessels,
and possess a complete set of musical instruments
is contrary to ritual,
and this is called throwing the state into disorder.
9.15 "Thus, those who serve the duke are called chén (ministers),
while those who serve a household are called pú (servants).
For those in the three-year mourning period
or newly married,
they should not be assigned tasks for a year.
To enter the court wearing mourning garments
and mingle with household servants as equals
is contrary to ritual,
and this is called the ruler and ministers sharing the state.
Thus, the Son of Heaven has land to settle his descendants,
the feudal lords have states to settle their descendants,
and the ministers have fiefs to settle their descendants—
this is called the system of regulations.
When the Son of Heaven visits a feudal lord,
he must lodge in the ancestral temple,
and if he enters without following the ritual records,
this is called the Son of Heaven undermining laws and disrupting order.
If a feudal lord enters the homes of his ministers
other than to inquire about illness or offer condolences,
this is called the ruler and ministers jesting with each other.
9.16 "Therefore,
ritual is the great handle of the ruler,
used to distinguish ambiguities and clarify subtleties,
serve the ghosts and spirits,
examine institutions,
differentiate benevolence and righteousness,
and thereby govern the state and secure the ruler.
Thus, if governance is not correct,
the ruler's position is endangered;
if the ruler's position is endangered,
then high ministers will rebel,
and petty officials will steal.
When punishments are severe and customs decay,
laws become unstable.
If laws are unstable,
ritual loses its order.
If ritual loses its order,
then scholars will not serve.
When punishments are severe and customs decay,
the people will not return—
this is called a flawed state.
9.17 "Thus, governance is
how the ruler conceals himself.
Therefore, governance
must be rooted in heaven,
modeled after it to issue commands.
Commands issued from the altar of the land are called modeling after earth;
from the ancestral temple, they are called benevolence and righteousness;
from the mountains and rivers, they are called initiatives;
from the five sacrifices, they are called institutions.
This is how the sage firmly conceals himself.
9.18 "Thus, the sage aligns with heaven and earth,
associates with ghosts and spirits,
to govern the state.
Dwelling in what exists,
there is the sequence of ritual;
delighting in what is joyful,
there is the order of the people.
Thus, heaven produces the seasons and earth produces wealth,
while humans are born from their fathers and taught by their masters—
these four,
the ruler uses correctly,
so the ruler stands in a position without fault.
9.19 "Thus, the ruler is to be enlightened,
not to enlighten others;
the ruler is to be supported,
not to support others;
the ruler is to be served,
not to serve others.
If the ruler enlightens others, he errs;
if he supports others, he lacks;
if he serves others, he loses his position.
Thus, the people emulate the ruler to govern themselves,
support the ruler to secure themselves,
serve the ruler to glorify themselves.
Thus, when ritual is understood and roles are fixed,
people all cherish death and worry about life.
9.20 "Thus, employ people's wisdom but remove their deceit,
employ people's courage but remove their anger,
employ people's benevolence but remove their greed.
9.21 "Thus, when the state faces calamity,
the ruler dying for the altars of land and grain is called righteousness,
while a minister dying for the ancestral temple is called a deviation.
9.22 "Thus, for the sage to endure and treat the world as one family,
and the central states as one person,
is not arbitrary—
he must know their feelings,
understand their righteousness,
clarify their benefits,
and comprehend their calamities,
before he can achieve this.
9.23 "What are human feelings?
Joy, anger, sorrow, fear, love, hatred, and desire—
these seven
are innate without learning.
What is human righteousness?
Father's kindness,
son's filial piety,
elder brother's goodness,
younger brother's respect,
husband's righteousness,
wife's compliance,
elder's generosity,
younger's obedience,
ruler's benevolence,
minister's loyalty—
these ten
are called human righteousness.
Cultivating trust and harmony
is called human benefit.
Struggling, seizing, and killing each other
is called human calamity.
Thus, how can the sage govern the seven feelings,
cultivate the ten righteousnesses,
promote trust and harmony,
honor deference,
and eliminate strife
without ritual?
Food, drink, and sexual relations
are the great desires of humans.
Death, loss, poverty, and suffering
are the great aversions of humans.
Thus, desires and aversions
are the great beginnings of the heart.
Humans conceal their hearts,
making them immeasurable;
beauty and ugliness are in their hearts, unseen in their countenances.
To uniformly exhaust them,
how can it be done without ritual?
9.24 "Thus, humans
embody the virtue of heaven and earth,
the interaction of yīn and yáng,
the communion of ghosts and spirits,
and the finest energy of the five phases.
9.25 "Thus, heaven holds yáng,
suspending the sun and stars;
earth holds yīn,
piercing through mountains and rivers.
It disseminates the five phases through the four seasons,
and harmony gives birth to the moon.
Hence, it waxes full in three fives,
and wanes in three fives.
The movements of the five phases
successively exhaust each other.
The five phases, four seasons, and twelve months
alternate as their basis.
The five tones, six pitches, and twelve tubes
alternate as the gōng note.
The five flavors, six harmonies, and twelve foods
alternate as their substance.
The five colors, six patterns, and twelve garments
alternate as their substance.
9.26 "Thus, humans are
the heart of heaven and earth,
the culmination of the five phases,
born to taste flavors, distinguish sounds, and wear colors.
Therefore, when the sage arises,
he must take heaven and earth as the foundation,
yīn and yáng as the starting point,
the four seasons as the handle,
the sun and stars as the guideline,
the moon as the measure,
ghosts and spirits as companions,
the five phases as the substance,
ritual and righteousness as tools,
human feelings as the field,
and the four numinous creatures as livestock.
Taking heaven and earth as the foundation,
all things can be raised.
Taking yīn and yáng as the starting point,
feelings can be observed.
Taking the four seasons as the handle,
tasks can be encouraged.
Taking the sun and stars as the guideline,
tasks can be ordered.
Taking the moon as the measure,
achievements have standards.
Taking ghosts and spirits as companions,
tasks have guardians.
Taking the five phases as the substance,
tasks can be repeated.
Taking ritual and righteousness as tools,
actions have examinations,
taking human feelings as the field,
humans are considered profound.
Taking the four numinous creatures as livestock,
food and drink have their sources.
What are the four numinous creatures?
The qílín, fènghuáng, turtle, and lóng
are called the four numinous creatures.
Thus, when the lóng is kept as livestock,
fish and sturgeon do not flee.
When the phoenix is domesticated,
birds do not flee wildly.
When the qilin is domesticated,
beasts do not bolt.
When the turtle is domesticated,
human feelings do not go astray.
9.27 "Thus the ancient kings held the divining stalks and tortoise shells,
arranged sacrifices,
buried silk offerings,
proclaimed prayers and benedictions,
established institutions and measures,
so the state had rituals,
officials had duties,
affairs had functions,
and rituals had order.
9.28 "Thus the ancient kings worried that rituals might not reach the common people.
9.29 "Therefore they sacrificed to Di in the suburbs,
to establish heaven's position;
sacrificed to the soil god in the capital,
to display earth's benefits;
the ancestral temple served as the root of benevolence;
mountains and rivers served to host spirits;
the five sacrifices served as the basis of affairs.
Thus the ancestral invocator was in the temple,
the three dukes at court,
the three elders in the school.
The king
had shamans before him and historians behind,
diviners and blind musicians all at his sides,
while the king at the center
remained non-active,
preserving perfect rectitude.
9.30 "Thus when rituals are performed in the suburbs
all spirits receive their duties;
when rituals are performed at the soil altar
all goods reach their utmost;
when rituals are performed in the ancestral temple
filial piety and parental love are practiced;
when rituals are performed for the five sacrifices
correct laws and standards are established.
Thus from suburban and soil sacrifices, ancestral temple, mountains and rivers, to the five sacrifices -
these are where righteousness is cultivated and rituals are stored.
9.31 "Therefore this ritual
must be rooted in the Great One,
divided to form heaven and earth,
transformed to become yin and yang,
changed to form the four seasons,
arrayed to become spirits.
Its descent is called mandate,
its office is in heaven.
9.32 "Ritual must be rooted in heaven,
move to reach earth,
array to form affairs,
change to follow seasons,
harmonize with distinctions.
Its residence in humans is called cultivation,
its practice through goods, labor,
and deferential speech:
drinking, eating,
capping, marriage,
mourning, sacrifice,
archery, charioteering,
audience, visitation.
9.33 "Thus ritual and righteousness
are the great foundations of humanity,
through which trust is cultivated and harmony established,
securing the connections of skin and flesh,
the binding of sinews and bones.
They are the great means for nourishing the living, sending off the dead, and serving spirits.
They are the great passage for reaching heaven's way and complying with human feelings.
9.34 "Thus only sages know that ritual cannot be abandoned,
so when states crumble, families perish, and people are lost,
ritual must first have been discarded.
Thus ritual's relation to humans
is like yeast to wine -
gentlemen use it richly,
petty men use it thinly.
9.35 "Thus sage kings cultivate righteousness's handle,
ritual's sequence,
to govern human feelings.
Thus human feelings
are the sage king's field.
Cultivate ritual to plow it,
display righteousness to seed it,
discuss learning to weed it,
root in benevolence to gather it,
spread music to settle it.
Thus ritual
is the substance of righteousness.
When harmonized with righteousness and found fitting,
even if previous kings lacked it,
ritual can arise from righteousness.
Righteousness is the distinction of arts,
the measure of benevolence.
Harmonized with arts,
discussed through benevolence,
those who attain it become strong.
Benevolence
is the root of righteousness,
the substance of compliance,
those who attain it become honored.
Thus governing a state without ritual
is like plowing without a plowshare.
Practicing ritual without rooting in righteousness
is like plowing without seeding.
Practicing righteousness without discussing it through learning
is like seeding without weeding.
Discussing it through learning
without uniting it with benevolence
is like weeding without harvesting.
Uniting it with benevolence
without settling it with music
is like harvesting without eating.
Settling it with music
without reaching compliance
is like eating without growing stout.
When the four limbs are correct,
skin and flesh充盈,
this is human stoutness.
When father and son are devoted,
brothers harmonious,
husband and wife concordant,
this is family stoutness.
When great ministers follow laws,
petty officers are honest,
offices are ordered mutually,
ruler and ministers correct each other,
this is state stoutness.
When the son of heaven takes virtue as his chariot,
music as his driver;
feudal lords interact through ritual;
great officers order themselves by laws;
scholars examine each other through trust;
common people preserve each other through harmony;
this is the stoutness of all under heaven.
This is called great compliance.
Great compliance
is the constant way for nourishing the living, sending off the dead, and serving spirits.
Thus affairs accumulate greatly without congestion,
proceed together without conflict,
and minor actions are not neglected.
Deep yet penetrating,
dense yet with intervals.
Connected without interfering,
moving without harming,
this is the ultimate of compliance.
Thus understanding compliance,
one can then preserve in peril.
9.36 "Thus ritual's distinctions
are neither excessive
nor deficient,
thereby maintaining feelings and uniting perils.
Thus the way sage kings achieve compliance:
they don't make mountain dwellers live by rivers,
nor island dwellers inhabit plains,
thus avoiding exhaustion.
Using water, fire, metal, wood,
and food and drink must be timely.
Joining men and women,
bestowing ranks and positions,
must match age and virtue.
Employing the people must be compliant.
Thus there are no floods, droughts, or insect calamities,
nor do people suffer famine, evil, or monstrous ailments.
Thus heaven does not grudge its way,
earth does not grudge its treasures,
humans do not grudge their feelings.
Thus heaven sends down sweet dew,
earth produces sweet springs,
mountains yield vessels and carriages,
rivers produce horse-charts,
phoenixes and qilin dwell in suburban marshes,
turtles and dragons reside in palace ponds;
the eggs and fetuses of other birds and beasts
can all be viewed by bending down.
This is for no other reason
than that ancient kings could cultivate ritual to reach righteousness,
embody trust to reach compliance,
this being the substance of compliance."
10.1 Ritual vessels
thus achieve great completeness.
Great completeness is abundant virtue.
Ritual dispels distortion,
enhances beautiful substance.
When established, it is correct;
when implemented, it works.
In humans,
it is like the green bark of bamboo arrows;
like the heart of pine and cypress.
These two represent the great foundations of the world.
Thus they persist through four seasons without changing branches or leaves.
Thus when gentlemen have ritual,
they are harmonious externally and unresentful internally,
so all things embrace their benevolence,
and spirits enjoy their virtue.
10.2 The ancient kings established rituals,
which have both substance and form.
Loyalty and sincerity
are the substance of rituals;
righteousness and principle
are the form of rituals.
Without substance, they cannot be established;
without form, they cannot be practiced.
10.3 Rituals
harmonize with the timing of heaven,
utilize the resources of earth,
accord with the spirits and gods,
conform to human hearts,
and bring order to all things.
Thus, the timing of heaven gives life,
the principles of earth provide suitability,
human offices possess capabilities,
and all things have their particular benefits.
Therefore, if heaven does not produce it,
or earth does not nurture it,
a noble person does not use it in rituals,
and the spirits and gods will not enjoy it.
To use fish and turtles as offerings in the mountains,
or deer and pigs as offerings in the marshes,
a noble person would call this ignorance of ritual.
Thus, one must consider the fixed resources of the state,
to establish the great constants of ritual,
the great order of ritual.
Based on the breadth or narrowness of the land,
the richness or simplicity of rituals,
and the abundance or scarcity of the year.
Therefore, even in a year of great scarcity,
the people are not filled with fear.
This shows that the ruler's establishment of rituals is measured.
10.4 In ritual,
timeliness is foremost,
accord comes next,
embodiment follows,
suitability after that,
and appropriateness last.
Yáo passed the throne to Shùn,
Shùn passed it to Yǔ.
Tāng exiled Jié,
King Wǔ attacked Zhòu.
This is timeliness.
The Book of Songs says:
"Not by hastening his plans,
but by pursuing filial piety."
10.5 The sacrifices to heaven and earth,
the affairs of the ancestral temple,
the way between father and son,
the righteousness between ruler and minister,
these are the principles.
10.6 The affairs of the altars of soil and grain and the mountains and rivers,
the sacrifices to the spirits and gods,
these are embodiments.
10.7 The uses in mourning and sacrifices,
the interactions with guests,
these are righteousness.
10.8 Using a lamb
and a piglet for sacrifice,
all officials are satisfied;
using a grand sacrifice with ox, sheep, and pig,
there is not necessarily surplus,
this is called appropriateness.
Feudal lords consider tortoise shells as treasures,
and jade tablets as auspicious tokens.
Common families do not treasure tortoise shells,
do not store jade tablets,
do not have tower gates,
this speaks of appropriateness.
10.9 In ritual,
there are cases where more is esteemed:
the Son of Heaven has seven temples,
feudal lords have five,
great officers have three,
scholars have one.
The Son of Heaven has twenty-six sacrificial vessels,
dukes have sixteen,
feudal lords have twelve,
senior great officers have eight,
junior great officers have six.
Feudal lords have seven attendants and seven sets of sacrificial animals,
great officers have five attendants and five sets.
The Son of Heaven's mats are five layers,
feudal lords' mats are three layers,
great officers' mats are two layers.
When the Son of Heaven dies, burial is after seven months,
with five layers and eight feather banners;
feudal lords are buried after five months,
with three layers and six feather banners;
great officers are buried after three months,
with two layers and four feather banners.
This is where more is esteemed.
10.10 There are cases where less is esteemed:
The Son of Heaven has no attendants.
Sacrificing to heaven uses a single bull.
When the Son of Heaven visits feudal lords,
the feudal lords serve a calf.
When feudal lords visit each other,
they use aromatic wine for libation,
without offerings of bamboo and wooden vessels.
Great officers use dried meat and paste in their courtesy visits.
The Son of Heaven eats one meal,
feudal lords two,
great officers and scholars three,
laborers eat without fixed number.
The grand carriage has one row of tassels,
the secondary carriage has seven rows.
Jade tablets and scepters are presented alone,
tiger and half-ring jades are presented with wine.
Sacrifices to spirits and gods use a single mat.
When feudal lords hold court,
great officers are introduced individually,
scholars as a group.
This is where less is esteemed.
10.11 There are cases where larger is esteemed:
the size of palaces and rooms,
the dimensions of utensils,
the thickness of inner and outer coffins,
the size of burial mounds.
This is where larger is esteemed.
10.12 There are cases where smaller is esteemed:
In ancestral temple sacrifices,
the noble offer with a small cup,
the humble offer with a large cup;
the honored raise a small vessel,
the lower raise a horn vessel.
For the five-offering ceremony, the wine vessels:
outside the gate, earthenware jars,
inside the gate, pots,
the ruler's vessel is a pottery jar.
This is where smaller is esteemed.
10.13 There are cases where higher is esteemed:
the Son of Heaven's hall is nine feet high,
feudal lords' seven feet,
great officers' five feet,
scholars' three feet.
The Son of Heaven and feudal lords have tower gates,
this is where higher is esteemed.
10.14 There are cases where lower is esteemed:
the highest reverence uses no altar,
but sweeps the ground for sacrifice.
The Son of Heaven and feudal lords dispense with stands for their wine vessels,
great officers and scholars use simple stands
or footed stands,
this is where lower is esteemed.
10.15 There are cases where ornamentation is esteemed:
the Son of Heaven wears a dragon robe,
feudal lords wear embroidered garments,
great officers wear patterned garments,
scholars wear black upper garments and red lower garments.
The Son of Heaven's crown,
with red and green strings, has twelve tassels,
feudal lords have nine,
senior great officers seven,
junior great officers five,
scholars three,
this is where ornamentation is esteemed.
10.16 There are cases where plainness is esteemed:
the highest reverence has no ornament,
before one's father's kin, no elaborate demeanor,
the great jade tablet is unpolished,
the grand broth is unseasoned,
the grand carriage is plain with rush mats,
the sacrificial vessel has a coarse cloth cover,
and a plain ladle;
this is where plainness is esteemed.
Confucius said:
"Rituals,
one cannot but examine!
Rituals differ,
should not be excessive,
nor insufficient."
This refers to this.
It speaks of appropriateness.
10.17 The aspect of ritual that esteems more
is due to its outward-directed mind;
virtue that is displayed and promoted,
extends to all things,
the great principle governs vast things,
thus,
how can it not esteem more?
Therefore, the noble person delights in its manifestation.
The aspect of ritual that esteems less
is due to its inward-directed mind.
The essence of virtue's production is subtle,
observing that nothing under heaven can match one's virtue,
thus,
how can it not esteem less?
Therefore, the noble person is cautious in solitude.
10.18 The sages of old,
inwardly esteemed reverence,
outwardly esteemed joy,
esteemed less in some respects,
esteemed more in others.
Therefore, when the ancient kings established rituals,
they could not make them too many,
nor too few,
but only appropriate.
10.19 Therefore,
when a gentleman offers a grand sacrifice with a full set of animal sacrifices,
it is called propriety;
when a common officer does the same,
it is called usurpation.
Guǎn Zhòng had carved guǐ vessels and red hat strings,
hill-shaped brackets and painted pillars,
which gentlemen considered excessive.
Yàn Píngzhòng, when sacrificing to his ancestors,
used pig's shoulders so small they did not cover the dòu vessels.
He wore washed clothes and cleaned hats to court,
which gentlemen considered too frugal.
10.20 Therefore,
in practicing rituals,
a gentleman cannot but be cautious;
they are the guiding principles for the multitude,
and if the principles are scattered, the multitude will be in disorder.
Confucius said:
"When I fight, I conquer;
when I sacrifice, I receive blessings,
because I have grasped the Way."
A gentleman said:
"In sacrifices, one does not pray for specific outcomes,
does not rush the timing,
does not delight in grandeur,
does not seek auspicious events,
the sacrificial animals need not be excessively large,
and the offerings need not be numerous."
10.21 Confucius said:
"How could Zāng Wénzhòng know ritual!
When Xiàfù Fúqí reversed the order of sacrifices,
he did not stop him.
He offered a burnt sacrifice to the household god,
but the household god
is worshiped by old women,
with offerings in a basin,
and honored with a vase."
10.22 Ritual
is like the body.
If the body is incomplete,
a gentleman says one is not fully human.
If it is arranged improperly,
it is as if it were incomplete.
Ritual has its major and minor aspects,
its evident and subtle points.
The major cannot be reduced,
the minor cannot be expanded,
the evident cannot be concealed,
the subtle cannot be magnified.
Thus, there are three hundred major rituals,
and three thousand detailed rituals,
but their purpose is one.
No one enters a room without going through the door.
In practicing ritual,
a gentleman exhausts his sincerity and caution,
expressing reverence with genuine compliance,
and beautifying it with elegance and genuine compliance.
In practicing ritual,
a gentleman sometimes acts directly,
sometimes indirectly with reduction,
sometimes consistently with equality,
sometimes sequentially with gradation,
sometimes spreading it widely,
sometimes pushing it forward,
sometimes imitating and embellishing,
sometimes imitating without fully achieving,
sometimes following and selecting.
The rituals of the three dynasties are one in essence,
and the people all follow them.
Some use plain colors, some use dark,
the Xia initiated them and the Yin inherited them.
10.23 In the Zhōu, the representative of the deceased sits,
with instructions and assistance from all sides;
their rituals are like this,
their principle is one;
the Xià set up the representative and concluded the sacrifice;
the Yīn had the representative sit.
The Zhōu have toasts among six representatives,
Zēngzǐ said:
"The rituals of Zhōu are like a communal feast!"
10.24 A gentleman said:
"Rituals that are close to human feelings
are not the highest.
The suburban sacrifice uses blood,
the great feast uses raw meat,
the triple offering uses parboiled meat,
the single offering uses cooked meat."
Therefore,
in practicing ritual,
a gentleman does not force his emotions artificially,
but has a basis for starting.
Thus, seven introductions are used for meetings,
otherwise it would be too simple.
Three declinations and three yieldings lead to the ceremony,
otherwise it would be too hurried.
Thus, when the people of Lǔ were to serve God,
they first served at the Pàngōng.
When the people of Jìn were to serve the Hé River,
they first served at the Èchí.
When the people of Qí were to serve Mount Tàishān,
they first served at the Pèilín.
They tied the animals for three months,
fasted for seven days,
purified for three days,
such was the height of caution.
10.25 Thus, ritual has ushers and guides,
music has pace-setters,
such is the height of refinement.
Ritual
returns to the root and follows antiquity,
not forgetting its origins.
Thus, for mournful events, no instructions are given,
for court events, music is used.
While sweet wine is used,
plain water is honored.
While the cutting knife is used,
the bell-decorated knife is esteemed.
While the comfort of fine mats is enjoyed,
rough mats are also set out.
Therefore,
when the ancient kings instituted rituals,
there was always a main principle,
so they could be transmitted and widely learned.
10.26 A gentleman said:
"Those without inner restraint
cannot examine things clearly.
To try to examine things without following ritual
is impossible.
Thus, to act without ritual
shows lack of respect.
To speak without ritual
lacks credibility.
Therefore it is said:
Ritual
is the ultimate standard of things."
10.27 Therefore,
when the ancient kings instituted rituals,
they used available resources to express their meaning.
Thus, in undertaking great affairs
one must follow the timing of heaven,
for morning and evening ceremonies one must model on the sun and moon,
for high places one must use hills and mounds,
for low places one must use rivers and marshes.
Thus, with the timely rains from heaven,
the gentleman achieves diligent success.
10.28 Therefore,
the ancient kings
honored those with virtue,
respected those with the Way, and employed those with ability.
They recommended the worthy and placed them in position,
gathered the masses and made pledges to them.
Thus, they served heaven according to heaven's ways,
served earth according to earth's ways,
ascended famous mountains to report accomplishments to heaven,
and used auspicious lands to sacrifice to God in the suburbs.
When accomplishments were reported to heaven,
phoenixes descended,
and tortoises and dragons appeared.
When God was sacrificed to in the suburbs,
wind and rain were regulated,
and cold and heat came in season.
Thus, when the sage faces south and stands,
all under heaven is greatly ordered.
10.29 The Way of Heaven is the ultimate teaching,
the sage has the ultimate virtue.
In the temple hall,
the lěi vase is in the eastern station,
the sacrificial vase is in the west.
Below the temple hall,
the suspended drum is in the west,
the answering drum is in the east.
The lord is in the eastern station,
the lady is in the chamber.
The great brightness (sun) is born in the east,
the moon is born in the west,
this is the division of yin and yang,
the positions of husband and wife.
10.30 The lord ladles from the west with the sacrificial vase,
the lady ladles from the east with the lěi vase,
ritual interactions move above,
musical responses echo below,
such is the height of harmony.
10.31 Ritual
returns to its origins;
music
delights in its completion.
Thus, the ancient kings instituted ritual to regulate affairs,
cultivated music to guide intentions.
Therefore, by observing their rituals and music,
one can know order or disorder.
Qú Bóyù said:
"The gentleman is perceptive."
Thus, by observing the implements,
one knows the skill of the artisan;
by observing the actions,
one knows the wisdom of the person.
Therefore it is said:
The gentleman is cautious about what he presents to others.
10.32 Within the grand temple, how reverent it is!
The ruler personally leads the sacrificial animal,
while the senior officials follow bearing the silk offerings.
The ruler personally prepares the sacrifice,
and his wife presents the vessel of clear wine.
The ruler personally cuts the sacrificial animal,
and his wife offers the wine.
The ministers and senior officials accompany the ruler,
and the appointed ladies accompany his wife.
How profoundly reverent they are,
how earnestly loyal,
how diligently they desire the spirits to enjoy the offerings!
The presentation of the animal is announced in the courtyard,
the blood and hair are announced in the chamber,
and when the broth is ready, it is announced in the hall.
These three announcements are made at different positions,
perhaps because the way is sought but not yet attained.
The sacrifice is set up in the hall,
and the invocation is made outside.
Hence it is said:
Is it there?
Or is it here?
10.33 A single offering is simple,
three offerings are elaborate,
five offerings are discerning,
seven offerings are divine.
10.34 The great feast—is it the affair of the king?
The three sacrificial animals, fish, and dried meats
are the delicious flavors from all within the four seas and nine provinces.
The offerings in the bamboo and wooden vessels
are the harmonious products of the four seasons.
The inclusion of metal
signifies harmony.
The bundled silk with the jade disc on top
honors virtue.
The tortoise shells placed at the front
represent foreknowledge.
Metal comes next,
to reveal true feelings.
Cinnabar, lacquer, silk, floss, bamboo, and arrowheads
are shared resources with the people.
The remaining items are not fixed goods;
each state contributes what it has,
thus bringing distant things.
When they depart,
they are sent off with the "Sì Xià" music,
showing the importance of ritual.
10.35 Sacrificing to the Di in the suburbs
is the ultimate in reverence.
The sacrifices in the ancestral temple
are the ultimate in humanity.
The funeral rites
are the ultimate in loyalty.
Preparing the grave goods and vessels
is the ultimate in humanity.
The use of silk in receiving guests
is the ultimate in righteousness.
Thus, if the noble person wishes to observe the ways of humanity and righteousness,
ritual is their foundation.
The noble person says:
"Sweetness accepts harmony,
white accepts color;
a person who is loyal and trustworthy
can learn ritual.
If there is no loyal and trustworthy person,
then ritual cannot be practiced emptily.
Therefore, it is precious to have the right person."
10.36 Confucius said:
"Reciting three hundred poems
is not enough for a single offering.
The ritual of a single offering
is not enough for the great feast.
The ritual of the great feast
is not enough for the grand assembly.
Even if the grand assembly is fully prepared,
it is not enough to feast the Di.
Do not lightly discuss ritual!"
10.37 Zǐlù was steward to the Jì family.
When the Jì family sacrificed,
they began at dawn
and the day was not enough,
so they continued by candlelight.
Even with strong physical endurance
and a solemn, reverent heart,
everyone became weary.
The officers leaned wearily during the sacrifice,
which was greatly disrespectful.
Another day during a sacrifice,
Zǐlù participated.
Indoor affairs were exchanged at the door,
hall affairs were exchanged at the steps.
They began at full daylight
and retired by late morning.
Confucius heard of this and said:
"Who says Yóu does not understand ritual?"
11.1 For the suburban sacrifice, a single beast is used,
but for the Shè and Jì sacrifices, a grand sacrifice of three beasts is used.
When the Son of Heaven visits the feudal lords,
the feudal lords serve a calf for the meal;
when the feudal lords visit the Son of Heaven,
the Son of Heaven rewards them with the grand sacrifice of three beasts:
this is the principle of valuing sincerity.
Thus, the Son of Heaven does not eat pregnant animals,
nor uses them in sacrifices to the Di.
The great carriage has one row of tassels,
the first carriage has three rows,
the secondary carriage has five rows.
The suburban sacrifice uses blood,
the great feast uses raw meat,
three offerings use lightly cooked meat,
a single offering uses well-done meat;
the highest reverence does not enjoy flavors
but values the aroma.
When feudal lords are guests,
they are presented with scented liquor.
The presentation uses fragrance,
and in the great feast,
only dried spiced meat is elevated.
11.2 In the great feast,
the ruler sits on three layers of mats when toasting.
For the envoy in a three-offering ceremony,
the ruler sits on a single mat when toasting.
This is lowering the noble to approach the humble.
11.3 The feast and the Dì sacrifice have music,
but the Shí and Cháng sacrifices have no music,
reflecting the principle of yīn and yáng.
All drinking
nourishes yáng energy;
all eating
nourishes yīn energy.
Hence, the Dì sacrifice is in spring and the Cháng sacrifice in autumn;
in spring, the orphaned are feasted,
in autumn, the elderly are fed:
the principle is the same.
Thus, the Shí and Cháng sacrifices have no music.
Drinking,
nourishing yáng energy,
therefore has music;
eating,
nourishing yīn energy,
therefore is silent.
All sound
belongs to yáng.
11.4 The dǐng and zǔ are odd in number, while the biān and dòu are even,
reflecting the principle of yīn and yáng.
The contents of the biān and dòu
are products of water and earth.
They dare not use common flavors but value variety,
which is the principle of interacting with the divine and enlightened.
11.5 When a guest enters the main gate, the "Sì Xià" is played,
showing ease and respect.
When the cup is emptied, the music stops,
which Confucius often praised.
After the ceremonial toast, the musicians ascend to sing,
to express virtue.
The singers are above,
while the gourd and bamboo instruments are below,
valuing the human voice.
Music comes from yáng,
ritual is made from yīn,
and when yīn and yáng harmonize, all things attain their place.
11.6 The ceremonial gifts have no fixed form,
to distinguish what is suitable from each land,
and regulate the timing for near and far.
Tortoise shells are placed at the front,
for foreknowledge,
followed by bells,
using harmony to accompany them.
The skins of tigers and leopards
show the taming of the fierce.
Bundled silk with a jade disc
honors virtue.
11.7 The hundred torches in the courtyard
began with Duke Huán of Qí.
The senior officials playing the "Sì Xià"
began with Zhào Wénzǐ.
11.8 For court audiences,
a senior official's private audience
is against ritual.
A senior official holds a jade tablet on missions
to demonstrate trust;
he dares not have a private audience,
to show respect;
so why would a private audience with court gifts
be in the feudal lord's court?
As a subject,
one should have no external ties,
daring not to be disloyal to the ruler.
11.9 For a senior official to feast his ruler
is against ritual.
If a senior official becomes powerful and the ruler executes him,
it is righteous;
this began with the Sān Huán.
The Son of Heaven has no guest rituals,
for none dare act as host.
When the ruler visits his subject,
he ascends by the eastern steps,
not daring to claim the house as his own.
The ceremony of royal audience,
where the Son of Heaven does not descend from the hall to receive the feudal lords.
If he descends from the hall to receive them,
it is a breach of etiquette by the Son of Heaven,
starting from King Yí onward.
11.10 The feudal lords having their bells hung in a full set like the palace arrangement,
offering sacrifices with a white bull,
striking jade chimes,
using vermilion shields adorned with metal ornaments,
and performing the "Great War" dance in ceremonial caps—
riding in the grand carriage—
these are usurpations of ritual by the feudal lords.
Having tower gates and rows of trees,
reversed stands for cups,
embroidered axes,
crimson inner garments—
these are usurpations of ritual by the high officials.
Thus, when the Son of Heaven is weak,
the feudal lords usurp.
When the high officials are strong,
the feudal lords are coerced.
In this way, they honor each other by rank,
present themselves with gifts,
bribe each other for profit,
and the rites of the world fall into chaos.
Feudal lords dare not claim ancestry from the Son of Heaven,
nor high officials from the feudal lords.
Yet establishing ducal temples in private families
is against the rites,
beginning with the Sān Huán.
11.11 The Son of Heaven preserves the descendants of two preceding dynasties,
still honoring the worthy.
Honoring the worthy does not extend beyond two generations.
Feudal lords do not treat exiled dukes as subjects.
Therefore, in ancient times, exiled dukes did not continue for generations.
11.12 The ruler faces south,
responding to the principle of yang.
The ministers face north,
responding to their ruler.
11.13 A high official's servants do not kowtow,
not to honor the household servants,
but to avoid usurping the ruler's prerogative.
When a high official has a gift to present, he does not do it personally;
when the ruler bestows a favor, he does not bow in person—
this is to avoid the ruler having to respond to him.
11.14 When the villagers performed the exorcism ritual,
Confucius stood in his court robes at the eastern steps,
to preserve the spirits of the house.
11.15 Confucius said:
"Shooting to music,
how can one listen?
How can one shoot?"
Confucius said:
"A scholar,
if asked to shoot,
and unable,
should decline on grounds of illness—
the meaning of hanging the bow."
Confucius said:
"Three days of fasting,
used in one day,
still fear insufficient reverence;
two days of drum-beating,
what is the reason?"
11.16 Confucius said:
"Holding the continuous sacrifice inside the treasury gate,
the border sacrifice in the east,
the morning market in the west—
this is a mistake."
11.17 The altar of the soil sacrifices to the earth and honors the yin energy.
The ruler faces south by the northern wall,
responding to the principle of yin.
The day used is jiǎ,
the beginning of the days.
The Son of Heaven's great altar must be exposed to frost, dew, wind, and rain, to connect with the energies of heaven and earth.
Therefore, the altar of a destroyed state is roofed over,
not receiving the yang of heaven.
The Bó Shè has a northern window,
to let in the yin light.
The altar is the way to deify the earth.
The earth carries all things,
heaven hangs forth its signs.
We take resources from the earth,
and models from heaven,
hence we honor heaven and cherish the earth,
teaching the people to make beautiful return.
The family honors the central hearth and the state the altar of the soil,
showing the root.
Only for the altar affairs
does the whole village turn out.
Only for the altar hunt
do all the people participate.
Only for the altar
do the districts contribute the millet offerings,
to repay the root and return to the beginning.
11.18 In late spring, they bring out the fire
for burning the fields.
Then they inspect the chariots and assignments,
and organize the troops,
and the ruler personally pledges at the altar,
to drill the army.
Moving left and right,
sitting and rising,
to observe their adaptability;
displaying the game to them,
and tempting them with profits,
to see that they do not disobey orders.
Seeking to subdue their will,
not coveting their gains,
thus in war they conquer,
in sacrifice they receive blessings.
11.19 When the Son of Heaven goes to the four quarters,
he first offers a burnt offering of firewood.
11.20 The suburban sacrifice
welcomes the arrival of the longest day,
greatly repaying heaven and focusing on the sun.
The site is in the southern suburbs,
taking the yang position.
Sweeping the ground and sacrificing
emphasizes simplicity.
Using earthenware and gourds
symbolizes the nature of heaven and earth.
Being in the suburbs,
it is called the suburban sacrifice.
The victim is a red ox,
favoring the color red.
Using a calf
values sincerity.
The suburban sacrifice uses a xīn day,
as the beginning of the Zhōu suburban sacrifice was on the winter solstice.
Divining for the suburb,
receiving the mandate in the ancestral temple,
consulting the tortoise in the father's temple,
shows honoring the ancestor and cherishing the father.
On the day of divination,
the king stands at the marsh,
personally hearing the pledges and commands,
showing he accepts instruction and advice.
Presenting commands inside the treasury gate
warns the officials.
The command in the great temple
warns the hundred surnames.
On the day of sacrifice,
the king wears a leather cap to hear the sacrifice report,
showing the people reverence for superiors.
Mourners do not weep,
none dare wear mourning clothes,
everywhere they sweep and reverse the earth,
and in the countryside, torches light the fields.
Without orders, the people obey their superiors.
On the day of sacrifice,
the king wears a dragon robe to symbolize heaven,
dons the ceremonial cap,
with twelve pendants of jade beads,
matching the number of heaven.
He rides in a plain carriage,
valuing its simplicity.
The banner has twelve streamers,
with dragon patterns and sun and moon,
symbolizing heaven.
Heaven hangs forth its signs,
the sage takes them as models.
The suburban sacrifice illuminates the way of heaven.
If the emperor's ox is not auspicious,
it is used as the millet god's ox.
The emperor's ox must be purified for three months,
the millet god's ox only needs to be complete.
This distinguishes serving the heavenly spirits from the human ghosts.
All things have their root in heaven,
humans have their root in ancestors,
this is why they are paired with the Supreme Deity.
The suburban sacrifice
is the great repayment of the root and return to the beginning.
11.21 The Son of Heaven's great wax sacrifice includes eight things.
The Yǐqí Shì first started the wax,
wax means
searching.
In the twelfth month of the year,
they gather all things and search to offer them.
The wax sacrifice:
focuses on the first reaper
and sacrifices to the controller of harvests.
Sacrificing to the hundred seeds
repays the harvest.
Offering to the farmers, the field markers and paths,
and the birds and beasts,
is the utmost in benevolence,
the fullest in righteousness.
The ancient noblemen,
if they used something, surely repaid it.
Welcoming the cat,
for it eats the field mice;
welcoming the tiger,
for it eats the wild boars,
they welcome and sacrifice to them.
Sacrificing to the dikes and water channels,
is part of the service.
It is said:
"Let the soil return to its dwelling,
the waters return to their channels,
let no insects cause harm,
and let grasses and trees return to their marshes."
They offer sacrifices wearing leather caps and plain garments.
The plain garments
are to send off the deceased.
The hempen girdle and hazel staff
signify the reduction in mourning.
The Zhà sacrifice
represents the utmost in benevolence
and the fullest expression of righteousness.
Wearing yellow robes and yellow caps to sacrifice
is to give rest to the farmers.
The country folk wear yellow caps;
the yellow caps
are rustic attire.
11.22 The Grand Luóshì,
who is the Son of Heaven's officer in charge of birds and beasts,
receives the tribute offerings from the feudal lords.
They come wearing straw hats,
honoring the rustic attire.
The Luóshì presents deer and women,
and announces to the guests,
cautioning the feudal lords, saying:
"Those who indulge in hunting
and women will lose their states.
The Son of Heaven plants melons and flowers,
not the kinds that are stored away."
The Eight Zhà sacrifices are used to record the conditions of the four directions.
If the years in the four directions are not favorable,
the Eight Zhà sacrifices are not conducted,
to be cautious with the people's wealth.
In regions with favorable years,
the Zhà sacrifices are conducted,
to shift the people's attention.
After the Zhà sacrifices, harvests are gathered,
and the people rest.
Therefore, after the Zhà sacrifices,
the noblemen do not initiate labor.
11.23 The pickled vegetables in the constant dòu vessels
are the harmonious qi of aquatic plants;
the meat pastes
are products of the land.
The additional dòu vessels
contain land products;
their meat pastes
are aquatic products.
The offerings in biān and dòu vessels
are products of water and land,
not daring to use common, familiar flavors
or to value variety,
which is the principle of interacting with the divine and bright,
not the way of savoring flavors.
The offerings of the former kings
could be eaten
but were not to be craved.
The ceremonial robes and chariots
could be displayed
but were not to be favored.
The "Wǔ" dance, though majestic,
was not for enjoyment.
The awe of the ancestral temple
was not for comfort.
The vessels of the ancestral temple
could be used
but not for convenient benefit,
because interacting with the divine and bright
cannot be the same as the principle of seeking comfort and pleasure.
The excellence of fine wines,
yet the preference for plain water and clear water,
values the origin of the five flavors.
The beauty of embroidered silks,
yet the preference for coarse cloth,
returns to the beginning of women's work.
The comfort of fine mats,
yet the preference for rush and straw mats,
clarifies this.
The grand broth is not seasoned,
valuing its simplicity.
The great jade tablet is not carved,
appreciating its natural state.
The beauty of red lacquer and carved patterns,
yet riding in plain carriages,
honors their plainness,
valuing their simplicity alone.
Therefore, interacting with the divine and bright
cannot be the same as seeking excessive comfort and familiarity.
Only then is it appropriate.
The tripods and stands are odd-numbered, while the biān and dòu vessels are even-numbered,
reflecting the principle of yīn and yáng.
The yellow-eyed vessel,
is the highest尊 of fragrant liquor.
Yellow represents the center;
the eye represents clarity and brightness of qì.
It means drawing from within and being clear and bright on the outside.
In sacrificing to Heaven,
they sweep the ground and sacrifice there,
focusing on its simplicity.
The excellence of pickled pastes,
yet the preference for boiled salt,
values natural products.
The use of cutting knives,
yet the honor given to the bell-adorned knife,
values its significance.
It is after the sound harmonizes that the cutting is done.
11.24 The meaning of the capping ceremony:
At the first capping,
it is the black cloth cap.
In great antiquity, caps were of cloth,
and for solemn occasions, they were dyed black.
As for its tassels,
Confucius said:
"I have not heard of this.
It is acceptable to discard the cap after use."
The eldest son is capped at the zuò position,
to signify succession.
The libation is offered at the guest's position,
to honor his maturity.
The three additions of caps increase in尊贵,
symbolizing his aspirations.
After capping, he is given a style name,
to respect his personal name.
The wěimào cap
is the way of the Zhōu.
The zhāngfǔ cap
is the way of the Yīn.
The móuzhuī cap
is the way of the Xià Hòu shì.
The Zhōu biàn,
the Yīn xǔ,
and the Xià shōu.
The Three Dynasties all used leather caps and plain accumulations.
There is no capping rite for great officers,
but there is a marriage rite for them.
In ancient times,
one received rank only after fifty,
so how could there be a capping rite for great officers?
The existence of a capping rite for feudal lords
was a late development of the Xià.
The eldest son of the Son of Heaven
is a scholar.
Under Heaven, none are noble by birth.
Succeeding to become a feudal lord
is to emulate the worthy.
Appointing people to office and rank
is based on the degree of their virtue.
Posthumous names are given after death,
which is the current practice;
in ancient times, one had no rank in life,
and no posthumous name in death.
What is尊贵 in ritual
is尊贵 its meaning.
Losing its meaning
and displaying its forms
is the task of the invocators and scribes.
Thus, the forms can be displayed,
but the meaning is difficult to know.
Knowing its meaning and reverently preserving it
is how the Son of Heaven governs the world.
11.25 Heaven and Earth unite, and then all things flourish.
Marriage rites
are the beginning of ten thousand generations.
Taking a wife from a different surname
is to ally with distant families and emphasize distinction.
The betrothal gifts must be sincere,
and the words must not be insincere.
They are told to be upright and faithful;
faithfulness
is for serving others;
faithfulness
is the virtue of a wife.
Once united with him,
she does not change her whole life.
Therefore, if the husband dies, she does not remarry.
The man personally goes to meet the bride,
the man precedes the woman,
which is the principle of the firm and the soft.
Heaven precedes Earth,
the ruler precedes the subject,
the principle is the same.
Holding gifts to meet each other
respectfully makes distinctions clear.
When men and women are distinct,
then father and son are close.
When father and son are close,
then righteousness arises.
When righteousness arises,
then ritual is established.
When ritual is established,
then all things are at peace.
Without distinction and without righteousness,
it is the way of birds and beasts.
The groom personally hands her the carriage strap,
showing his affection.
Showing his affection
means he cherishes her.
Revering and cherishing her—
this is how the former kings gained the empire.
Going out the main gate first,
the man leads the woman,
the woman follows the man:
the principle of husband and wife begins here.
A woman
is one who follows others.
In youth, she follows her father and elder brothers;
married, she follows her husband;
when her husband dies, she follows her sons.
A husband
is a leader;
a husband
is one who leads others with wisdom.
Wearing the dark ceremonial cap and fasting
are for the spirits and the forces of yin and yang.
Since she will become the mistress of the state,
the successor to the ancestors,
how can one not show her reverence?
Eating from the same sacrificial animal
shows shared honor and humility.
Thus a woman holds no rank of her own,
but follows her husband's rank,
and is seated according to her husband's seniority.
Vessels of earthenware and gourds
are used to uphold ritual.
The three dynastic kings used earthenware and gourds for the sacrificial feast.
The next morning,
the wife washes and presents food;
after the parents-in-law have eaten,
she eats their leftovers,
showing their intimacy.
The parents-in-law descend by the western steps,
the wife by the eastern steps,
indicating the transfer of the household to her.
No music is used in the wedding ceremony,
reflecting the principle of quiet solemnity.
Music
belongs to the yang energy.
The wedding is not congratulated,
as it marks the natural succession of generations.
11.26 The sacrifices of the Yǒuyú clan
valued the vital energy.
Offering blood, raw meat, and half-cooked meat in sacrifice
was to use the vital energy.
11.27 The Yīn people valued sound.
Before the aromas had developed,
they cleansed the air with music.
After three repetitions of the music,
they went out to welcome the sacrificial animal.
The calls of the sounds
were to announce to heaven and earth.
The Zhōu people valued scent.
They poured out offerings of fragrant liquor.
Blended aromatic herbs with the liquor.
The scent
penetrated downward to the springs.
They poured it with jade scepters,
using the energy of jade.
After the pouring,
they welcomed the sacrificial animal,
to draw forth the yin energy.
Blending artemisia with millet;
the scent
rose to the roofs and walls.
Thus after the libation,
they burned artemisia mixed with the smells of fat and grains.
In all sacrifices,
they were careful in these matters.
The ethereal soul returns to heaven,
the bodily soul returns to earth.
Therefore, in sacrifice,
they sought the meaning of yin and yang.
The Yīn people first sought the yang,
the Zhōu people first sought the yin.
They announced prayers in the chamber,
seated the representative of the deceased in the hall,
slaughtered the animal in the courtyard,
and presented its head in the chamber.
In the direct sacrifice,
they prayed before the spirit tablet;
in the searching sacrifice,
they prayed at the side altar.
Not knowing where the spirit resided—
was it there? Or here?
Or perhaps among distant people?
Sacrificing at the side altar
was like seeking it among the distant ones.
Bēng means "distant",
qí means "reverence".
Wealth means blessing.
The head
symbolizes uprightness.
Xiàng
means to offer a feast.
Jiǎ
means long
and great.
Shī
means to display.
The hair and blood
announce the whole and hidden offering.
Announcing the whole and hidden offering
is the way to honor purity.
Offering blood
honors the abundant vital energy.
Offering the lung, liver, and heart
honors the organs that govern the energy.
Offering millet with the lung,
and the libation with clear water,
repays the yin.
Taking the fat and burning it,
and presenting the head,
repays the yang.
Mixing the libation with clear water
values freshness.
All mixing
is to renew it.
It is called "clear water"
because the master's purity is manifested in this water.
The ruler bows twice and touches his head to the ground,
bares his arm and personally cuts the meat,
showing the utmost reverence.
The utmost reverence
is submission.
Bowing
is submission;
touching the head to the ground
is deep submission;
baring the arm
is complete submission.
In sacrifice, they are called "filial grandson" or "filial son",
according to the meaning;
called "so-and-so, the great-grandson",
refers to the state.
The assistants in sacrifice
allow the host to express his reverence
and perfect his good wishes
without yielding.
With raw, prepared, half-cooked, and cooked offerings,
how can one know what the spirits enjoy?
The host simply expresses his reverence to the utmost.
Raising the jia and horn cups,
they request the representative to be seated.
In ancient times,
the representative stood when inactive,
and sat when there was something to do.
The representative
is the image of the spirit.
The invocator
conveys the messages.
Filtering the wine with mao grass
makes it clear.
Mixing the zhan wine with clear wine,
and the aromatic wine with zhan wine,
is like mixing clear and zhan wines with aged wine.
Sacrifices may be for prayer,
for thanksgiving,
or for averting evil.
The dark robes of fasting
deepen solemn thoughts in yin quietude.
Thus, after three days of fasting,
the gentleman must see those he sacrifices to.
12.1 The later kings ordered the prime minister
to bestow virtue upon the millions of people.
12.2 In serving his parents,
at the first crow of the cock,
the son washes his hands and rinses his mouth,
combs his hair, binds it with a silk ribbon, inserts a hairpin, and ties it all together,
brushes his cap tassels, puts on his cap with its hanging ribbons and strings,
dons his ceremonial robe, knee covers, and girdle,
and inserts his tablet.
He wears various objects on left and right:
on the left, a duster, knife, whetstone, small spike, and metal sun-mirror;
on the right, a thumb ring, arm guard, tube case, knife sheath, large spike, and wood fire-drill;
leg bindings, and shoes with laces tied.
12.3 A wife serving her parents-in-law
does so as she would her own parents.
At the first crow of the cock,
she washes her hands and rinses her mouth,
combs her hair and binds it with a silk ribbon,
inserts a hairpin and ties it all together,
and puts on her robe and girdle.
On the left, she wears a duster, knife, whetstone, small spike, and metal sun-mirror;
on the right, needles, case, thread, and silk floss,
placed in a small pouch, along with a large spike and wood fire-drill;
a neck ribbon,
and laced shoes.
When going to the place of parents or parents-in-law,
upon arrival,
one should lower one's voice and speak cheerfully.
Inquire if their clothes are warm or cold,
and if they have any pains, irritations, or itches,
respectfully soothe and scratch them.
When they go out or come in,
either walk ahead or follow behind,
and respectfully support them.
When presenting water for washing,
the younger one holds the basin,
the elder pours the water,
requesting to wash,
and after washing, hand them a towel.
Ask what they desire and respectfully offer it,
with a gentle expression to warm their hearts.
Whether they want thick congee, thin congee, wine, sweet wine, vegetables with meat, soup, beans, wheat, hemp seeds, rice, millet, sorghum, or glutinous millet,
add dates, chestnuts, malt sugar, or honey to sweeten them;
use violet leaves, shepherd's purse, white elm bark, elm bark, fresh or dried ingredients, and seasoned sauces to smooth them;
apply animal fats or oils to moisten them.
Parents and parents-in-law must taste the food before retiring.
12.4 For boys and girls who have not yet reached capping or hair-pinning age,
at the first crow of the rooster,
all wash their faces and rinse their mouths,
comb their hair and tie it up,
brush their bangs, bind their hair in horns,
fasten their sashes,
and all wear scent pouches.
At dawn, they pay their respects,
asking, "What have you eaten and drunk?"
If they have already eaten, they withdraw;
if not,
they assist the elders in preparing the meal.
12.5 In all households, inside and out,
at the first crow of the rooster,
all wash their faces and rinse their mouths,
put on clothes,
put away pillows and mats,
sprinkle water and sweep the rooms, hall, and courtyard,
spread out mats,
and each attends to their duties.
12.6 Young children may sleep early and rise late,
as they wish,
and eat at no fixed times.
12.7 From the rank of appointed officials upward,
fathers and sons live in separate residences.
At dawn, they pay their respects,
offering kind words and sweet delicacies;
after sunrise, they withdraw,
each attending to their duties.
At sunset, they pay evening respects,
again offering kind words and sweet delicacies.
12.8 When parents or parents-in-law are about to sit,
present the mat and ask which direction to face.
When they are about to lie down,
the elder presents the mat and asks where to place their feet.
The younger holds the bed and assists them to sit.
Attendants bring the small table,
put away the mat and fine mat,
hang up the quilt and store the pillow in a box,
roll up the fine mat and cover it.
12.9 The clothes,
quilts, mats, pillows, and small tables of parents and parents-in-law should not be moved arbitrarily.
Their staffs and shoes should be treated with reverence,
and one dare not approach them.
Vessels like dūn, móu, zhī, and yí
should not be used unless with leftover food;
for regular food and drink,
unless it is leftovers,
one dare not consume it.
12.10 When parents are alive,
during regular morning and evening meals,
sons and daughters-in-law assist with the leftovers.
After eating, they always finish the leftovers.
If the father has died but the mother is alive,
the eldest son serves the meal,
and the other sons and daughters-in-law assist with leftovers as before.
Sweet and tender foods are given to the young children as leftovers.
12.11 In the presence of parents or parents-in-law,
if they give an order,
respond with "yìng" or "wéi" and answer respectfully.
In moving forward, backward, or turning around, be cautious and composed.
When ascending, descending, entering, exiting, bowing, or moving freely,
one must not belch, sigh, sneeze, cough, yawn, stretch, stand unevenly, lean, or glance sideways.
One must not spit or snivel;
if cold, one must not add more clothes;
if itchy, one must not scratch;
unless engaged in respectful tasks,
one must not bare the arms or chest;
unless wading through water, one must not lift the garments;
undergarments and quilts should not show their inner lining.
If parents spit or snivel, do not look.
If their hats or belts are soiled,
prepare ashes and request to wash them;
if their clothes are dirty,
prepare ashes and request to launder them;
if their clothes are torn,
thread a needle and request to mend them.
Every five days,
prepare warm water and request they bathe;
every three days, prepare for hair washing.
If their faces are dirty in between,
prepare rice water and request they wash their faces;
if their feet are dirty,
prepare warm water and request they wash their feet.
The young serving the elder,
the lowly serving the noble,
all follow these rules.
12.12 Men do not discuss internal affairs,
women do not discuss external affairs.
Unless during sacrifices or mourning,
they do not hand objects directly to each other.
If they must hand something,
the woman receives it in a basket;
if there is no basket,
both sit, place the object on the ground, and then retrieve it.
Men and women do not share a well,
do not share a bathing area,
do not share sleeping mats,
do not borrow or lend from each other,
do not exchange clothes,
internal words do not go out,
external words do not come in.
When a man enters the inner quarters,
he must not whistle or point,
at night he must use a candle,
if there is no candle, he should not go.
When a woman goes out,
she must cover her face,
at night she must use a candle,
if there is no candle, she should not go.
On the road,
men keep to the right,
women keep to the left.
For filial and respectful sons and daughters-in-law,
the commands of parents and parents-in-law
must not be opposed or neglected.
