If they are given food or drink,
even if not fond of it,
they must taste it and wait;
if given clothes,
even if unwilling,
they must wear them and wait;
if assigned tasks,
and someone else does them,
even if they do not wish it,
let them do it temporarily,
and let them handle it,
then later resume it.
If sons or daughters-in-law have laborious tasks,
even if deeply loved,
let them do it temporarily,
but rather allow them frequent rest.
If sons or daughters-in-law are not filial or respectful,
do not resent them immediately,
but teach them first;
if they cannot be taught,
then show displeasure;
if displeasure does not work,
the son may be expelled, and the daughter-in-law sent away,
but without publicizing the breach of ritual.
If parents have faults,
advise them with a subdued voice, pleasant expression, and gentle tone.
If the advice is not heeded,
increase respect and filial piety;
if they are pleased, advise again;
if displeased,
rather than letting them offend the local community,
persist in earnest advice.
If parents are angry and displeased,
even if beaten until bleeding,
one must not resent or complain,
but increase respect and filial piety.
If parents have maidservants' children or concubines' children and grandchildren,
and deeply love them,
even after parents pass away,
respect them lifelong without decline.
If a son has two concubines,
and parents love one,
while the son loves the other,
in matters of clothing, food, and drink,
or in duties,
the son must not treat his favored one equally to the parents' favored one,
even after parents pass away, without decline.
If a son is very fond of his wife,
but parents are displeased,
he should divorce her.
If a son is not fond of his wife,
but parents say:
"She serves us well,"
the son should perform the husband-wife rituals,
lifelong without decline.
Even after parents pass away,
when about to do good,
thinking to leave a good name for parents,
one must act resolutely.
When about to do wrong,
thinking it would bring shame to parents,
one must refrain.
12.13 When the father-in-law has passed away and the mother-in-law is elderly,
the principal wife, in matters of sacrifices
and receiving guests,
must consult the mother-in-law on every occasion,
while the secondary wives consult the principal wife.
If the father-in-law and mother-in-law assign tasks to the principal wife,
she must not be negligent, unfriendly, or disrespectful toward the secondary wives.
If the father-in-law and mother-in-law assign tasks to a secondary wife,
she must not dare to act as an equal to the principal wife,
not daring to walk side by side with her,
not daring to issue commands together,
not daring to sit together.
In all cases, a wife,
unless ordered to go to her private room,
does not dare to withdraw.
If a wife has any matter to attend to,
whether great or small, she must seek permission from her father-in-law and mother-in-law.
A wife should have no private wealth,
no private livestock,
no private utensils,
not daring to lend privately,
not daring to give privately.
If a wife is gifted with food and drink, clothing, cloth and silk, sashes, or fragrant herbs,
she should receive them and present them to her father-in-law and mother-in-law.
If they accept them, she is pleased,
as if she herself had just received the gift.
If they return the gift to her, she should decline,
but if they insist,
she accepts it as if receiving a new gift,
storing it away for future need.
If a wife has private relatives or brothers and wishes to give them something,
she must again report the reason for it,
and only after it is granted may she give it to them.
12.14 The legitimate sons and collateral sons
should reverently serve the clan heir and his wife.
12.15 Even if they are noble and wealthy,
they should not enter the house of the clan heir with an air of nobility and wealth.
Even if they have many carriages and followers,
they should leave them outside,
entering with humility and simplicity.
If younger members of the clan are given utensils, clothing, furs, quilts, carriages, or horses,
they must offer the best of them
before daring to use the next best themselves.
If what they have is not worthy of offering,
they should not dare to bring it into the clan heir's gate,
nor dare to flaunt their wealth and status before their fathers, elder brothers, or the clan.
If they are wealthy,
they should prepare two sacrificial animals,
offering the superior one to the clan heir,
and both husband and wife should fast and show reverence to the clan,
only after the ceremony daring to conduct their private sacrifices.
12.16 Grains for meals:
broomcorn millet, foxtail millet, rice, and fine millet;
white broomcorn millet, yellow fine millet, sprouted grain, and early-harvested grain.
Dishes for meals:
beef soup, mutton soup, pork soup, minced meat, and roasted beef.
Minced meat, sliced beef; minced meat, beef cut into thin slices.
Roasted mutton, sliced mutton, minced meat, roasted pork.
Minced meat, sliced pork, mustard sauce, sliced fish.
Pheasant, rabbit, quail, and quail-like bird.
12.17 Drinks:
double-fermented sweet wine,
clear and unfiltered rice wine,
clear and unfiltered millet wine,
clear and unfiltered fine millet wine,
or sometimes using thin gruel to make sweet wine,
millet gruel,
sour drink, water, plum juice, and sweetened water.
12.18 Wines: clear and white.
12.19 Delicacies:
parched grain, cakes, rice powder, and fermented gruel.
12.20 Foods:
snail paste with wild rice stems,
pheasant soup;
wheat food,
with dried meat soup,
chicken soup;
polished rice,
dog meat soup,
rabbit soup;
seasoned with rice paste but without smartweed.
Boiled pork,
wrapped with bitter herbs and stuffed with smartweed;
boiled chicken,
with meat paste and stuffed with smartweed;
boiled fish,
with fish roe sauce and stuffed with smartweed;
boiled turtle,
with meat paste and stuffed with smartweed.
Dried seasoned meat,
ant egg paste,
dried meat soup,
rabbit paste,
sliced elk meat,
fish paste,
sliced fish,
mustard sauce,
raw elk meat,
minced meat, sauce,
pickled peaches,
pickled plums,
egg-shaped salt.
12.21 In general, the temperature of solid foods should be like that of spring;
that of soups like summer;
that of sauces like autumn;
that of drinks like winter.
12.22 In general, for seasoning,
spring should have more sour,
summer more bitter,
autumn more pungent,
winter more salty,
and all should be harmonized with smooth and sweet flavors.
12.23 Beef pairs well with rice,
mutton with broomcorn millet,
pork with foxtail millet,
dog with fine millet,
goose with wheat,
fish with wild rice stems.
12.24 Spring is suitable for lamb and suckling pig, cooked with fragrant fat;
summer for dried pheasant and dried fish, cooked with mutton fat;
autumn for calf and fawn, cooked with beef fat;
winter for fresh fish and wild fowl, cooked with lard.
12.25 Beef jerky,
venison jerky,
wild boar jerky,
elk jerky,
roe deer jerky;
elk, deer, wild boar, and roe deer
can all be sliced raw;
pheasant and rabbit are both served with vegetables.
Sparrow, quail-like bird, cicada, bee, mushroom and bracket fungus,
water caltrop, Chinese quince, jujube, chestnut, hazelnut,
persimmon, melon, peach, plum, apricot,
Chinese hawthorn, pear, ginger, cinnamon.
12.26 A minister's casual meal
may include sliced meat but not dried meat,
or dried meat but not sliced meat.
A scholar should not have two soups or sliced meat dishes,
and commoners, even the elderly, do not eat meat alone without grain.
12.27 For sliced meat:
use spring onion in spring,
mustard in autumn.
For pork:
use leek in spring,
smartweed in autumn.
For animal fat, use spring onion;
for oil, use Chinese chive;
for the three sacrificial animals, use Chinese prickly ash;
for seasoning, use vinegar;
for game, use plum.
Quail soup,
chicken soup,
and rice bird
are cooked with smartweed.
Steamed bream and chub,
roasted young bird,
pheasant,
with fragrant herbs, but without smartweed.
12.28 Do not eat young turtle,
remove the intestines of wolf,
remove the kidneys of dog,
remove the backbone of raccoon dog,
remove the rump of rabbit,
remove the head of fox,
remove the brain of pig,
remove the spine bone of fish,
remove the anus of turtle.
12.29 For meat, it is called "stripping";
for fish, "preparing";
for jujubes, "renewing";
for chestnuts, "selecting";
for peaches, "wiping";
for hawthorns and pears, "piercing".
12.30 If an ox bellows at night, its meat is putrid;
if a sheep has thin, tangled wool, its meat is rank;
if a dog has red thighs and is restless, its meat is foul;
if a bird's feathers are discolored and its cry hoarse, its meat is stale;
if a pig looks upward and its eyelashes cross, its meat is腥;
if a horse has a black spine and spotted forelegs, its meat is worm-infested;
if a young bird's tail is not a handful,
do not eat it;
the tail fat of goose,
the rib meat of swan and owl,
the tail fat of duck,
chicken liver,
goose kidney,
the lower part of bustard,
deer tripe.
12.31 Raw meat, when finely minced, is called "kuài" (sliced meat);
when in large pieces, is called "xuān" (sliced raw);
some say: elk, deer, and fish are made into "zū" (pickled meat);
roe deer is made into "pì jī" (minced);
wild boar is sliced raw;
rabbit is made into "wǎn pí" (thin slices);
chop spring onions or Chinese chives,
and soak them in vinegar to soften them.
12.32 Thick soups and cooked grains
were equally consumed by all from nobles down to commoners without distinction.
Grandees did not have regular provisions,
but those over seventy had storage shelves.
The Son of Heaven's shelves
had five compartments on the left
and five on the right.
Dukes, marquises, and earls had five in their chambers,
grandees had three shelves,
and officers had one ledge.
12.33 Regarding the care of the elderly:
The Yǒuyú clan used the banquet ritual,
the Xiàhòu clan used the feast ritual,
the Yīn people used the food ritual,
and the Zhōu people refined and combined them all.
At fifty, one was cared for in the local districts,
at sixty in the capital,
at seventy in the national academy,
applying up to the feudal lords.
At eighty,
when receiving the ruler's command,
one knelt once and touched the ground twice;
the blind did likewise,
and at ninety, someone was sent to receive it.
At fifty, one had different grains;
at sixty, meat was kept overnight;
at seventy, two meals were served;
at eighty, delicacies were constant;
at ninety, food and drink were not withheld from the bedside,
and meals could follow one on outings.
At sixty, burial items were prepared yearly;
at seventy, seasonally;
at eighty, monthly;
at ninety, daily—
except for the shroud, burial cloths, quilt, and cover,
which were made only after death.
At fifty, one begins to decline;
at sixty, without meat one is not satisfied;
at seventy, without silk one is not warm;
at eighty, without others' warmth one is not warm;
at ninety, even with others, one is not warm.
At fifty, one used a staff at home;
at sixty, in the district;
at seventy, in the capital;
at eighty, at court;
at ninety,
if the Son of Heaven wished to consult him,
he visited his home with delicacies.
At seventy, one did not wait at court;
at eighty, one was inquired after monthly;
at ninety, daily provisions were sent.
At fifty, one was exempt from labor service;
at sixty, from military duties;
at seventy, from receiving guests;
at eighty, from fasting and mourning observances.
At fifty, one received rank;
at sixty, no longer attended school;
at seventy, retired from office;
all over seventy,
only wore mourning hemp for bereavement.
The Three Dynasties all honored the elderly according to age:
for an eighty-year-old,
one son was exempt from service;
for a ninety-year-old,
his whole household was exempt;
the blind received the same.
As long as parents were alive,
children, though old, did not sit in their presence.
The Yǒuyú clan cared for state elders at the Shàngxiáng,
and common elders at the Xiàxiáng;
the Xiàhòu clan, state elders at the Dōngxù,
common elders at the Xīxù;
the Yīn people, state elders at the Yòuxué,
common elders at the Zuǒxué;
the Zhōu people, state elders at the Dōngjiāo,
common elders at the Yúxiáng,
located in the western suburbs.
The Yǒuyú clan wore ceremonial caps for sacrifices
and deep robes for elderly care;
the Xiàhòu clan wore headgear for sacrifices
and banquet robes for elderly care;
the Yīn people wore ritual caps for sacrifices
and plain white robes for elderly care;
the Zhōu people wore crowns for sacrifices
and black robes for elderly care.
12.34 Zēngzǐ said:
"A filial son in caring for the elderly
delights their hearts without opposing their wishes,
pleases their ears and eyes, and comforts their rest,
faithfully nourishing them with food and drink.
A filial son's duty lasts a lifetime—
'lifetime' meaning
not just the parents' lifetime,
but his own entire life;
thus, what parents loved he also loved,
what they revered he also revered,
even to dogs and horses, all the more so,
how much more for people!"
In elderly care,
the Five Emperors set examples,
the Three Kings sought advice.
The Five Emperors, as models,
nourished the body and spirit without seeking words,
but recorded good deeds as instructive history.
The Three Kings also set examples,
cared for the elderly and then sought advice,
moderating the rituals,
all with instructive histories.
12.35 Chún'ǎo: minced meat fried,
placed on upland rice,
drenched with fat,
called chún'ǎo.
Chúnwú: minced meat fried,
placed on millet,
drenched with fat,
called chúnwú.
Páo:
take a suckling pig or lamb,
slaughter and clean it,
fill its belly with dates,
wrap in reed mats,
plaster with clay,
roast it,
when the clay dries,
crack it open,
wash hands and rub the meat,
remove the membrane,
make rice powder, mix with water for paste,
coat the pig, fry in fat,
fat fully covering it,
in a large cauldron of boiling water,
place a small tripod with spiced meat inside,
keeping the water below the tripod rim,
for three days and nights without extinguishing the fire,
then season with vinegar and meat sauce.
12.36 Dǎozhēn:
take meat from ox, sheep, elk, deer, or river deer—
only the tenderloin—equal portions of each to the ox's, pound
on both sides,
remove the tendons,
cook, take out,
remove the membrane,
tenderize the meat.
take freshly slaughtered beef,
slice thinly,
cutting across the grain;
soak in fine wine,
by the next morning
eat it with sauce or vinegar marinade.
pound the meat,
remove the membrane,
lay reeds,
spread beef on them,
sprinkle powdered cinnamon and ginger,
sprinkle with salt,
dry and eat.
Do the same with lamb,
and with elk, deer, or river deer,
all like ox and sheep.
For moist meat,
soak and fry with sauce;
for dried meat,
pound and eat.
take meat from ox, sheep, or pig,
equal parts of three, mince finely,
mix with rice,
two parts rice to one part meat,
form into cakes, and fry.
12.40 Gānliáo:
take one dog liver,
wrap it
in its fat, moisten and roast,
until the fat
is crisp, without adding herbs.
Take rice, mix with water,
mince wolf fat finely,
and combine with rice to make porridge.
12.41 Ritual
begins with the careful distinction between husband and wife,
in building houses,
separating inner and outer quarters.
Men reside outside,
women inside,
with deep chambers and secure gates,
guarded by doorkeepers and eunuchs,
so men do not enter,
nor women leave.
Men and women do not share clothes racks,
wives dare not hang clothes on their husband's rack,
nor store them in his boxes,
nor bathe together.
When the husband is absent,
store his pillow in a case, and roll up and put away his mat and coverings.
The young serve the elder,
the lowly serve the noble,
all in like manner.
The rites for husband and wife
only allow cohabitation without separation
when they reach seventy.
Thus, although a concubine may be old,
if her age has not reached fifty,
she must participate in the rotational intimate service every five days.
When preparing to serve,
she purifies herself,
rinses her mouth and bathes,
carefully attends to her clothing,
combs her hair, ties it with a silk ribbon, inserts a hairpin, and binds it at the back,
adorns with horn ornaments and trims her bangs,
fastens her lapel ribbons, and dons her plain shoes.
Even for maids and concubines,
in matters of clothing and food and drink,
they must defer to their elders.
If the wife is absent,
no concubine dares to assume the nightly service.
12.42 When the wife is about to give birth,
as the month of delivery arrives,
she resides in a side chamber.
The husband sends someone to inquire twice daily about her condition.
When labor begins, he inquires personally,
but the wife dares not appear before him,
instead having her governess dress formally to respond.
Until the child is born,
the husband again sends someone to inquire twice daily.
If the husband is observing purification,
he does not enter the door of the side chamber.
When the child is born,
for a boy, a bow is set outside the left of the door;
for a girl, a handkerchief is set outside the right of the door.
On the third day,
the child is first carried,
with a bow used for a boy but not for a girl.
12.43 When the heir of a feudal lord is born,
it is reported to the lord.
The child is received with a grand sacrifice of a bull, sheep, and pig,
with the steward overseeing the preparations.
On the third day,
a diviner selects a scholar to carry the child.
The chosen one, having fasted and purified overnight,
dons court robes and stands outside the inner chamber door.
Chanting, he carries the child,
while an archer uses a mulberry bow
and six arrows of cogongrass
to shoot toward heaven, earth, and the four directions.
The guardian then receives and carries the child.
The steward offers a sweet wine toast to the carrier,
presenting him with a bundle of silk.
The wife of the divined scholar
or a concubine of a high official
is appointed to nurse the child.
12.44 For all receptions of a newborn,
an auspicious day is chosen.
For the eldest son, a grand sacrifice is used;
for commoners, a single suckling pig;
for lower officials, a single pig;
for high officials, a lesser sacrifice of a sheep and pig;
for the heir of a feudal lord, a grand sacrifice.
If it is not the eldest son,
then all ranks are reduced by one grade.
12.45 A separate nursery is established for the child within the palace.
From among the various mothers and suitable women,
one must seek those who are generous and kind,
gentle, respectful,
cautious, and sparing in speech,
to appoint as the child's instructor.
The next is appointed as the nurturing mother,
and the next as the protecting mother.
All reside in the child's chamber,
and others do not enter without reason.
At the end of the third month,
a day is chosen to cut the hair, leaving some unshorn;
for a boy, horn-shaped locks; for a girl, cross-shaped locks;
otherwise, left for boys and right for girls.
On this day,
the wife presents the child to the father.
Noble persons dress formally;
from appointed scholars downward,
all rinse and bathe.
Men and women rise early,
bathe, and dress in clean clothes.
They prepare food as for the first day of the month.
The husband enters the gate,
ascends by the eastern steps,
and stands facing west on the eastern platform.
The wife carries the child out from the side room,
standing under the central beam, facing east.
The governess first
announces on her behalf:
"The mother, so-and-so, dares to reverently present the child to you on this day."
The husband responds:
"May he respectfully have a guide."
The father grasps the child's right hand,
strokes his chin and names him.
The wife responds:
"May he remember to accomplish."
She then turns to the left,
and hands the child to the instructor.
The instructor fully informs the various wives and mothers of the name.
The wife then returns to her chamber.
The husband reports the name to the steward,
who fully informs the various men of the name.
It is written:
"In such year, such month, such day, so-and-so was born,"
and stored away.
The steward informs the local historian,
who writes it in duplicate:
one copy stored in the local archive,
the other presented to the district historian.
The district historian presents it to the district chief,
who orders it stored in the district archive.
The husband then dines according to the nurturing rites.
12.46 When the heir is born,
the lord bathes, dons court robes,
and the lady does the same.
Both stand on the eastern steps, facing west.
A palace matron carries the child up from the western steps.
The lord names him,
then descends.
Legitimate sons and secondary sons are presented in the outer chamber,
where he pats their heads, strokes their chins, and names them,
following the initial rites,
without the exchange of words.
12.47 In general, when naming a child,
one does not use sun or moon,
nor the name of a state,
nor a hidden ailment.
Sons of high officials and scholars
dare not have the same name as the heir.
When a concubine is about to give birth,
as the month of delivery arrives,
the husband sends someone to inquire once daily about her condition.
At the end of the third month after the child's birth,
she rinses, bathes, and fasts overnight.
She is presented in the inner chamber,
treated with the same rites as when she first entered the household.
After the lord has eaten,
the leftovers are cleared
and specially given to her to consume,
after which she enters to serve.
12.48 When a secondary son of a lord is born,
the birth occurs in a side chamber.
At the end of the third month,
his mother bathes, dons court robes, and is presented to the lord.
An usher presents her child,
and if the lord wishes to bestow a gift,
he names the child.
For other sons,
he orders an official to name them.
12.49 Commoners who lack a side chamber,
when the month of delivery arrives,
the husband moves out to other quarters.
The inquiries about her
and the rites for the child meeting the father
are no different.
Whenever the father is alive,
a grandchild presented to the grandfather
is also named by him,
with rites like those for a son meeting the father,
without the exchange of words.
12.50 Those who nurse a child
are released after three years.
When seen in the lord's palace, they are rewarded for their toil.
Sons of high officials have nursing mothers;
wives of scholars raise their own children.
12.51 From appointed scholars upward and sons of high officials,
they are presented after ten days.
The eldest son is presented before the meal,
and his right hand must be held.
Legitimate and secondary sons are presented after the meal,
and their heads must be stroked.
12.52 When a child can eat,
teach him to use his right hand.
When he can speak,
boys respond firmly, girls respond gently.
Boys wear leather girdle pouches,
girls wear silk girdle pouches.
At six years,
teach him numbers and directional names.
At seven years,
boys and girls do not share the same mat,
nor eat together.
At eight years,
when entering or exiting doors and when sitting for meals,
they must defer to their elders,
beginning to teach them deference.
At nine years,
teach them to count the days.
At ten years,
they go out to study with an external tutor,
residing away from home,
learning writing and arithmetic.
They do not wear silk jackets or trousers,
following initial rites,
studying juvenile etiquette morning and evening,
and practicing simplicity and honesty.
At age thirteen,
one learns music,
recites poetry,
dances the "Sháo",
as an older child dances the "Xiàng",
and learns archery and charioteering.
At twenty, one is capped,
begins to learn rituals,
may wear furs and silks,
dances the "Dàxià",
diligently practices filial piety and fraternal duty,
studies broadly but does not teach,
keeping knowledge within and not expressing it outwardly.
At thirty, one takes a wife,
begins to manage men's affairs,
studies broadly without fixed methods,
befriends respectfully and observes aspirations.
At forty, one begins official service,
deliberates on matters and devises plans,
follows if the Way aligns,
leaves if it does not.
At fifty, one is appointed as a senior official,
handles governmental duties,
at seventy, retires from affairs.
12.53 In all, when men bow,
the left hand is placed on top.
12.54 Girls do not leave home from age ten,
governesses teach them gentleness, grace, and obedience;
they handle hemp and flax,
process silk cocoons,
weave fabrics, make ribbons and cords,
learn women's work to supply clothing,
observe sacrifices,
present wine, offerings, pickles, and sauces,
and assist in laying out rituals.
At fifteen, they receive the hairpin,
at twenty, they marry;
if there is a reason,
they marry at twenty-three.
Those betrothed become wives,
those who elope become concubines.
When women bow,
the right hand is placed on top.
13.1 The Son of Heaven wears a jade-adorned cap,
with twelve tassels,
long front and back,
and a dragon robe for sacrifices.
In dark robes, he worships the sun outside the eastern gate,
receives the new moon outside the southern gate;
in a leap month,
he closes the left door,
standing inside it.
In leather cap, he holds daily court,
then dines,
at midday has a light meal,
with music while eating.
Daily fare is a shǎoláo,
on the new moon, a tàiláo;
five drinks:
water, fermented juice, wine, sweet wine, and thin gruel.
After eating,
he wears dark robes at leisure.
Actions are recorded by the left historian,
words by the right historian,
and blind musicians note the tones of his speech.
In a year of poor harvest,
the Son of Heaven wears plain clothes,
rides a plain carriage,
and eats without music.
13.2 Feudal lords wear dark robes for sacrifices,
ceremonial caps for court,
leather caps to receive the new moon in the ancestral temple,
court robes for daily audiences in the inner court.
At court,
they enter at first light.
The ruler appears at sunrise,
retires to the main chamber
to handle governance,
sends to check on his officials,
who then withdraw;
afterward, he goes to his private chamber
to change clothes.
Again in court robes, he dines,
with a single sacrifice, three stands, and offering lungs;
in evening, wears deep robes,
offers sacrificial meat,
on new moon, a shǎoláo,
five stands and four guǐ vessels,
on zǐ-mǎo days, millet and vegetable soup,
his wife sharing the kitchen with him.
The ruler kills no ox without reason,
senior officials kill no sheep without reason,
scholars kill no dog or pig without reason.
A nobleman keeps distant from the kitchen,
for all creatures with blood and breath,
he does not personally tread on them.
If no rain falls by the eighth month,
the ruler does not feast.
In a poor harvest year,
the ruler wears cloth and a plain girdle,
tolls at passes and bridges are waived,
mountains and marshes are regulated without taxes,
earthworks are halted,
and senior officials may not build carriages or horses.
13.3 Diviners determine the turtle shell,
scribes fix the ink lines,
the ruler interprets the cracks.
13.4 The ruler's carriage has lamb-skin covering and tiger-hide trim,
senior officials' ritual carriages
have deer-skin covering and leopard-hide trim,
court carriages,
scholars' ritual carriages
have deer-skin covering and leopard-hide trim.
13.5 A nobleman's seat always faces the door,
he sleeps with head to the east;
if there are fierce winds, loud thunder, or heavy rain,
he must change demeanor,
rising even at night,
donning clothes and cap to sit.
He washes five times daily,
bathes with millet water and rinses with grain broth,
combs with a boxwood comb,
dries hair with an ivory comb,
then presents refreshments and delicacies,
musicians ascending to sing.
Bathing uses two towels,
fine cloth above, coarse below.
Exiting the tub, he steps on a rush mat,
rinses with warm water,
steps on a cattail mat,
dries with a cloth,
then puts on shoes and takes a drink.
When going to the ruler's place,
he fasts and abstains overnight,
stays in the outer chamber,
bathes and washes,
the scribe presents an ivory tablet,
he writes down thoughts, responses, and orders;
after dressing,
he practices demeanor and the sound of his jades,
then goes out,
bows in his private court,
radiantly,
and upon boarding the carriage, shines with light.
The Son of Heaven carries a straight jade tablet,
square and upright to the world;
feudal lords carry curved tablets,
bent in front and straight behind,
yielding to the Son of Heaven;
senior officials have tablets bent front and back,
yielding in all matters.
13.6 When attending a seated ruler,
one must withdraw from the mat;
if not withdrawing,
then must draw back from the ruler's side.
Ascending a mat not from the front
is considered stepping over it.
When merely sitting, do not occupy the full mat by a foot;
when reading,
or eating,
align with the edge,
with dishes a foot from the mat.
13.7 If granted food and the ruler treats one as a guest,
one offers sacrifice only after being commanded to do so;
then sacrifices;
tastes the food first, samples all dishes,
then drinks and waits.
If there is someone to taste the food,
then wait until the ruler eats
before eating;
after eating,
drink and wait.
If the ruler commands one to try a dish,
try the nearest one;
if commanded to sample all,
then do as one wishes.
When tasting distant food,
always start with the near.
Before the ruler has wiped his hands,
one dare not eat hurriedly;
after the ruler has eaten,
one may eat more,
meaning
three additional mouthfuls.
After the ruler has cleared the dishes,
take the rice and sauce,
and give them to attendants.
13.8 When urged to eat more,
do not finish all;
when eating with others, do not eat to fullness.
Only water and fermented juice are not offered in sacrifice;
if sacrificed,
it is considered too demeaning.
13.9 If the ruler bestows a cup of wine,
cross the mat, bow twice, kowtow, and receive it,
ascend the mat, offer it in sacrifice,
drink, finish the cup,
and wait; after the ruler finishes his cup,
then return the empty vessel.
When a gentleman drinks wine,
he accepts one cup and maintains a dignified demeanor.
With the second cup, his speech becomes harmonious,
and the rites are already
observed by the third cup,
after which he withdraws composedly.
Upon withdrawing, he sits to retrieve his shoes,
concealing himself before putting them on,
sitting on the left to slip on the right shoe,
sitting on the right to slip on the left shoe.
13.10 In all cases, the honored vessel must have plain water placed above wine;
only the ruler faces the尊 (zūn) vessel directly.
Only when entertaining rural folk is all wine served;
for a senior official, the尊 (zūn) is placed to the side, using a棜 (yù);
for a gentleman, the尊 (zūn) is placed to the side, using a禁 (jìn).
13.11 For the initial capping, a black cloth cap is worn;
from the feudal lords downward,
it is permissible to discard the cap after the capping ceremony.
A black cap with a crimson silk cord:
this is the cap of the Son of Heaven.
A black cloth cap with adorned tassels:
this is the cap of a feudal lord.
A black cap with a red silk cord:
this is the fasting cap of a feudal lord.
A black cap with a dark silk cord:
this is the fasting cap of a gentleman.
A plain silk cap with a black border:
this is the cap for descendants.
A plain silk cap with a plain edging:
this is the cap worn after the end of mourning.
Tassels hanging five inches:
this is for idle wanderers.
A black cap with a plain silk border:
this is the attire for those not ranked.
For a cap worn at home, the border is attached;
from the Son of Heaven downward,
tassels are added only for formal events.
At fifty, one does not scatter offerings in farewell;
after parents pass away, one does not wear the máo (youthful hairstyle);
a plain white silk cap has no tassels.
A black cap with purple tassels:
this began with Duke Huán of Lǔ.
13.12 In the morning, wear dark formal robes;
in the evening, wear the deep garment.
The deep garment has three tucks;
the hem is double the waist width,
with the lapel at the side,
and sleeves that allow the elbow to turn.
The length reaches the ankle, covering a foot.
The collar is two inches wide,
the cuff one foot two inches,
and the edging one and a half inches wide.
Using silk to line cloth
is contrary to ritual.
Gentlemen do not wear woven silk;
those without a ruler do not use dual colors.
Robes are of pure colors;
skirts are of mixed colors.
Without proper layered colors, one does not enter the duke's gate;
fine or coarse hemp garments are not worn into the duke's gate;
fur coats without cover are not worn into the duke's gate;
covered fur coats are not worn into the duke's gate.
Wadded silk makes a lined jacket;
hemp wadding makes a robe;
unlined garments are called jiǒng;
silk makes a pleated garment.
13.13 Wearing a plain silk court robe:
this began with Jì Kāngzǐ.
Confucius said:
"One wears court robes to court,
and after the new moon announcement, then wears them."
He also said:
"If the state is not following the Way,
then one does not fully wear its prescribed attire."
Only the ruler has a fur-trimmed robe for oath-taking inspections;
the great fur robe is not ancient.
13.14 The ruler wears a white fox fur robe,
with a brocade gown draped over it.
The ruler's right attendant wears a tiger fur robe;
the left attendant wears a wolf fur robe.
Gentlemen do not wear white fox fur.
A gentleman wears a dark blue fox fur robe with leopard cuffs,
draped with a black sheer silk gown;
a fawn fur robe with dark blue àn (wild dog) cuffs,
draped with a cross-patterned gown;
a lamb fur robe with leopard trim,
draped with a black gown;
a fox fur robe,
draped with a yellow gown.
A brocade gown over a fox fur robe:
this is the attire of feudal lords.
Dog or sheep fur robes
are not draped,
as they lack ornamental elegance,
and thus are not draped.
Draping over a fur robe
reveals its beauty.
When mourning, one covers it fully,
not displaying all ornamentation;
in the ruler's presence, one drapes it,
displaying full ornamentation.
Covering the garment fully
conceals its beauty;
thus, the corpse is covered,
and when holding jade or a turtle, one covers up,
but when not engaged in duties, one drapes it,
not daring to conceal the beauty.
13.15 The scepter:
the Son of Heaven uses jade;
feudal lords use ivory;
senior officials use bamboo with fish-whisker patterning;
gentlemen may use bamboo with an ivory base.
When appearing before the Son of Heaven or in archery,
one does not remove the scepter;
entering the ancestral temple to remove the scepter
is not ancient practice.
During minor mourning, one does not remove the scepter;
only when involved in affairs requiring bare head does one remove it.
After inserting it, one must wash hands;
even if holding it at court,
one does not wash again.
Whenever pointing or drawing before the ruler,
use the scepter;
when receiving commands before the ruler,
write them on the scepter.
The scepter is for all purposes,
and thus is adorned.
The scepter's length is two feet six inches,
with a central width of three inches,
tapering by one-sixth at the ends.
As for the plain belt,
it is adorned all around;
for a senior official, the plain belt
has adorned hanging ends;
for a gentleman, a boiled silk belt,
edged, with adorned lower part;
for recluses, a brocade belt;
for disciples, a plain silk belt.
All have fastened knots, using silk cords.
The knee cover: for the ruler, vermilion;
for a senior official, plain;
for a gentleman, russet leather.
Round, tapered, or straight:
the Son of Heaven's is straight;
dukes and marquises have square fronts and backs;
senior officials have square fronts
and rounded backs;
gentlemen have straight fronts and backs.
The knee cover is two feet wide at the bottom,
one foot wide at the top,
three feet long,
with a neck of five inches,
shoulder straps and a leather belt
two inches wide.
A senior official's great belt is four inches wide.
The mixed belt:
for the ruler, vermilion and green;
for a senior official, black and flowery;
for a gentleman, black-edged,
two inches wide,
wound twice to four inches.
All belts have edging,
without needlework.
With one appointment, a red knee cover and dark pendant;
with two appointments, a crimson knee cover and dark pendant;
with three appointments, a crimson knee cover and green pendant.
The Son of Heaven's belt is plain,
with red lining,
adorned all around.
The queen wears a huī (pheasant) robe;
the consort wears a yú (pheasant) robe,
three inches wide,
length even with the belt.
The sash length is regulated:
for gentlemen, three feet;
for officers, two feet five inches.
Zǐyóu said:
"Divide the area below the belt into three parts,
the sash occupying two."
The sash, knee cover, and knot align evenly.
The ruler's consort wears a què (pheasant) robe.
With two appointments, a huī robe;
with one appointment, a tǎn robe;
for gentlemen, a tuàn robe.
Only the shìfù (palace ladies) receive their rank at the cocoon offering;
all others follow the male's rank.
Whenever attending the ruler,
the sash hangs down,
feet as if stepping on the hem,
chin inclined, hands clasped,
gazing downward but listening upward,
sight resting between the belt and collar,
listening directed, favoring the left.
Whenever the ruler summons,
it is with three tokens:
with two tokens, one runs;
with one token, one hastens;
in office, one does not wait for shoes;
outside, one does not wait for a carriage.
13.16 A shì towards a dàfū
does not dare to bow when welcoming, but bows when sending off.
A shì towards a superior,
first bows, then approaches face to face;
if the superior returns the bow, he retreats.
When a shì speaks of the ruler,
if a dàfū has passed away,
he refers to him by his posthumous name or courtesy name,
but calls a shì by his given name.
When speaking with a dàfū,
he calls a shì by his given name,
and a dàfū by his courtesy name.
In the presence of a dàfū,
there is public avoidance
but no private avoidance.
In all sacrifices, there is no avoidance;
in the temple, there is no avoidance;
in teaching, learning, and facing texts, there is no avoidance.
13.17 The noble person of ancient times always wore jade pendants,
with zhǐ and jué on the right,
and gōng and yǔ on the left.
They quickened their steps to the rhythm of "Cǎi Qí,"
and walked to the rhythm of "Sì Xià."
Circling around, they followed a circular path;
turning corners, they followed a square path.
Advancing, they bowed slightly;
retreating, they raised the pendants,
after which the jade would tinkle clearly.
Thus, when the noble person is in a carriage,
one hears the sound of luán and hé bells;
when walking, the pendant jades chime,
so that improper thoughts
find no way to enter.
13.18 In the ruler's presence, one does not wear jade pendants;
on the left, the pendants are tied up;
on the right, pendants are set.
At rest, pendants are set;
at court, pendants are tied up;
during fasting, the pendants are tied up with colorful cords and a noble's knee cover is worn.
All girdles must have pendant jades,
except during mourning.
Pendant jades have a chōngyá piece;
the noble person without reason
does not remove the jade from their body,
for the noble person compares virtue to jade.
The Son of Heaven wears white jade with black silk cords,
dukes and marquises wear dark mountain jade with vermilion silk cords,
dàfū wear blue-green water jade with pure-colored silk cords,
the crown prince wears fine jade with variegated silk cords,
shì wear stone-like jade with reddish silk cords,
and Confucius wore an ivory ring five cun in diameter
with variegated silk cords.
13.19 The etiquette for a child includes
wearing black cloth garments with brocade trim,
a brocade sash,
joined fastenings, and brocade
to tie the hair, all in vermilion brocade.
The tied bundle and the belt
are gathered up by an attendant when there is business,
and held when running.
A child does not wear fur or silk,
nor shoes with upturned toes,
and has no mourning attire for distant relatives.
When listening to affairs, they do not wear hemp;
when not occupied,
they stand north of the host, facing south.
When meeting a teacher,
they follow others in.
13.20 When serving a meal to a teacher or someone of higher rank,
one offers sacrifice after them but eats first.
If a guest offers sacrifice,
the host declines, saying:
"It is not worthy of sacrifice."
If the guest eats heartily,
the host apologizes for the "meager fare."
If the host sets out the sauce himself,
the guest clears it away himself.
In a household,
if not entertaining guests,
one person clears the dishes.
Among those eating together,
one person clears.
In all informal meals,
women do not clear away.
13.21 When eating dates, peaches, or plums,
do not discard the pits on the ground;
with melons, offer the top part in sacrifice,
eat the middle, and discard the part held.
When eating fruits, let the superior eat first;
with cooked foods, the superior eats first.
On celebratory occasions,
one does not offer congratulations unless bestowed by the ruler.
Those in mourning
have their attire gathered by attendants when there is business,
and held when running.
When Confucius ate at the Jì family's,
he did not decline,
but ate the meat without finishing the meal.
If the ruler bestows a chariot or horses,
one rides in them to bow in thanks;
if clothing,
one wears it to bow in thanks;
unless the ruler commands,
one dare not immediately ride or wear them.
When receiving the ruler's gift,
one kowtows,
placing palms on the ground;
for gifts of wine or meat,
one does not bow twice.
All gifts
are given to noble persons and commoners on different days.
13.22 When presenting gifts to the ruler,
a dàfū sends his steward,
a shì goes personally,
both kowtowing twice to send it off.
When offering food to the ruler,
include garlic, peach wood, and reeds;
to a dàfū, omit the reeds;
to a shì, omit the garlic,
all presented to the kitchen steward.
A dàfū does not bow personally,
to avoid the ruler returning the bow.
A dàfū bows for a gift and withdraws;
a shì waits for acknowledgment before withdrawing,
bows again,
but receives no return bow.
If a dàfū personally gives a gift to a shì,
the shì bows to accept it,
and bows again at the dàfū's home.
For clothing,
one does not wear it to bow.
If an equal is absent,
one bows at their home.
When presenting to a superior,
one dare not make it known.
A shì does not accept congratulations from a dàfū;
a lower dàfū accepts congratulations from a higher dàfū.
While parents are alive,
when performing rites for others, one refers to one's father;
if someone gives a gift,
one refers to the father and bows.
13.23 If the rite is not grand,
the attire is not full,
hence a great fur robe is not covered,
and one does not bow in a royal carriage.
13.24 When called by the father's command,
respond with "wéi" not "nuò,"
if holding work, drop it;
if food is in the mouth, spit it out;
run, do not just walk briskly.
With elderly parents,
do not change destinations when going out,
and return without delay.
When parents are ill, one's expression should not be cheerful;
these are the basic points of a filial child.
After the father's death, one cannot read his books,
as the touch of his hand remains;
after the mother's death, one cannot drink from her cup,
as the moisture of her breath remains.
13.25 When the ruler enters the gate,
his escort brushes against the door pivot;
a dàfū passes between the middle post and the pivot,
and a shì's escort brushes against the post.
13.26 A guest does not walk through the center of the gate,
nor step on the threshold;
for public affairs, enter west of the pivot;
for private affairs, enter east of the pivot.
13.27 The ruler and the impersonator walk with overlapping steps;
a dàfū with successive steps;
a shì with medium-spaced steps;
slow walking all follows this.
In quick walking, one intends to start,
but without moving hands and feet;
walking in circles, without lifting feet,
even as flowing water;
the same on mats.
Walking upright,
the chin should be like an arrow's line;
walking in formal dress,
the shoes should lift sharply;
holding turtle shells or jade,
lift the front and drag the heels,
stepping cautiously.
13.28 In all walking, the demeanor should be respectful.
13.29 In the temple, be reverent;
at court, be dignified and composed.
13.30 The noble person's demeanor is calm and deliberate,
but when seeing a respected one, it becomes prompt.
The feet should be steady,
the hands respectful,
the eyes straightforward,
the mouth still,
the voice quiet,
the head erect,
the breath solemn,
the stance virtuous,
the countenance dignified,
sitting like an impersonator.
13.31 In leisure at home, one's speech should be gentle.
13.32 In all sacrifices,
one's countenance and complexion
should be as if seeing the one being sacrificed to.
13.33 In mourning, the appearance should be weary and exhausted,
the facial expression distressed and anxious,
the gaze startled and uncertain,
and the speech faint and weak.
13.34 In military demeanor, the appearance should be resolute and determined,
the speech firm and decisive,
the expression severe and stern,
the gaze clear and bright.
The standing posture should be distinguished,
humble but not flattering,
the head and neck must be upright,
firm as a mountain, moving in due time,
with vital energy充盈坚实
radiating magnificence, and a jade-like complexion.
13.35 In all self-references,
the Son of Heaven says "yǔ yī rén" (I, the one man),
a feudal lord says "Tiānzǐ zhī lì chén" (the Son of Heaven's strong servant).
When a feudal lord addresses the Son of Heaven,
he says "mǒu tǔ zhī shǒu chén mǒu" (so-and-so, the guarding servant of such-and-such land),
if at a border town,
he says "mǒu píng zhī chén mǒu" (so-and-so, the screening servant of such-and-such).
To those of equal or lower status,
he says "guǎrén" (the morally deficient one),
the ruler of a small state says "gū" (the orphaned one),
and the usher also calls him "gū".
A high-ranking minister calls himself "xià chén" (the lower servant),
and the usher calls him "guǎ jūn zhī lǎo" (our ruler's elder).
A lower-ranking minister uses his personal name,
and the usher calls him "guǎ dàfū" (our minister).
The crown prince uses his personal name,
and the usher calls him "guǎ jūn zhī shì" (our ruler's designated heir).
A prince says "chén niè" (your servant, the branch).
A scholar says "chuán jù zhī chén" (your servant, the courier).
To a minister, he says "wài sī" (the external private servant).
When a minister is on a private mission,
if introduced by a private usher, he uses his personal name;
if introduced by a public usher, he is called "guǎ dàfū" (our minister)
or "guǎ jūn zhī lǎo" (our ruler's elder).
When a minister goes somewhere,
he must have a public usher as his attendant.
14.1 In the past, the Duke of Zhōu arranged the positions for the feudal lords in the Míngtáng:
The Son of Heaven stood facing south with his back to the axe-embroidered screen;
the Three Dukes
were in front of the central steps,
facing north with the highest-ranking on the east.
The positions of the feudal lords
were east of the eastern steps,
facing west with the highest-ranking on the north.
The states of the various Bó
were west of the western steps,
facing east with the highest-ranking on the north.
The states of the various Zǐ
were east of the gate,
facing north with the highest-ranking on the east.
The states of the various Nán
were west of the gate,
facing north with the highest-ranking on the east.
The states of the nine Yí tribes were outside the east gate,
facing west with the highest-ranking on the north.
The states of the eight Mán tribes,
outside the south gate,
facing north with the highest-ranking on the east.
The states of the six Róng tribes,
outside the west gate,
facing east with the highest-ranking on the south.
The states of the five Dí tribes,
outside the north gate,
facing south with the highest-ranking on the east.
The states of the nine tribute-paying regions,
outside the Yìngmén gate,
facing north with the highest-ranking on the east.
Those from the four remote regions
reported their arrival generation after generation.
This was the arrangement of positions in the Duke of Zhōu's Míngtáng.
The Míngtáng
was to clarify the尊卑 of the feudal lords.
In the past, King Zhòu of Yīn brought chaos to the world,
making dried meat of the Guǐhóu to feast the feudal lords.
Therefore, the Duke of Zhōu assisted King Wǔ in attacking Zhòu.
When King Wǔ died,
and King Chéng was young and weak,
the Duke of Zhōu ascended to the position of the Son of Heaven
to govern the world;
in the sixth year,
he received the feudal lords in the Míngtáng,
established rituals and created music,
promulgated standards and measures,
and the world became greatly submissive;
in the seventh year,
he returned the government to King Chéng;
King Chéng, because the Duke of Zhōu had rendered great service to the world,
therefore enfeoffed the Duke of Zhōu at Qūfù,
with a territory of seven hundred lǐ square,
a thousand war chariots,
and commanded the Duke of Lǔ to sacrifice to the Duke of Zhōu with the rituals and music of the Son of Heaven for generations.
Therefore, the ruler of Lǔ,
in the first month of spring, rides the great carriage,
carrying the bow case;
with a banner of twelve tassels,
adorned with the sun and moon;
sacrifices to the Emperor in the suburbs,
accompanied by Hòujì.
This is the ritual of the Son of Heaven.
14.2 In the sixth month of late summer,
they sacrifice to the Duke of Zhōu in the great temple with the dì ritual,
using a white bull as the sacrificial animal;
wine vessels include the xī, elephant-shaped,
and mountain-patterned léi;
the fragrant wine vessel is a yellow-eyed one;
for the libation, a jade zàn
and large jade tablet are used;
offerings are presented in jade dòu vessels,
carved bamboo baskets;
cups are jade zhǎn,
still carved,
with additional
bì-shaped sǎn and jiǎo vessels;
the stands are kuǎn jué;
they sing the "Qīng Miào" ascending,
and play the "Xiàng" descending;
with vermilion shields and jade axes,
they dance the "Great Wǔ" in ceremonial caps;
in leather caps and white robes,
they dance the "Great Xià" with open robes.
"Mèi",
is the music of the eastern Yí;
"Rén",
is the music of the southern Mán.
Incorporating the music of the Yí and Mán into the great temple
signifies spreading Lǔ's influence throughout the world.
14.3 The ruler, in rolled-up ceremonial robes and crown, stands at the eastern steps,
the lady, with headdress and pheasant-patterned robe, stands in the inner chamber.
The ruler bares his arm to welcome the sacrificial animal at the gate;
the lady offers the dòu
and biān vessels.
High ministers assist the ruler,
and appointed ladies assist the ruler's wife:
each fulfills their duty.
Any official who neglects their duty suffers severe punishment,
and the world becomes greatly submissive.
14.4 Therefore,
the summer yuè, autumn cháng, and winter zhēng sacrifices,
the spring shè, autumn xǐng,
and then the great zhà sacrifice,
are the sacrifices of the Son of Heaven.
14.5 The great temple
is the Son of Heaven's Míngtáng.
The storehouse gate
is the Son of Heaven's gāo gate.
The pheasant gate
is the Son of Heaven's yìng gate.
14.6 Shaking the wooden bell in the court
is the governance of the Son of Heaven.
14.7 Mountain-shaped brackets, algae-carved posts,
double-eaved roofs, layered屋檐,
scraped pillars,通达 windows,
returning stands, prominent wine vessels,
elevated stands, resting jade tablets,
ornamented screens;
these are the temple decorations of the Son of Heaven.
14.8 The luán carriage
was the vehicle of the Yǒuyú shì.
The gōu carriage
was the vehicle of the Xiàhòu shì.
The great carriage
was the vehicle of the Yīn.
The shèng carriage
was the vehicle of the Zhōu.
14.9 The banner of the Yǒuyú shì,
the streamers of the Xiàhòu shì,
the great white of the Yīn,
the great red of the Zhōu.
14.10 The Xiàhòu shì had white horses with black manes,
black manes.
The Yīn people had white horses,
with black heads.
The Zhōu people had yellow horses,
with abundant manes.
14.11 The Xiàhòu shì
preferred black for sacrificial animals,
the Yīn used white bulls,
the Zhōu used red stallions.
14.12 The tài vessel
was the wine vessel of the Yǒuyú shì.
The mountain-patterned léi
was the wine vessel of the Xiàhòu shì.
The zhù vessel
was the wine vessel of the Yīn.
The xī and elephant-shaped vessels
were the wine vessels of the Zhōu.
14.13 For cups,
the Xiàhòu shì used zhǎn,
the Yīn used jiǎ,
the Zhōu used jué.
14.14 The ceremonial wine vessel:
the Xiàhòu clan used the jīyí,
the Yīn used the jiǎ,
and the Zhōu used the huángmù.
14.15 Their ladles:
the Xiàhòu clan used the lóngsháo,
the Yīn used the shūsháo,
and the Zhōu used the púsháo.
14.16 The earthen drum, kuài-fiber drumsticks, and reed yuè pipe
were the instruments of the Yīqíshì.
The fǔbó, jade qìng, and jiē jī,
the great qín and great sè,
the medium qín and small sè—
these were the musical instruments of the four dynasties.
14.17 The temple of the Duke of Lǔ
was the Wén Shìshì.
The temple of Duke Wǔ
was the Wǔ Shìshì.
14.18 The Mǐlǐn
was the Xiáng of the Yǒuyúshì;
the Xù
was the Xù of the Xiàhòu clan;
the Gǔzōng
was the school of the Yīn;
the Pàngōng
was the school of the Zhōu.
14.19 The Chóng dǐng,
Guàn dǐng,
Great Huáng,
and Fēngfǔ tortoise shell
were vessels of the Son of Heaven.
The Yuè jí
and great bow
were the weapons of the Son of Heaven.
14.20 The Xiàhòu clan's
footed drum.
The Yīn,
pillar drum;
the Zhōu,
suspended drum.
14.21 Chuí's harmonious bells,
Shū's arranged qìng stones,
and Nǚwā's shēng reeds.
14.22 The Xiàhòu clan's dragon-shaped sǔnjù stand,
the Yīn's chóngyá,
the Zhōu's bìshà.
The Yǒuyúshì's two duì vessels,
the Xiàhòu clan's four lián,
the Yīn's six hú,
the Zhōu's eight guǐ.
14.23 The zǔ stand:
the Yǒuyúshì used the kuǎn,
the Xiàhòu clan used the jué,
the Yīn used the jǔ,
the Zhōu used the fángzǔ.
14.24 The Xiàhòu clan used the qièdòu,
the Yīn used jade dòu,
the Zhōu used xiàndòu.
14.25 The Yǒuyúshì wore the fú,
the Xiàhòu clan had mountains,
the Yīn had fire,
the Zhōu had dragon patterns.
14.26 The Yǒuyúshì sacrificed the head,
the Xiàhòu clan sacrificed the heart,
the Yīn sacrificed the liver,
the Zhōu sacrificed the lungs.
14.27 The Xiàhòu clan esteemed míngshuǐ,
the Yīn esteemed lǐ,
the Zhōu esteemed wine.
14.28 The Yǒuyúshì had fifty officials,
the Xiàhòu clan had a hundred,
the Yīn two hundred,
the Zhōu three hundred.
The Yǒuyúshì's suí,
the Xiàhòu clan's chóuliàn,
the Yīn's chóngyá,
the Zhōu's bìshà.
All the clothing, vessels, and officials of the four dynasties
were used together in Lǔ.
Therefore,
Lǔ
practiced royal rites,
and this was long transmitted throughout the land.
Ruler and minister
never killed each other;
rites and music, punishments and laws, governance and customs
never changed.
The land considered it a state with the Way.
Therefore,
the land drew upon its rites and music.
15.1 For zhǎncuī mourning,
the hair is bound with hemp;
for one's mother,
the hair is bound with hemp,
and when wearing the miǎn, it is with cloth.
For zīcuī mourning,
a coarse hairpin is worn until the mourning ends.
Men wear the guān and women the jī,
men wear the miǎn and women the zhuā.
The principle:
for men, the miǎn;
for women, the zhuā.
15.2 The jūzhàng staff
is of bamboo;
the xuēzhàng staff
is of paulownia.
15.3 When the grandfather dies,
then the one succeeding the grandmother observes three years.
15.4 For parents
and the eldest son, one kowtows.
When a senior official condoles,
even for sī mourning, one must kowtow.
A woman kowtows for her husband and eldest son,
but not for others.
15.5 The male presiding mourner must be of the same surname,
the female presiding mourner must be of a different surname.
15.6 One who succeeds the father
wears no mourning for a divorced mother.
15.7 In loving kin,
from three, it becomes five;
from five, it becomes nine.
Diminishing upward,
diminishing downward,
diminishing sideways,
and kinship ends.
15.8 The king performs the dì sacrifice to the origin of his ancestor,
matching it with his ancestor,
and establishes four temples.
A son of a concubine becoming king
does likewise.
15.9 A collateral son becomes the ancestor,
continuing the collateral line becomes the great lineage,
continuing the father becomes the minor lineage.
There is a lineage that shifts after five generations,
which continues from the high ancestor.
Therefore,
the ancestor shifts above,
the lineage changes below.
Honoring the ancestor, thus respecting the lineage;
respecting the lineage is how one honors the ancestor and father.
A son of a concubine does not sacrifice to the ancestor,
to clarify his lineage.
A son of a concubine does not observe zhǎncuī for his eldest son,
because he does not continue the ancestor and father.
A son of a concubine does not sacrifice to those who died young or without heirs,
they are attached to the ancestor's sacrifice.
15.10 A son of a concubine does not sacrifice to his father,
to clarify his lineage.
15.11 Loving kin, honoring the honorable, respecting elders,
and the distinction between men and women
are the great principles of human conduct.
15.12 In following mourning,
if the one followed dies,
it stops.
In attached following,
even if the one followed has died, mourning is worn.
If a concubine leaves with her mistress,
she does not mourn for the mistress's son.
15.13 In rites, one who is not king does not perform the dì.
15.14 The heir apparent does not reduce mourning for his wife's parents;
for his wife,
it is the same as for a senior official's eldest son.
15.15 If the father was a shì,
and the son is Son of Heaven or a feudal lord,
then he sacrifices as Son of Heaven or feudal lord,
but the corpse wears shì attire.
If the father was Son of Heaven or a feudal lord,
and the son is a shì,
he sacrifices as a shì,
and the corpse wears shì attire.
15.16 If a woman is divorced during mourning,
then it ends.
For parents' mourning,
if divorced before the liàn sacrifice,
then three years.
If divorced after the liàn sacrifice,
then it ends.
If returning before the liàn sacrifice,
then one year;
if returning after the liàn sacrifice,
then continue it.
15.17 A double-cycle mourning
is three years;
a single-cycle mourning
is two years.
Nine-month and seven-month mournings,
are three seasons;
five-month mourning,
two seasons,
three-month mourning,
one season.
Thus, sacrificing at the cycle,
is ritual;
ending mourning at the cycle,
is principle.
Sacrifice is not for ending mourning.
If burial occurs three years later, there must be two sacrificial ceremonies,
performed at different times between which mourning garments are removed.
For major gōng mourning when managing another's funeral,
if it involves a three-year mourning period,
then one must perform two sacrificial ceremonies for them.
For friends,
only the yú and fù sacrifices are performed.
If a servant-concubine has borne a child,
one wears sī mourning for her;
if she has no child, then it is not done.
If one was born after the deaths of grandparents, uncles, or brothers,
and the father retroactively observes mourning for them,
oneself does not.
For the ruler's parents, wife, or eldest son,
if the ruler has already removed mourning garments before hearing of the death,
then one does not observe retroactive mourning.
If the mourning grade is reduced to sī or xiǎo gōng,
then one observes retroactive mourning.
For close attendants,
they wear whatever mourning the ruler wears.
For others,
they follow in wearing mourning if present,
but do not observe retroactive mourning if absent.
Even if the ruler is unaware of the death,
the ministers already wear mourning.
15.18 For the yú sacrifice,
the staff is not brought into the chamber;
for the fù sacrifice,
the staff is not ascended to the hall.
15.19 One who succeeds a legal mother,
when the legal mother dies,
does not wear mourning for her natal family.
15.20 The dié mourning band is reduced by one-fifth in width,
and the staff is as large as the dié.
15.21 A concubine's mourning for the ruler's eldest son
is the same as the wife's.
When removing mourning garments,
remove the heavier first;
when changing mourning garments,
change the lighter first.
Do not open the temple door without reason.
All weeping should be at their positions.
15.22 The calling back of the soul and writing the inscription,
from the Son of Heaven down to the shì,
follow the same wording.
For men, state their personal name;
for women, write their surname and birth order,
or if the surname is unknown, write their clan name.
15.23 The gé mourning of zhǎn cuī is the same as the hemp of zī cuī.
The gé mourning of zī cuī is the same as the hemp of dà gōng mourning;
when the hemp is the same,
both are worn together.
15.24 For hasty burials, perform hasty yú sacrifices,
with the卒哭 ceremony after three months.
15.25 When both parents' deaths occur together,
for the first buried, neither yú nor fù is performed,
but wait until the later matters.
For the burial,
wear zhǎn cuī mourning.
15.26 A senior official reduces mourning for his庶子,
but the grandson does not reduce mourning for his father.
A senior official does not preside over a shì's funeral.
15.27 One does not wear mourning for the parents of a慈母.
15.28 If a husband becomes an heir to another line,
his wife wears dà gōng mourning for her parents-in-law.
15.29 When a shì is附葬 to a senior official, change the sacrificial animal.
15.30 A stepfather who is not co-residing
must have previously co-resided.
Both have no primary heir.
Sharing resources and sacrificing to his ancestors constitutes co-residence;
having a primary heir constitutes separate residence.
15.31 When mourning for a friend,
stand outside the gate to the right, facing south.
15.32 For附葬, do not divine the burial site.
15.33 Shì and senior officials cannot be附葬 to feudal lords;
they are附葬 to paternal grandfathers who were shì or senior officials,
their wives to paternal grandaunts.
Concubines are附葬 to concubine grandaunts.
If none exist, then skip one generation and附葬 upward.
附葬 must follow the zhāo-mù order.
Feudal lords cannot be附葬 to the Son of Heaven;
the Son of Heaven, feudal lords, and senior officials can be附葬 to shì.
15.34 For the mother's legal mother,
when the mother dies, one does not wear mourning.
15.35 The clan heir,
if his mother is alive, performs the dàn sacrifice for his wife.
15.36 One who succeeds a慈母
may also succeed a庶母,
or a paternal grandmother who was a庶母.
15.37 Perform the dàn sacrifice for parents, wife, and eldest son.
15.38 For慈母 and concubine mothers,
sacrifices are not continued for generations.
15.39 Males who have been capped are not considered yāo,
females who have undergone the hair-pinning ceremony are not considered yāo.
15.40 One who succeeds a yāo,
wears mourning according to the prescribed garments.
15.41 For long-delayed burials,
only the chief mourner does not remove mourning;
others who wear hemp for the full month count
remove mourning and that is all.
15.42 The arrow hairpin is worn for the full three-year mourning.
For three-month zī cuī mourning that is the same as dà gōng,
wear rope sandals.
15.43 For the liàn ceremony,
divine the day and the impersonator,
and inspect the washing,
all while wearing the waist dié, staff, and rope sandals.
When the officers announce everything is ready,
then remove the staff.
For divining the day and the impersonator,
after the officers announce the completion, then take up the staff again,
and bow while seeing off guests.
For the dà xiáng ceremony,
wear auspicious garments to divine the impersonator.
15.44 A庶子 living in the father's house
does not perform the dàn sacrifice for his mother.
A庶子 does not take his staff to his position.
If the father does not preside over a庶子's funeral,
then the grandson may take his staff to his position.
If the father is alive,
a庶子 for his wife
may take his staff to his position.
15.45 When a feudal lord condoles with a minister of another state,
that state's ruler acts as host.
15.46 When a feudal lord offers condolences,
he must wear a leather cap and fine hemp mourning clothes.
Even if the deceased has been buried,
the host must wear the miǎn headband.
If the host has not yet put on mourning garments,
then the lord also does not wear fine hemp.
15.47 Those nursing the sick do not wear mourning garments,
but subsequently manage the funeral.
If non-nursing persons join in managing the funeral,
they do not change their own mourning garments.
Those nursing superiors must change garments,
those nursing inferiors need not.
15.48 If a concubine has no concubine grandaunt,
she may be附葬 to the wife with a change of sacrificial animal.
15.49 For a woman's funeral, yú, and卒哭 ceremonies,
her husband or son presides.
For the fù ceremony,
the father-in-law presides.
A shì does not act as proxy for a senior official.
A shì acting as proxy for a senior official
is only permissible for the clan heir.
If the host has not removed mourning,
and brothers arrive from another state,
the host presides without wearing the miǎn headband.
The principle for displaying grave goods:
display many but bury few is acceptable;
display few but bury all is acceptable.
15.50 When rushing to a brother's funeral,
go first to the grave and then to the home,
take a position and weep.
For an acquaintance's funeral,
weep at the temple first and then go to the grave.
15.51 A father does not reside outside for his众子.
One wears zhǎn cuī mourning for brothers who are feudal lords.
For xiǎo gōng mourning for older yāo,
the belt
is of washed hemp with roots intact,
bent and doubled back to fasten.
A wife is附葬 to a paternal grandaunt;
if there are three paternal grandaunts,
she is附葬 to the closest.
15.52 If a wife dies while her husband is a senior official,
and later her husband is no longer a senior official,
when she is附葬, the sacrificial animal is not changed.
If the wife dies and later the husband becomes a senior official,
when she is附葬,
then use the sacrificial animal of a senior official.
15.53 One who succeeds his father
wears no mourning for an expelled mother.
Wearing no mourning
is because the mourner does not sacrifice to her.
15.54 Cases where women do not preside but carry a staff:
a wife carries a staff for her husband if the mother-in-law is alive;
a mother uses a pared-down staff for her eldest son.
An unmarried daughter for her parents—
if the chief mourner does not carry a staff,
then one daughter carries a staff.
15.55 For sī and xiǎo gōng mourning,
wear the miǎn headband for the yú and卒哭 ceremonies.
If buried but the yú is not promptly performed,
then even the host wears a cap,
and at the yú, all wear the miǎn.
For brothers,
after mourning is removed,
at their burial,
resume wearing the mourning garments.
If the yú and卒哭 are performed promptly, wear the miǎn.
If the yú is not performed promptly, then remove mourning.
Those who accompany the distant burial all wear caps;
when they reach the outskirts, they then remove them and return weeping.
When the ruler comes to offer condolences,
even if it is not the time to remove the cap,
the host must remove it,
but not loosen the hemp mourning cloth.
Even for the ruler of another state,
the cap is removed.
All close relatives remove their caps.
For those who conclude the mourning for a minor,
the sacrifice must be in dark attire.
15.56 For those who conclude the mourning for an adult,
the sacrifice is performed
in court robes and a plain white cap.
15.57 When rushing to a father's funeral,
one binds the hair in the hall,
bares the shoulders, descends, and leaps,
then dons the mourning headband in the eastern section.
When rushing to a mother's funeral,
one does not bind the hair,
but bares the shoulders in the hall,
descends, and leaps,
then dons the cap and removes it in the eastern section,
puts on the headband, takes position, and completes the leaping,
exits the gate, and ceases weeping.
Over three days, there are five weepings and three bare-shoulderings.
15.58 If the principal wife does not produce an heir for the father-in-law,
then the mother-in-law wears minor mourning for her.
16.1 In rites:
one who is not a king does not perform the dì sacrifice.
The king performs the dì sacrifice to the origin of his ancestors,
with his ancestor as the counterpart.
Feudal lords extend to their great ancestor,
while grand masters and officers, for great affairs,
seek approval from their ruler,
and through the xiá sacrifice,
reach their high ancestor.
At Mùyě,
King Wǔ's great affair was completed.
After the affair concluded, he withdrew,
offered a burnt sacrifice to the Supreme Deity,
prayed at the altar of the soil,
and set up offerings in the chamber at Mù.
Then he led the feudal lords of the world
holding dòu and biān vessels,
hurrying and running;
he posthumously honored King Tàiwáng Dǎnfù,
King Jì Lì, and King Wén Chāng;
not allowing the lowly to oversee the noble.
16.2 Governing upwards to ancestors and father,
honors the honorable;
governing downwards to sons and grandsons,
cherishes the dear;
governing sideways to brothers,
unites the clan with feasts,
orders by zhāo-mù distinctions,
differentiates with ritual and righteousness,
thus exhausting the way of humanity.
The sage faces south and governs the world,
with five priorities,
among which the people are not included.
First is governing kin,
second is repaying merit,
third is promoting the worthy,
fourth is employing the capable,
fifth is preserving love.
If these five are achieved in the world,
the people will lack nothing,
and have no insufficiency.
If in these five,
one thing is amiss,
the people may not die naturally.
The sage faces south and governs the world,
necessarily starting from the way of humanity.
Establishing weights, measures, and capacities,
examining documents,
correcting the calendar,
changing ceremonial colors,
distinguishing insignia,
varying tools,
differentiating garments—
these are what can be changed with the people.
What cannot be changed includes:
cherishing the dear,
honoring the honorable,
respecting elders,
distinguishing between men and women—
these cannot be changed with the people.
16.3 Those of the same surname follow the lineage head,
uniting the clan members;
those of different surnames focus on titles,
managing interactions.
When titles are clear,
men and women are distinguished.
If the husband
belongs to the father's generation,
the wife is in the "mother" category.
If the husband
belongs to the son's generation,
the wife is in the "daughter-in-law" category.
To call a younger brother's wife "daughter-in-law"—
then can an elder brother's wife be called "mother"?
Naming is a great matter in human governance,
can one not be cautious?
16.4 Four generations, and the mourning is sī,
the limit of mourning attire;
five generations, bare shoulders and cap removal,
reducing ties with the same surname.
Six generations,
kinship is exhausted.
If collateral branches differentiate above,
and closeness fades below,
can marriage be allowed?
Linking by "surname" without distinction,
connecting through feasts without separation,
even after a hundred generations, marriage is not permitted—
such is the way of Zhōu.
16.5 There are six principles of mourning:
first, cherishing the dear;
second, honoring the honorable;
third, by title;
fourth, by status (as married/unmarried);
fifth, by age;
sixth, following another's mourning.
16.6 Following another's mourning has six types:
following by relation,
following by association,
following where there is mourning but one has none,
following where there is no mourning but one has it,
following from heavy to light,
following from light to heavy.
16.7 From humaneness, following parents,
ascending step by step,
to the ancestors,
is called light.
From righteousness, following ancestors,
descending in order,
to the father,
is called heavy.
One light and one heavy,
such is the principle.
16.8 The ruler has the way to unite the clan,
but clansmen may not use kinship to relate to the ruler—
due to his position.
16.9 A son by a concubine does not offer sacrifices,
to clarify the main line.
A son by a concubine does not observe three years' mourning for his eldest son,
as he does not continue the main ancestral line.
A collateral son becomes an ancestor,
continuing him forms a main lineage,
continuing the father forms a minor lineage.
There are lineages that do not change for a hundred generations,
and those that change after five generations.
Those that do not change for a hundred generations
are descendants of collateral sons;
the lineage that continues the collateral son's origin
is the one unchanged for a hundred generations.
The lineage that continues the high ancestor
changes after five generations.
Honoring the ancestor thus respects the lineage.
Respecting the lineage
is the meaning of honoring the ancestor.
16.10 There are cases with a minor lineage but no main lineage,
with a main lineage but no minor lineage,
or with no lineage and none to lineage with—
such as with the ruler's sons.
The ruler's sons have a lineage way:
the ruler of the ruler's sons,
for those who are officers or grand masters by concubines,
they lineage with those who are officers or grand masters by the principal wife—
this is the lineage way of the ruler's sons.
16.11 For severed clans, there is no transferred mourning,
closeness is by connection.
16.12 From humaneness, following parents,
ascending step by step,
to the ancestors;
from righteousness, following ancestors,
descending in order,
to the father.
Therefore,
the way of humanity is to cherish the dear.
Cherishing the dear thus honors ancestors,
honoring ancestors thus respects the lineage,
respecting the lineage thus gathers the clan,
gathering the clan thus solemnizes the ancestral temple,
solemnizing the ancestral temple thus values the altars of land and grain,
valuing the altars thus loves the people,
loving the people thus penalties are just,
penalties just thus the common people are secure,
the common people secure thus resources are sufficient,
resources sufficient thus all aims are achieved,
all aims achieved thus rituals and customs are formed,
rituals and customs formed then there is joy.
The Book of Songs says:
"How illustrious, how honored,
never wearying of it among men."
This refers to this.
17.1 When first meeting a nobleman, one should say:
"I sincerely wish to have my name heard by your messenger."
One should not directly address the host.
To an equal, say:
"I sincerely wish to see you."
For rare meetings, say
"I've heard of your reputation."
For frequent meetings, say
"I see you morning and evening."
A blind person says
"I've heard of your reputation."
17.2 When going to someone in mourning, say
"I come to assist."
A youth says
"I come to handle affairs."
When attending the funeral of a minister or high official,
then say
"I come to serve under the Sītú."
17.3 When the ruler is about to travel elsewhere,
if a minister presents gold, jade, goods, or currency to the ruler,
he should say:
"I present travel expenses to the officials";
to an equal, say:
"I give this to your attendants."
17.4 When a minister presents burial clothes to the ruler,
he should say:
"I present discarded clothes to the merchants";
to an equal, say:
"Burial clothes."
Among close relatives and brothers,
the burial clothes are presented directly.
When a minister contributes goods and currency for the ruler's funeral,
he should say:
"I submit my district's tribute to the officials."
Horses presented for funeral expenses enter the temple gate;
horses for condolence gifts with their silks,
and large white military chariots,
do not enter the temple gate.
17.5 After the condolence gift presenter has delivered his message,
he sits and places the gift down,
and the usher picks it up.
The host does not receive it personally.
17.6 When receiving or giving while standing, one does not kneel.
Only those who are naturally upright do so.
Upon entering, there is a polite refusal,
saying:
"Please decline."
When taking the seat,
say:
"It is acceptable."
Only one person should remove shoes inside the door by pushing the door leaves aside.
If elders are present, this is not done.
17.7 When asking about food preferences, say:
"Do you often eat such-and-such?"
When asking about skills and arts, say:
"Have you studied such-and-such?"
"Are you skilled in such-and-such?"
Do not harbor doubts about yourself,
do not measure others' possessions,
do not covet wealthy households,
do not criticize valuable vessels.
General sweeping is called sǎo,
sweeping in front of the mat is called fèn;
do not use a broom's bristles to sweep the mat.
Hold the dustpan facing oneself.
17.8 Do not ask twice.
When consulting divination, ask:
"Is it for righteousness?
Or for personal desire?"
If for righteousness, one may ask;
if for personal desire, one may not.
17.9 For elders superior to oneself,
one dare not ask their age.
In informal visits, no announcement is made.
Meeting on the road,
if seen, face them,
but do not ask where they are going.
During mourning, wait for the proper time and do not make special condolence visits.
When attending a seated person, unless instructed,
do not hold qín or sè,
do not draw on the ground,
do not gesture with hands,
and do not use a fan.
If the person is resting, sit and deliver the message.
When attending archery, gather the arrows;
when attending pitching games, hold the arrows.
If winning, wash the cup and offer a toast;
the guest does likewise.
Do not use horn cups,
do not move the horse piece.
17.10 When holding the ruler's carriage, sit.
The driver wears his sword on the right,
carries the good reins on his back,
extends them forward,
drapes them over the cover,
ascends using the spare reins,
and takes the reins before walking.
17.11 Request an audience but do not request to leave.
In court, it is called "withdrawing";
in leisure outings, "returning";
in military campaigns, "ceasing."
17.12 When attending a seated nobleman,
if the nobleman yawns and stretches,
twirls his scepter,
polishes his sword hilt,
turns his shoes,
or asks the time of day,
one may request to leave.
17.13 Those serving a ruler should assess their capability before taking office,
not take office and then assess;
similarly for borrowing from others
or working for someone.
Thus,
the superior holds no grudges,
and the subordinate avoids offenses.
Do not pry into secrets,
do not be overly familiar,
do not speak of past affairs,
do not show playful expressions.
17.14 As subordinates,
offer remonstrance but not slander,
leave but not resent;
praise without flattery,
advise without arrogance;
if the ruler is negligent, encourage and assist him;
if he neglects duties, rectify and renew them;
this is called service to the state.
17.15 Do not act hastily,
do not come and go frequently,
do not disrespect the gods,
do not follow wrong paths,
do not speculate about the future.
Scholars rely on virtue,
and practice arts;
craftsmen rely on standards,
and practice discourse.
Do not criticize clothing or finished utensils,
do not personally guarantee words.
The beauty of speech
lies in reverence and dignity;
the beauty of court
lies in order and grace;
the beauty of sacrifices
lies in solemnity and grandeur;
the beauty of chariots and horses
lies in majesty and order;
the beauty of carriage bells
lies in solemn harmony.
17.16 When asking about the age of a ruler's son,
if older,
say
"He can participate in state affairs";
if younger,
say
"He can drive"
or "He cannot yet drive."
When asking about a minister's son,
if older,
say
"He can follow the musicians' duties";
if younger,
say
"He can be instructed by musicians"
or "He cannot yet be instructed by musicians."
When asking about a scholar's son,
if older,
say
"He can plow";
if younger,
say
"He can carry firewood"
or "He cannot yet carry firewood."
17.17 When holding jade or turtle shells, do not hurry;
do not hurry in the hall,
do not hurry on city walls.
Do not bow in military chariots;
armored soldiers do not bow.
Women, in auspicious events,
even with a ruler's gift,
perform a sù bài.
