When acting as the ancestral representative, sitting,
they do not bow with hands,
but perform a sù bài;
when presiding over mourning, they do not bow with hands.
Wear hempen mourning with hemp girdle.
Taking or presenting the sacrificial stand does not require sitting.
17.18 Hold the empty as if holding the full,
enter emptiness as if people are present.
In all sacrifices in the chamber
or hall, do not go barefoot,
but in banquets, it is allowed.
Never fails to partake of the new harvest.
17.19 When serving a gentleman,
when the gentleman ascends or descends the carriage, hand him the mounting cord;
when starting the carriage, bow forward;
after the gentleman descends,
then turn around and stand.
17.20 In a secondary carriage, bow forward,
but not in an auxiliary carriage.
For secondary carriages,
feudal lords have seven,
high-ranking ministers five,
lower-ranking ministers three.
The horses and carriages of those with secondary carriages are not ranked by age.
When observing a gentleman's clothing,
sword,
or carriage horses,
do not appraise their value.
If giving someone a vessel of wine,
a bundle of dried meat,
and a dog,
or presenting them to someone,
then display the wine and hold the meat to convey the message,
also saying:
"A vessel of wine,
a bundle of dried meat,
and a dog."
If it is meat in a tripod,
then hold it to convey the message.
If the game birds exceed a pair,
hold one pair to convey the message,
and set aside the remainder.
For dogs, hold the leash;
guard dogs
and hunting dogs,
hand them to the usher,
and after receiving them,
then ask the dog's name.
For oxen, hold the nose rope;
for horses, hold the bridle,
both with the right hand.
For servants, use the left hand.
For carriages, remove the mounting cord,
and hold it to convey the message.
For armor, if there is something preceding it,
hold it to convey the message;
if not,
bare the case and present the helmet.
For vessels, hold the lid.
For bows, use the left hand to bend the cover and hold the grip.
For swords, open the case, cover it,
and place the scabbard and sword inside.
Tablets, documents, dried meat, wrapped gifts, bows, mats, pillows, small tables, torches, staffs, zithers, lutes, dagger-axes with blades in cases, whips, and flutes—
all are held with the left hand uppermost.
For knives, present the back of the blade and the tip.
For small knives, present the handle.
All bladed objects,
when handing to others, avoid the sharp edge.
In a war chariot,
when exiting, blades face forward;
when entering, blades face backward.
The army honors the left,
soldiers honor the right.
With guests, emphasize respect;
in sacrifices, emphasize reverence;
in funerals, emphasize grief;
in assemblies, emphasize eloquence.
In military campaigns, consider dangers,
and conceal intentions to anticipate.
17.21 When dining with a gentleman informally,
start eating first and finish last;
do not return food to the dish,
do not drink noisily;
take small bites and eat quickly;
chew frequently, do not make mouth movements.
If a guest clears his own dishes,
dissuade him and then stop.
17.22 The guest's cup is placed on the left,
the drinking cup on the right;
the mediator's cup, the toast cup,
and the assistant's cup are all on the right.
17.23 For serving moist fish, present the tail;
in winter, the right side is the belly;
in summer, the right side is the fin;
offer the belly fat in sacrifice.
17.24 For all seasonings,
hold them with the right hand,
place them with the left.
17.25 Assisting with gifts is done from the left,
conveying words from the right.
17.26 Pouring for the impersonator's attendant
is like pouring for the ruler's attendant.
In the chariot, hold the reins with the left hand, receive the cup with the right,
sacrifice to the left and right wheel tracks, then drink.
17.27 For all dishes served on a stand,
sacrifice within the stand.
A gentleman does not eat the belly fat of pigs.
Young boys run but do not hasten;
when raising a cup, sit to sacrifice and stand to drink.
Before washing, always rinse the hands.
For the lungs of oxen and sheep,
separate without detaching the core.
For all dishes with broth,
do not add seasonings.
When selecting scallions or shallots for a gentleman,
remove the ends.
For dishes with heads,
present the beak and offer the ear in sacrifice.
For esteemed vessels, the pourer's left is the position of honor.
Vessels and pots face their spouts forward.
Those drinking, performing rituals, or pledging—
if there is a broken stand, do not sit.
Before passing the cup,
do not taste the dishes.
17.28 For raw beef, mutton, or fish,
slice and mince them for kuài;
elk and deer are made into zǔ,
wild boar into xuān,
both sliced but not minced;
river deer become pì jī,
rabbit becomes wǎn pí,
both sliced and minced.
Mince scallions or shallots,
soak them in vinegar to soften.
17.29 For those with a broken stand,
take the sacrificial lung,
return it,
without sitting;
roasted meat is treated the same.
The impersonator sits.
17.30 If clothes are on one's body,
but their names are unknown, it is ignorance.
17.31 If there are no candles and someone arrives later,
inform them of those present.
Guiding the blind is the same.
In all drinking, the host
holds the candle and carries the torch,
the guest rises to decline,
then it is handed to another.
When holding a candle, do not yield,
do not decline,
do not sing.
Those washing, rinsing, or handling food and drink should not breathe on them;
if asked a question,
turn the head and answer.
17.32 Offering sacrifice for others is called "conveying blessings";
offering sacrifice for oneself and presenting food to a gentleman is called "presenting a meal";
for fù and liàn sacrifices, it is called "announcing."
In all meal announcements to a gentleman,
the host inspects it,
hands it to the messenger south of the eastern steps,
facing south, bows twice with head to the ground to send him off;
upon his return report,
the host again bows twice with head to the ground.
The protocol:
for a grand sacrifice, use the ox's left shoulder, arm, and leg broken into nine segments;
for a minor sacrifice, use the sheep's left shoulder in seven segments;
for a single pig, use the pig's left shoulder in five segments.
17.33 When the state is impoverished,
carriages are not carved,
armor is not laced,
eating vessels are not engraved,
gentlemen do not wear silk shoes,
horses are not regularly fed grain.
18.1 Pondering laws,
seeking the virtuous and good,
is enough to gain a slight reputation,
but not enough to move the masses;
approaching the worthy and caring for the distant,
is enough to move the masses,
but not enough to transform the people.
If a gentleman wishes to transform the people and perfect customs,
must it not be through learning!
18.2 Jade uncut
does not become a vessel;
people without learning
do not understand the Way.
Therefore, the ancient kings,
in establishing states and ruling the people,
made teaching and learning primary.
The "Yuè Mìng" says:
"Think constantly from start to finish of the classics in learning."
Is this not referring to it!
Though there be fine food,
if one does not eat it,
one does not know its flavor;
though there be the perfect Way,
if one does not learn it,
one does not know its goodness.
Therefore, learn and then know inadequacy,
teach and then know difficulty.
Knowing inadequacy,
then one can reflect on oneself;
knowing difficulty,
then one can strengthen oneself.
Hence it is said:
"Teaching and learning promote each other."
The "Yuè Mìng" says:
"Teaching is half of learning." Is this not referring to it.
In ancient education,
there were village schools,
local academies in the districts,
regional colleges,
and state universities.
Students entered annually,
and were examined every other year.
In the first year, they were tested on parsing texts and discerning aspirations;
in the third year, on dedication to studies and harmony with peers;
in the fifth year, on broad learning and closeness to teachers;
in the seventh year, on discussing scholarship and choosing friends—
this was called the minor achievement.
In the ninth year, they understood categories and achieved thorough comprehension,
standing firm without regression,
which was called the great achievement.
Only then were they fit to transform the people and change customs,
so that those nearby were pleased and submitted,
and those afar cherished them—
this is the Way of the Great Learning.
The Record says:
"The ant continually learns the art."
This expresses it indeed.
18.3 At the commencement of Great Learning,
ceremonial caps and vegetable offerings
show reverence for the Way;
studying three odes from Xiǎoyǎ
initiates official duties;
entering school to the drumbeat and unpacking satchels
cultivates respect for studies;
the two implements of warning
restrain overbearingness;
not inspecting studies before the Di sacrifice
allows aspirations to develop;
observing without immediate instruction
nurtures inner reflection;
the young listening without questioning
prevents skipping grades.
These seven aspects
are the great principles of education.
The Record says:
"In all learning, officials prioritize duties,
scholars prioritize aspirations."
This expresses it indeed.
Great Learning's teaching is timely,
instruction follows proper subjects,
and retreats have their places.
Learning—
without practicing basic melodies,
one cannot master strings;
without learning varied analogies,
one cannot compose poetry;
without studying diverse rituals,
one cannot understand rites;
without cultivating arts,
one cannot delight in learning.
Thus the noble person towards learning
stores it within,
cultivates it,
rests with it,
and wanders in it.
This being so,
they find peace in learning and closeness to teachers,
joy in friends and faith in the Way.
Thus even when leaving mentors, they do not regress.
The Yuè Mìng says:
"Reverent, respectful, timely, and diligent—
then cultivation arrives."
This expresses it indeed.
18.4 Modern teachers
chant from texts mechanically,
multiply interrogations
and hurried explanations,
advancing without regard for comprehension,
compelling without sincerity,
teaching without developing potential;
their implementation is contradictory,
their demands unreasonable.
Thus,
students conceal their learning and resent teachers,
suffer difficulties unaware of benefits,
and though completing studies,
rapidly forget them.
Education's failure
stems from this!
The methods of Great Learning:
preventing before occurrence is called precaution;
acting when appropriate is called timeliness;
teaching without overstepping stages is called sequence;
mutual observation for improvement is called polishing.
These four
are why education flourishes.
18.5 If restraining after occurrence,
resistance arises uncontrollably;
learning after the time has passed,
toil brings meager results;
haphazard teaching without sequence
causes chaos and lack of cultivation;
studying alone without friends
leads to isolation and ignorance;
frivolous companions defy teachers;
idle talk wastes learning.
These six
are why education fails.
18.6 The noble person, knowing both why education flourishes
and why it fails,
may then become a teacher.
Thus the noble person's teaching enlightens
by guiding without dragging,
strengthening without suppressing,
opening without fully revealing.
Guiding without dragging creates harmony;
strengthening without suppression brings ease;
opening without full revelation prompts thought;
harmony, ease, and thoughtfulness—
this may be called skillful enlightenment.
18.7 Learners have four shortcomings
teachers must know.
In human learning,
some err in excess,
some in deficiency,
some in superficiality,
some in halting.
These four
stem from differing minds.
Knowing their minds,
one can then correct their shortcomings.
Teaching means
nurturing goodness and saving from shortcomings.
Skilled singers
make others continue their melody;
skilled teachers
make others continue their aspirations.
Their words are concise yet penetrating,
subtle yet profound,
seldom using analogies yet illuminating—
this may be called continuing aspirations.
18.8 The noble person knows the difficulty and ease of advanced learning
and recognizes quality and flaws,
then can broadly enlighten;
able to broadly enlighten, then can teach;
able to teach, then can lead;
able to lead, then can rule.
Thus a teacher
is one from whom we learn to rule.
Therefore choosing teachers cannot be done carelessly.
The Record says:
"The Three Sovereigns and Four Dynasties valued only their teachers."
This expresses it.
18.9 In all learning principles,
revering teachers is most difficult.
Teachers revered, then the Way is honored;
the Way honored, then people respect learning.
Thus there are two cases where a ruler does not treat subjects as subjects:
when acting as ceremonial representative, not as subject;
when serving as teacher, not as subject.
In Great Learning's rites,
even when instructing the Son of Heaven,
one does not face north;
this is how teachers are honored.
Good learners
give teachers ease with doubled achievement,
and credit them thereafter;
poor learners
make teachers toil with halved achievement,
and blame them thereafter.
Good questioners
attack hard wood:
starting with soft parts,
then tackling knots,
until with time,
they separate smoothly;
poor questioners do the opposite.
Good answerers
resound like bells:
tapped lightly, they chime softly;
struck strongly, they ring loudly;
awaiting composure,
then sounding fully;
poor answerers do the opposite.
These all are ways to advance learning.
18.10 Rote-memorized learning
does not qualify one as teacher.
One must listen to questions,
and if unable to ask,
then explain;
if explaining brings no understanding,
setting it aside is permissible.
A skilled smith's child
must learn to make fur garments;
a skilled archer's child
must learn to make baskets;
horses trained for carriage start reversed,
with the cart before them.
The noble person contemplating these three things
may thereby aspire to learning.
18.11 The learners of old:
compared things and grouped categories.
Drums do not equate to the five tones,
yet without them the five tones would not harmonize.
Water does not equate to the five colors,
yet without it the five colors would not manifest.
Learning does not equate to the five senses,
yet without it the five senses would not be ordered.
A teacher does not equate to the five degrees of mourning,
yet without one the five degrees would not foster closeness.
18.12 The noble person says:
"Great virtue is not confined to office,
the great Way is not limited to utility,
great trust requires no pledge,
great timing is not uniform.
Understanding these four aspects,
one can aspire to learning."
When the three kings sacrificed to rivers,
they always gave precedence to the river before the sea;
some are sources,
some are outlets.
This is called attending to the root.
19.1 All music arises
from the human heart.
The stirrings of the human heart
are caused by external things.
Moved by things and stirred,
it takes form in sound.
Sounds responding to each other
produce variations;
when variations form patterns,
it is called melody;
combining melodies with instruments,
along with shields, axes, feathers, and plumes,
is called music.
Music
is what gives rise to melody;
its root lies in the human heart being moved by things.
Thus, when the sorrowful heart is moved,
the sound is anxious and fading.
When the joyful heart is moved,
the sound is expansive and relaxed.
When the delighted heart is moved,
the sound is vibrant and dispersing.
When the angry heart is moved,
the sound is harsh and severe.
When the reverent heart is moved,
the sound is straightforward and restrained.
When the loving heart is moved,
the sound is harmonious and gentle.
These six
are not innate nature,
but are stirred by things and then activated.
Therefore, the ancient kings were cautious about what could stir them.
Thus, ritual guides their aspirations,
music harmonizes their sounds,
government unifies their conduct,
punishments prevent their wrongdoing.
Ritual, music, punishments, and government
share the same ultimate goal;
they unite the people's hearts and bring forth the way of order.
All melody
is born from the human heart.
Emotions stirred within
take form in sound.
Sound patterned
is called melody.
Therefore,
the music of a well-governed age is peaceful and joyful,
reflecting harmonious governance.
The music of a chaotic age is resentful and angry,
reflecting perverse governance.
The music of a perishing state is sorrowful and thoughtful,
reflecting the people's hardship.
The way of sound and music
is interconnected with governance.
The gōng note represents the ruler,
the shāng note represents the ministers,
the jué note represents the people,
the zhǐ note represents affairs,
the yǔ note represents things.
If these five are not disordered,
then there is no discordant music.
If gōng is disordered, it becomes wild,
and the ruler is arrogant.
If shāng is disordered, it becomes biased,
and the officials are corrupt.
If jué is disordered, it becomes worried,
and the people are resentful.
If zhǐ is disordered, it becomes sorrowful,
and affairs are laborious.
If yǔ is disordered, it becomes perilous,
and resources are depleted.
If all five are disordered,
overlapping and encroaching,
it is called decadence.
In such a case,
the state's destruction is imminent.
The music of Zhèng and Wèi
is the music of a chaotic age,
akin to decadence.
The music of Sāngjiān and Púshàng
is the music of a perishing state,
its governance fragmented,
its people adrift,
deceiving superiors and pursuing selfish ends uncontrollably.
All melody
is born from the human heart.
Music
connects with ethical principles.
Therefore,
those who know sound but not melody
are like beasts;
those who know melody but not music
are the common people.
Only the noble person can understand music.
Thus,
discern sound to know melody,
discern melody to know music,
discern music to know governance,
and the way of order is complete.
Therefore,
one who does not know sound cannot discuss melody,
one who does not know melody cannot discuss music.
Knowing music,
one is close to ritual.
Having both ritual and music,
is called having virtue.
Virtue is attainment.
Thus,
the grandeur of music
is not in extreme sounds.
The rituals of feasting
are not about ultimate flavors.
The zither in the "Qīngmiào"
has red strings and wide-spaced frets,
one chant followed by three sighs,
leaving an enduring resonance.
The great feast ritual
honors dark wine and offers raw fish on stands,
the grand broth unseasoned,
leaving an enduring taste.
Thus, when the ancient kings instituted ritual and music,
it was not to satisfy the desires of mouth, belly, ears, and eyes,
but to teach the people to balance likes and dislikes
and return to the proper way of humanity.
Humans are born tranquil,
which is their heavenly nature;
stirred by things and moved,
is the desire of nature.
Things arrive and knowledge perceives,
then likes and dislikes take form.
If likes and dislikes are unregulated within,
and knowledge is seduced from without,
unable to reflect inwardly,
heavenly principle is extinguished.
Since things stir humans endlessly,
and human likes and dislikes are unregulated,
then when things arrive, humans become transformed by things.
Humans transformed by things
extinguish heavenly principle and exhaust human desires.
Then arise rebellious, deceitful, and hypocritical hearts,
and licentious, chaotic deeds.
Thus,
the strong oppress the weak,
the many brutalize the few,
the clever deceive the simple,
the brave torment the timid,
the sick are uncared for,
the old, young, orphaned, and solitary find no place,
this is the path to great chaos.
Therefore, the ancient kings instituted ritual and music,
as human regulations;
mourning garments and weeping
regulate funeral observances;
bells, drums, shields, and axes
harmonize and pacify joy;
marriage, capping, and hair-pinning
distinguish male and female;
archery, village gatherings, feasts, and banquets
rectify social interactions.
Ritual regulates the people's hearts,
music harmonizes the people's sounds,
government implements them,
punishments prevent wrongdoing,
ritual, music, punishments, government,
these four extend everywhere without conflict,
then the kingly way is complete.
Music creates unity,
ritual creates distinction.
Unity fosters affection,
distinction fosters respect.
If music prevails, it leads to dissipation;
if ritual prevails, it leads to alienation.
Harmonizing emotions and adorning appearances
is the work of ritual and music.
When ritual principles are established,
then the distinctions between noble and humble are equalized;
when musical forms are unified,
then superiors and inferiors are harmonized;
when preferences and aversions are made clear,
then the worthy and unworthy are distinguished.
Punishments prohibit violence,
ranks promote the worthy,
then governance is balanced.
Benevolence to love them,
righteousness to correct them,
in this way,
then the people's governance is practiced.
Music emerges from within,
ritual operates from without.
Music emerges from within, hence it is tranquil;
ritual operates from without, hence it is patterned.
Great music must be simple,
great ritual must be unadorned.
When music reaches perfection, there is no resentment;
when ritual reaches perfection, there is no conflict.
To govern the world through courteous yielding,
this is what is meant by ritual and music.
When violent people do not arise,
when feudal lords submit as guests,
when weapons and armor are not tested,
when the five punishments are not used,
when the common people have no troubles,
when the Son of Heaven is not angered,
in this way,
then music has achieved its purpose.
To unite the affection between father and son,
to clarify the order between elder and younger,
to reverence the Son of Heaven within the four seas,
in this way,
then ritual is practiced.
19.2 Great music harmonizes with heaven and earth,
great ritual aligns with the rhythms of heaven and earth.
Harmony ensures nothing is lost among all things,
rhythm enables sacrifice to heaven and earth,
in the visible realm there are ritual and music,
in the invisible realm there are spirits and deities.
In this way,
within the four seas,
all join in reverence and share love.
Ritual distinguishes affairs but unites in reverence;
music varies in form but unites in love.
The essence of ritual and music is the same,
thus enlightened kings follow this tradition.
Therefore affairs accord with the times,
and names match achievements.
19.3 Thus bells, drums, pipes, and chime stones,
feathers, yu flutes, shields, and axes,
are the instruments of music.
Bending, stretching, lowering, raising,
formation, movement, slow, fast,
are the patterns of music.
Food vessels, grain containers, sacrificial stands, and ritual dishes,
regulations, measures, and ornamental designs,
are the instruments of ritual.
Ascending, descending, going up, coming down,
circling, turning, baring, covering,
are the patterns of ritual.
Thus those who understand the essence of ritual and music can create,
those who recognize the patterns of ritual and music can transmit.
Creators are called sagely,
transmitters are called enlightened;
enlightened and sagely means
transmitting and creating.
19.4 Music is
the harmony of heaven and earth;
ritual is
the order of heaven and earth.
Harmony makes all things transform;
order makes all things distinct.
Music is made according to heaven,
ritual is modeled on earth.
Excessive regulation leads to chaos,
excessive creation leads to violence.
Understanding heaven and earth,
then one can promote ritual and music.
Harmonious without harm,
is the essence of music;
joy, happiness, affection, love,
are the function of music.
Upright and without evil,
is the substance of ritual;
dignified, respectful, reverent, obedient,
are the regulation of ritual.
As for applying ritual and music to metal and stone,
expressing through sounds,
using in ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain,
serving mountains, rivers, spirits, and deities,
this is shared with the people.
19.5 When kings achieve merit, they create music;
when governance is settled, they establish ritual.
Those with great merit have complete music;
those with comprehensive governance have full ritual.
Dances with shields and axes are not complete music;
cooking sacrifices are not perfected ritual.
The Five Emperors had different eras,
they did not follow the same music;
the Three Kings had different ages,
they did not copy the same ritual.
Music carried to extremes leads to worry,
ritual made coarse leads to bias.
As for enjoying music without worry,
and having complete ritual without bias,
is this only for the great sage?
19.6 Heaven above, earth below,
all things scattered and distinct,
thus ritual principles operate.
Flowing without ceasing,
blending together and transforming,
thus music arises.
Spring growth and summer maturation,
is benevolence;
autumn harvest and winter storage,
is righteousness.
Benevolence is close to music,
righteousness is close to ritual.
Music promotes harmony,
following the spiritual and aligning with heaven;
ritual distinguishes what is appropriate,
residing with the ghosts and following earth.
Thus the sage creates music to respond to heaven,
establishes ritual to match earth.
When ritual and music are clear and complete,
heaven and earth fulfill their functions.
Heaven honored, earth humble,
so ruler and minister are fixed.
High and low positions arranged,
so noble and humble are properly placed.
Movement and stillness have constancy,
so small and great are distinguished.
beings divide by category,
so natures and destinies differ.
In heaven they form images,
on earth they take shape;
in this way,
ritual represents the distinctions of heaven and earth.
Earth's vapors rise upward,
heaven's vapors descend downward,
yin and yang rub against each other,
heaven and earth shake each other,
thunder and lightning drum upon them,
wind and rain arouse them,
four seasons move them,
sun and moon warm them,
and the transformation of all things flourishes.
In this way,
music represents the harmony of heaven and earth.
Transformation untimely produces no growth,
men and women undistinguished leads to disorder arising:
this is the nature of heaven and earth.
When ritual and music reach to heaven and coil around earth,
operating through yin and yang and communicating with spirits and deities;
they penetrate the highest and farthest and measure the deep and thick.
Music manifests the great beginning,
while ritual resides in completed things.
Manifesting ceaseless motion is heaven,
manifesting motionless stability is earth.
One moving, one still
between heaven and earth.
Therefore the sage speaks of "ritual and music."
19.7 In ancient times,
Shùn made a five-stringed qín to sing the "South Wind,"
Kuí began creating music to reward the feudal lords.
19.8 Thus when the Son of Heaven creates music,
it is to reward virtuous feudal lords.
When virtue flourishes and teaching is honored,
when the five grains ripen in season,
then he rewards them with music.
Thus for those who govern with toil for the people,
their dance formations have wide spacing;
for those who govern with ease for the people,
their dance formations have close spacing.
Thus observing their dance,
one knows their virtue;
hearing their posthumous title,
one knows their conduct.
19.9 The "Dà Zhāng"
makes things manifest.
The "Xián Chí"
is complete.
The "Sháo"
continues.
The "Xià"
is great.
The music of Yīn and Zhōu
is exhaustive.
The way of Heaven and Earth is such that
if cold and heat are untimely, sickness arises;
if wind and rain are unregulated, famine occurs.
Education is to the people
what cold and heat are to the year;
if education is untimely, it harms the world.
Governance is to the people
what wind and rain are to the year;
if governance is unregulated, it achieves no merit.
Thus, when the ancient kings created music,
they did so to model it on law,
so that excellence would manifest in conduct and virtue.
19.10 Raising pigs to make wine
was not intended to create calamity,
yet lawsuits and disputes increased greatly—
this shows how the flow of wine gives rise to misfortune.
Therefore, the ancient kings established the rituals of drinking:
in the ceremony of a single toast,
host and guest bow a hundred times,
so that even drinking all day, one cannot become intoxicated.
This is how the ancient kings prepared against the calamity of wine.
Thus, food and drink are for fostering joy;
music is for symbolizing virtue;
ritual is for restraining excess.
Hence, when the ancient kings faced great sorrows,
they necessarily used ritual to express grief;
when they had great blessings,
they necessarily used ritual to express joy.
The distinctions of grief and joy
are all finalized through ritual.
Music is what
the sages delighted in,
for it can improve the people's hearts,
deeply move people,
and easily transform customs and practices.
Therefore, the ancient kings established its teachings.
19.11 The people have natures of blood, breath, mind, and awareness,
but lack constancy in sorrow, joy, anger, or pleasure.
They respond to stimuli and are moved by things,
after which the inclinations of the heart take form.
Thus, when subtle and mournful sounds arise,
the people grow pensive and sorrowful.
When harmonious, gentle,
elaborate, and simple sounds arise,
the people become healthy and joyful.
When harsh, forceful,
vigorous, and expansive sounds arise,
the people become firm and resolute.
When upright, strong, dignified, and sincere sounds arise,
the people become respectful and reverent.
When generous, smooth, fluent, and harmonious sounds arise,
the people become kind and loving.
When decadent, deviant, excessive, and dissipating sounds arise,
the people become licentious and disorderly.
19.12 Therefore,
the ancient kings based music on human nature,
examined it by measures and numbers,
and regulated it with ritual and righteousness.
They harmonized the vital breaths,
guided the movements of the five constants,
so that the yang would not scatter,
the yin would not congest,
the hard energy would not rage,
and the soft energy would not fear.
The four permeate each other within
and manifest outwardly,
each resting in its place without usurping others.
Then they established levels of learning,
broadened the rhythms,
refined the patterns,
to measure moral depth.
They balanced the proportions of small and large,
arranged the sequence of beginning and end,
to symbolize affairs and conduct.
They made the principles of closeness and distance, nobility and lowliness, elder and younger, male and female
all visible in music.
Hence it is said:
"Observing music, one perceives its depth."
When the earth is exhausted, plants do not grow;
when waters are disturbed, fish and turtles do not grow large;
when the vital energy declines, living things do not flourish;
when the age is chaotic, ritual becomes corrupt and music becomes licentious.
Therefore, its sound is sorrowful but not dignified,
joyful but not tranquil;
negligent and violating measure,
dissipated and forgetting the root.
Broad, it tolerates evil;
narrow, it stirs desires;
arousing reckless energy
and extinguishing the virtue of peace and harmony.
Thus, the gentleman holds it in low esteem.
19.13 Generally, when depraved sounds move people,
rebellious energy responds;
when rebellious energy takes form,
licentious music arises.
When upright sounds move people,
harmonious energy responds;
when harmonious energy takes form,
balanced music arises.
Stimulus and response answer each other;
crooked and straight,
each returns to its category.
And the principles of all things
move according to their kinds.
Therefore,
the gentleman returns to his nature to harmonize his will,
classifies things to complete his conduct.
Depraved sounds and disorderly sights
do not remain in his ears and eyes;
licentious music and corrupt rituals
do not connect with his heart.
Indolent, arrogant, and perverse energies
are not set in his body,
so that ears, eyes, nose, mouth, mind, and all parts
follow harmony and correctness to practice righteousness.
Then he expresses it in sounds,
adorns it with qín and sè,
moves with shield and axe,
decorates with feathers and ox-tails,
accompanies with panpipes.
He displays the light of ultimate virtue,
stirs the harmony of the four energies,
to manifest the principles of all things.
Thus, clarity and brightness symbolize heaven;
vastness and greatness symbolize earth;
beginning and end symbolize the four seasons;
circulation symbolizes wind and rain.
The five colors form patterns without disorder;
the eight winds follow pitch without deviation;
all measures obtain their numbers with constancy.
Small and large complete each other;
beginning and end generate each other.
Stimulus and response, clear and turbid,
alternate as warp and woof.
Thus, when music is practiced, human relations are clear,
ears and eyes are perceptive,
blood and breath are peaceful,
customs are transformed,
and all under heaven is tranquil.
19.14 Hence it is said:
"Music (yuè) is joy (lè)."
The gentleman rejoices in attaining the Way;
the petty person rejoices in attaining desires.
Using the Way to control desire,
one rejoices without disorder;
letting desire make one forget the Way,
one is confused and without joy.
19.15 Therefore,
the gentleman returns to his nature to harmonize his will,
spreads music to complete his teaching.
When music is practiced,
the people turn toward direction,
and virtue can be observed.
Virtue is the pinnacle of nature.
Music is
the flower of virtue.
Metal, stone, silk, and bamboo
are the instruments of music.
Poetry speaks its will;
song chants its sounds;
dance moves its appearance.
These three originate in the heart,
and then the energy of music follows.
Thus, when feeling is deep, culture is bright;
when energy is abundant, transformation is divine.
Harmony and obedience accumulate within, and elegance blossoms without—
only in music can there be no pretense.
19.16 Music is
the movement of the heart;
sound is
the image of music.
Patterns and rhythms
are the adornment of sound.
The gentleman moves from the root,
images it in music,
and then orders its adornment.
Therefore, he first drums to warn and alert,
takes three steps to show direction,
repeats the beginning to emphasize progress,
returns to the finale to regulate the conclusion.
Fervent yet not excessive,
profound yet not obscure.
He delights solely in his will,
never tiring of the Way;
fully practicing the Way,
he does not indulge his desires.
Thus, feeling is revealed and righteousness established;
music ends and virtue is honored.
The gentleman thereby loves goodness;
the petty person thereby hears his faults.
Hence it is said:
"In the way of nurturing the people,
music is of great importance."
19.18 Music is about giving;
rites are about reciprocation.
Music
rejoices in its origins;
while rites
return to their beginnings.
Music manifests virtue;
rites reciprocate feelings and revert to origins.
19.19 The so-called grand carriage
is the chariot of the Son of Heaven.
The dragon banner with nine tassels
is the pennant of the Son of Heaven.
The tortoise shell with green and black edges
is the precious tortoise of the Son of Heaven.
Followed by herds of cattle and sheep,
these are what are used to bestow upon feudal lords.
19.20 Music is
that which cannot be altered in emotion.
Rites are
that which cannot be changed in principle.
Music unifies the common;
rites distinguish differences.
The doctrine of rites and music
governs human emotions.
19.21 To explore the roots and understand transformations
is the essence of music;
to manifest sincerity and eliminate falsity
is the constant principle of rites.
Rites and music embody the emotions of heaven and earth,
communicate the virtue of the divine and bright,
summon the spirits above and below,
consolidate the forms of the refined and coarse,
and regulate the norms between father and son, ruler and minister.
19.22 Therefore,
when the great man promotes rites and music,
heaven and earth will become illuminated.
Heaven and earth harmoniously unite,
yīn and yáng complement each other,
nurturing and fostering all things.
Then grasses and trees flourish,
buds sprout forth,
wings take flight,
antlers grow,
hibernating insects awaken revitalized,
birds brood over their eggs,
furry creatures carry and nurture their young,
the viviparous do not suffer miscarriage,
and the oviparous do not have their eggs broken.
This is where the way of music culminates.
19.23 Music
does not merely refer to Huángzhōng, Dàlǚ, strings, singing, shields, and dances;
these are the minor details of music,
hence performed by children.
Spreading mats and carpets,
setting out wine vessels and stands,
arranging bamboo and wooden dishes,
and using bowing and rising as rites
are the minor details of rites,
hence managed by officials.
Music masters understand the sounds and poetry,
thus they play strings facing north;
the temple priests and invocators understand the rites of the ancestral temple,
thus they follow behind the impersonator of the deceased;
the funeral directors understand mourning rites,
thus they follow behind the host.
Therefore,
moral accomplishment is superior,
while technical skill is inferior;
virtuous conduct comes first,
while mere tasks come after.
Hence, the ancient kings established superior and inferior,
first and last,
and only then could they institute order throughout the world.
19.24 Wèi Wénhóu asked Zǐxià:
"When I listen to ancient music in formal attire,
I fear I might fall asleep;
but when I hear the music of Zhèng and Wèi,
I do not feel tired.
May I ask,
why is ancient music like that?
And why is new music like this?"
Zǐxià replied:
"Now, ancient music
advances and retreats in unison,
harmonious, proper, and expansive.
Strings, gourds, shēngs, and reeds
all follow the fǔ and drum,
beginning with civil tunes,
concluding with martial themes,
using the xiàng to regulate order and chaos,
and the yǎ to control tempo.
Gentlemen then discourse,
recount the past,
cultivate themselves and their families,
and bring balance to the world.
This is the expression of ancient music."
19.25 "Now, new music
advances and retreats haphazardly,
with corrupt sounds running wild,
drowning without cease;
involving actors and dwarfs,
mixing men and women promiscuously,
disregarding the relationship between father and son.
When the music ends, one cannot discourse,
nor recount the past.
This is the expression of new music.
What you, my lord, ask about is music,
but what you enjoy is mere sound!
Music
is close to sound but not the same."
Wénhóu said:
"May I ask how they differ?"
Zǐxià replied:
"In ancient times,
heaven and earth were harmonious and the four seasons timely,
the people were virtuous and the five grains abundant,
diseases did not arise and there were no omens.
This is called great harmony.
Then the sages established the roles of father, son, ruler, and minister,
as the guiding principles.
Once the principles were rectified,
the world was greatly settled.
With the world greatly settled,
they then standardized the six pitch pipes,
harmonized the five notes,
and set the Shī and Sòng to strings and songs.
This is called virtuous sound;
virtuous sound is what is meant by music.
The Shī says:
'His virtuous sound is profound,
his virtue can shine brightly.
Shining brightly, he can categorize,
he can lead, he can rule,
king over this great state;
he can comply, he can assist,
assisting King Wén,
his virtue knows no regret.
Having received divine blessings,
he extends them to his descendants.'
This is what it means.
What you, my lord, enjoy,
must be the drowning sounds?"
Wénhóu said:
"May I ask where these drowning sounds come from?"
Zǐxià replied:
"The music of Zhèng is overly indulgent and corrupts the will;
the music of Sòng is seductive and drowns the will;
the music of Wèi is hurried and troubles the will;
the music of Qí is arrogant and perverts the will.
These four all indulge in sensuality
and harm virtue,
hence they are not used in sacrifices.
The Shī says:
'Solemn and harmonious in their resonance,
the ancestral lords listen.'
Solemn
signifies reverence;
harmonious
signifies accord.
With reverence and accord,
what task cannot be accomplished?
As a ruler,
one must be cautious about one's likes and dislikes.
If the ruler likes it,
the ministers will do it.
If those above practice it,
the people will follow.
The Shī says:
'To guide the people is very easy.'
This is what it means.
Then
the sages made the táo, drum, qiāng, qià, xūn, and chí;
these six are the sounds of virtuous sound.
Then bells, stone chimes, yú, and sè are used to harmonize them,
shields, axes, ox-tails, and pheasant feathers to dance with them.
These are used to sacrifice in the temples of the ancient kings,
for presenting, toasting, rinsing, and responding,
to arrange the noble and humble in offices each appropriately,
and to show later generations the order of respect and humility, elder and younger.
The sound of bells is resonant,
resonance establishes commands,
commands establish boldness,
boldness establishes martial spirit.
When a gentleman hears bell sounds,
he thinks of martial ministers.
The sound of stone chimes is clear,
clarity establishes distinction,
distinction leads to readiness for death.
When a gentleman hears stone chime sounds,
he thinks of ministers who would die defending the borders.
The sound of strings is sorrowful,
sorrow establishes integrity,
integrity establishes resolve.
When a gentleman hears the sounds of qín and sè,
he thinks of ministers of resolve and righteousness.
The sound of bamboo is expansive,
expansiveness establishes assembly,
assembly gathers the multitude.
When a nobleman hears the sounds of the yú, shēng, xiāo, and guǎn,
he thinks of ministers who gather and store resources.
The sounds of war drums are stirring,
stirring to initiate action,
action to mobilize the masses.
When a nobleman hears the sounds of war drums,
he thinks of ministers who are commanders and generals.
When a nobleman listens to music,
he does not merely listen to its clanging and ringing;
he also seeks what resonates with him."
19.26 Bīnmóu Jiǎ
was sitting in attendance with Confucius.
Confucius spoke with him, and when the conversation turned to music,
he said:
"Why is it that in the 'Wǔ' dance, the preparatory warnings last so long?"
He replied:
"It symbolizes the worry over not gaining the support of the masses."
"Why are there prolonged sighs
and lingering, drawn-out melodies?"
He replied:
"It reflects the fear of not accomplishing the task in time."
"Why do the vigorous movements and stomping begin so early?"
He replied:
"It signifies seizing the moment for action."
"In the 'Wǔ' dance posture, why is the right knee grounded and the left raised?"
He replied:
"That is not a posture of the 'Wǔ' dance."
"Why does the music excessively involve the shāng note?"
He replied:
"That is not the music of the 'Wǔ'."
The Master said:
"If it is not the music of the 'Wǔ',
then what music is it?"
He replied:
"It is due to the officials losing the tradition.
If it were not for the officials losing the tradition,
then King Wǔ's intent would be considered neglected."
The Master said:
"Ah!
What I heard from Cháng Hóng
is indeed as you have said."
Bīnmóu Jiǎ rose,
stepped away from his mat, and asked:
"Regarding the 'Wǔ' dance's prolonged preparatory warnings,
I have already received your explanation,
but may I ask
why the delays are so extended and lengthy?"
The Master said:
"Sit!
I will tell you.
Music
represents accomplishment;
holding shields and standing firm like a mountain
symbolizes King Wǔ's task;
the vigorous movements and stomping
express the ambition of Tàigōng.
The 'Wǔ' concludes with all seated,
representing the governance of the Duke of Zhōu and the Duke of Shào.
Moreover, the 'Wǔ'
begins with marching north,
the second part depicts the destruction of Shāng,
the third part turns south,
the fourth part establishes the southern states as borders,
the fifth part divides with the Duke of Zhōu on the left and the Duke of Shào on the right,
and the sixth part returns to the starting positions,
to honor the Son of Heaven.
With paired振 and four strikes,
it demonstrates awe throughout the central states.
Dividing and advancing in pairs
signifies the early completion of the task.
Long standing at the starting positions
awaits the arrival of the feudal lords.
And have you not heard the accounts of Mùyě?
When King Wǔ conquered Yīn,
he returned to Shāng.
Before even descending from his chariot,
he enfeoffed the descendants of Huángdì at Jì,
the descendants of Emperor Yáo at Zhù,
and the descendants of Emperor Shùn at Chén.
After descending, he enfeoffed the descendants of the Xiàhòu clan at Qǐ,
and relocated the descendants of Yīn to Sòng.
He restored the tomb of Prince Bǐgān:
released Jīzǐ from imprisonment,
and had him reinstate Shāng Róng to his position.
He relaxed governance for the common people,
and doubled the salaries of officials.
Crossing the river westward,
he released the horses
on the sunny side of Huà Shān
and never rode them again;
the oxen
were set free in the fields of Táolín
and never used again.
Chariots and armor were smeared and stored in armories,
never to be used again.
Weapons were inverted
and wrapped in tiger skins;
the officers and generals
were made feudal lords;
this was called
'jiàngāo'.
Thereafter,
all under heaven knew that King Wǔ would not use arms again.
Disbanding the army for archery in the suburbs,
shooting to the left with 'Lí Shǒu',
and to the right with 'Zōu Yú',
the piercing arrow shots ceased.
Officials wore ceremonial robes and held tablets,
while tiger-warriors laid aside their swords.
Sacrificing in the míngtáng taught the people filial piety.
Through court audiences,
feudal lords learned their duties as subjects;
through plowing the imperial field,
they learned respect.
These five acts
were the great teachings for all under heaven.
Feeding the Sānlǎo and Wǔgēng in the Great Academy,
with the Son of Heaven baring his arm to cut the sacrificial animal,
serving sauce and offering food,
holding the cup and presenting wine,
and wearing the crown while holding shields,
taught the feudal lords brotherly deference.
Thus,
the way of Zhōu reached everywhere,
with rituals and music interflowing.
So, is it not fitting
that the 'Wǔ' dance is prolonged and extensive?"
The nobleman said:
"Ritual and music must not be separated from oneself for even a moment.
Applying music to cultivate the heart
causes a heart of ease, straightforwardness, kindness, and sincerity to naturally arise.
When such a heart arises, there is joy,
joy brings peace,
peace brings endurance,
endurance leads to heavenliness,
and heavenliness leads to spirituality.
Heavenliness means trust without speaking,
spirituality means awe without anger—
this is applying music to cultivate the heart.
Applying ritual to cultivate the body brings solemnity and reverence,
solemnity and reverence bring dignity and awe.
If the heart is disharmonious and unjoyful for even a moment,
then base and deceitful thoughts enter it.
If the appearance is unsolemn and irreverent for even a moment,
then careless and disrespectful thoughts
enter it.
Thus, music
is what moves within;
ritual
is what moves without.
Music achieves harmony,
ritual achieves compliance,
inner harmony and outer compliance
make people observe one's countenance
and not contend;
gazing upon one's demeanor,
people do not generate disrespect.
Thus, when virtue shines within,
all people heed and listen;
when principle emanates without,
all people comply and follow.
Therefore, it is said:
"Master the way of ritual and music,
apply it
throughout the world,
and nothing will be difficult."
Music
is what moves within;
ritual
is what moves without.
Thus, ritual emphasizes restraint,
music emphasizes fullness.
Ritual restrains yet promotes,
taking promotion as its refinement;
music is full yet reverts,
taking reversion as its refinement.
If ritual restrains without promotion, it wanes;
if music is full without reversion, it becomes indulgent;
thus, ritual has its reciprocation and music its return.
When ritual attains reciprocation, there is joy;
when music attains return, there is peace;
the reciprocation of ritual
and the return of music
share the same meaning.
Music is joy,
an unavoidable aspect of human emotion.
Joy must be expressed in sounds,
manifested in movements and stillness,
which is the way of humans.
Sounds, movements, and stillness
encompass all changes
in the nature and methods of humanity.
Thus people cannot be without joy,
and joy cannot be without expression,
but if expressed without being guided by the Way,
it cannot avoid chaos.
19.27 The ancient kings were ashamed of such chaos,
so they created the sounds of the Yǎ and Sòng to guide it,
making their sounds sufficiently joyful but not excessive,
making their lyrics eloquent but not exhausting,
making their melodic twists, complexity or simplicity, sharpness or fullness, and rhythm
sufficient to move people's good hearts and nothing more.
They did not allow restless hearts and evil influences to connect with it—
this was the method by which the ancient kings established music.
19.28 Therefore, when music is performed in the ancestral temple,
and rulers and ministers, high and low, listen to it together,
none fail to be harmoniously reverent;
in clan gatherings or village communities,
when elders and youth listen together,
none fail to be harmoniously obedient;
within the household,
when fathers and sons, brothers listen together,
none fail to be harmoniously affectionate.
Thus music
examines the fundamental tone to establish harmony,
compares instruments to adorn the rhythm;
rhythms combined form the pattern.
It serves to harmonize fathers and sons, rulers and ministers,
and unite the myriad people in closeness—
this was the method by which the ancient kings established music.
So when hearing the sounds of the Yǎ and Sòng,
one's will and mind are broadened;
grasping the shield and axe,
practicing the bowing and stretching movements,
one's demeanor becomes dignified;
following the dance formations,
keeping to the rhythm,
the ranks become correct,
advancing and retreating become uniform.
Thus music
is the mandate of Heaven and Earth,
the guiding principle of balance and harmony,
something human emotions cannot do without.
Now music
is what the ancient kings used to adorn joy,
while armies and battle-axes
are what they used to adorn anger.
Thus the joys and angers of the ancient kings
all found their proper counterparts.
When joyful, all under Heaven harmonized with them;
when angry, those who were violent and chaotic feared them.
In the Way of the ancient kings,
ritual and music can be said to have flourished.
19.29 Zǐgòng met Shī Yǐ and asked him,
saying:
"I have heard that sounds and songs each have their appropriateness—
for someone like me,
what should I sing?"
Shī Yǐ said:
"I, Yǐ, am a lowly musician—
how could I presume to speak of what is appropriate?
Let me recite what I have heard,
and you, sir, can judge for yourself.
The loving are appropriate to sing the Shāng;
the gentle and good yet decisive are appropriate to sing the Qí.
Now singing
is to express oneself and display virtue.
When one is moved, Heaven and Earth respond,
the four seasons harmonize,
the stars and planets align,
and the myriad things flourish.
Thus the Shāng
is the legacy sound of the Five Emperors.
The broad-minded and calm,
gentle and upright are appropriate to sing the Sòng.
The magnanimous and calm,
open-minded and trustworthy are appropriate to sing the Dàyǎ.
The respectful, frugal, and fond of ritual
are appropriate to sing the Xiǎoyǎ;
the upright and calm,
incorruptible and humble are appropriate to sing the Fēng.
Frank and straightforward yet kind and loving."
(This is the legacy sound of the Shāng,
the Shāng people preserved it,
thus it is called the Shāng.
The Qí
is the legacy sound of the Three Dynasties,
the Qí people preserved it,
thus it is called the Qí.)
Those who understand the sound of Shāng
face affairs and repeatedly decide;
those who understand the sound of Qí
see profit and yield.
Facing affairs and repeatedly deciding—
this is courage;
seeing profit and yielding—
this is righteousness.
Having both courage and righteousness—
if not through song, how could one preserve this?
Therefore in singing,
the high notes are like lifting,
the low notes like falling,
turning notes like breaking,
stopping like withered wood;
angular as a square,
curved as a hook,
continuous and even like strung pearls.
Thus singing as speech
is elongated speech.
Delighting in it,
one speaks it;
when speech is insufficient,
one elongates it;
when elongated speech is insufficient,
one sighs it;
when sighing is insufficient,
unconsciously the hands dance it
and the feet tap it."
Zǐgòng asks about music.
20.1 If a feudal lord dies while traveling at a lodge,
then the ritual to summon his soul
is conducted as if in his own state.
If he dies on the road,
then they ascend the left wheel of his carriage,
and use its tassels to summon the soul.
His hearse has curtains,
with black cloth for the lower curtains and plain brocade forming a chamber, then they proceed.
Upon reaching the temple gate,
they do not dismantle the surrounding walls,
but enter directly to the place of encoffining;
only the hearse is detached outside the temple gate.
20.2 If a high official or scholar dies on the road,
they ascend the left wheel of his carriage,
and use its tassels to summon the soul.
If he dies at a lodge,
then the summoning of his soul
is conducted as if at home.
The high official uses cloth for the hearse and proceeds;
upon reaching home, the hearse is detached,
and the body is transferred to a flat-top carriage;
they enter through the gate,
reach below the eastern steps and detach the carriage,
lift it from the eastern steps,
and ascend to the place of encoffining.
For a scholar's hearse,
reed mats form the chamber,
and rush mats form the lower curtains.
20.3 When announcing a death to one's ruler,
say:
"Your servant So-and-so has died."
For parents, wife, or eldest son,
say:
"Your servant So-and-so's Such-and-such has died."
When a ruler announces to the ruler of another state,
say:
"Our unworthy ruler has passed away,
daring to inform your attendant."
For the ruler's wife,
say:
"Our unworthy consort has passed away."
For the crown prince's funeral,
say:
"Our ruler's designated son So-and-so has died."
When a high official announces to the same state:
to an equal,
say:
"So-and-so has passed away";
when announcing to a scholar,
also say:
"So-and-so has passed away."
When announcing to the ruler of another state,
say:
"Your external minister, our unworthy high official So-and-so, has died."
When announcing to an equal,
say:
"Your external associate, our unworthy high official
So-and-so has passed away,
sent by So-and-so to report."
When announcing to a scholar,
also say:
"Your external associate, our unworthy high official So-and-so has passed away,
sent by So-and-so to report."
When a scholar announces to the same state's high official,
say:
"So-and-so has died."
When announcing to a scholar,
also say:
"So-and-so has died."
When announcing to the ruler of another state,
say:
"Your external minister So-and-so has died."
When announcing to a high official,
say:
"Your external associate So-and-so has died."
When announcing to a scholar,
also say:
"Your external associate So-and-so has died."
High-ranking officials reside at the ducal residence to complete the mourning period,
while lower-ranked officials return after the first anniversary ceremony.
Lower-ranked officials stay at the ducal residence,
high-ranking officials dwell in mourning huts,
and lower-ranked officials occupy plastered chambers.
When high-ranking officials mourn for their parents or brothers who were not high-ranking officials,
they wear the mourning attire of lower-ranked officials.
When lower-ranked officials mourn for their parents or brothers who were high-ranking officials,
they also wear the mourning attire of lower-ranked officials.
The legitimate son of a high-ranking official
wears the mourning attire of a high-ranking official.
20.4 If a secondary son of a high-ranking official becomes a high-ranking official,
he wears high-ranking official mourning attire for his parents;
his position
is ranked alongside those who are not high-ranking officials.
20.5 If the son of a lower-ranked official becomes a high-ranking official,
his parents cannot preside over his funeral;
his son presides instead.
If he has no son,
an heir is established for him.
When a high-ranking official divines for a burial site and date,
the officers wear hemp garments, cloth mourning clothes, and cloth belts,
with mourning shoes,
and plain black cloth caps without tassels;
the diviner wears a leather cap.
If using milfoil stalks for divination,
the scribe wears a refined cap and a long garment to perform the divination.
The diviner wears court attire.
At the funeral of a high-ranking official,
after the horses are presented.
Those presenting the horses
wail and leap,
then exit,
after which the offerings are wrapped, and the funeral eulogy is read.
At the funeral of a high-ranking official,
the chief ritualist assists,
the deputy ritualist instructs the tortoise shell,
and the diviner applies heat to the shell.
The principal wife wears a jūyī,
a bāoyī,
with plain silk underneath.
Lower-ranking officials wear a tǎnyī,
while others dress as lower-ranked officials.
For the summoning of the soul,
feudal lords use a bāoyī, a miǎnfú,
and a juébiàn fú.
Their wives wear a shuìyī and a yáodí,
with the dí and shuì made of plain silk.
The soul-summoning is conducted facing west as the superior direction.
High-ranking officials do not have hanging silk
attached below the coffin canopy.
A high-ranking official is buried alongside lower-ranked officials,
but a lower-ranked official is not buried alongside a high-ranking official;
he is buried alongside the brothers of a high-ranking official.
If there are no brothers,
he follows the order of zhāomù.
Even if paternal grandparents are alive,
this is still the case.
A wife is buried alongside the consort her husband is buried with,
if there is no such consort,
she follows the zhāomù order for consorts.
A concubine is buried alongside her husband's grandmother who was a concubine,
if there is no such grandmother,
she follows the zhāomù order for concubines.
If a man is buried with his grandfather, he is paired with him;
if a woman is buried with her grandmother,
she is not paired.
A son of a feudal lord is buried with other sons of feudal lords.
20.6 When the ruler passes away,
the crown prince is referred to as "zǐ",
but is treated as the ruler.
20.7 If one is wearing the refined cap of the three-year mourning period,
it is replaced by the hemp of the nine-month mourning;
only the staff and shoes are not changed.
If one has the mourning for parents ongoing,
and is still in the reduced mourning period,
but buries a young sibling who died prematurely, then the refined cap is worn.
When burying one who died prematurely,
refer to them as "yáng tóng mǒu fǔ",
not by name,
to treat them as a spirit.
20.8 For those living separately,
upon first hearing of a sibling's death,
it is acceptable
to only respond with weeping.
Initially, they wear hemp
with loose belts and headbands.
If one rushes to the funeral without having donned hemp,
and before the host has completed the headband:
distant relatives
complete it with the host;
close relatives
continue wearing the hemp belt and headband for the full number of days.
20.9 For the funeral of a principal concubine,
the burial is arranged by herself, but until the first anniversary and second anniversary ceremonies,
her son presides over it.
Her encoffining and sacrifices
are not held in the main chamber.
The ruler does not comfort servants or concubines.
20.10 If the principal wife dies,
the concubines wear mourning for the principal wife's family.
If acting as the principal wife,
they do not mourn for the previous principal wife's family.
Upon hearing of a sibling's death,
for those in the nine-month mourning or closer,
they weep when they see the direction of the deceased's home.
If one misses accompanying a sibling's funeral procession,
but meets the host on the road,
one goes directly to the tomb.
When presiding over a sibling's funeral,
even if distant, one performs the yú sacrifice.
20.11 If the mourning period is not yet over,
and there is a condolence visit,
one takes their position to weep, bow, and leap.
When a high-ranking official weeps for another high-ranking official,
he wears a cap with a hemp band;
when a high-ranking official attends the encoffining,
he also wears a cap with a hemp band.
If a high-ranking official has the hempen mourning replaced by lighter mourning,
but for a lighter mourning of a sibling,
he wears a cap with a hemp band.
20.12 If a father uses a staff for his eldest son's funeral,
the son does not use a staff to take his position.
For one's wife,
if parents are alive,
one does not use a staff,
nor kowtow.
If the mother is alive,
one does not kowtow.
When kowtowing,
one bows for gifts received.
When leaving a feudal lord to serve a high-ranking official,
one does not return to mourn.
When leaving a high-ranking official to serve a feudal lord,
one does not return to mourn.
The mourning cap has a continuous band,
to distinguish it from auspicious occasions.
The refined cap of the three-year mourning
also has a continuous band,
sewn on the right side,
while for five-month mourning and below, it is on the left.
The three-month mourning cap has a coiled cord.
For nine-month mourning and above, the belt is loose.
Court attire is made of fifteen-sheng cloth,
halved for three-month mourning;
with ash added,
it becomes the finest mourning cloth.
When feudal lords present burial clothes to each other,
they use the secondary carriage and ceremonial robes.
The primary carriage and bāoyī
are not used for such presentations.
The number of funeral carriages corresponds to the sacrificial animals.
They have coarse cloth coverings,
with decorations on all four sides,
and are placed at the four corners.
They carry grain,
but a disciple said:
"This is not according to ritual.
Funeral offerings
should only include dried meat and pickles."
In sacrifices, one refers to oneself as "filial son" or "filial grandson".
In funerals, one refers to oneself as "grieving son" or "grieving grandson".
The mourning garment
and the funeral carriage
have no distinctions of rank.
The plain white cap
and the black cloth cap
have no tassels.
Only caps with xuan and gao decorations have tassels afterwards.
A high-ranking official wears a ceremonial cap when sacrificing for the lord,
but a leather cap when sacrificing for himself.
A lower-ranked official wears a leather cap when sacrificing for the lord,
but a regular cap when sacrificing for himself.
A lower-ranked official wears a leather cap when fetching his bride,
thus
it is acceptable for him to wear a leather cap when sacrificing for himself.
For making sacrificial wine, the mortar is made of juniper,
the pestle of phoenix tree wood.
The ladle is made of mulberry wood,
three feet long;
some say five feet.
The bì is made of mulberry wood,
three feet long,
with its handle and tip trimmed.
20.13 The embroidered banner
for feudal lords and high-ranking officials has five colors;
for lower-ranked officials, two colors.
20.14 The sweet wine
is made from rice.
Jars, pots, baskets, and beams
are filled and displayed,
then folded and placed inside.
20.15 The symbolic tablet,
is buried after the yú sacrifice.
20.16 In all cases, a woman
follows the rank and position of her husband.
During the minor dressing, the major dressing, and the opening of the coffin,
she acknowledges all bows.
20.17 During the morning and evening wailings,
there are no curtains.
If there is no coffin, there are no curtains.
20.18 If the ruler comes to offer condolences after the coffin has been loaded,
then the host faces east and bows,
then moves to the right of the gate, faces north, and leaps.
He then goes out to wait,
and returns afterward to set out the offerings.
20.19 Regarding Zì Gāo's shroud:
one set of silk garments with a dull red robe and crimson-edged skirt,
one plain formal robe,
one leather cap,
one ceremonial cap,
and one black ceremonial cap.
Zēngzǐ said:
"He was not shrouded in women's attire."
20.20 If one dies while on a mission for the ruler,
the calling back of the soul takes place at a public lodging;
it does not take place at a private lodging.
A public lodging refers to
the ruler's palace or a place provided by the ruler.
A private lodging refers to
the residences of ministers, high officials, and below.
20.21 For a ruler, there are seven leaps,
for a high official, five leaps,
with women participating in between;
for a scholar, three leaps,
and women all participate in between.
The ruler's shroud includes:
one rolled garment,
one black formal robe,
one court robe,
one plain pleated skirt,
one crimson skirt,
two ceremonial caps,
one black ceremonial cap,
and one embroidered robe.
A red and green belt is worn,
and over it, a great belt is added.
For the minor dressing, a circular hempen band is used,
the same for the ruler, high officials, and scholars.
When the ruler attends the major dressing,
the ruler ascends,
the shāngzhǔ spreads the mat,
and then the dressing is performed.
The people of Lǔ's gifts for the dead are:
three black and two crimson pieces,
one foot wide,
and the full width of the cloth in length.
The condoler takes his position to the west of the gate,
facing east;
his attendants are to his southeast,
facing north, with the highest ranking to the west,
west of the gate.
The orphaned host faces west.
The usher receives the command and says:
"The orphan so-and-so sends so-and-so to inquire your business."
The guest says:
"My ruler sends me, to express sorrow for this misfortune";
the usher goes in to report,
comes out and says:
"The orphan so-and-so awaits."
The condoler enters,
the host ascends to the hall,
facing west.
The condoler ascends by the western steps,
faces east,
and delivers his message, saying:
"My ruler has heard of your lord's passing,
my ruler sends me,
to express sorrow for this misfortune!"
The son bows with his head to the ground,
the condoler descends,
and returns to his position.
The one offering the mouth-jade holds a disk and announces his mission, saying:
"My ruler sends me to offer the mouth-jade."
The usher goes in to report,
comes out and says:
"The orphan so-and-so awaits."
The offerer enters,
ascends to the hall,
and delivers his message.
The son bows twice with his head to the ground.
The offerer sits and places it to the southeast of the bier,
on a reed mat;
after burial,
a rush mat is used.
He then descends,
goes out,
and returns to his position.
The steward, in court attire,
and mourning shoes, ascends by the western steps,
faces west,
sits to take the disk,
descends by the western steps, and goes eastward.
The one presenting burial clothes says:
"My ruler sends me to present burial clothes."
The usher goes in to report,
comes out and says:
"The orphan so-and-so awaits."
The presenter holds the ceremonial cap and robes:
left hand holding the collar,
right hand holding the waist, enters,
ascends to the hall, and delivers his message, saying:
"My ruler sends me to present burial clothes."
The son bows with his head to the ground.
He places the clothes to the east of the bier.
The presenter descends,
receives the ceremonial cap and robes inside the gate at the eaves,
announces his mission,
the son bows with his head to the ground,
as before.
He receives the leather cap and robes in the central courtyard,
the court robe at the western steps,
the black formal robe from the hall,
announces his mission,
the son bows with his head to the ground,
all as before.
The presenter descends,
goes out,
and returns to his position.
Five stewards
lift them and carry them eastward.
They descend by the western steps.
Those lifting them also face west.
The chief attendant presents the funeral gift:
holding a scepter, he announces his mission,
saying:
"My ruler sends me to present the funeral gift."
The usher goes in to report,
returns with the message:
"The orphan so-and-so awaits."
They set out a team of yellow horses
and a great carriage in the central courtyard,
with the carriage pole facing north.
He holds the scepter and announces his mission.
The guest's attendants come from below,
passing west of the carriage.
The son bows with his head to the ground,
and the offerer sits to place it at the southeastern corner of the bier.
The steward lifts it and carries it eastward.
In all cases of announcing a mission,
one announces it facing the bier,
and the son bows with his head to the ground.
Facing west, one sits
and places it.
The steward lifts the disk and scepter,
the stewards lift the burial clothes,
ascend by the western steps,
face west,
sit to take them,
and descend by the western steps.
The presenter of the funeral gift goes out,
and returns to his position outside the gate.
The chief guest comes to lament,
saying:
"My ruler has affairs of the ancestral temple,
and cannot attend in person,
so he sends an old retainer like me to assist in holding the cords."
The usher returns with the message,
saying:
"The orphan so-and-so awaits."
The lamenter enters by the right of the gate,
his attendants all follow him,
and stand to his left, with the highest ranking to the east.
The director of ceremonies admits the guest,
ascends,
receives commands from the ruler;
descends and says:
"The orphan dares to decline the honor of your presence,
and requests that you return to your position."
The guest replies:
"My ruler commanded me
not to dare act as a guest,
so I dare to decline."
The director of ceremonies returns with the message:
"The orphan dares to firmly decline the honor of your presence,
and requests that you return to your position."
The guest replies:
"My ruler commanded me
not to dare act as a guest,
so I dare to firmly decline."
The director of ceremonies returns with the message:
"The orphan dares to firmly decline the honor of your presence,
and requests that you return to your position."
The guest replies:
"My ruler commanded,
sending your servant so-and-so
not to dare act as a guest,
therefore I dare to firmly decline.
Having firmly declined without receiving permission,
how dare I not respectfully comply."
The guest stands at the west of the gate,
with his attendant standing to his left,
arranged in order from east to west.
The orphaned descendant descends from the eastern steps,
bows to them,
ascends,
and weeps,
then joins the guest in three alternating leaps of mourning.
When the guest departs,
he sees them off outside the gate,
bowing and touching his forehead to the ground.
20.22 If the state is in mourning for its ruler,
one should not accept condolences.
20.23 The female relatives of the external lineage face south in the side room,
while the minor official spreads the mat,
the shāng ritualist spreads the shroud, wrapping cloth, and coverlet,
and the officer washes his hands north of the basin.
They lift and move the corpse onto the burial garments,
and when the enshrouding is completed,
the steward announces it,
whereupon the son embraces the corpse and leaps in mourning.
The wife, sitting facing east,
embraces it and rises to leap.
There are three aspects in which the mourning of an officer is the same as that of the Son of Heaven:
keeping torches burning all night,
using men to pull the carriage,
and proceeding along a dedicated path.
21.1 If, during the mourning period for one's father,
the mother dies before the father's mourning is completed,
when it is time to remove the mourning for the father,
one wears the garments for its removal.
After the ceremony,
one resumes the mourning garments for the mother.
21.2 Even for the mourning of paternal uncles or brothers,
if it coincides with that for one's parents,
when removing the mourning for the uncles or brothers,
one wears the garments for their removal.
After the ceremony,
one resumes the parental mourning garments.
If it is the three-year mourning,
after the headband is changed,
both the xián and xiáng ceremonies are performed.
If the grandfather dies,
and the grandson dies before the xián or xiáng ceremonies for the grandfather,
he is still attached in burial to the grandfather.
21.3 If there is a coffin in the home,
and one hears of an external mourning,
one weeps in another room.
Then one enters to make offerings,
and after completing them,
exits,
changes clothes, and takes position,
following the ritual as at the initial positioning.
21.4 When an officer or great officer is to participate in the state sacrifice,
and after inspecting the washing of vessels,
his parent dies,
he still participates in the sacrifice,
but stays in a separate residence.
After the sacrifice,
he removes his sacrificial robes, exits the ducal gate,
and returns home weeping.
In other respects,
he follows the rites of hastening to mourning.
If he has not yet inspected the washing,
he sends someone to inform.
When the messenger returns,
then he weeps.
If it is mourning for a paternal uncle, brother, aunt, or sister,
once he has lodged for the sacrifice,
he participates in it.
After the ceremony,
he exits the ducal gate,
removes his robes, and then returns.
In other respects, he follows the rites of hastening to mourning.
If they shared the same residence,
he stays in a separate one.
21.5 Zēngzǐ asked:
"If a minister or great officer is to serve as the impersonator of the dead in the state sacrifice,
and has received the order to fast,
but then has a mourning of zīcuī within the family,
what should he do?"
Confucius said:
"He goes out and lodges at the ducal palace to await the ceremony,
as is ritually proper."
Confucius said:
"When the impersonator goes out in his ceremonial cap,
ministers, great officers, and officers all descend from their carriages.
The impersonator must bow to the crossbar and have attendants clearing the way."
21.6 During the mourning for parents,
if a brother dies just before the sacrifice,
the sacrifice is performed after the encoffining.
If they shared the same residence,
even for servants,
the sacrifice is held after the burial.
During the sacrifice,
the host ascends and descends the steps without holding the rail,
and the attendants also do not hold the rail.
This applies to the yú and fù sacrifices as well.
21.7 From the feudal lords down to the officers,
at the xiǎo xiáng sacrifice,
the host only tastes the wine presented to him;
the other guests and brothers
merely sip it.
At the dà xiáng:
the host sips it,
and the other guests and brothers may all drink it.
21.8 Those attending at sacrifices or mournings
are told to offer the delicacies but not to eat them.
Zǐgòng asked about mourning,
and the Master said:
"Reverence is paramount,
grief comes next,
and physical emaciation is the least.
One's countenance should match the feelings;
the sorrowful expression should match the mourning garments."
"May I ask about mourning for brothers?"
The Master said:
"For mourning brothers,
the rules are preserved in the books and records."
A gentleman does not deprive others of their mourning,
nor should his own mourning be deprived.
Confucius said:
"Shǎolián and Dàlián were good at observing mourning,
showing no negligence for three days,
no relaxation for three months,
sorrowful through the first year,
and anxious for three years.
They were sons of the Eastern Yí."
21.9 During the three-year mourning,
one speaks but does not converse,
answers but does not question.
In the hut
or the earthen house,
one does not sit with others.
While in the earthen house,
unless at the appointed time to see one's mother,
one does not enter the gate.
Those in lighter mourning all stay in the earthen house, not the hut.
The hut
is for the most severe mourning.
21.10 Mourning for a wife is equivalent to that for paternal uncles and aunts,
for aunts and sisters equivalent to that for brothers,
and for those who die in childhood equivalent to that for adults.
21.11 Mourning for parents is outwardly removed,
while mourning for brothers is inwardly removed.
21.12 Mourning for the ruler's mother or wife
is equated to that for brothers.
Things that affect one's complexion
should not be consumed.
21.13 Beyond the period of mourning,
when walking on the road,
seeing someone who resembles the deceased startles the eyes,
and hearing the name startles the heart.
When condoling the dead or inquiring after the sick,
one's countenance and sorrowful expression must differ from others.
Only thus
is one fit to observe the three-year mourning.
For other mournings,
one follows the straightforward way
as is proper.
21.14 For the xiáng ceremony,
the host's removal of mourning
is scheduled the evening before,
wearing court robes.
The xiáng uses the same robes.
Zǐyóu said:
"After the xiáng,
even if it is not time for plain silk, one must wear it,
and then resume the mourning garments."
When one should be bared,
if a great officer arrives,
even if it is time to leap,
one interrupts the leaping to bow to him,
then returns to complete the leaping,
and only then covers the shoulder.
For an officer,
after the ceremony and completing the leaping,
one covers the shoulder and then bows,
without repeating the leaping.
The yú sacrifice for a high-ranking great officer
uses a shàoláo offering.
At the completion of weeping and the establishment of the affair,
and the fù sacrifice,
a tàiláo offering is used.
The yú sacrifice for a lower-ranking great officer
uses a single animal.
At the completion of weeping and the establishment of the affair,
and the fù sacrifice,
a shàoláo offering is used.
21.15 The invocator, in announcing the burial or yú sacrifice divination,
for a son or grandson says "the sorrowful one,"
for a husband says "so-and-so,"
for a brother says "a certain one,"
and for divining the burial of a brother says "the elder son so-and-so."
21.16 In ancient times,
both the noble and the humble used canes.
Shūsūn Wǔshū was at court,
and saw a wheelwright using his cane to pass through the hub and scrape the wheel.
From then on,
only those with rank used canes afterward.
21.17 To cover the cloth over the face while feeding rice,
Gōngyáng Jià did this.
21.18 What is the shroud for?
It is used to conceal the body.
From the dressing of the body to the minor enshrouding,
if the shroud is not set, the body is exposed.
Therefore, the shroud is set after dressing the body.
21.19 Someone asked Zēngzǐ:
"After the offering is sent off, the remainder is wrapped up;
is it like wrapping up the leftovers after a meal?
Does a gentleman, after eating,
then wrap up the leftovers?"
Zēngzǐ said:
"Have you not seen the grand feast?
At the grand feast,
after the feast,
the platters of the three sacrificial animals are rolled up and returned to the guesthouse.
To treat parents as guests,
this is what makes it sorrowful!
Have you not seen the grand feast!"
21.20 It is not for others' mourning,
that one inquires or gives gifts.
21.21 For the three-year mourning,
one bows in mourning;
for mourning less than three years,
one bows auspiciously.
During the three-year mourning,
if someone gives wine or meat,
it is accepted, but one must decline three times.
The host, in mourning clothes and hempen band, accepts it.
If it is by the ruler's command,
one dares not decline,
but accepts and offers it.
One in mourning does not give to others;
if others give to him,
even if it is wine or meat,
it is accepted.
