For cousins and below,
after the cessation of crying,
it is permissible to give to others.
Xiànzǐ said:
"The three-year mourning,
is like being cut.
The one-year mourning,
is like being sliced."
For the one-year mourning,
in the eleventh month, the练 ceremony is held;
in the thirteenth month, the祥 ceremony;
in the fifteenth month, the禫 ceremony.
During the three-year mourning,
even if in light mourning, one does not offer condolences,
from the nobles down to the scholars.
If there is a mourning relationship and one goes to weep,
then one goes in the appropriate mourning clothes.
After the练 ceremony, one may offer condolences.
After burial,
for great功 mourning, one offers condolences,
weeps and withdraws,
without participating in the affairs.
For one-year mourning,
if not yet buried,
when offering condolences to villagers,
one weeps and withdraws,
without participating in the affairs.
In light mourning, when offering condolences,
one waits on the affairs but does not handle them.
For small功 and sil mourning,
one handles affairs but does not participate in the rituals.
21.22 If they came for the sake of haste,
they leave after exiting the palace.
If they came for a bow,
they withdraw at the mourning station.
If they came to inquire,
they withdraw after the sealing of the tomb.
If they came for a visit,
they withdraw after returning and weeping.
For friends,
they withdraw after the虞 and (附) ceremonies.
21.23 Condolence
is not following the host.
Those forty years old hold the cords:
villagers fifty years old follow the return weeping,
those forty wait until the pit is filled.
21.24 Mourning food, though poor, must satisfy hunger;
to be hungry and neglect duties,
is not ritual;
to be full and forget sorrow,
is also not ritual.
If vision is unclear,
hearing is not sharp,
walking is unsteady,
and one does not know sorrow,
the gentleman considers it a fault.
Therefore, if ill, one may drink wine and eat meat;
at fifty, one does not extreme emaciation;
at sixty, no emaciation;
at seventy, drink wine and eat meat,
all for fear of death.
21.25 If in mourning,
and someone invites to eat,
one does not go.
For great功 and below,
after burial,
one may go to others,
and if others feed him,
or his kinsmen feed him,
it is acceptable; if not his kinsmen, he does not eat.
In light mourning, one eats vegetables and fruits,
drinks water and broth,
without salt or dairy.
If unable to eat food,
salt and dairy are permissible.
Confucius said:
"If the body has sores, bathe;
if the head has wounds, wash the hair;
if ill, drink wine and eat meat.
To become emaciated and ill,
the gentleman does not do.
If one dies from emaciation,
the gentleman says he has no son."
21.26 Unless following the coffin or returning weeping,
one does not remove the mourning band on the road.
21.27 In all mourning,
from small功 upward,
unless for虞, 附, 练, or 祥 ceremonies,
one does not bathe or wash hair.
21.28 For coarse mourning,
after burial,
if people request to see him,
he sees them;
he does not request to see others.
For small功 mourning,
it is permissible to request to see others.
For great功 mourning, one does not hold gifts.
Only for parents' mourning,
one does not avoid tears and sees people.
21.29 For three-year mourning,
after the祥 ceremony, one resumes governance;
for one-year mourning,
after the cessation of crying, one resumes governance;
for nine-month mourning,
after burial, one resumes governance;
for small功 and sil mourning,
after encoffining, one resumes governance.
Zēng Shēn asked Zēngzǐ:
"Is there a constant sound when weeping for parents?"
He said:
"Like an infant on the road who has lost its mother,
what constant sound could there be?"
After the cessation of crying, avoidance begins.
For paternal grandparents, brothers,
uncles,
aunts, and sisters.
The son avoids the same as the father.
For the mother's taboos,
they are avoided within the household.
For the wife's taboos,
they are not mentioned in her presence;
if having the same name as a cousin, they are avoided.
To cap during mourning,
even for three-year mourning
is permissible.
After capping in the temporary shelter,
one enters, weeps, and leaps,
three times three,
then exits.
At the end of great功 mourning,
one may cap a son,
and may marry off a daughter.
For a father,
at the end of great功 mourning,
one may cap a son,
marry off a daughter,
and take a daughter-in-law.
For oneself,
even in small功 mourning,
after the cessation of crying,
one may cap,
and take a wife;
but for small功 mourning for a child who died between 8 and 11,
it is not permissible.
21.30 All with hempen bands and caps,
their mourning clothes have wide sleeves.
If the father is in mourning,
those in the household do not participate in music.
If the mother is in mourning,
if her sounds are heard, music is not played.
If the wife is in mourning,
music is not played in her presence.
When great功 mourning approaches,
avoid zithers and lutes.
When small功 mourning comes,
music is not stopped.
21.31 When an aunt or sister dies,
and her husband has passed away,
with no brothers in the husband's clan,
the husband's relatives should manage the funeral.
The wife's relatives,
even if close, should not take charge.
If the husband has no clan,
then the neighbors to the front and back,
or east and west;
if none exist,
the village chief manages it.
Some say:
they manage it,
but are attached to the husband's clan.
21.32 Those in hemp mourning do not wear a sash;
one holding jade does not wear hemp.
Hemp is not worn over colored silk.
21.33 When the state bans mourning,
it stops; for the morning and evening offerings,
taking one's position is done as usual.
A child's wailing is not drawn out,
they do not leap in grief,
do not use a staff,
do not wear straw sandals,
nor dwell in a hut.
Confucius said:
"For a paternal aunt or sister-in-law,
in light mourning,
leaping does not leave the ground.
For an aunt or sister in moderate mourning,
leaping clears the ground.
Those who understand this,
how refined they are!
How refined they are!"
21.34 When Shì Liǔ's mother died,
the assistants stood on the left.
When Shì Liǔ died,
his followers had assistants on the right.
Having assistants on the right
was instituted by Shì Liǔ's followers.
21.35 The Son of Heaven is buried with nine cowries;
feudal lords with seven,
high ministers with five,
and scholars with three.
Scholars are buried in three months,
and cease wailing that month;
high ministers in three months,
ceasing wailing in five;
feudal lords in five months,
ceasing wailing in seven.
Scholars have three 'yú' sacrifices,
high ministers five,
feudal lords seven.
When a feudal lord sends condolences,
the order is:
placing pearls in the mouth, offering burial clothes, presenting gifts, and the visit,
all completed on the same day,
in that sequence.
For a high minister's illness,
the ruler inquires without limit;
for a scholar, once.
For a high minister,
the ruler abstains from meat until burial,
and music until wailing ceases;
for a scholar,
music stops until encoffining.
21.36 Raising the coffin upright,
feudal lords have five hundred men pulling the ropes,
four ropes,
all gagged,
with the Minister of War holding bells,
eight on the left,
eight on the right,
and craftsmen using feather banners to guide the coffin.
For a high minister's funeral,
raising the coffin upright
has three hundred pullers,
bell holders
four on each side,
guiding the coffin with reeds.
21.37 Confucius said:
"Guǎn Zhòng had carved vessels and red caps,
screen walls and reversed stands,
carved pillars and painted beams.
A worthy minister,
yet hard to be superior to.
Yàn Píngzhòng sacrificed to his ancestors
with pig shoulders not covering the dishes.
A worthy minister,
yet hard to be subordinate to.
The gentleman neither exceeds above nor oppresses below."
21.38 Women, unless in three-year mourning,
do not cross borders to condole.
If in three-year mourning,
then the ruler's wife may return.
The wife,
on her return, follows the condolence rites of feudal lords;
she is received
as if receiving a feudal lord.
Upon arrival,
she enters through the side gate,
ascends by the side steps,
with the ruler on the eastern steps.
The rest is like the hurried mourning rites.
21.39 A sister-in-law does not comfort a brother-in-law,
nor he her.
The gentleman has three worries:
not having heard,
he worries about not hearing;
having heard,
he worries about not learning;
having learned,
he worries about not practicing.
The gentleman has five shames:
holding a position
without the words,
he is ashamed.
Having the words
without the actions,
he is ashamed.
Having gained it and lost it,
he is ashamed.
Having land to spare but not enough people,
he is ashamed.
With equal numbers yet doubling others' output,
he is ashamed.
21.40 Confucius said:
"In a bad year, ride a nag.
For sacrifices,
use lesser animals."
21.41 At the mourning of Xù Yóu,
Duke Āi sent Rú Bēi to learn from Confucius
the "Scholars' Funeral Rites,"
and thus the "Scholars' Funeral Rites" were written.
21.42 Zǐgòng observed the Zhà sacrifice.
Confucius said:
"Cì, are you enjoying it?"
He replied:
"The whole state is as if mad—
I do not find it enjoyable!"
The Master said:
"After a hundred days of toil,
one day of release—
this is beyond your understanding.
Taut without relaxation,
even Wén and Wǔ could not sustain it;
relaxed without tension,
they would not do it.
Alternating tension and relaxation—
that is the way of Wén and Wǔ."
21.43 Mèng Xiànzǐ said:
"At the winter solstice in the first month,
one can sacrifice to the Supreme Deity;
at the summer solstice in the seventh month,
one can sacrifice to the ancestors."
Sacrificing in the seventh month
was initiated by Xiànzǐ.
21.44 Wives not being appointed by the Son of Heaven
began with Lǔ Zhāogōng.
21.45 External clan women serving the ruler and his wife
are like internal clan women.
21.46 When the stables burned,
Confucius bowed to villagers who came due to the fire.
He bowed once to scholars,
twice to high ministers.
This too is the way of mutual condolence.
Confucius said:
"Guǎn Zhòng encountered robbers
and selected two among them,
recommending them as ducal officers,
saying:
'They associated with the wicked due to their company.
They are capable men!'
When Guǎn Zhòng died,
Duke Huán had them mourn him.
Officers serving a minister mourning him
began with Guǎn Zhòng,
as there was the ruler's command."
21.47 If one mistakenly mentions the ruler's taboo name,
rise.
If one's name matches the ruler's taboo,
use the style name.
21.48 Do not participate in internal strife,
but do not avoid external threats.
21.49 The tablet,
for grand ceremonies called guī.
For a duke, nine cun;
for a marquis or earl, seven;
for a viscount or baron, five.
Width three cun,
thickness half a cun.
Pointed at the top,
left and right each one and a half cun,
made of jade.
The sacrificial ornaments have three colors and six grades.
Duke Āi asked Zìgāo:
"When did your family begin to receive official salary?"
He replied:
"Starting from a minor official under Duke Wén."
21.50 When a new temple is completed, it is consecrated with blood.
The ritual:
the invocator, the temple steward, the household steward, and the cook
all wear ceremonial caps and black robes.
The cook prepares a sheep,
the temple steward inspects it,
the household steward stands facing north
south of the stone tablet,
with the highest-ranking person on the east.
The cook lifts the sheep
and ascends to the roof, from the center,
faces south at the center of the roof,
cuts the sheep,
lets the blood flow in front,
then descends.
The gate and side chambers
all use chickens.
First the gate, then the side chambers.
The bloodletting
is all done below the roof.
The chicken is cut,
at the gate facing the gate,
in the side chambers facing the chamber.
The officials all stand facing the chamber,
at the gate the officials stand facing north toward the gate.
After the affair is completed,
the temple steward announces the completion,
and all withdraw.
They report to the ruler, saying:
"The consecration of such-and-such temple is completed."
They report in the residential chamber,
the ruler faces south inside the gate in court dress.
After receiving the report,
he withdraws.
When the main residential chamber is completed,
it is inspected but not consecrated with blood.
Consecrating a building with blood
is the way to communicate with the spirits.
All vessels for the ancestral temple,
when the famous ones
are completed, are consecrated with a boar piglet.
21.51 When a feudal lord sends away his wife,
the wife, until she reaches her own state,
travels with the rites due to a wife;
upon arrival,
she enters as a wife.
The envoy announces:
"Our unworthy ruler,
unable to continue serving together at the altars of soil and grain and the ancestral temple,
has sent me, so-and-so,
to dare report to your attendants."
The host replies:
"Our ruler had previously declined, saying 'untrained,'
how dare our ruler not respectfully await the command."
The officers display the vessels according to their offices;
the host's officers also receive them according to their offices.
When a wife is sent away,
the husband sends someone to escort her, saying:
"So-and-so is unworthy,
unable to continue together making the grain offerings,
has sent me to dare report to your attendants."
The host replies:
"So-and-so's daughter is unworthy,
dare not avoid punishment,
how dare I not respectfully await the command."
The envoy withdraws,
the host bows while sending him off.
If the father-in-law is alive,
then he is referred to.
If the father-in-law has died,
then the elder brother is referred to.
If there is no elder brother,
then the husband is referred to.
The host's words are:
"So-and-so's daughter is unworthy."
In the case of aunts and sisters,
they are all referred to similarly.
Confucius said:
"I ate at Shǎo Shī's house and was satisfied,
for Shǎo Shī served me food with ritual.
When I made an offering,
he rose and declined, saying:
'This coarse food is not sufficient for offering.'
When I ate,
he rose and declined, saying:
'This coarse food
I dare not let harm you.'"
The betrothal gifts consist of one bundle:
a bundle contains five pairs,
a pair is five xún.
When the bride meets her parents-in-law,
the brothers, aunts, and sisters
all stand below the hall,
facing west, with the northernmost being the highest ranking,
this is how she is received.
Meeting the uncles
each takes place in their respective chambers.
A girl, even if not yet betrothed,
at age twenty receives the hairpin,
with the ceremony
performed by married women.
For informal occasions, she wears her hair in a bun.
21.52 The knee cover
is three chǐ long,
two chǐ wide at the bottom,
one chǐ wide at the top.
The seam is five cùn from the top,
edged with six cùn of colored leather,
not reaching five cùn from the bottom.
Trimmed with white silk,
and laced with five colors.
22.1 When critically ill,
both inside and outside are swept.
22.2 The ruler and great officers remove their hanging musical instruments,
gentlemen remove their lutes and zithers.
The sick lies with head to the east under the north window.
The bed is removed.
Remove the inner garments,
add new clothes,
and support the body with one person.
Men and women change their clothes.
Put floss by the nose to wait for the last breath.
A man should not die in the hands of a woman,
a woman should not die in the hands of a man.
22.3 The ruler's wife dies in the main chamber,
a great officer's principal wife dies in the proper chamber,
a wife without rank
dies in the lower chamber.
Move the corpse to the chamber,
gentlemen and their wives all die in their chambers.
22.4 For calling back the soul,
if there are woods and hills,
the forester sets up the ladder;
if there are no woods and hills,
the musician sets up the ladder.
22.5 The minor officer calls back the soul,
the caller wears court dress.
For a ruler, use the dragon robe,
for his wife, the pheasant robe;
for a great officer, black and red,
for his principal wife, the ceremonial robe;
for a gentleman, the ceremonial cap,
for a gentleman's wife, the dark robe.
All ascend from the east gable,
walk on the ridge of the central roof,
call three times facing north,
roll up the clothes and throw them forward,
the robe officer receives them,
and descends from the northwest gable.
If serving as a guest,
then call back the soul at a public lodging,
not at a private lodging;
if in the countryside,
then ascend the left wheel of his carriage and call back the soul.
The clothes used for calling back the soul are not used to dress the corpse,
nor for enshrouding.
For calling back a woman's soul,
do not use her wedding robe.
In all soul callings,
for men, call the name,
for women, call the style name.
Only wailing comes before calling back the soul,
after calling back the soul, then proceed with the death matters.
22.6 At the moment of death,
the principal mourner wails,
brothers cry,
women wail and leap.
After the corpse is properly laid,
the son sits in the eastern position,
ministers, great officers, father, brothers, and sons stand in the eastern position,
officers and various officials cry below the hall, facing north;
the wife sits in the western position,
inner appointed women, aunts, sisters, and daughters stand in the western position,
outer appointed women lead the external clan members to cry in the hall, facing north.
22.7 At the funeral of a great officer,
the principal mourner sits in the eastern position,
the principal wife sits in the western position,
if there are appointed men and women, they sit,
if not, all stand.
At the funeral of a gentleman,
the principal mourner, father, brothers, and sons all sit in the eastern position,
the principal wife, aunts, sisters, and daughters all sit in the western position.
All who wail for the corpse in the chamber,
the principal mourner holds the coverlet with both hands and wails.
22.8 For a ruler's funeral,
before the minor dressing,
they go out to receive visiting rulers and state guests;
for a great officer's funeral,
before the minor dressing,
they go out to receive the ruler's envoy;
for a gentleman's funeral,
they go out to receive a great officer only when it is not during the dressing.
22.9 When the master goes out,
he walks barefoot, tucks his garment under his belt, beats his breast,
and descends from the western steps.
The ruler bows to the guest lords and state visitors at their positions;
for a great officer, when receiving a command from the ruler,
he meets the messenger outside the chamber door,
the messenger ascends the hall to deliver the command,
and the master bows below;
for a lower officer, if a great officer comes personally to offer condolences,
he weeps with him;
he does not go out to meet him beyond the gate.
22.10 The wife goes out for the wife of a guest lord,
a titled lady goes out for a command from the ruler's wife,
and the wife of a lower officer, if it is not during the enshrouding,
goes out for a titled lady.
22.11 For the minor enshrouding,
the master takes his position inside the door,
the mistress faces east,
and then the enshrouding is performed.
When the enshrouding is finished,
the master leans over the body and leaps in mourning,
and the mistress does likewise.
The master bares his shoulders, removes his cap,
ties his hair with hemp,
the women fasten their hair with hemp,
and all put on hemp girdles in the side room.
22.12 The curtains are removed,
men and women support the corpse and carry it to the hall,
then descend and bow.
22.13 The ruler bows to guest lords and state visitors,
great officers and lower officers bow to ministers and great officers at their positions,
and to lower officers, he bows three times to the side;
great officers also bow to the wives of guest lords on the hall,
the wives of great officers,
and the wives of lower officers specifically bow
to titled ladies,
and generally bow to all visitors on the hall.
The master takes his position,
dons the outer garment, girdle, hempen band, and leaps.
—For the mourning of a mother,
he takes his position with a mourning cap,
and then the offerings are set.
Condolers wear fur robes covered,
add a mourning band, girdle, and hempen band,
and take turns leaping with the master.
22.14 For the mourning of a ruler,
the forester brings out wood and horn,
the potter brings out the water clock,
the cook brings out the tripod,
the marshal hangs them up,
and then officials take turns wailing,
for a great officer, officials take turns wailing,
but the water clock is not hung,
for a lower officer, turns wailing are not taken by officials.
For a ruler, two torches in the hall
and two below;
for a great officer, one torch in the hall
and two below;
for a lower officer, one torch in the hall
and one below.
22.15 When visitors leave, the curtains are removed.
22.16 Wailing for the corpse is done in the hall,
with the master on the east side,
those coming from outside on the west side,
and the women facing south.
22.17 Women do not descend the hall to greet or see off guests;
if they descend the hall, they do not wail;
men, when going out of the chamber door,
do not wail upon seeing others.
If there is no mistress of the house,
then the master bows to female visitors inside the chamber door;
if there is no master of the house,
then the mistress bows to male visitors below the eastern steps.
If a son is young,
he is held in mourning clothes,
and others bow for him;
if the heir is absent,
then those with rank decline on his behalf,
and those without rank
have others bow for them.
If within the borders, they wait for him;
if outside the borders, the encoffining and burial may proceed.
In mourning, there may be no heir,
but never no master.
22.18 For the mourning of a ruler:
on the third day,
the son and the wife take the staff,
on the fifth day after encoffining,
the staff is given to great officers and palace ladies.
The son and great officers use the staff outside the chamber door,
but carry it respectfully inside;
the wife and palace ladies use the staff in their quarters,
but when taking positions, have it held by others.
The son, if receiving a royal command, sets aside the staff,
for a command from another ruler, he carries it respectfully,
for listening to divination or serving the corpse, he sets it aside.
A great officer, in the presence of the ruler, carries it respectfully,
in the presence of another great officer, uses it.
22.19 For the mourning of a great officer:
on the morning of the third day after encoffining,
the master, mistress, and steward all take the staff.
The great officer, if receiving a ruler's command, sets aside the staff,
for a command from another great officer, carries it respectfully;
his wife, for a command from the ruler's wife, sets aside the staff,
for a command from a palace lady, has it held by others.
22.20 For the mourning of a lower officer:
encoffining on the second day,
and on the third day morning,
the master takes the staff,
and all women take the staff.
For commands from the ruler or his wife, they act like great officers,
for commands from great officers or palace ladies, they act like great officers.
All sons take the staff,
but not when taking positions.
Great officers and lower officers use the staff when wailing before the coffin,
but carry it respectfully when wailing before the bier.
Those discarding the staff
break it and discard it in a hidden place.
22.21 For a ruler, a large basin is set to hold ice,
for a great officer, a flat basin is set to hold ice,
for a lower officer, earthenware basins are joined without ice,
a bed with a bamboo mat is set,
with a pillow.
One bed for holding the mouth,
one bed for dressing the body,
and another bed for moving the corpse to the hall,
all have pillows—
the same for ruler, great officer, and lower officer.
22.22 At the beginning of death,
the corpse is moved to a bed,
covered with a shroud cloth,
the death clothes are removed,
a minor officer props the teeth open with a horn spoon,
and supports the feet with a small table,
the same for ruler, great officer, and lower officer.
22.23 The well-keeper draws water,
does not remove the rope, but coils it,
goes up the steps but not into the hall,
and hands it to the attendants;
the attendants enter to bathe the body:
four minor officers hold up the cover,
two attendants bathe the body,
using a basin for bath water,
a ladle for pouring water,
a fine cloth for bathing,
and a bath robe for drying, as in life; the minor officers trim the feet,
and the leftover bath water is discarded in a pit.
For the mourning of his mother,
then female attendants hold up the cover and bathe her.
22.24 The well-keeper draws water,
hands it to the attendants,
and the attendants prepare the hair wash on the hall.
—The ruler washes with millet water,
a great officer with panicled millet water,
a lower officer with millet water.
The field officer makes a stove under the western wall,
the potter brings out the double-legged cauldron,
the well-keeper receives the wash water,
and then boils it;
the field officer takes the firewood from the northwest corner of the temple,
to fuel the fire.
The well-keeper gives the wash water to the attendants,
and then the hair is washed;
washing is done with an earthenware basin,
drying with a cloth, as in life,
the minor officers trim the nails and beard,
and the used water is discarded in a pit.
22.25 For the mourning of a ruler,
the son, great officers, other sons, and all lower officers fast for three days.
The son, great officers, and other sons then eat porridge,
taking in food,
one yi of rice in the morning,
one yi in the evening,
eating without counting meals;
lower officers eat coarse food and drink water,
eating without counting meals;
the wife, palace ladies, and various consorts all eat coarse food and drink water,
eating without counting meals.
22.26 For the mourning of a great officer,
the master, steward, and sons all eat porridge;
other lower officers eat coarse food and drink water;
wives and concubines eat coarse food and drink water.
The same for a lower officer.
22.27 After burial,
the master eats coarse food and drinks water,
not eating vegetables or fruits;
women also do the same,
—the same for ruler, great officer, and lower officer.
After the first anniversary, they eat vegetables and fruits,
after the second anniversary, they eat meat.
22.28 Eating porridge from a vessel does not require washing hands,
eating from a basket requires washing hands.
Eating vegetables with vinegar and sauce,
those beginning to eat meat start with dried meat,
those beginning to drink alcohol start with sweet wine.
22.29 For the one-year mourning period,
one does not eat for three meals;
when eating:
it is coarse food and plain water,
without consuming vegetables or fruits.
After three months and the burial,
one may eat meat and drink alcohol.
At the end of the one-year mourning,
one does not eat meat,
nor drink alcohol,
if the father is alive, for the mother,
or for the wife.
For the nine-month mourning period,
eating and drinking are the same as for the one-year mourning,
but when eating meat and drinking alcohol,
one does not share enjoyment with others.
22.30 For the five-month or three-month mourning periods,
one may abstain from one meal or two meals.
Before the burial,
one may eat meat and drink alcohol,
but not share enjoyment with others.
For mourning an uncle's wife, a paternal aunt,
a former ruler, or the clan heir,
one may eat meat and drink alcohol.
If unable to eat porridge,
it is permissible to flavor it with vegetables;
if ill,
it is permissible to eat meat and drink alcohol.
At fifty, one does not complete the full mourning rites,
at seventy, only the mourning garments and hemp remain on the body.
22.31 After burial,
if the ruler offers food,
one eats it;
if a high official or a friend of the father offers food,
one eats it.
One does not avoid fine grains or meat,
but if there is wine or sweet liquor, one declines.
22.32 The minor dressing is done inside the door,
the major dressing on the eastern steps.
The ruler uses a bamboo mat,
high officials use rush mats,
scholars use reed mats.
22.33 For the minor dressing:
cloth bindings are used,
one lengthwise,
three crosswise.
The ruler has a brocade coverlet,
high officials a plain white coverlet,
scholars a black coverlet,
each one only.
There are nineteen sets of clothing,
the ruler displays them in the east wing;
high officials and scholars display them in the side room;
all with collars facing west, arranged north as the superior,
—bindings and shrouds are not included in the display.
23.1 For the major dressing:
cloth bindings are used,
three lengthwise,
five crosswise,
cloth shrouds, two coverlets,
—this is the same for the ruler, high officials, and scholars.
The ruler displays the clothes in the courtyard,
one hundred sets,
collars facing north, with west as superior;
high officials display clothes in the east wing,
fifty sets,
collars facing west, with south as superior;
scholars display clothes in the east wing,
thirty sets,
collars facing west, with south as superior.
Bindings and shrouds are like court robes,
the bindings are one bolt of cloth divided into three,
without openings,
the shroud is five bolts,
without tassels.
23.2 For the clothes in the minor dressing,
sacrificial robes are not turned inside out.
The ruler does not have donated clothes,
high officials and scholars use all the sacrificial robes of the deceased;
clothes from relatives
are accepted but not displayed.
For the minor dressing,
the ruler, high officials, and scholars all use lined clothes and lined coverlets;
for the major dressing,
the ruler, high officials, and scholars have an unlimited number of sacrificial robes,
the ruler uses unlined clothes and unlined coverlets,
high officials and scholars are as in the minor dressing.
23.3 A robe must have an outer garment,
not unlined,
an upper garment must have a lower garment,
this is called one set.
23.4 All those displaying clothes
place them in a box,
those taking clothes also use a box,
those ascending and descending use the western steps.
When displaying clothes, they are not folded,
colored robes not of the proper rank are not included,
fine hemp, coarse hemp, or ramie are not included.
23.5 Those performing the dressing bared their arms,
those moving the corpse covered them.
For the ruler's funeral,
the senior attendant performs the dressing,
assisted by the junior attendants;
for a high official's funeral,
the senior attendant supervises,
the junior attendants perform the dressing;
for a scholar's funeral,
the attendant supervises,
the scholars perform the dressing.
23.6 In both minor and major dressings,
sacrificial robes are not turned inside out,
all are left-lapped,
bindings are tied, not buttoned.
23.7 Those dressing must wail after the dressing.
Scholars who have served together with the deceased may dress him,
and for doing so, they abstain from one meal.
There are six people in total for the dressing.
23.8 The ruler has a brocade covering, with an axe-patterned lower part,
and seven ties on the sides;
high officials have a black covering, with an axe-patterned lower part,
and five ties on the sides;
scholars have a black covering, with a red lower part,
and three ties on the sides.
The main part of the covering is as long as the hands,
the lower part is three feet,
after the minor dressing, a burial shroud is used,
the burial shroud has a main and lower part,
cut similarly to the covering.
23.9 When the ruler is to be dressed in the major dressing,
the son wears a mourning cap and headband,
and takes his position at the end of the east wing,
ministers and high officials take their positions at the west side of the pillars on the hall's edge,
facing north with east as superior,
paternal uncles and brothers face north below the hall,
the wife and noblewomen face east west of the corpse,
external female relatives face south in the side room.
Attendants spread the mat,
the funeral director spreads the bindings, shroud, coverlet, and clothes,
scholars wash their hands over a basin
, then scholars lift and move the corpse onto the dressing clothes.
After the dressing is completed,
the steward announces,
the son leans over the corpse and leaps in grief,
the wife facing east does the same.
23.10 For a high official's funeral,
when preparing for the major dressing,
after spreading the bindings, shroud, coverlet, and clothes,
the ruler arrives, the host greets him,
first entering to the right of the door,
the shaman stops outside the door,
the ruler offers vegetables,
the invocator enters first and ascends the hall,
the ruler takes his position at the end of the east wing,
ministers and high officials take their positions at the west side of the pillars on the hall's edge,
facing north with east as superior,
the host faces south outside the side room,
the hostess faces east west of the corpse.
The corpse is moved, and after the dressing is completed,
the steward announces,
the host descends,
facing north below the hall,
the ruler touches the corpse,
the host bows and touches his head to the ground,
the ruler descends, then the host ascends and leans over the corpse,
and the hostess is ordered to lean over the corpse.
23.11 For a scholar's funeral,
when preparing for the major dressing,
if the ruler is not present,
the rest of the rites are like those for a high official.
23.12 When spreading the bindings and shroud, leap in grief;
when spreading the coverlet, leap in grief;
when spreading the clothes, leap in grief;
when moving the corpse, leap in grief;
when dressing with clothes, leap in grief;
when dressing with the coverlet, leap in grief;
when dressing with the bindings and shroud, leap in grief.
23.13 The ruler touches the corpse for high officials,
and for inner noblewomen;
high officials touch the corpse for their stewards,
and for their nieces and younger sisters.
The ruler and high officials lean over the corpse for father, mother, wife, and eldest son,
but not for secondary sons;
scholars lean over the corpse for father, mother, wife, eldest son, and secondary sons,
but if a secondary son has a son,
then the parents do not lean over his corpse.
For those leaning over the corpse,
parents go first,
wife and children after.
The ruler touches the corpse for ministers,
parents hold the corpse for their son,
a son leans over the corpse for parents,
a wife supports the corpse for parents-in-law,
parents-in-law touch the corpse for the wife,
a wife embraces the corpse for her husband,
a husband holds the corpse for his wife and brothers.
Leaning over the corpse should not be at the place the ruler did.
Whenever leaning over the corpse,
rising must be accompanied by leaping in grief.
23.14 During the mourning for parents,
one dwells in a lean-to hut, unplastered,
sleeps on a rush mat with a clod of earth as a pillow,
and does not speak except on matters related to the funeral.
For a ruler, a hut is built and enclosed with a wall;
for high officials and scholars, it is left open.
23.15 After the burial, the ridgepole is raised,
and the hut is plastered, but not in conspicuous places.
For the ruler, high officials, and scholars, it is enclosed with a wall.
23.16 For all who are not the eldest son,
from before the burial until after, the hut is built in a secluded spot.
23.17 After the burial,
when standing with others:
the ruler speaks of the king's affairs,
not of state affairs;
high officials and scholars speak of public duties,
not of family matters.
23.18 After the ruler's burial,
the king's governance extends into the state,
and after the wailing ends, the ruler attends to the king's affairs;
after high officials and scholars are buried,
public governance enters their homes,
and after the wailing ends,
with their caps, mourning bands, and girdles,
they do not avoid matters of war and metal.
23.19 After the first anniversary rite,
one moves to a plastered room,
and does not live with others.
The ruler plans state affairs,
high officials and scholars plan family matters.
After the second anniversary rite,
the room is blackened and plastered.
After the second anniversary, there is no wailing outside;
after the final mourning rite, there is no wailing inside,
because music begins to be played.
23.20 After the final rite, one resumes marital relations,
and after the auspicious sacrifice, returns to the normal bedroom.
For the one-year mourning period, dwelling in the hut,
and abstaining from relations throughout the mourning,
applies when the father is alive for the mother or wife;
for those in one-year even mourning hemp,
and those in nine-month coarse hemp mourning,
all abstain from relations for three months.
Women do not dwell in the hut,
nor sleep on rush mats.
For mourning parents,
they return home after the first anniversary;
for one-year or nine-month mourning,
they return after the burial.
23.21 For the funeral of a duke,
high officials wait until the first anniversary,
scholars return after the wailing ends.
23.22 For high officials and scholars, during the mourning for parents,
they return after the first anniversary.
On the first of the month and death anniversaries,
they return to wail in the ancestral temple.
For the mourning of uncles or brothers,
they return after the wailing ends.
23.23 A father does not take precedence over his son,
an elder brother does not take precedence over his younger brother.
23.24 For a ruler towards a high official,
he attends the great dressing of the chief concubine;
if granting a favor,
he attends the small dressing.
23.25 For external appointed women,
the ruler arrives after the coffin lid is added.
For scholars,
he goes after the encoffining;
if granting a favor,
he attends the great dressing.
The ruler's wife, for the chief concubine,
attends the great dressing;
if granting a favor,
she attends the small dressing.
For the various wives,
if granting a favor,
she attends the great dressing.
For high officials and external appointed women,
she goes after the encoffining.
When the ruler goes to a high official or scholar after encoffining,
he sends a messenger to announce it,
the host prepares the grand offering ceremony,
and waits outside the gate.
Upon seeing the horse's head,
he first enters to the right of the gate,
the shaman stops outside the gate,
the invocator takes his place leading,
the ruler offers vegetables inside the gate.
The invocator first ascends from the eastern steps,
stands with his back to the wall facing south.
The ruler takes his position on the eastern steps.
Two attendants hold spears standing in front,
two stand behind.
The usher advances,
the host bows and touches his head to the ground.
The ruler speaks,
looks to the invocator and leaps in mourning,
the host leaps.
23.26 For a high official, the offering may then be made;
for a scholar, he goes out to wait outside the gate,
is commanded to return for the offering,
and then returns to make the offering.
After the offering,
the host first waits outside the gate,
the ruler departs,
the host escorts him outside the gate,
bowing and touching his head to the ground.
For a high official's illness, the ruler
inquires three times;
if encoffined,
he goes three times;
for a scholar's illness,
he inquires once;
if encoffined,
he goes once.
23.27 If the ruler comes to condole, they resume the encoffining attire.
23.28 When the ruler's wife condoles with a high official or scholar,
the host comes out to welcome her outside the gate,
upon seeing the horse's head,
he first enters to the right of the gate.
The wife enters,
ascends the hall and takes her position.
The host's wife descends from the western steps,
bows and touches her head to the ground below.
The wife looks to the heir and leaps.
The offering follows the ritual as when the ruler arrives.
When the wife departs,
the host's wife escorts her inside the gate,
bowing and touching her head to the ground;
the host escorts her outside the main gate,
without bowing.
23.29 For a high official acting as lord, he is not welcomed outside the gate.
He enters and takes his position below the hall.
The host faces north,
the other mourners face south;
the women take their positions in the room.
If there are commands from the ruler,
or from appointed men or women,
or guests from the four neighbors,
the lord bows after the host.
23.30 When the ruler condoles,
he sees the corpse or coffin before leaping.
23.31 If the ruler goes to a high official or scholar unannounced,
the grand offering is not prepared;
after the ruler leaves, the offering must be made.
23.32 The ruler's outer coffin is eight inches thick,
the middle coffin six inches,
the inner coffin four inches;
a senior high official's outer coffin is eight inches,
the middle coffin six inches;
a junior high official's outer coffin is six inches,
the middle coffin four inches,
a scholar's coffin is six inches.
23.33 The ruler's inner coffin is lined with red and green,
fastened with mixed metal nails;
a high official's inner coffin is lined with black and green,
fastened with ox bone nails;
a scholar's is not lined with green.
23.34 The ruler's lid is lacquered,
with three folds and three bindings;
a high official's lid is lacquered,
with two folds and two bindings;
a scholar's lid is not lacquered,
with two folds and two bindings.
23.35 For the ruler and high officials, hair and nails
are placed in a bag;
for scholars, they are buried.
23.36 The ruler's encoffining uses a hearse,
piled up to the top,
fully plastered like a house;
a high official's encoffining uses a cover,
piled in the western wall,
plastered not reaching the coffin;
a scholar's encoffining exposes the folds,
plastered on top. It is screened.
23.37 Parched grains:
for the ruler, four kinds in eight baskets,
for a high official, three kinds in six baskets,
for a scholar, two kinds in four baskets,
with fish and dried meat added.
23.38 Decorating the coffin:
for the ruler, a dragon curtain,
three pendants,
shaking ornaments.
Axe-patterned canopy,
three rows of fire symbols,
three rows of axe symbols.
Plain brocade lining,
covered with a false canopy.
Six crimson cords.
The plume
has five colors, five shells.
Two axe-patterned fans,
two bow-patterned fans,
two painted fans,
all topped with jade tablets.
Fish leap and brush the pond.
The lord has six crimson cords on the cap,
and six crimson drapes.
Great officers have painted curtains, two ponds,
without shaking ornaments.
Painted canopies,
with three rows of fire patterns,
and three rows of axe patterns.
Plain brocade linings.
Two crimson ties,
two black ties.
The fringe has three colors, three cowries.
Two axe-patterned fans,
two painted fans,
all adorned with tassels.
Fish leap and brush the pond.
Great officers wear crimson in front and black in back on the cap,
and the drapes are the same.
Officers have cloth curtains, cloth canopies,
one pond,
with hempen trimmings.
Two crimson ties,
two black silk ties.
The fringe
has three colors, one cowrie.
Two painted fans,
all adorned with tassels.
Officers wear crimson in front and black silk in back on the cap,
two drapes, using crimson.
23.39 The lord is buried using a hearse,
with four ropes and two stone tablets,
guiding the coffin with feather-decorated canopies.
Great officers are buried using a hearse,
with two ropes and two stone tablets,
guiding the coffin with reeds.
Officers are buried using a state carriage,
with two ropes and no stone tablets,
until leaving the palace,
guiding the coffin with coarse cloth.
23.40 For all burials,
ropes are used to pull away from the tablets bearing the load,
the lord's burial uses a crossbeam,
great officers and officers use a collective pull.
For the lord, orders are given to silence noise,
using drums for the burial;
for great officers, orders are given to stop weeping;
for officers, those weeping restrain each other.
23.41 The lord has a pine outer coffin,
great officers have a cypress outer coffin,
officers have a mixed wood outer coffin.
23.42 Between the inner and outer coffins,
the lord's space fits a bell-stand,
a great officer's fits a jar,
an officer's fits a wine vessel.
23.43 The lord lines the outer coffin and prepares a basket,
great officers do not line the outer coffin,
officers do not prepare a basket.
24.1 Sacrificial methods:
The Yǒu Yú shì sacrificed to Huángdì in the dì sacrifice and to Kù in the jiāo sacrifice,
venerated Zhuānxū as ancestor and Yáo as patriarch.
The Xià Hòu shì also sacrificed to Huángdì in the dì sacrifice and to Gǔn in the jiāo sacrifice,
venerated Zhuānxū as ancestor and Yǔ as patriarch.
The Yīn people sacrificed to Kù in the dì sacrifice and to Míng in the jiāo sacrifice,
venerated Qì as ancestor and Tāng as patriarch.
The Zhōu people sacrificed to Kù in the dì sacrifice and to Jì in the jiāo sacrifice,
venerated Wénwáng as ancestor and Wǔwáng as patriarch.
24.2 Burning firewood on the Tài Tán,
is for sacrificing to heaven;
burying offerings at the Tài Zhé,
is for sacrificing to earth;
using a red
calf.
24.3 Burying a shǎoláo at the Tài Zhāo,
is for sacrificing to the seasons;
offering at pits and altars nearby,
is for sacrificing to cold and heat.
The Wáng Gōng,
is for sacrificing to the sun;
the Yè Míng,
is for sacrificing to the moon;
the Yōu Zōng,
is for sacrificing to the stars;
the Yú Zōng,
is for sacrificing for water and drought;
the four pits and altars,
are for sacrificing to the four directions.
Mountains, forests, rivers, valleys, hills,
that can produce clouds, wind, and rain,
and reveal strange creatures, are all called spirits.
Those who possess the world
sacrifice to the hundred spirits.
Feudal lords,
sacrifice to those in their territory,
but not to those whose lands they have lost.
24.4 Generally, all that are born between heaven and earth,
are called life.
When the myriad things die,
it is called perishing;
when humans die,
they are called ghosts;
this has not changed through the five dynasties.
What the seven dynasties established differently:
the dì, jiāo, zōng, and zǔ sacrifices;
the rest remain unchanged.
24.5 When the world has a king,
he divides the land to establish states,
sets up capitals and cities,
and erects temples, distant shrines, altars, and open platforms for sacrifices,
determining the numbers based on closeness and distance.
Thus,
the king establishes seven temples,
one altar, and one open platform:
called the father's temple,
the grandfather's temple,
the great-grandfather's temple,
the great-great-grandfather's temple,
and the ancestral temple;
all are sacrificed to monthly.
Distant temples become distant shrines,
there are two such shrines,
where offerings are made only at seasonal sacrifices.
Beyond the distant shrines are altars,
beyond the altars are open platforms.
For altars and open platforms,
sacrifices are made when prayers are offered;
without prayers,
they cease.
Beyond the open platforms, they are called ghosts.
Feudal lords establish five temples,
one altar, and one open platform:
called the father's temple,
the grandfather's temple,
the great-grandfather's temple,
all sacrificed to monthly;
the great-great-grandfather's temple,
and the ancestral temple,
receive offerings only at seasonal sacrifices.
Beyond the ancestral temple are altars,
beyond the altars are open platforms.
For altars and open platforms,
sacrifices are made when prayers are offered,
without prayers
they cease.
Beyond the open platforms, they are ghosts.
Great officers establish three temples,
two altars:
called the father's temple,
the grandfather's temple,
the great-grandfather's temple,
receiving offerings only at seasonal sacrifices.
The great-great-grandfather and ancestral father have no temples,
when prayers are offered,
sacrifices are made at an altar.
Beyond the altar, they are ghosts.
Senior officers have two temples,
one altar:
called the father's temple,
the grandfather's temple,
receiving offerings only at seasonal sacrifices.
The great-great-grandfather has no temple,
when prayers are offered,
sacrifices are made at an altar.
Beyond the altar, he is a ghost.
Official masters have one temple:
called the father's temple.
The grandfather has no temple but is sacrificed to,
beyond the grandfather, he is a ghost.
Common officers and common people have no temples,
at death, they are called ghosts.
24.6 The king establishes a shrine for the multitude of surnames,
called the Great Shrine.
The king establishes a shrine for himself,
called the King's Shrine.
Feudal lords establish a shrine for the hundred surnames,
called the State Shrine.
Feudal lords establish a shrine for themselves,
called the Lord's Shrine.
Below great officers,
groups establish shrines, called Established Shrines.
24.7 The king establishes seven sacrifices for the multitude of surnames:
called the Director of Fate,
the Center of the House,
the Gate of the State,
the Roads of the State,
the Great Wandering Spirit,
the Door,
and the Hearth.
The king establishes seven sacrifices for himself.
Feudal lords establish five sacrifices for the state,
called the Director of Fate,
the Center of the House,
the Gate of the State,
the Roads of the State,
the Public Wandering Spirit.
Feudal lords establish five sacrifices for themselves.
High officials establish three sacrifices:
to the lineage spirits,
to the gate,
and to the path.
Senior scholars establish two sacrifices:
to the gate
and to the path.
Lower scholars
and common people
establish one sacrifice,
either to the door
or to the hearth.
24.8 The king offers sacrifices downward to five generations of deceased minors:
his proper son,
proper grandson,
proper great-grandson,
proper great-great-grandson,
and proper great-great-great-grandson.
Feudal lords offer sacrifices downward to three generations;
high officials offer sacrifices downward to two generations;
senior scholars and common people
only offer sacrifices to their sons.
24.9 The sage kings established the rules for sacrifices thus:
those who established laws for the people
are sacrificed to;
those who died in diligent service
are sacrificed to;
those who labored to stabilize the state
are sacrificed to;
those who could ward off great calamities
are sacrificed to;
those who could resist great disasters
are sacrificed to.
Therefore,
when Lìshānshì ruled the world,
his son, named Nóng,
could cultivate all grains;
when the Xià dynasty declined,
Zhōu Qì succeeded him,
so they are sacrificed to as the gods of grain.
When Gònggōngshì dominated the Nine Provinces,
his son, named Hòutǔ,
could pacify the Nine Provinces,
so he is sacrificed to as the god of earth.
Dìkù could order the stars and constellations to illuminate the people;
Yáo could impartially reward and punish according to law and died righteously;
Shùn diligently served the people's affairs and died in the wilderness.
Gǔn blocked the flood and was executed,
but Yǔ could continue Gǔn's work.
Huángdì gave correct names to all things to enlighten the people and share resources,
and Zhuānxū could continue this.
Xiè served as Minister of Education and the people became accomplished;
Míng diligently performed his duties and died in the water.
Tāng governed the people with leniency and removed their oppressor;
Wénwáng ruled with culture,
Wǔwáng with military achievements
removed the people's calamities.
These all had meritorious services for the people.
As for the sun, moon, stars, and constellations,
they are what the people look up to;
mountains, forests, rivers, valleys, hills, and mounds
are where the people obtain their resources.
Those not of these categories
are not included in the sacrificial codes.
25.1 Sacrifices should not be too frequent;
if too frequent, it becomes burdensome,
and when burdensome, respect is lost.
Sacrifices should not be too sparse;
if too sparse, it leads to neglect,
and when neglected, they are forgotten.
Therefore,
the gentleman harmonizes with the way of Heaven:
offering the Dì sacrifice in spring and the Cháng sacrifice in autumn.
When frost and dew have descended,
the gentleman treads upon them,
inevitably feeling a sorrowful heart,
not because of the cold.
In spring,
when rain and dew have moistened,
the gentleman treads upon them,
inevitably feeling a cautious heart,
as if about to see them.
With joy, he welcomes their coming;
with sorrow, he sends them off.
Hence, the Dì sacrifice has music
while the Cháng sacrifice has no music.
25.2 Inner purification is conducted indoors,
outer purification outdoors.
On the days of purification:
think of their dwelling places,
think of their laughter and speech,
think of their will and intentions,
think of what they enjoyed,
think of what they delighted in.
After three days of purification,
one then sees the one for whom he is purifying.
25.3 On the day of sacrifice:
upon entering the chamber,
one must dimly perceive them in their positions;
when turning around and exiting the door,
one must solemnly hear their voices and demeanor;
upon going out and listening,
one must deeply hear their sighs.
25.4 Therefore,
in the filial piety of the former kings,
their appearances are not forgotten by the eyes,
their voices do not cease in the ears,
their hearts' wills and desires are not forgotten in the heart.
With utmost love, they remain present;
with utmost sincerity, they become manifest.
When manifest and present are not forgotten in the heart,
how can one not be respectful?
25.5 The gentleman, while they live, respectfully cares for them;
after death, respectfully offers sacrifices,
thinking never to bring disgrace throughout life.
The gentleman has a lifelong mourning,
which refers to the anniversary of death.
On the death anniversary, one does not conduct affairs,
not because it is inauspicious,
but because on that day,
one's thoughts are fully devoted,
and dare not indulge personal matters.
25.6 Only the sage can offer sacrifices to God,
and only the filial son can offer sacrifices to his parents.
Offering sacrifice means
to face toward.
Facing toward them,
then one can offer sacrifice.
Therefore,
the filial son, facing the representative of the deceased, feels no shame.
The lord leads the sacrificial animal,
the lady sets out the wine vessel.
The lord offers wine to the representative,
the lady presents the sacrificial dishes.
High ministers assist the lord,
titled ladies assist the lady.
How reverent they are in their respect,
how joyful in their loyalty,
how earnest in their desire for the spirits to enjoy the sacrifice!
25.7 King Wénwáng's sacrifices:
he served the dead as if serving the living,
missed the dead as if not wishing to live,
on death anniversaries, he was necessarily sorrowful,
mentioning their names as if seeing his parents.
In the loyalty of sacrifice:
as if seeing what his parents loved,
like desiring with eager expression;
was this not Wénwáng?
The Book of Songs says:
"Awake throughout the night,
longing for two people."
This refers to Wénwáng.
The day after the sacrifice,
awake throughout the night,
he offers sacrifices to bring them,
and then continues to think of them.
On the day of sacrifice,
joy and sorrow are half and half;
offering sacrifice must be joyful,
but when it ends, sorrow necessarily comes.
25.8 When Zhòngní conducted the autumn sacrifice,
holding the offerings and presenting them,
his demeanor was sincere,
and his steps were hurried and frequent.
After the sacrifice,
Zǐgòng asked:
"You, Master, speak of sacrifice
as being dignified and reverent;
yet now in your sacrifice,
there is no dignity or reverence—
why is that?"
The Master said:
"Dignity
is a demeanor of distance;
reverence
is a demeanor of self-reflection.
If demeanor creates distance,
or if demeanor turns inward,
how can there be communion with the spirits?
What place is there for dignity and reverence then?
When the sacrifice returns,
music is completed,
the offerings and meats are presented,
the rituals and music are in order,
and all officials are prepared,
the gentleman expresses his dignity and reverence—
how can there be any confusion?
Words
cannot be one-sided,
for each has its appropriate context."
25.9 When a filial son is about to sacrifice,
he must consider the affairs and cannot fail to prepare beforehand;
he must gather the objects for the occasion,
and cannot fail to have them complete;
he must empty his mind to manage them.
25.10 When the temple chambers have been repaired,
the walls and buildings arranged,
and all the objects prepared,
husband and wife observe abstinence, bathe,
and put on their full attire,
then reverently bring the offerings forward,
with an appearance of cautious reverence,
and an air of earnest devotion,
as if they were unable to sustain the burden,
as if they would let it fall—
such is the utmost of their reverential mind in filial duty!
They present the offerings on the stands and the meat on the stands,
arrange the ceremonies and music in order,
and prepare all the officers,
reverently bringing them forward.
25.11 Thereupon
they make their intentions understood,
and with their abstracted and indistinct state of mind, they commune with the spirits,
hoping perhaps that the spirits will enjoy the offerings.
"Hoping perhaps that they will enjoy them"—
this is the aim of the filial son.
25.12 In sacrificing, the filial son
gives the utmost to his earnestness and is earnest,
gives the utmost to his sincerity and is sincere,
gives the utmost to his reverence and is reverent,
gives the utmost to his ritual and does not exceed or fall short.
In advancing and retiring, he must be reverent,
as if personally hearing the orders,
as if they were directing him.
25.13 The filial son's sacrifice
can be known:
in standing,
he is reverent and humble;
in advancing,
he is reverent and pleased;
in presenting the offerings,
he is reverent and desirous;
when he retires and stands,
it is as if he were about to receive orders;
when the removal is done and he withdraws,
the expression of reverent gravity does not leave his face.
In sacrificing, if the filial son
stands without humility,
it is stiffness;
advances without pleasure,
it is alienation;
presents offerings without desire,
it is lack of love;
retires and stands not as if receiving orders,
it is arrogance;
when the removal is done and he withdraws,
without the expression of reverent gravity,
it is forgetting the root.
To sacrifice in such a manner
is to fail in it.
25.14 The filial son who has deep love
must have a harmonious spirit;
he who has a harmonious spirit
must have a pleased expression;
he who has a pleased expression
must have a gentle demeanor.
The filial son is as if holding jade,
as if carrying a full vessel,
with cautious reverence and earnest devotion,
as if unable to sustain it,
as if about to let it fall.
Stern dignity and severe gravity
are not the way to serve parents;
they belong to the way of a mature person.
25.15 The reasons why the ancient kings governed the world are five:
honoring the virtuous,
honoring the noble,
honoring the aged,
respecting the elders,
and being kind to the young.
These five
are how the ancient kings stabilized the world.
Honoring the virtuous—
why is that?
Because they are close to the Way.
Honoring the noble—
because they are close to the ruler.
Honoring the aged—
because they are close to one's parents.
Respecting the elders—
because they are close to one's elder brothers.
Being kind to the young—
because they are close to one's children.
Therefore,
perfect filial piety is close to kingly virtue,
and perfect fraternal duty is close to hegemonic virtue.
Perfect filial piety is close to kingly virtue—
even the Son of Heaven
must have a father;
perfect fraternal duty is close to hegemonic virtue—
even the feudal lords
must have elder brothers.
The teachings of the ancient kings,
followed and not changed,
are how they led the world and the states.
25.16 The Master said:
"Establish love beginning with parents,
to teach the people harmony.
Establish respect beginning with elders,
to teach the people obedience.
Teaching with kindness and harmony,
the people value having parents;
teaching with respect for elders,
the people value following commands.
With filial piety to serve parents,
with obedience to heed commands,
applying this throughout the world,
there is nowhere it does not prevail."
25.17 In the suburban sacrifice,
those in mourning do not dare to weep,
and those in mourning attire do not dare to enter the city gate—
such is the height of reverence.
25.18 On the day of sacrifice,
the ruler leads the victim,
the chief minister responds to the ruler,
and the high ministers and great officers follow in order.
After entering the temple gate,
it is tied to the stone pillar,
the high ministers and great officers bared their arms,
and the hair of the ox is offered with the ear foremost,
the bell-knife is used to cut,
taking the fat and the net,
then they retire.
They offer the boiled and roasted meat,
offer the raw meat and retire—
such is the height of reverence.
25.19 The suburban sacrifice
greatly repays Heaven with the sun as the main focus,
and the moon as the associate.
The Xiàhòu shì sacrificed in the dark,
the Yīn rén sacrificed at daylight,
the Zhōu rén sacrificed to the sun,
from morning till dark.
25.20 They sacrifice to the sun on an altar,
and to the moon in a pit,
to distinguish the dark and the bright,
and to regulate high and low.
25.21 They sacrifice to the sun in the east,
and to the moon in the west,
to distinguish the outer and the inner,
and to correct their positions.
25.22 The sun rises in the east,
the moon is born in the west.
The dark and bright, long and short,
end and begin in mutual succession,
thereby bringing about the harmony of the world.
25.23 The rites of the world
serve to bring back to the beginning,
to serve the spirits and gods,
to achieve harmony and utility,
to achieve righteousness,
and to achieve yielding.
Bringing back to the beginning
serves to thicken the root;
serving the spirits and gods
serves to honor the high;
achieving material utility
serves to establish the people's discipline;
achieving righteousness,
then high and low do not rebel against each other;
achieving yielding,
serves to eliminate contention.
Combining these five
to govern the rites of the world,
even if there are strange and evil elements,
those that are not governed are few.
25.24 Zǎi Wǒ said:
"I have heard the names 'spirit' and 'god',
but I do not know what they mean."
The Master said:
"The vital breath
is the abundance of the spirit;
the animal soul
is the abundance of the ghost;
uniting ghost and spirit
is the height of teaching."
25.25 All living beings must die,
and dying must return to the earth—
this is called ghost.
The bones and flesh decay below,
and hidden become the wild soil.
25.26 The vital breath is sent forth and rises above,
becoming the shining brightness,
The vapors and fragrances,
the sorrow and grief,
these are the essence of all things,
the manifestation of spirits.
25.27 Based on the essence of things,
they established the ultimate standards,
clearly designated them as guǐshén,
to serve as rules for the common people.
The masses thereby stood in awe,
and the myriad people submitted.
25.28 The sages considered this insufficient,
so they built palaces and temples,
established ancestral shrines and distant temples,
to distinguish between close and distant relatives,
teaching people to return to antiquity and recover their origins,
not forgetting whence they were born.
The people's submission stems from this,
hence their obedience is swift.
25.29 Once these two aspects were established,
they were repaid with two rituals.
They arranged the morning ceremony,
burning fat and fragrant herbs,
revealing them with the light of wormwood,
to repay the vital energy.
This teaches the masses to return to their origins.
Offering millet and grains,
presenting livers, lungs, heads, and hearts,
displayed between paired wine vessels,
supplemented with aromatic wine,
to repay the earthly soul.
Teaching people to love one another,
superiors and inferiors employing genuine feelings,
this is the pinnacle of ritual.
25.30 The noble person returns to antiquity and recovers their origins,
not forgetting whence they were born,
therefore expressing their reverence,
revealing their feelings,
exerting all efforts in their tasks,
to repay their parents,
daring not to be less than thorough.
25.31 Thus,
in ancient times,
the Son of Heaven plowed a thousand mǔ of ceremonial fields,
wearing a crown with red strings,
personally holding the plow.
The feudal lords plowed a hundred mǔ,
wearing crowns with blue strings,
personally holding the plows,
to serve Heaven, Earth, mountains, rivers, the state altars, and ancient ancestors,
providing sweet wine, fermented beverages, and sacrificial grains,
which were taken from here,
the ultimate in reverence.
25.32 In ancient times,
the Son of Heaven and feudal lords necessarily had officials in charge of breeding animals,
and at the appropriate seasons,
they would fast, bathe, and personally inspect them.
Sacrificial animals, pure-colored victims, and offerings
were necessarily selected from these,
the ultimate in reverence.
The ruler would summon the oxen,
bring them in and examine them,
select their hair and divine with it,
if auspicious,
then they would be raised.
The ruler wore a leather cap and plain garments,
on the first day
and the middle of the month,
the ruler inspected the sacrificial animals,
thereby devoting his efforts,
the ultimate in filial piety.
25.33 In ancient times, the Son of Heaven and feudal lords
necessarily had public mulberry trees and silkworm chambers,
established near rivers.
They built palaces, with walls seven and a half feet high,
surrounded by thorny fences and closed from the outside.
At the dawn of the great day,
the ruler wore a leather cap and plain garments,
divined to select the auspicious ones among the three palaces' ladies and official wives,
sending them into the silkworm chambers to tend silkworms;
they would take the silkworm eggs and wash them in the river;
they gathered mulberry leaves from the public trees,
dried by the wind to feed the silkworms.
When the year's work was completed:
the official wives finished rearing silkworms,
presented the cocoons to show the ruler,
then offered them to the primary wife.
The primary wife would say:
"Are these for making the ruler's garments?"
Then she would don her ceremonial headdress and robe to receive them,
and perform a shàoláo sacrifice to honor them.
Those who presented cocoons in ancient times,
did they generally follow this practice?
On an auspicious day,
the primary wife would reel the silk,
dipping her hands three times in basins,
then distribute it to the auspiciously selected ladies of the three palaces and official wives,
having them reel the silk;
then dye it red and green,
black and yellow,
to make the patterns of ceremonial robes.
When the garments were completed,
the ruler would wear them to sacrifice to previous kings and dukes,
the ultimate in reverence.
25.34 The noble person said:
"Ritual and music cannot be separated from oneself for even a moment.
Applying music to cultivate the heart
causes a heart of ease, straightforwardness, kindness, and sincerity
to naturally arise.
When this heart arises, there is joy,
joy brings peace,
peace brings endurance,
endurance brings heavenly connection,
heavenly connection brings spiritual connection.
Heaven does not speak yet is trusted,
spirits are not angry yet are awe-inspiring.
This is applying music to cultivate the heart.
Applying ritual to cultivate the body brings dignity and reverence,
dignity and reverence bring solemn authority.
If the heart is discordant and unjoyful for even a moment,
then base and deceitful thoughts enter it;
if the appearance is undignified and irreverent for even a moment,
then negligent and disrespectful thoughts enter it.
Thus music
moves within,
while ritual
moves without.
Music achieves harmony,
ritual achieves compliance.
Harmonious within and compliant without,
then people observe one's countenance and do not contend;
they behold one's demeanor,
and the masses feel no negligence or disrespect.
Thus when virtue shines within,
the people all heed;
when principle manifests without,
the masses all comply.
Therefore it is said:
'Master the way of ritual and music,
and fill the world with it,
then implementing it everywhere will be without difficulty.'
Music
moves within;
ritual
moves without.
Thus ritual emphasizes restraint,
music emphasizes fullness.
Ritual restrained yet advancing,
takes advancement as its pattern;
music full yet returning,
takes return as its pattern.
Ritual restrained without advancement wanes,
music full without return becomes indulgent.
Thus ritual has its recompense and music its return.
When ritual attains its recompense, there is joy;
when music attains its return, there is peace.
The recompense of ritual
and the return of music
share the same meaning."
25.35 Zēngzǐ said:
"There are three kinds of filial piety:
the greatest is honoring one's parents,
the next is not disgracing them,
the lowest is being able to support them."
Gōngmíng Yí asked Zēngzǐ:
"Can the master be considered filial?"
Zēngzǐ replied:
"What kind of talk is this?
What kind of talk is this?
What the noble person calls filial piety means:
anticipating their wishes and continuing their aims,
guiding parents with the Way.
I, Shēn,
merely provide support!
How can that be considered filial piety?"
Zēngzǐ said:
"The body
is the legacy of one's parents.
Using this legacy of one's parents,
how dare one not be reverent?
If daily conduct is not dignified,
it is unfilial;
if serving the ruler is not loyal,
it is unfilial;
if holding office is not respectful,
it is unfilial;
if with friends one is not trustworthy,
it is unfilial;
if in battle one is not courageous,
it is unfilial;
if these five are not accomplished,
disaster will reach one's parents,
how dare one not be reverent?"
Offering cooked, ripe, fragrant, and savory foods,
tasting and presenting them,
is not filial piety,
but mere provision.
What the noble man calls filial piety
is when the people of the state exclaim with admiration:
" 'How fortunate to have a son
like this!' "
This is what is called filial piety.
The fundamental teaching for the masses is called filial piety,
and its practice is called provision.
Provision
is possible,
but respect is difficult;
respect
is possible,
but ease is difficult;
ease
is possible,
but perseverance is difficult.
After parents have passed away,
to be cautious in one's conduct,
not leaving a bad name for one's parents,
can be called capable of completion.
Benevolence
is to be benevolent in this;
ritual
is to practice this;
righteousness
trustworthiness
is to be trustworthy in this;
strength
is to be strong in this.
Joy arises from following this,
punishment arises from opposing this."
Zēngzǐ said:
"Filial piety,
when established, fills heaven and earth;
when spread, extends across the four seas;
when applied to later ages, it knows no morning or evening;
extended and applied to the Eastern Sea, it is the standard;
extended and applied to the Western Sea, it is the standard;
extended and applied to the Southern Sea, it is the standard;
extended and applied to the Northern Sea, it is the standard.
The Book of Songs says:
'From west, from east, from south, from north,
none think but to submit.'
This expresses it."
Zēngzǐ said:
"Trees are felled in their season,
birds and beasts are killed in their season.
The Master said:
' 'To cut down a single tree,
to kill a single beast,
not in its proper season,
is not filial.'
There are three degrees of filial piety:
minor filial piety uses effort,
medium filial piety uses toil,
great filial piety is inexhaustible.
Thinking of parental love and forgetting toil
can be called using effort.
Honoring benevolence,
being at ease with righteousness,
can be called using toil.
Broadly bestowing and fully providing
can be called inexhaustible.
When parents love one,
rejoice and do not forget;
when parents dislike one,
be fearful but without resentment;
when parents have faults,
remonstrate but do not oppose;
after parents have passed away,
must seek grain from the benevolent to sacrifice to them.
This is called completing the rites."
25.36 Yuèzhèng Zǐchūn came down from the hall and injured his foot,
and for several months did not go out,
still wearing a worried expression.
His disciples said:
"Master, your foot has healed,
yet for several months you have not gone out,
still wearing a worried expression;
why is this?"
Yuèzhèng Zǐchūn said:
"Excellent is your question!
Excellent is your question!
I heard from Zēngzǐ,
and Zēngzǐ heard from the Master, who said:
' 'What heaven gives birth to,
what earth nourishes,
nothing is greater than humans.
Parents give birth to one whole,
and the child returns whole,
this can be called filial.
Not damaging one's body,
not disgracing oneself,
can be called whole.
Therefore, the noble man does not dare forget filial piety even for a half-step.'
Now I have forgotten the way of filial piety,
hence I have this worried expression.
With each step, one dares not forget parents;
with each word spoken, one dares not forget parents.
With each step, one dares not forget parents,
therefore one takes the main road and not bypaths,
uses boats and does not swim,
not daring to risk the body inherited from parents.
With each word spoken, one dares not forget parents,
therefore harsh words do not leave the mouth,
and angry words do not reach one's person.
Not disgracing oneself,
not shaming one's parents,
can be called filial."
25.37 In ancient times,
the Yú dynasty valued virtue and honored age,
the Xiàhòu dynasty valued rank and honored age,
the Yīn people valued wealth and honored age,
the Zhōu people valued kinship and honored age.
Yú, Xià, Yīn, and Zhōu,
the illustrious kings of the world,
none neglected age.
The honor of age in the world
is long-standing;
it is next to serving parents.
25.38 Therefore,
at court, those of the same rank honor age.
At seventy, one leans on a staff at court,
and if the ruler asks, a mat is provided.
At eighty, one does not wait for court,
and if the ruler asks, he goes to them,
thus fraternal duty reaches the court.
25.39 When walking,
shoulders do not come side by side,
but if not staggered, then one follows.
When seeing an elder,
those in carriages or on foot give way;
the grey-haired do not carry burdens on the road,
thus fraternal duty reaches the roads.
In the village, age is honored,
and the old and poor are not neglected,
the strong do not oppress the weak,
the many do not bully the few,
thus fraternal duty reaches the neighborhoods.
25.40 According to the ancient way,
at fifty one does not serve as a hunter,
and game is distributed generously to the elders,
thus fraternal duty reaches the hunts.
In military ranks,
those of the same rank honor age,
thus fraternal duty reaches the army.
25.41 Filial and fraternal duties emanate from the court,
are practiced on the roads,
reach the neighborhoods,
extend to the hunts,
follow into the army,
and the multitude would die for righteousness,
not daring to violate it.
25.42 Sacrificing in the Míngtáng
teaches the feudal lords filial piety;
feasting the Three Elders and Five Seniors in the Great Academy
teaches the feudal lords fraternal duty.
Sacrificing to former worthies in the Western Academy
teaches the feudal lords virtue;
plowing the imperial field
teaches the feudal lords provision;
attending court
teaches the feudal lords ministerhood.
These five
are the great teachings of the world.
25.43 Feasting the Three Elders and Five Seniors in the Great Academy,
the Son of Heaven bares his arm to cut the sacrifice,
holds the sauce to serve,
holds the cup to offer drink,
and wearing the crown, leads the dance with shield,
thus teaching the feudal lords fraternal duty.
Therefore,
in the villages, age is honored,
and the old and poor are not neglected,
the strong do not oppress the weak, the many do not bully the few,
this comes from the Great Academy.
The Son of Heaven establishes four schools,
and when entering to study,
the crown prince honors age.
25.44 When the Son of Heaven tours the domains,
the feudal lords wait at the borders.
The Son of Heaven first visits those over a hundred years old.
Those eighty or ninety: if going east,
those going west dare not pass without paying respects;
if going west,
those going east dare not pass without paying respects.
Those wishing to speak about governance,
the ruler may go to them.
25.45 With one appointment, one takes precedence by age among the village neighbors;
with a second appointment, one takes precedence by age among the clan;
with a third appointment, one does not take precedence by age.
If there is a seventy-year-old in the clan,
one dares not precede them.
Those who are seventy,
unless there is a major reason, do not enter the court;
if they enter due to a major reason,
the ruler must exchange courtesies with them,
and only then attend to those of higher rank.
25.46 When the Son of Heaven has merits,
he attributes the virtue to Heaven;
when the feudal lords have merits,
they ascribe them to the Son of Heaven;
when the high ministers and great officers have merits,
they present them to the feudal lords;
when the scholars and common people have merits,
they trace them to their parents,
and present them to the elders;
emoluments, ranks, celebrations, and rewards
are all completed in the ancestral temple;
this is to show compliance.
In ancient times,
the sages established the principles of yīn and yáng, Heaven and Earth,
and set them up as the Yì.
The diviner holds the tortoise shell facing south,
while the Son of Heaven, in ceremonial dress, faces north;
even if he possesses a wise and knowing mind,
he must advance and have his intentions decided by it.
This shows he does not dare to act arbitrarily,
in order to honor Heaven.
He attributes goodness to others,
and faults to himself.
He teaches not to boast in order to honor the worthy.
25.47 When a filial son is about to offer sacrifices,
he must have a reverent and solemn heart to consider the affairs,
to prepare the garments and objects,
to repair the ancestral temples,
and to manage all matters.
On the day of the sacrifice,
his countenance must be gentle,
his actions must be cautious,
as if fearing he will not reach the beloved.
When he sets forth the offerings,
his appearance must be warm,
his body must be bowed,
as if speaking and not yet finished.
After all the participants have left,
he stands humble and quiet, upright,
as if he will not see them again.
After the sacrifice,
he is deeply content and fulfilled.
as if about to enter again.
Therefore,
sincerity and goodness do not leave his person,
his ears and eyes do not stray from his heart,
his thoughts do not stray from his parents.
They are tied in his heart,
manifested in his expression,
and examined through reflection;
this is the aim of a filial son.
25.48 In establishing the spiritual positions of the state;
the altar to the gods of soil and grain is on the right,
and the ancestral temple is on the left.
26.1 In the way of governing people,
nothing is more urgent than ritual.
There are five classics of ritual,
and none is more important than sacrifice.
Sacrifice is not something
that comes from outside;
it emerges from within, born from the heart;
the heart is moved and presents it with ritual.
Therefore,
only the worthy can fully realize the meaning of sacrifice.
26.2 The sacrifice of the worthy
is sure to receive blessings.
Not the blessings that the world speaks of.
Blessings mean
completeness;
completeness means
the name for all that is favorable.
When there is nothing that is not favorable,
it is called completeness.
This means
inwardly exhausting oneself in effort,
and outwardly complying with the Way.
The loyal minister in serving his ruler,
the filial son in serving his parents,
their root is one.
Above, they comply with the spirits and gods,
