outwardly they comply with rulers and elders,
inwardly they are filial to their parents.
This is called completeness.
Only the worthy can achieve completeness,
and only after achieving completeness can they sacrifice.
Therefore,
the sacrifice of the worthy:
expresses their sincerity and trustworthiness
along with their loyalty and reverence,
presents it with objects,
guides it with ritual,
settles it with music,
and correlates it with the seasons.
They clearly offer it, that is all,
not seeking anything in return.
This is the heart of a filial son.
Sacrifice is
the means to continue providing for and extending filial piety.
Filial piety means nurturing.
Complying with the Way,
not going against the moral order,
this is called nurturing.
26.3 Therefore,
in a filial son's service to his parents,
there are three ways:
in life, he nurtures them;
after death, he mourns them;
after mourning, he sacrifices to them.
In nurturing, observe his compliance;
in mourning, observe his grief;
in sacrifice, observe his reverence and timeliness.
Fulfilling these three ways
is the conduct of a filial son.
26.4 After exhausting efforts inwardly,
one also seeks help outwardly;
this is the meaning of the marriage ceremony.
Thus, the words when a ruler takes a wife are:
"I request your jade-like daughter
to share our humble state with me,
to serve the ancestral temple and the altars of soil and grain."
This is the root of seeking help.
As for sacrifice,
it must be personally attended by husband and wife,
thereby completing the offices both inside and outside;
when the offices are complete, the preparations are complete.
Pickles from aquatic plants,
minced meats from land products,
small items are thus prepared;
the stands with the three sacrificial animals,
the contents of the eight guǐ vessels,
fine items are thus prepared;
the unusual among insects,
the fruits of trees and plants,
the things of yīn and yáng are thus prepared.
26.5 All that is born by Heaven,
and grown by Earth,
if it can be offered,
nothing is omitted,
showing the exhaustion of things.
Outwardly, things are exhausted;
inwardly, intention is exhausted;
this is the heart of sacrifice.
Therefore,
the Son of Heaven personally plows in the southern suburb
to supply the grain offerings;
the Queen sericultures in the northern suburb
to supply the pure robes.
The feudal lords plow in the eastern suburb
also to supply the grain offerings;
their Ladies sericulture in the northern suburb
to supply the ceremonial robes.
It is not that the Son of Heaven and feudal lords have no one to plow for them,
nor that the Queen and Ladies have no one to sericulture for them;
they personally express their sincerity and trustworthiness.
Sincerity and trustworthiness are called exhaustion,
exhaustion is called reverence,
and only after reverence and exhaustion can one serve the spirits and gods;
this is the Way of sacrifice.
26.6 When the time for sacrifice approaches,
the noble person fasts.
Fasting means to purify.
One purifies what is not pure to achieve purity.
Therefore, unless there is a great affair,
unless there is reverence and respect,
the noble person does not fast.
Without fasting, there is no guarding against things,
and desires have no stop.
When about to fast,
one guards against evil things,
puts an end to desires,
and the ears do not listen to music.
Thus, the record says:
"One who fasts does not enjoy music."
This means one does not dare to scatter one's will.
The mind does not think carelessly,
but must rely on the Way;
the hands and feet do not move carelessly,
but must follow ritual.
Therefore, the fasting of the noble person
is solely to express its clear and bright virtue.
Thus, there is dispersed fasting for seven days to settle it,
and intense fasting for three days to purify it.
Settling it is called fasting.
Fasting is
the ultimate in clarity and brightness,
and only then can one communicate with the spirits and gods.
Therefore,
ten days before the ceremony,
the palace steward informs the lady,
who then observes seven days of dispersed purification,
followed by three days of intensive purification.
The lord undergoes intensive purification outside,
while the lady does so inside,
after which they meet in the grand temple.
The lord stands at the eastern steps in a plain ceremonial cap,
while the lady, adorned with headdress and pheasant-embroidered robe, stands in the eastern chamber.
The lord holds the jade libation cup to pour libation to the impersonator,
and the chief lineage officer holds the jade tablet cup for the secondary libation.
When the sacrificial animal is welcomed,
the lord holds the leading rope,
with ministers and high officials following,
while lower officers hold the fodder.
The lineage women follow with basins, and the lady presents the filtered water.
The lord wields the bell-adorned knife
to offer a taste,
and the lady presents the vessels;
this is what is meant by
"the husband and wife personally participate."
26.7 When it comes to the dance entry,
the lord holds shield and axe
to take his dance position,
with the lord positioned east as the superior,
wearing the ceremonial cap and holding the shield,
leading his assembled ministers
to delight the imperial impersonator.
Thus, the Son of Heaven's sacrifice
is shared in joy with all under heaven;
the feudal lords' sacrifices
are shared in joy within their domains.
Wearing the ceremonial cap and holding the shield,
leading his assembled ministers
to delight the imperial impersonator—
this embodies the meaning of sharing joy within the domain.
26.8 In sacrifices, there are three emphases:
among the offerings,
none is more emphasized than the libation;
in music, none is more emphasized than the ascending song;
in dance, none is more emphasized than the "Warrior's Night Bivouac";
this is the way of Zhōu.
These three ways
utilize external means
to enhance the noble's intent,
thus advancing or receding with the intent;
if the intent is light, they are light,
if the intent is heavy, they are heavy.
To lighten the intent while seeking external emphasis
is something even a sage cannot achieve.
Therefore, in sacrifice, the noble
must personally exert utmost effort,
thereby demonstrating emphasis.
Guided by ritual,
he presents the three emphases
and offers them to the imperial impersonator—
this is the way of the sages.
26.9 Sacrifices involve the consumption of leftovers;
this consumption
occurs at the sacrifice's conclusion,
which must not be overlooked.
Hence,
the ancients said:
"A good ending is like the beginning."
This applies to the consumption.
Therefore,
the noble ancients said:
"The impersonator also consumes the spirits' leftovers,"
which is a method of beneficence,
allowing observation of governance.
Thus,
when the impersonator rises,
the lord and four ministers consume.
When the lord rises,
six high officials consume.
This is ministers consuming the lord's leftovers.
When high officials rise,
eight lower officers consume.
This is the lowly consuming the noble's leftovers.
When lower officers rise,
each takes his utensils out,
arranges them in the courtyard,
where all officials advance,
clear them away,
and the lower consume the superiors' leftovers.
The principle of consumption
changes with increasing participants,
distinguishing noble and base ranks,
and manifesting the image of bestowed beneficence.
Therefore,
with four vessels of millet, the temple's abundance is shown.
The temple
symbolizes the entire domain.
Sacrifice
represents great bounty.
Hence,
when there is great bounty above,
beneficence must reach below,
though superiors precede and inferiors follow.
It is not that above accumulates excess while below has freezing and starving people.
Therefore, with great bounty above,
the people await downstream,
knowing beneficence will surely arrive—
seen through the consumption.
Thus it is said:
"It allows observation of governance."
26.10 Sacrifice as an institution is grand,
evoking comprehensive offerings.
Compliance leads to completeness,
is this not the foundation of teaching?
Therefore,
the noble's teaching
externally instructs respect for rulers and elders,
internally instructs filial piety toward parents.
Thus,
with an enlightened ruler above,
all ministers obey;
honoring temple and state altars
ensures descendants' obedience and filiality.
Fulfilling this way,
rectifying its righteousness,
teaching thereby arises.
Therefore, in serving the ruler, the noble
must personally practice it;
what is unacceptable from above
should not be imposed below;
what is despised below
should not be used to serve above;
blaming others
while practicing it oneself
is not the way of teaching.
Thus, the noble's teaching
must follow its root,
achieving ultimate compliance—
is this not sacrifice?
Hence it is said:
"Sacrifice
is the foundation of teaching."
26.11 Sacrifice embodies ten relationships:
it shows the way of serving spirits,
shows the righteousness between ruler and minister,
shows the relationship between father and son,
shows the distinction between noble and base,
shows the gradations of intimacy and distance,
shows the bestowal of ranks and rewards,
shows the separation between husband and wife,
shows the balance in governance,
shows the order of elder and younger,
shows the interaction between high and low.
These are called the ten relationships.
26.12 Spreading mats and sharing one armrest
serves to rely on the spirits;
prayers in the chamber
extending to the side altar
represent the way of communicating with the divine.
26.13 The lord welcomes the animal but not the impersonator,
to avoid ambiguity.
Outside the temple gate, the impersonator
appears as a minister,
but inside becomes fully the ruler;
outside, the lord appears as ruler,
but entering becomes fully minister
and fully son.
Therefore,
not going out
clarifies the ruler-minister righteousness.
26.14 In sacrificial practice,
a grandson acts as impersonator for the royal grandfather.
The chosen impersonator
belongs to the sacrificer's son's generation;
the father faces north serving him,
demonstrating how a son serves his father.
This is the father-son relationship.
26.15 After the impersonator drinks five times,
the lord cleanses the jade cup to offer to ministers;
after seven drinks,
he offers with the jasper cup to high officials;
after nine drinks,
he offers with the plain cup to lower officers
and various officers—
clarifying the noble-base hierarchy.
26.16 Sacrifices follow the zhāo-mù arrangement,
which
distinguishes the sequences of father-son, distance-closeness, elder-younger, intimacy-distance without confusion.
Therefore,
during ceremonies in the grand temple,
all zhāo and mù lineages are present
without losing proper order.
This is called the gradation of intimacy and distance.
26.17 In ancient times,
enlightened rulers enfeoffed the virtuous and salaried the meritorious,
always bestowing ranks and emoluments in the grand temple,
showing they dared not act arbitrarily.
Therefore, on the day of the sacrifice,
after the first offering,
the ruler descends and stands south of the eastern steps,
facing south.
The appointed official faces north,
and the historian, from the ruler's right, holds the bamboo slip to announce the appointment.
The official bows twice and touches his head to the ground,
receives the document, and returns,
then performs a libation at his own ancestral temple.
This is the bestowal of rank and reward.
26.18 The ruler, in dragon-embroidered robe and crown, stands at the eastern steps,
while the lady, with her headdress and pheasant-patterned robe, stands in the eastern chamber.
When the lady presents the bean vessel, she holds its stem,
and when handing over the sweet liquor, she receives the base.
When the impersonator toasts the lady, he holds the handle,
and the lady receives it by holding the foot.
Husband and wife hand and receive
without occupying the same position,
and for toasts, they must change cups.
This clarifies the distinction between husband and wife.
26.19 In preparing the sacrificial stand,
bones are the main focus.
Bones have their noble and humble parts;
the Yīn people valued the thigh,
while the Zhōu people valued the shoulder,
generally the front parts being more esteemed than the rear.
The sacrificial stand
serves to show that the sacrifice must bring blessings.
Thus,
the noble take the noble bones,
and the humble take the humble bones.
The noble do not receive double,
nor do the humble go empty,
demonstrating fairness.
When blessings are equal, governance is effective;
effective governance leads to successful affairs;
successful affairs establish achievements.
The reason achievements are established
must not be unknown.
The sacrificial stand
illustrates that blessings must be distributed equally.
Those skilled in governance act thus,
hence it is said:
"Observe the fairness in governance."
26.20 In conferring cups of wine,
the Zhāo lineage is one group,
the Mù lineage is another.
Those of Zhāo rank by age among themselves,
and those of Mù rank by age among themselves,
all officials are ordered by age,
this is called the sequence of elder and younger.
26.21 In sacrifices, there are those given to the Huī, Bāo, Dí, and Hūn—
this is the way to bestow kindness upon the lowly.
Only a virtuous ruler can practice this,
with clarity enough to perceive it,
and benevolence enough to grant it.
"Bì" means to give,
able to share the surplus with those below.
The Huī
are the lowliest of armor officials;
the Bāo
are the lowliest of meat officials;
the Dí
are the lowliest of music officials;
the Hūn
are the lowly gatekeepers.
In ancient times, punished men were not made gatekeepers;
these four custodians
are the humblest of officials.
The impersonator is the most honored;
for the most honored, at the sacrifice's end,
not to forget the lowliest,
but to share the remnants with them—
therefore,
under an enlightened ruler above,
none within the borders suffer cold or hunger,
this is called the connection between high and low.
26.22 Sacrifices are held in the four seasons:
spring sacrifice is called Yuè,
summer sacrifice is called Dì,
autumn sacrifice is called Cháng,
winter sacrifice is called Zhēng.
Yuè and Dì
embody the principle of yang;
Cháng and Zhēng
embody the principle of yin.
Dì
represents the peak of yang,
while Cháng
represents the peak of yin.
Hence it is said: "None are more important than Dì and Cháng."
In ancient times, at the Dì sacrifice,
ranks were conferred and robes bestowed,
following the yang principle;
at the Cháng sacrifice,
fields and towns were allocated,
and autumn governance was promulgated,
following the yin principle.
Thus the record says:
"On the day of Cháng,
the state treasury is opened,
to show rewards";
when grass is cut, punishments are imposed;
if autumn governance is not promulgated,
the people dare not cut grass.
Therefore it is said:
"The significance of Dì and Cháng is great.
They are the foundation of governing the state,
and must not be unknown."
To understand their meaning
is the ruler's role;
to carry out their affairs
is the minister's duty.
Without understanding the meaning,
the ruler is incomplete;
unable to perform the duties,
the minister is incomplete.
Meaning
is what fulfills the will,
the manifestation of all virtues.
Therefore,
those with abundant virtue
have profound will,
those with profound will
display clear meaning,
those with clear meaning
perform sacrifices with reverence.
If sacrifices are reverent,
then no descendant within the borders dares to be irreverent.
Hence,
in the sacrifices of the noble person,
they must personally attend;
if there is a reason,
sending a representative is acceptable.
Even when sending a representative,
the ruler does not lose the meaning,
because the ruler understands the meaning.
Those with shallow virtue
have frivolous will,
doubtful of the meaning
yet seeking to sacrifice;
to make them reverent
is impossible.
To sacrifice without reverence—
how can one be a parent to the people?
26.23 The tripod bears an inscription;
the inscription
is a self-naming.
Self-naming
serves to praise the virtues of one's ancestors
and make them clear to later generations.
Among ancestors,
all have virtues,
and all have faults;
the principle of inscription
is to praise virtues and not faults,
this being the heart of filial sons and grandsons.
Only the worthy can do this.
The inscription
recounts the virtuous deeds of one's ancestors,
their achievements, merits, honors, rewards, and fame,
displayed to the world,
and斟酌ed into the sacrificial vessel,
thus establishing one's own name
to sacrifice to the ancestors.
To glorify the ancestors
is to honor filial piety.
To include oneself
is accord.
To clearly show later generations
is instruction.
The inscription,
with one praise, benefits both high and low.
Therefore, when the noble person observes an inscription,
they admire what is praised,
and also admire the act itself.
The one who creates it
has clarity enough to perceive it,
benevolence enough to grant it,
wisdom enough to benefit from it—
they may be called worthy.
Worthy yet not boastful,
they may be called respectful.
Thus, the inscription on the tripod of Kǒng Kuī of Wèi says:
"On the ding-hai day of the sixth month,
the duke arrived at the grand temple."
The duke said:
"Uncle!
Your ancestor Zhuāng Shū
assisted Lord Chéng.
Lord Chéng then commanded Zhuāng Shū
to follow him in hardship to Hànyáng,
settled at the court in Zōngzhōu,
serving untiringly.
He guided and assisted Lord Xiàn.
Lord Xiàn then commanded Chéng Shū
to continue your ancestor's duties."
Then examining Wén Shū,
he revived the old aspirations,
led the auspicious officers,
personally cared for the state of Wèi,
diligently served the public household,
day and night without slackening,
the people all said:
"How excellent!"
The duke said:
"Uncle!
I give you an inscription,
to continue your father's duties."
Kuǐ bowed and touched his head to the ground, saying:
"In response to this honor and to avoid it,
I diligently fulfill the great command
by applying it to the steaming sacrificial tripod."
This is the tripod inscription of Kǒng Kuǐ of Wèi.
The noble persons of old
discoursed and recorded the virtues of their ancestors,
and clearly displayed them to later generations.
By comparing themselves to these,
they thus honored their state and family
in this way.
Those descendants who guard the ancestral temple and altars of land and grain—
if their ancestors had no virtues yet they praise them,
that is deceit;
if they have goodness but are unaware of it,
that is ignorance;
if they know it but do not transmit it,
that is unkindness.
These three things
are what the noble person considers shameful.
26.24 In the past,
Zhōu Gōng Dàn had meritorious service to the world.
After Zhōu Gōng passed away,
King Chéng and King Kāng, recalling Zhōu Gōng's meritorious service,
wished to honor Lǔ;
therefore they bestowed upon it grand sacrifices.
External sacrifices
were those at the suburban altar and altar of land and grain;
internal sacrifices
were the Great Tasting and Dì sacrifice.
In the Great Tasting and Dì sacrifice,
they ascended to sing the "Qīng Miào";
descending, they played pipes
for the "Xiàng";
with vermilion shields and jade axes,
they danced the "Great Wǔ";
with eight rows of dancers
they danced the "Great Xià";
this was the music of the Son of Heaven.
To honor Zhōu Gōng,
it was therefore bestowed upon Lǔ.
Descendants continued it,
unabated to this day,
thereby illuminating Zhōu Gōng's virtue,
and also honoring their state.
27.1 Confucius said:
"Entering a state,
its teachings can be known.
If its people are:
gentle and sincere,
that is the teaching of the Shī;
broad-minded and far-sighted,
that is the teaching of the Shū;
expansive and good-natured,
that is the teaching of the Yuè;
pure and subtle,
that is the teaching of the Yì;
respectful and dignified,
that is the teaching of the Lǐ;
skillful in language and comparing events,
that is the teaching of the Chūn Qiū.
Thus the fault of the Shī
is foolishness;
the fault of the Shū
is deceit;
the fault of the Yuè
is extravagance;
the fault of the Yì
is harm;
the fault of the Lǐ
is fussiness;
the fault of the Chūn Qiū
is disorder.
If a person is:
gentle and sincere without foolishness,
then they are profound in the Shī.
Broad-minded and far-sighted without deceit,
then they are profound in the Shū.
Expansive and good-natured without extravagance,
then they are profound in the Yuè.
Pure and subtle without harm,
then they are profound in the Yì.
Respectful and dignified without fussiness,
then they are profound in the Lǐ.
Skillful in language and comparing events without disorder,
then they are profound in the Chūn Qiū."
27.2 The Son of Heaven
forms a triad with Heaven and Earth.
Thus his virtue matches Heaven and Earth,
benefits all things,
shines with the sun and moon,
illuminating the four seas without neglecting the small.
At court,
he promotes the order of benevolence, wisdom, and righteousness;
at leisure,
he listens to the sounds of the Yǎ and Sòng;
walking,
he has the sound of jade pendants;
boarding a carriage,
he has the sound of bells.
His dwelling is with ritual,
his advances and retreats with measure,
all officials find their proper place,
all affairs find their order.
The Shī says:
"The good man, the noble man,
his demeanor is without fault.
His demeanor without fault,
he rectifies the four states."
This refers to this.
Issuing commands and the people rejoicing
is called harmony.
Superiors and inferiors loving each other
is called benevolence.
The people obtaining their desires without seeking
is called trust.
Removing the harms of Heaven and Earth
is called righteousness.
Righteousness and trust,
harmony and benevolence,
are the tools of the hegemon and king.
Having the will to govern the people but not the tools,
then one does not succeed.
27.3 Ritual in governing a state
is like the scale for weight,
the marking line for straightness,
the compass and square for shape.
Thus
if the scale is truly hung,
one cannot be deceived about weight;
if the marking line is truly laid out,
one cannot be deceived about straightness;
if the compass and square are truly set,
one cannot be deceived about shape;
if the noble person examines ritual,
he cannot be deceived by treachery.
Therefore
honoring and following ritual
is called being a person of principle;
not honoring or following ritual
is called being a person without principle.
This is the way of respect and deference.
Thus, serving in the ancestral temple, there is reverence;
entering the court,
there is position for noble and humble;
dwelling in the household,
there is affection between father and son, harmony among brothers;
dwelling in the village,
there is order between elder and younger.
Confucius said:
"For securing the high and governing the people,
nothing is better than ritual."
This refers to this.
27.4 Thus the rituals of court audience
clarify the duty between ruler and minister.
The rituals of diplomatic visits
cause feudal lords to respect each other.
The rituals of mourning and sacrifice
clarify the gratitude of ministers and sons.
The ritual of village drinking
clarifies the order between elder and younger.
The rituals of marriage
clarify the distinction between male and female.
Ritual
prevents disorder from arising,
like a dam stopping the source of water.
Thus, if an old dam is considered useless and destroyed,
there will surely be flood damage;
if old rituals are considered useless and abandoned,
there will surely be disorder and calamity.
27.5 Thus if the rituals of marriage are abandoned,
then the way of husband and wife is difficult,
and crimes of licentiousness abound.
If the ritual of village drinking is abandoned,
then the order between elder and younger is lost,
and disputes and fights proliferate.
If the rituals of mourning and sacrifice are abandoned,
then the gratitude of ministers and sons becomes thin,
and those who betray the dead and forget ancestors are many.
If the rituals of diplomatic visits and court audience are abandoned,
then the positions of ruler and minister are lost,
feudal lords act wickedly,
and failures of betrayal and aggression arise.
27.6 Thus, the transformative influence of ritual is subtle,
it stops evil before it takes form,
causing people daily to move towards goodness and distance themselves from crime without even realizing it.
This is why the former kings esteemed it.
The *Yì* says:
"The nobleman is cautious about the beginning.
A discrepancy as small as a hair's breadth
leads to an error of a thousand miles."
This expresses the idea.
28.1 Duke Āi asked Confucius:
"What is the Great Lǐ like?
When noblemen speak of lǐ,
why do they hold it in such high esteem?"
Confucius said:
"I, Qiū, am but a petty man,
insufficient to understand lǐ."
The Duke said:
"No!
Please, you must speak of it."
Confucius said:
"I have heard that,
among the means by which the people live,
lǐ is the greatest.
Without lǐ, there is no means to properly serve the spirits of Heaven and Earth;
without lǐ, there is no means to distinguish the positions of ruler and minister, superior and inferior, elder and younger;
without lǐ, there is no means to differentiate the relationships between men and women, father and son, elder and younger brothers,
the bonds of marriage, and distant or close associations;
the nobleman, because of this, holds it in respect and honor.
Only then does he use what he is capable of to teach the common people,
not neglecting their gatherings and seasonal nodes.
When affairs are accomplished,
then he adorns them with carvings, patterns, and embroidered symbols to continue the tradition.
Following this order,
he then speaks of the mourning calculations,
prepares the dǐng and zǔ vessels,
sets out the pork and dried meats,
maintains the ancestral temple,
respectfully offers sacrifices according to the seasons,
to put the clan in order.
He then settles peacefully in his dwelling,
is moderate and plain in his clothing,
keeps his palace humble,
his carriage not overly carved,
his vessels not engraved,
his meals without duplicate flavors,
so as to share benefits with the people.
This is how the noblemen of old practiced lǐ."
The Duke said:
"Why do the noblemen of today
not practice it?"
Confucius said:
"The noblemen of today
are fond of material gain without satiety,
indulge in excess virtue without weariness,
are neglectful, idle, arrogant, and disrespectful,
stubbornly exhaust the people,
and oppose the masses to attack those who possess the Dào;
they seek to obtain and satisfy their desires,
not by the proper means.
Those of old who led the people followed the former way,
those of today who use the people follow the latter.
The noblemen of today
do not practice lǐ."
28.2 Confucius was sitting in attendance with Duke Āi,
Duke Āi said:
"May I ask, in the way of humanity, what is the greatest?"
Confucius, with a changed countenance and serious expression, replied:
"That you, my lord, have come to speak of this
is a virtue for the common people!
How dare I, your servant, not respond without words?
In the way of humanity,
government is the greatest."
The Duke said:
"May I ask what is meant by government?"
Confucius replied:
"Government means rectitude.
If the ruler is rectified,
then the common people will follow the government.
What the ruler does,
the common people follow.
If the ruler does not do it,
what will the common people follow?"
The Duke said:
"May I ask how to carry out government?"
Confucius replied:
"Husband and wife are distinguished,
father and son are affectionate,
ruler and minister are respectful.
If these three are rectified,
then all things will follow accordingly."
The Duke said:
"Although I am unworthy,
I wish to hear the way to practice these three sayings.
May I hear it?"
Confucius replied:
"In ancient times, in governing,
loving people was the greatest.
The means to govern and love people,
lǐ is the greatest.
The means to govern lǐ,
reverence is the greatest.
The utmost of reverence
is the Great Marriage.
The Great Marriage is paramount!
When the Great Marriage comes,
the ruler dons the ceremonial cap and personally greets the bride,
showing his closeness to her.
To be close to her
is to show intimacy.
Therefore,
the nobleman fosters reverence to be close;
abandoning reverence
is to forsake closeness.
Without love, there is no closeness;
without reverence, there is no rectitude.
Are not love and reverence
the foundation of government?"
The Duke said:
"I wish to say something,
truly.
To don the ceremonial cap and personally greet the bride,
is that not overly solemn?"
Confucius, with a changed countenance and serious expression, replied:
"To unite the harmony of two families,
to continue the line of the former sages,
to provide the mistress for Heaven and Earth, the ancestral temple, and the state altars—
how can you, my lord, say it is overly solemn?"
The Duke said:
"I am stubborn!
If not for my stubbornness,
how would I have heard these words?
I wished to ask,
but could not find the right words.
Please, elaborate a little!"
Confucius said:
"If Heaven and Earth do not harmonize,
the myriad things do not grow.
The Great Marriage
is for the lineage of ten thousand generations.
How can you, my lord, say it is overly solemn!"
Confucius then said:
"Inwardly, to practice the lǐ of the ancestral temple
is sufficient to match the divine brilliance of Heaven and Earth;
outwardly, to practice the lǐ of straightforward speech
is sufficient to establish the respect between superior and inferior.
If things are disgraced,
it is sufficient to rouse them;
if the state is disgraced,
it is sufficient to revive it.
In governing, prioritize lǐ.
Lǐ—
is it not the foundation of government?"
Confucius then said:
"The government of the enlightened kings of the three ancient dynasties
necessarily involved reverence for their wives and children.
There is a principle
in this.
The wife
is the mainstay of kinship—
how dare one not revere her?
The son
is the continuation of kinship—
how dare one not revere him?
The nobleman reveres everything.
In reverence,
revering one's own person is the greatest.
The person
is the branch of kinship—
how dare one not revere it?
If one cannot revere one's own person,
it harms one's kin;
harming one's kin
is harming the root;
harming the root,
the branches follow and perish.
These three—
are the image for the common people.
From one's own person to others' persons,
from one's own son to others' sons,
from one's own wife to others' wives—
if the ruler practices these three,
then his influence spreads throughout the world;
this is the way of the Great King.
Thus,
the state and family will be in harmony."
28.3 The Duke said:
"May I ask what is meant by revering one's person?"
Confucius replied:
"If the nobleman errs in speech,
the people will imitate his words;
if he errs in action,
the people will take it as a model.
If the nobleman's speech does not err in words,
and his actions do not err in principles,
the common people will be respectful and reverent without being commanded.
Thus,
he is able to revere his own person;
being able to revere his own person,
he is then able to bring honor to his parents."
28.4 The Duke said:
"May I ask what is meant by 'fulfilling one's parents'?"
Confucius replied:
"A gentleman is
one who achieves renown among people.
When the common people bestow upon him the name,
they call him 'the son of a gentleman.'
This makes his parents become gentlemen,
thus fulfilling the name of his parents!"
Confucius then continued:
"In ancient governance,
loving people was paramount.
If one cannot love people,
one cannot preserve oneself.
If one cannot preserve oneself,
one cannot be content with the land.
If one cannot be content with the land,
one cannot delight in heaven.
If one cannot delight in heaven,
one cannot perfect oneself."
28.5 The Duke said:
"May I ask what is meant by 'perfecting oneself'?"
Confucius replied:
"Not exceeding the nature of things."
28.6 The Duke said:
"May I ask why the gentleman values the Way of Heaven?"
Confucius replied:
"He values its 'ceaselessness.'
Like the sun and moon following each other east and west without ceasing,
this is the Way of Heaven;
not obstructing its endurance,
this is the Way of Heaven;
acting through non-action yet things are accomplished,
this is the Way of Heaven;
when accomplished, it becomes clear,
this is the Way of Heaven."
28.7 The Duke said:
"I am dull and foolish.
I am fortunate to trouble you for your sincere thoughts."
Confucius rose respectfully from his mat and replied:
"A benevolent person does not exceed the nature of things,
a filial son does not exceed the nature of things.
Therefore,
a benevolent person serves his parents as he serves Heaven,
and serves Heaven as he serves his parents,
thus the filial son perfects himself."
The Duke said:
"Having heard these words,
what if I still commit faults hereafter!"
Confucius replied:
"That you, my lord, speak thus,
is the blessing of your servant."
29.1 Zhòngní was leisurely at home,
with Zǐzhāng, Zǐgòng, and Yányóu in attendance,
and their free conversation turned to ritual.
The Master said:
"Sit!
You three,
I will tell you about ritual,
so that you may circulate through ritual
without omitting anything."
Zǐgòng stepped forward from his mat and replied:
"May I ask how?"
The Master said:
"Respect that does not accord with ritual
is called rudeness;
deference that does not accord with ritual
is called fawning;
courage that does not accord with ritual
is called rebellion."
The Master said:
"Fawning robs one of kindness and benevolence."
29.2 The Master said:
"Shī,
you go too far;
while Shāng
does not go far enough.
Zǐchǎn is like the mother of the multitude -
she can feed them, but cannot teach them."
Zǐgòng stepped forward from his mat and replied:
"May I ask what should be taken as the mean?"
The Master said:
"Ritual, indeed ritual!
Ritual is what establishes the mean."
29.3 Zǐgòng withdrew,
and Yányóu came forward saying:
"May I ask whether ritual
is that which governs what is bad and preserves what is good?"
The Master said:
"Yes."
"Then how is this so?"
The Master said:
"The meaning of the suburban and state sacrifices
is to show benevolence to the spirits and gods;
the rituals of the seasonal and ancestral sacrifices
are to show benevolence in the order of ancestors;
the rituals of funeral offerings and sacrifices
are to show benevolence in death and mourning;
the rituals of archery and village ceremonies
are to show benevolence to the local community;
the rituals of feasting and entertainment
are to show benevolence to guests."
The Master said:
"Understanding the meaning of suburban and state sacrifices,
and the rituals of seasonal and ancestral sacrifices,
governing a state is as easy as pointing to one's palm!
Therefore,
when dwelling places have ritual,
then elders and juniors are distinguished.
When within the women's quarters there is ritual,
then the three clans are harmonious.
When the court has ritual,
then offices and ranks are orderly.
When hunting has ritual,
then military affairs are well-managed.
When the army has ritual,
then military achievements are accomplished.
Therefore,
palaces and buildings attain their proper measure,
vessels and tripods attain their proper forms,
flavors attain their proper seasons,
music attains its proper rhythm,
carriages attain their proper models,
spirits and gods receive their proper offerings,
mourning observances attain their proper grief,
discussion and persuasion attain their proper following,
officials attain their proper substance,
government affairs attain their proper implementation;
applied to oneself and arranged before one,
all movements of the multitude attain their propriety."
The Master said:
"What is ritual?
It is the proper ordering of affairs.
When a gentleman has affairs,
he must have their proper ordering.
Governing a state without ritual
is like a blind man without a guide -
how can he know where to go, groping in confusion?
It is like searching all night in a dark room -
without a torch, what can one see?
Without ritual,
hands and feet have no place to put themselves,
ears and eyes have nothing to attend to,
advancing, retreating, bowing, and yielding have no regulation.
Therefore,
in dwelling places,
elders and juniors lose their distinction;
in the women's quarters,
the three clans lose their harmony;
at court,
offices and ranks lose their order;
in hunting,
military affairs lose their strategy;
in the army,
military achievements lose their regulation;
palaces and buildings
lose their proper measure;
vessels and tripods
lose their proper forms;
flavors
lose their proper seasons;
music
lose their proper rhythm;
carriages
lose their proper models;
spirits and gods
lose their offerings;
mourning observances
lose their proper grief;
discussion and persuasion
lose their following;
officials
lose their substance;
government affairs
lose their implementation;
applied to oneself and arranged before one,
all movements of the multitude lose their propriety.
Thus,
there is no means to lead and harmonize the multitude."
29.4 The Master said:
"Listen carefully!
You three,
I will tell you
there are nine aspects of ritual,
and four in the grand entertainment.
If you understand these,
even while working in the fields,
you would be sages.
When two rulers meet;
they bow and yield entering the gate,
and upon entering, the suspended instruments sound.
They bow and yield ascending the hall,
and upon ascending, the music ceases.
Below, the 'Xiàng' and 'Wǔ' are played with pipes,
followed in sequence by the 'Xià' with flutes.
They arrange the offerings and stands,
order the rituals and music,
and prepare all the officials."
Thus,
the noble person understands benevolence.
Their steps follow the compass,
their turns follow the square,
the harmony of carriage bells matches the "Cǎi Qí",
guests depart to the "Yōng",
and clearing is done to the "Zhèn Yǔ".
Therefore,
there is nothing in which the noble person is not guided by ritual.
Upon entering the gate, metal instruments sound,
showing emotion.
Ascending to sing the "Qīng Miào",
shows virtue.
Descending to play the "Xiàng" with pipes,
shows affairs.
Therefore,
the noble people of old,
did not necessarily need to speak with each other personally,
but conveyed meaning through ritual and music alone."
The Master said:
"Ritual
is principle,
music
is moderation.
The noble person does not act without principle,
nor create without moderation.
Unable to recite poetry,
one errs in ritual;
unable in music,
ritual becomes plain;
lacking in virtue,
ritual becomes empty."
The Master said:
"Institutions lie in ritual,
refinements lie in ritual,
to practice them,
does it depend on the person?"
Zǐgòng stepped over his mat and replied:
"May I ask
was Kuí limited?"
The Master said:
"The people of old?
The people of old.
Those proficient in ritual but not in music
are called plain;
those proficient in music but not in ritual
are called one-sided.
Kuí
was proficient in music but not in ritual,
hence he transmitted this name,
as one of the ancients."
29.5 Zǐzhāng asked about governance,
the Master said:
"Shī!
Come forward,
have I not told you?
The noble person understands ritual and music,
and applies them, that is all."
Zǐzhāng asked again.
The Master said:
"Shī,
do you think it must involve spreading mats and tables,
ascending and descending, pouring, offering, toasting, and responding,
only then is it called ritual?
Do you think it must involve forming ranks and positions,
raising feather wands and flutes,
playing bells and drums,
only then is it called music?
To speak and practice it
is ritual.
To act and delight in it
is music.
The noble person exerts effort in these two to stand facing south,
thus the world is greatly peaceful.
Feudal lords attend court,
all things submit to order,
and no official dares not to perform their duties.
Where ritual flourishes,
the masses are well-governed;
where ritual is abandoned,
the masses fall into chaos.
In a room designed with visual skill,
there are inner chambers and eastern steps,
mats have upper and lower positions,
carriages have left and right,
walking has following order,
standing has sequence,
this is the principle of antiquity.
A room without inner chambers and eastern steps
causes chaos between hall and room.
Mats without upper and lower
cause chaos on the mats.
Carriages without left and right
cause chaos in the carriage.
Walking without following order
causes chaos on the road.
Standing without sequence
causes chaos in positions.
Former sage emperors, enlightened kings, and feudal lords
distinguished noble and base, elder and younger, far and near, male and female, outer and inner,
none dared to overstep each other,
all emerged from this path."
The three disciples,
having heard these words from the Master,
were enlightened as if emerging from blindness.
30.1 Confucius was at leisure,
Zǐxià in attendance.
Zǐxià said:
"May I ask,
the Odes say:
'Kindly brotherly noble person,
parent of the people',
how can one be called parent of the people?"
Confucius said:
"Parent of the people!
One must understand the source of ritual and music,
achieve the five arrivals,
practice the three non-beings,
spreading across the world,
when disasters occur in the four directions,
one must know of them first.
This is called parent of the people."
Zǐxià said:
"Parent of the people,
I have heard about;
may I ask what are the five arrivals?"
Confucius said:
"Where intention arrives,
poetry also arrives.
Where poetry arrives,
ritual also arrives.
Where ritual arrives,
music also arrives.
Where music arrives,
sorrow also arrives.
Joy and sorrow generate each other.
Therefore
straightening one's eyes to look at it,
it cannot be seen;
inclining one's ear to listen to it,
it cannot be heard;
intention and vital force fill heaven and earth,
this is called the five arrivals."
30.2 Zǐxià said:
"Having heard about the five arrivals,
may I ask what are the three non-beings?"
Confucius said:
"Music without sound,
ritual without form,
mourning without garments,
these are called the three non-beings."
Zǐxià said:
"Having briefly heard about the three non-beings,
may I ask which odes approximate them?"
Confucius said:
"Day and night upholding its mandate, broad and tranquil",
is music without sound.
"Dignified deportment, orderly,
cannot be faulted",
is ritual without form.
"Whenever people have mourning,
crawl to rescue them",
is mourning without garments."
30.3 Zǐxià said:
"The words are great!
Beautiful!
Magnificent!
Is this all there is to say?"
Confucius said:
Why would it be so!
When the noble person practices them,
there are still five manifestations."
Zǐxià said:
"How so?"
Confucius said:
"Music without sound:
vital force and intention do not contradict;
ritual without form:
dignified deportment is leisurely;
mourning without garments:
inner compassion is profoundly sorrowful.
Music without sound:
vital force and intention are attained;
ritual without form:
dignified deportment is reverent;
mourning without garments:
extends to the four states.
Music without sound:
vital force and intention are followed;
ritual without form:
superiors and inferiors harmonize;
mourning without garments:
nurtures all states.
Music without sound:
daily heard throughout the four directions;
The formless rites,
day by day and month by month progress;
the unrobed mourning,
pure virtue is greatly bright.
The soundless music,
when the spirit and will are aroused;
the formless rites,
extend to the four seas;
the unrobed mourning,
extend to descendants."
30.4 Zǐxià said:
"The virtue of the three kings
matched Heaven and Earth.
I dare to ask:
how can it be said to match Heaven and Earth?"
Confucius said:
"Serve the three selflessnesses to labor for the world."
Zǐxià said:
"I dare to ask what are the three selflessnesses?"
Confucius said:
"Heaven covers without selfishness,
Earth carries without selfishness,
sun and moon shine without selfishness.
Serving these three to labor for the world,
this is called the three selflessnesses.
It is in the 'Shī' said:
'The Di's command was not disobeyed,
until to Tāng it was uniform.
Tāng's descent was not delayed,
his sage reverence daily rose.
Clearly and slowly he arrived,
reverencing God on high.
The Di's command regulated the nine regions';
this was the virtue of Tāng."
30.5 "Heaven has four seasons,
spring, autumn, winter, summer,
wind, rain, frost, dew,
all are teachings.
Earth carries the divine energy,
divine energy, wind, thunder,
wind, thunder flow and form,
all things appear and grow,
all are teachings."
30.6 "Pure and bright in person,
spirit and will like divine,
when desires are about to come,
there must be an opening beforehand.
Heaven sends timely rain,
mountains and rivers produce clouds.
It is in the 'Shī' said:
'High are the mountains,
their peaks reaching to Heaven.
The mountains sent down spirits,
who gave birth to Fǔ and Shēn.
It was Shēn and Fǔ,
who were the bulwark of Zhōu.
The four states were guarded,
the four quarters proclaimed';
this was the virtue of King Wén and King Wǔ."
30.7 "The kings of the three dynasties,
must first have good fame,
the 'Shī' says:
'Intelligent was the Son of Heaven,
his good fame unceasing'.
This was the virtue of the three dynasties.
'He extended his civil virtue,
harmonizing these four states'.
This was the virtue of King Tài."
Zǐxià started up suddenly,
stood with his back to the wall,
and said:
"How dare your disciple not receive it?"
31.1 The Master said:
"Is the way of the gentleman
not like a dike?
It dams up what the people lack.
Even when greatly dammed,
the people still overflow it.
Therefore the gentleman uses rites to dam up virtue,
punishments to dam up licentiousness,
decrees to dam up desires."
31.2 The Master said:
"The small man when poor becomes straitened,
when rich becomes proud,
straitened becomes a thief,
proud becomes disorderly.
Rites
are the ornamental regulations of human feelings,
serving as dikes for the people.
Therefore the sage's regulation of wealth and honor
makes the people's wealth insufficient for pride,
poverty not reaching to straits,
honor not dissatisfying superiors,
so disorder increasingly perishes."
31.3 The Master said:
"Those who are poor yet love joy,
rich yet love rites,
numerous yet love tranquility,
how few are there in the world!
The 'Shī' says:
'The people's greed for disorder,
would rather inflict cruelty.'
Therefore it is regulated:
states should not exceed a thousand chariots,
capital cities should not exceed a hundred zhì,
family wealth should not exceed a hundred chariots.
Using this to dam the people,
feudal lords still have rebels."
31.4 The Master said:
"Rites
are to clarify doubts and distinguish subtleties,
serving as dikes for the people.
Therefore noble and base have ranks,
clothing has distinctions,
at court there are positions,
then the people have something to yield."
The Master said:
"Heaven has not two suns,
earth has not two kings,
family has not two masters,
honor has not two superiors,
showing the people the distinction between ruler and minister.
The 'Chūnqiū' does not mention the funeral of
the kings of Chǔ and Yuè,
in rites, the ruler is not called 'Heaven',
a great officer is not called 'ruler',
fearing the people's confusion.
The 'Shī' says:
'Look at that night-bird,
still it is worried.'"
The Master said:
"The ruler does not share a carriage with one of the same surname,
sharing a carriage with one of different surname, they wear different robes,
showing the people to avoid suspicion.
Using this to dam the people,
people still kill their ruler with the same surname."
31.5 The Master said:
"The gentleman declines honor but not lowliness,
declines wealth but not poverty,
then disorder increasingly perishes.
Therefore the gentleman would rather have people float above food
than have food float above people."
The Master said:
"A cup of wine, a dish of meat,
yielding and accepting the worse,
people still offend against age;
on the mat yielding
and sitting lower,
people still offend against rank;
at court positions yielding and taking the lower,
people still offend against the ruler.
The 'Shī' says:
'The people are not good,
mutually complaining in one place;
receiving rank without yielding,
until themselves they perish.'"
The Master said:
"The gentleman honors others and debases himself,
puts others first and himself last,
then the people practice yielding.
Therefore calling another's ruler 'ruler',
one calls his own ruler 'humble ruler'."
The Master said:
"Benefits and emoluments,
first to the dead then to the living,
then the people will not betray;
first to the perished then to the surviving,
then the people can be entrusted.
The 'Shī' says:
'Thinking of the former ruler,
to cherish your humble servant.'
Using this to dam the people,
people still betray the dead and cry with no one to appeal to."
31.6 The Master said:
"Those who have states and families,
honor people and debase emoluments,
then the people promote yielding;
value skill and debase chariots,
then the people promote arts.
Therefore the gentleman is sparing in words,
the small man speaks first."
31.7 The Master said:
"When superiors consider the people's words,
then inferiors regard superiors' gifts as from Heaven;
when superiors do not consider the people's words,
then there is offense;
when inferiors do not regard superiors' gifts as from Heaven,
then there is disorder.
Therefore the gentleman with trust and yieldiness oversees the hundred surnames,
then the people's return of rites is heavy.
The 'Shī' says:
'The ancients had a saying,
"Consult the grass and firewood gatherers."'"
31.8 Master said:
"Attribute the good to others,
and the faults to oneself,
then the people will not contend;
attribute the good to others,
and the faults to oneself,
then resentment will increasingly vanish.
The Book of Songs says:
'You divined by tortoise shell and by milfoil,
and the omens showed no words of blame.'"
Master said:
"Attribute the good to others,
and the faults to oneself,
then the people will yield goodness.
The Book of Songs says:
'The king consulted the oracle,
planned for the capital at Hàojīng,
the tortoise shell confirmed it,
and King Wǔ accomplished it.'"
Master said:
"Attribute the good to the ruler,
and the faults to oneself,
then the people will practice loyalty.
The Jūn Chén says:
'When you have excellent plans and schemes,
report them to your ruler within,
then you should comply with them without,
saying:
"These plans and schemes
are due to our ruler's virtue."
Alas!
This is how goodness becomes manifest!'"
Master said:
"Attribute the good to parents,
and the faults to oneself,
then the people will practice filial piety.
The Great Declaration says:
'If I overcome Zhòu,
it is not due to my martial prowess,
but because my deceased father Wén was without fault;
if Zhòu overcomes me,
it is not because my deceased father Wén was at fault,
but because I, the young son, lack virtue.'"
31.9 Master said:
"The gentleman overlooks his parents' faults,
and reveres their virtues.
The Analects says:
'If for three years he does not alter from the way of his father,
he may be called filial.'
Emperor Gāozōng said:
'For three years he did not speak,
and when he spoke, all rejoiced.'"
Master said:
"Obeying commands without negligence,
gently remonstrating without weariness,
laboring without complaint,
this may be called filial piety.
The Book of Songs says:
'The filial son's supply is endless.'"
Master said:
"Being harmonious with one's parents' kin,
this may be called filial piety.
Therefore the gentleman uses harmony to unite the clan.
The Book of Songs says:
'These good brothers
are generous and ample;
those bad brothers
mutually injure each other.'"
Master said:
"Regarding one's father's friends,
one may ride in their carriages,
but may not wear their clothes.
The gentleman thereby extends filial piety."
Master said:
"Even petty persons can feed their parents,
if the gentleman is not reverent,
how can they be distinguished?"
Master said:
"Father and son do not occupy the same position,
in order to deepen reverence.
The Book of Documents says:
'If the ruler does not act as ruler,
he disgraces his ancestors.'"
Master said:
"When parents are alive,
one does not call oneself old,
speaking of filial piety but not of parental kindness;
within the household,
one may jest but not sigh.
The gentleman uses this to guide the people,
yet the people still are meager in filial piety and excessive in parental kindness."
Master said:
"Those who govern the people,
if they revere the elderly at court,
then the people will practice filial piety."
Master said:
"The use of the impersonator in sacrifices,
and the tablet in the ancestral temple,
shows the people that there is service.
Repairing the ancestral temple,
reverently performing the sacrifices,
teaches the people to pursue filial piety.
Using this to guide the people,
the people still forget their parents."
31.10 Master said:
"For reverence, use sacrificial vessels.
Therefore the gentleman does not abolish rites due to meanness,
nor obscure rites with extravagance.
Thus in the dining rites:
if the host personally serves,
then the guest offers sacrifice;
if the host does not personally serve,
then the guest does not offer sacrifice.
Therefore if the gentleman lacks proper rites,
even if the food is fine, he will not eat it.
The Book of Changes says:
'The eastern neighbor slaying an ox
is not as good as the western neighbor's yuè sacrifice,
and truly receiving its blessings.'
The Book of Songs says:
'Drunk with wine,
sated with virtue.'
Using this to show the people,
the people still contend for profit and forget righteousness."
31.11 Master said:
"Seven days of preparation,
three days of fasting,
supporting one person as the impersonator,
those passing by him hurry quickly,
to teach reverence.
Sweet wine in the inner chamber,
clear wine in the hall,
sediment wine below,
showing the people not to be excessive.
The impersonator drinks three times,
the guests drink once,
showing the people there are superiors and inferiors.
Using the wine and meat,
gathering the clan,
to teach the people harmony.
Thus those in the hall observe the inner chamber,
those below the hall observe those above.
The Book of Songs says:
'The rituals are fully measured,
the laughter and talk fully appropriate.'"
31.12 Master said:
"In guest rites, with each advance there is yielding;
in funeral rites, with each step there is distancing.
Bathing under the central drip,
placing rice in the mouth under the window,
minor dressing inside the door,
major dressing on the eastern steps,
coffining in the guest's position,
baring the chest in the courtyard,
burial at the tomb,
this shows distancing.
The Yīn people condoled at the grave,
the Zhōu people condoled at the home,
showing the people not to turn away."
Master said:
"Death,
is the people's final affair,
I follow the Zhōu.
Using this to guide the people,
the feudal lords still have
those who die and are not buried."
31.13 Master said:
"Ascending by the guest's steps,
receiving condolences in the guest's position,
teaches the people to pursue filial piety.
Before the mourning period ends, not calling oneself ruler,
shows the people not to contend.
Thus the Lǔ Spring and Autumn records the Jìn mourning saying:
'They killed their ruler's son Xīqí and their ruler Zhuó.'
Using this to guide the people,
sons still have those who murder their fathers."
31.14 Master said:
"Using filial piety to serve the ruler,
using fraternal duty to serve elders,
shows the people not to be divided.
Therefore when the gentleman has a ruler, he does not seek office,
only on divination days does he refer to two rulers.
Mourning a father for three years,
mourning a ruler for three years,
shows the people no doubt.
When parents are alive,
one dares not claim one's own person,
dares not keep wealth private,
shows the people there are superiors and inferiors.
Therefore the Son of Heaven has no guest rites within the four seas,
none dare act as host.
Thus when the ruler goes to his minister,
he ascends by the eastern steps,
and takes position in the hall,
showing the people they dare not claim their own homes.
When parents are alive,
gifts do not include carriages and horses,
showing the people they dare not act arbitrarily.
Using this to guide the people,
the people still forget their parents and are divided against their ruler."
31.15 The Master said:
"Ritual takes precedence over gifts of silk and money,
desiring that the people attend to duties before thinking of emoluments.
If wealth is put before ritual,
then the people become greedy;
if actions follow emotions without proper words,
then the people contend.
Therefore, when a gentleman cannot receive someone who brings a gift,
he does not look at the gift.
The Book of Changes says:
'He who does not plow but reaps,
does not clear new land but harvests from cultivated fields,
meets with misfortune.'
Using this to guard the people,
still the people value emoluments and slight virtuous conduct."
31.16 The Master said:
"The gentleman does not take all the profits but leaves some for the people.
The Book of Songs says:
'There some sheaves are left standing,
here some grain unbound lies scattered -
these are for the benefit of widows.'
Therefore, when a gentleman serves in office, he does not farm;
when he hunts, he does not fish;
when eating, he does not strive for rare delicacies;
a great officer does not sit on a sheep mat;
a scholar does not sit on a dog mat.
The Book of Songs says:
'When gathering mustard greens and radishes,
do not reject them for their roots;
do not violate virtuous words,
and I will die with you.'
Using this to guard the people,
still the people forget righteousness and contend for profit,
thereby losing their lives."
31.17 The Master said:
"Ritual
guards the people against licentiousness,
makes clear the distinctions between people,
prevents suspicion among the people,
and serves as the people's standard.
Therefore, without a matchmaker, men and women do not meet;
without betrothal gifts, they do not see each other,
fearing that men and women might not maintain proper separation.
Using this to guard the people,
still there are those who offer themselves.
The Book of Songs says:
'How do we cut an axe handle?
Without an axe it cannot be done;
how do we take a wife?
Without a matchmaker it cannot be done.'
'How do we plant hemp?
We must plow the fields crosswise and lengthwise;
how do we take a wife?
We must inform our parents.'"
31.18 The Master said:
"One should not marry someone of the same surname,
to emphasize the distinction.
Therefore, if when buying a concubine one does not know her surname,
one divines about it.
Using this to guard the people,
the Lu Annals still omitted the surname of the lady from Wu,
and when she died recorded it as 'Mèngzǐ died.'"
31.19 The Master said:
"According to ritual,
except during sacrifices,
men and women do not exchange cups.
Using this to guard the people,
still Marquis Yáng killed Marquis Mù and stole his wife.
Therefore, the grand feast abolished the ritual involving ladies."
31.20 The Master said:
"Regarding a widow's son,
if one has not seen him,
one does not befriend him,
for the gentleman keeps his distance.
Therefore, in friendships,
if the host is absent,
without great cause,
one does not enter his gate.
Using this to guard the people,
still the people value physical beauty more than virtue."
The Master said:
"Love virtue as you love beauty.
Feudal lords should not fish for beauties within their domains.
Therefore, the gentleman keeps his distance from sensual beauty as a standard for the people.
Therefore, men and women do not touch hands when giving and receiving.
When driving a lady's carriage, one advances the left hand.
When paternal aunts, sisters, or daughters
return after marriage,
men do not sit on the same mat with them.
Widows do not weep at night.
When a woman is ill,
one inquires about her illness without asking about its nature.
Using this to guard the people,
still the people are licentious and disrupt clan relations."
31.21 The Master said:
"In the marriage ceremony,
the groom goes in person to meet the bride,
presents himself to her parents,
and her parents lead their daughter and give her to the groom,
fearing any violation of the procedure.
Using this to guard the people,
still there are brides who do not arrive."
32.1 What Heaven confers is called nature;
following nature is called the Way;
cultivating the Way is called education.
The Way
cannot be departed from for a single moment;
what can be departed from is not the Way.
Therefore the gentleman is cautious where he does not see,
and apprehensive where he does not hear.
Nothing is more visible than the hidden,
nothing more manifest than the minute;
therefore the gentleman is watchful over himself when alone.
When pleasure, anger, sorrow, and joy have not arisen,
it is called the mean.
When they arise and all hit their proper measure,
it is called harmony.
The mean
is the great foundation of the world.
Harmony
is the universal path of the world.
When mean and harmony are realized,
Heaven and Earth take their proper places,
and all things are nourished.
32.2 Zhòngní said:
"The gentleman embodies the mean;
the petty man acts contrary to the mean.
The gentleman's embodiment of the mean
consists in his being a gentleman who constantly hits the mean;
the petty man's violation of the mean
consists in his being a petty man who has no caution."
The Master said:
"Perfect is the mean!
For long few among the people have been able to practice it!"
The Master said:
"I know why the Way is not practiced:
the wise go beyond it,
and the foolish do not reach it.
I know why the Way is not understood:
the worthy go beyond it,
and the unworthy do not reach it.
There is no one who does not eat and drink,
but few are able to distinguish flavors."
The Master said:
"Alas! The Way is not practiced!"
32.3 The Master said:
"Shùn may be considered greatly wise!
Shùn loved to question others and examine their near-at-hand words,
concealing what was bad and displaying what was good.
Grasping the two extremes,
he applied the mean to the people.
This was how he became Shùn!"
32.4 The Master said:
"All say 'I am wise';
but when driven into nets, traps, or pitfalls,
none knows how to escape.
All say 'I am wise';
but having chosen the mean,
they cannot hold to it for a full month."
32.5 The Master said:
"Húi's way was this:
having chosen the mean,
when he got hold of one good thing,
he clasped it firmly to his bosom
and never lost it."
The Master said:
"The empire, states, and families may be ruled;
emoluments and ranks may be declined;
bare blades may be trodden;
but the mean cannot be attained."
32.6 Zǐlù asked about strength.
The Master said:
"Is it the strength of the south?
The strength of the north?
Or is it your strength?
To teach with gentleness and forbearance,
and not revenge wrongdoing -
this is the strength of the south;
the gentleman dwells in it.
To sleep in arms and armor,
and die without regret -
this is the strength of the north;
the strong dwell in it.
Therefore the gentleman is harmonious but not conformist -
how strong is his strength!
He stands in the middle without leaning -
how strong is his strength!
When the state has the Way,
he does not change from his former state -
how strong is his strength!
When the state lacks the Way,
he remains unchanged until death -
how strong is his strength!"
32.7 The Master said:
"To dwell in obscurity and practice strange deeds,
so that future generations may speak of them;
this I do not do.
The noble person follows the Way and proceeds,
but if they abandon it halfway,
I cannot persist in that.
The noble person relies on the Mean,
and though they withdraw from the world unknown, they do not regret it—
only the sage is capable of this."
The Way of the noble person is vast yet hidden.
Even the foolish among common men and women
can know something of it;
yet at its utmost,
even the sage has aspects he does not know.
The unworthy among common men and women
can practice it;
yet at its utmost,
even the sage has aspects he cannot practice.
Great as heaven and earth are,
people still find cause for regret.
Thus when the noble person speaks of its greatness,
nothing in the world can contain it;
when speaking of its smallness,
nothing in the world can split it.
The Book of Songs says:
"The hawk flies up to heaven;
the fish leaps in the deep."
This describes how it is examined above and below.
The Way of the noble person
begins with ordinary men and women;
yet at its utmost,
it is discernible in heaven and earth.
32.8 The Master said:
"The Way is not far from people;
if someone pursues the Way yet remains distant from people,
they cannot be practicing the Way.
The Book of Songs says:
"In hewing an axe handle, in hewing an axe handle,
the pattern is not far."
Grasping one axe handle to hew another,
and looking askance at it,
one still thinks it far.
Thus the noble person governs people according to their nature,
and stops when they reform.
Loyalty and reciprocity are not far from the Way:
what you do not wish done to yourself,
do not do to others.
The noble person's Way has four aspects,
yet I have failed in even one:
What I require from a son,
in serving my father
I have not achieved;
what I require from a minister,
in serving my ruler
I have not achieved;
what I require from a younger brother,
in serving my elder brother
I have not achieved;
what I require from a friend,
in first offering it
I have not achieved.
In the practice of ordinary virtue,
and the caution in ordinary speech;
where there is deficiency,
I dare not but strive;
where there is excess, I dare not indulge fully.
Speech should consider action,
action should consider speech;
how can the noble person not be sincere and earnest!"
The noble person acts according to their position,
without desiring what is beyond it.
Being in wealth and honor,
they act as befits wealth and honor.
Being in poverty and lowliness,
they act as befits poverty and lowliness.
Being among barbarian tribes,
they act as befits barbarian tribes.
Being in hardship and difficulty,
they act as befits hardship and difficulty.
The noble person finds contentment wherever they are.
In high position, they do not oppress those below;
in low position, they do not curry favor with those above.
They rectify themselves and seek nothing from others,
thus they have no resentment;
above, they do not blame heaven,
below, they do not blame people.
Thus the noble person dwells in ease awaiting destiny,
while the petty person takes risks seeking luck.
32.9 The Master said:
"Archery resembles the way of the noble person;
missing the target,
one turns to seek the cause in oneself."
The Way of the noble person,
is like traveling far—one must start from nearby;
like climbing high—one must start from below.
The Book of Songs says:
"Wife and children in harmony,
like strumming lute and zither.
Brothers united,
harmonious and joyful.
May your household be well-ordered,
and your wife and children content."
The Master said:
"How then parents must be at peace!"
32.10 The Master said:
"The power of ghosts and spirits
is indeed abundant!
Looking, we do not see them;
listening, we do not hear them;
yet they embody all things and cannot be neglected.
They cause all people under heaven
to fast, purify, and dress in splendid robes
to perform sacrifices,
so vast and overflowing,
as if above us,
as if to our left and right.
The Book of Songs says:
"The coming of the spirits,
cannot be fathomed;
how much less can we be weary of them!"
Thus the hidden becoming manifest—
so sincere and impossible to conceal is this!"
32.11 The Master said:
"Shùn was indeed greatly filial!
In virtue, he was a sage;
in honor, he was the Son of Heaven;
in wealth, he possessed all within the four seas;
the ancestral temple sacrificed to him,
and his descendants preserved his legacy.
Thus great virtue must attain its proper position,
must attain its proper emolument,
must attain its proper fame,
must attain its proper longevity.
For when heaven produces things,
it surely strengthens them according to their nature.
Thus what is planted is nurtured,
and what is leaning is toppled.
The Book of Songs says:
"The admirable and joyful noble person,
brilliant with splendid virtue.
He benefits the people and officials,
receiving emolument from heaven.
Heaven protects and appoints him,
and from heaven reiterates the command."
Thus one with great virtue must receive the mandate."
32.12 The Master said:
"The one without worries
was surely King Wén!
With King Jì as father,
and King Wǔ as son;
the father laid the foundation,
the son carried it on.
King Wǔ continued the enterprise of King Tài, King Jì, and King Wén,
and in one military campaign gained the world,
without losing his illustrious reputation in the world,
honored as the Son of Heaven,
possessing all within the four seas,
with the ancestral temple sacrificing to him,
and his descendants preserving his legacy.
King Wǔ received the mandate in his later years,
and the Duke of Zhōu completed the virtue of King Wén and King Wǔ,
posthumously honoring King Tài and King Jì as kings,
and sacrificing to previous lords with the rites of the Son of Heaven.
This practice of rites
extended to feudal lords and high officials
down to scholars and common people.
If the father was a high official
and the son a scholar,
the burial used the rites of a high official,
but the sacrifices used the rites of a scholar;
if the father was a scholar
and the son a high official,
the burial used the rites of a scholar,
but the sacrifices used the rites of a high official.
The one-year mourning period
extended to high officials.
The three-year mourning period
extended to the Son of Heaven.
In mourning parents,
there is no distinction between noble and base—
it is the same for all."
32.13 The Master said:
"King Wǔ and the Duke of Zhōu
were indeed perfectly filial!
For filial piety means
skillfully continuing the aspirations of predecessors,
and skillfully carrying on the undertakings of predecessors.
In spring and autumn, they repaired the ancestral temple,
displayed the ritual vessels,
laid out the ceremonial garments,
and offered the seasonal foods.
The rituals of the ancestral temple
serve to arrange the order of generations.
The ordering by rank
serves to distinguish the noble from the humble.
The arrangement of duties
serves to distinguish the worthy.
The toasting where inferiors offer to superiors
serves to include the lowly.
The seating by hair color
serves to order by age.
Treading in their positions,
performing their rituals,
playing their music,
revering those they honor,
loving those they cherish;
serving the dead as serving the living,
serving the departed as serving the present,
is the ultimate in filial piety.
The rituals of the suburban and state altars
serve to serve the Supreme Deity.
The rituals of the ancestral temple
serve to sacrifice to one's ancestors.
Understanding the rituals of the suburban and state altars,
and the meaning of the Dì and Cháng sacrifices,
governing a state would be as easy as looking at one's palm."
32.14 Duke Āi asked about governance.
The Master said:
"The governance of King Wén and King Wǔ
is recorded in historical documents.
When such men exist,
their governance prevails.
When such men perish,
their governance ceases.
Human way quickens governance,
earth way quickens growth.
Governance
is like the swift-growing reed.
Thus governance depends on the right people,
selecting people depends on self-cultivation,
self-cultivation depends on the Way,
cultivating the Way depends on benevolence.
Benevolence means being human;
loving one's kin is most important.
Righteousness means appropriateness;
honoring the worthy is most important.
The gradations in loving kin,
the hierarchy in honoring the worthy,
are what give rise to ritual.
If in lower position one doesn't gain trust from above,
the people cannot be governed.
Thus the gentleman cannot neglect self-cultivation;
thinking of self-cultivation,
one cannot neglect serving parents;
thinking of serving parents,
one cannot neglect understanding people;
thinking of understanding people,
one cannot neglect understanding Heaven.
There are five universal ways in the world,
and three means to practice them.
They are: ruler and minister,
father and son,
husband and wife,
elder and younger brothers,
and friendship between friends -
these five are the universal ways of the world.
Wisdom, benevolence, and courage - these three
are the universal virtues of the world.
The means to practice them is one.
Some know them by birth,
some learn to know them,
some know them through hardship,
but when known, they are the same.
Some practice them comfortably,
some for profit,
some through forced effort,
but when accomplished, the success is the same."
32.15 The Master said:
"Love of learning is close to wisdom,
earnest practice is close to benevolence,
knowing shame is close to courage.
Knowing these three,
one knows how to cultivate oneself;
knowing how to cultivate oneself,
one knows how to govern others;
knowing how to govern others,
one knows how to govern the world, state, and family."
There are nine standards for governing the world, state, and family:
they are:
self-cultivation,
honoring the worthy,
loving kin,
respecting high ministers,
understanding the masses of officials,
treating common people as children,
attracting various artisans,
being gentle to distant people,
and cherishing the feudal lords.
Self-cultivation establishes the Way,
honoring the worthy prevents confusion,
loving kin prevents resentment among uncles and brothers,
respecting high ministers prevents bewilderment,
understanding officials makes scholars reciprocate with heavy courtesy,
treating common people as children encourages the masses,
attracting artisans makes wealth and resources sufficient,
being gentle to distant people makes all quarters submit,
cherishing feudal lords makes the world stand in awe.
32.16 Purifying one's mind and wearing full dress,
not acting against ritual,
is how to cultivate oneself.
Rejecting slander and keeping distant from sensual pleasures,
despising wealth and valuing virtue,
is how to encourage the worthy.
Elevating their positions,
increasing their salaries,
sharing their likes and dislikes,
is how to encourage loving kin.
Providing ample staff and assistants,
is how to encourage high ministers.
Loyalty, trustworthiness and generous salaries,
is how to encourage scholars.
Using labor seasonably and lightening taxes,
is how to encourage the common people.
Daily inspection and monthly examination,
providing rations commensurate with work,
is how to encourage various artisans.
Welcoming those who come and seeing off those who go,
praising the good and compassionate to the incompetent,
is how to be gentle to distant people.
Continuing interrupted lines,
restoring fallen states,
bringing order to chaos and supporting the endangered,
receiving visits at proper times,
giving generously while taking little,
is how to cherish feudal lords.
32.17 For governing the world, state, and family, there are nine standards,
but the means to practice them is one.
All affairs succeed with preparation,
and fail without preparation.
Words predetermined won't stumble;
affairs predetermined won't be trapped;
actions predetermined won't cause regret;
the Way predetermined won't be exhausted.
32.18 If in lower position one doesn't gain trust from above,
the people cannot be governed.
Gaining trust from above has its way:
if not trusted by friends,
one won't gain trust from above.
Being trusted by friends has its way:
if not obedient to parents,
one won't be trusted by friends.
Being obedient to parents has its way:
if introspection finds no sincerity,
one won't be obedient to parents.
Being sincere in oneself has its way:
if not understanding goodness,
one cannot be sincere in oneself.
32.19 Sincerity
is the Way of Heaven.
Achieving sincerity
is the way of humans.
Sincerity means hitting the mark without effort,
gaining without thought,
naturally hitting the Mean -
this is the sage.
Achieving sincerity
means choosing goodness and firmly holding to it.
Study it broadly,
question it carefully,
ponder it prudently,
discriminate it clearly,
practice it earnestly.
If there's something not studied,
or studied but not mastered, don't abandon it;
if there's something not questioned,
or questioned but not understood, don't abandon it;
if there's something not pondered,
or pondered but not gained, don't abandon it;
if there's something not discriminated,
or discriminated but not clear, don't abandon it;
if there's something not practiced,
or practiced but not earnest, don't abandon it.
If others succeed with one effort, use a hundred;
if others succeed with ten efforts, use a thousand.
If one can truly follow this way,
though stupid, will become wise;
though weak, will become strong.
32.20 From sincerity to understanding
is called nature.
From understanding to sincerity
is called education.
With sincerity comes understanding;
with understanding comes sincerity.
Only the most sincere under heaven
can fully realize their own nature;
being able to fully realize their own nature,
they can fully realize the nature of others;
being able to fully realize the nature of others,
they can fully realize the nature of things;
being able to fully realize the nature of things,
they can assist in the transforming and nourishing powers of Heaven and Earth;
being able to assist in the transforming and nourishing powers of Heaven and Earth,
they can form a triad with Heaven and Earth.
32.21 Next are those who cultivate to the utmost the minor virtues;
from such cultivation, they can attain sincerity;
having sincerity, it becomes manifest;
being manifest, it becomes evident;
being evident, it becomes brilliant;
being brilliant, it moves others;
moving others, it transforms them;
transforming them, it completes the change.
Only the most sincere under
heaven can transform.
32.22 The way of the most sincere
can foreknow.
When a nation is about to flourish,
there are sure to be auspicious omens;
when a nation is about to perish,
there are sure to be signs of evil.
These appear in the milfoil and tortoise shell,
and in the movements of the four limbs.
When fortune or misfortune is about to come;
the good
can surely be foreknown;
the not good,
can surely be foreknown.
Therefore, the most sincere is like a spirit.
32.23 Sincerity is self-completion,
and the Way is self-directing.
Sincerity is the beginning and end of things;
without sincerity, there would be nothing.
Therefore, the superior man values sincerity.
Sincerity is not only the completion of oneself,
but also the completion of things.
Completing oneself is
benevolence;
completing things is
wisdom;
these are the virtues of nature,
and the way of uniting the inner and outer.
Hence, whenever applied, it is fitting.
Therefore, the most sincere is ceaseless;
being ceaseless, it continues long;
continuing long, it becomes evident;
becoming evident, it becomes far-reaching;
being far-reaching, it becomes broad and thick;
being broad and thick, it becomes high and brilliant.
Broad and thick
are what carry all things.
High and brilliant
are what cover all things.
Far-reaching and enduring
are what complete all things.
Broad and thick match the Earth;
high and brilliant match Heaven;
far-reaching and enduring are without limit.
Such being the case,
it manifests without showing,
changes without moving,
and completes without acting.
The Way of Heaven and Earth
can be completely described in one sentence:
"As a thing, it is unceasing,
and so in producing things, it is unfathomable."
The Way of Heaven and Earth is
broad,
thick,
high,
brilliant,
far-reaching,
and enduring.
32.24 Now this Heaven,
only a little brightness at first,
