and in its infinity,
the sun, moon, stars, and constellations are suspended in it,
and all things are covered by it.
Now this Earth,
only a handful of soil at first,
and in its breadth and thickness,
it carries Huà Yuè without feeling their weight,
contains the rivers and seas without leakage,
and all things are borne by it.
Now the mountains,
only a fistful of stones at first,
and in their vastness,
grass and trees grow on them,
birds and beasts dwell on them,
and precious stores are produced from them.
Now water,
only a spoonful at first,
and in its unfathomableness,
great turtles, alligators, dragons, fishes, and turtles are produced in it,
and wealth and articles of use are multiplied from it.
The Book of Poetry says:
'The ordinances of Heaven,
how profound and unceasing.'
This is meant to say that this is why Heaven is Heaven.
'How illustrious was the purity
of King Wén's virtue!'
This is meant to say that this is why King Wén was called Wén.
Pure and unceasing.
32.25 How great is the Way of the sage!
Overflowing,
it develops and nourishes all things,
and rises up to Heaven.
How great and abundant!
The three hundred rules of ceremony,
and the three thousand rules of demeanor,
wait for the right person before they can be practiced.
Hence it is said: Unless there is perfect virtue,
the perfect Way cannot be realized.
32.26 Therefore, the superior man honors the virtuous nature and follows the path of inquiry and learning,
strives to reach the greatest breadth and to exhaust the most subtle,
attains the highest brightness and follows the path of the Mean,
reviews the old and knows the new,
and is earnest and deep, and respects ceremony.
32.27 Thus, being in a high position, he is not proud;
in a low position, he is not insubordinate.
When the country is well-governed, his words are sufficient to raise it;
when the country is ill-governed, his silence is sufficient to preserve himself.
The Book of Poetry says:
'With intelligence and wisdom,
he guards his person,'
this expresses the meaning.
32.28 The Master said:
"Stupid, yet fond of using his own judgment;
low, yet fond of being autonomous;
living in the present age,
yet harking back to the ways of antiquity;
persons of this kind,
calamity will overtake them."
It is not the Son of Heaven
who does not discuss ceremonies,
does not define measures,
does not determine characters.
Now throughout the empire, carriages have all wheels of the same size;
all writing is with the same characters;
and for conduct, there are the same rules.
One may occupy the throne,
but if he does not have the proper virtue,
he may not dare to institute ceremonies or music;
one may have the virtue,
but if he does not occupy the throne,
he also may not dare to institute ceremonies or music.
32.29 The Master said:
"I can describe the ceremonies of Xià,
but Qǐ cannot sufficiently attest my words.
I have learned the ceremonies of Yīn,
and they are preserved in Sòng.
I have learned the ceremonies of Zhōu,
which are now used,
and I follow Zhōu."
He who attains the sovereignty of the world has three important things,
and by them few errors are made!
However excellent the institutions of the highest antiquity,
they cannot be attested;
not being attested, they cannot command credence;
not commanding credence, the people will not follow them.
However excellent the institutions of the lowest antiquity,
they are not honored;
not being honored, they cannot command credence;
not commanding credence, the people will not follow them.
Therefore, the Way of the superior man
is rooted in his own character,
attested by the common people,
examined by the three kings and found without error,
set up before Heaven and Earth and found without contradiction,
presented to the spirits and gods without doubt,
and ready to wait for a hundred ages for a sage without misgiving.
Presented to the spirits and gods without doubt,
he knows Heaven.
Ready to wait for a hundred ages for a sage without misgiving,
he knows humanity.
Therefore, his movements are a model for the world for generations;
his actions are a law for the world for generations;
his words are a rule for the world for generations.
Those who are far away look to him with hope;
those who are near never weary of him.
The Book of Poetry says:
'There, they do not dislike him;
here, they do not tire of him.
Thus, night and day, without ceasing,
they perpetuate his praise.'
Never has a superior man not obtained an early
reputation throughout the world in this way.
32.30 Zhòngní handed down the doctrines of Yáo and Shùn,
and displayed the regulations of Wén and Wǔ,
conforming himself to the times of Heaven above,
and following the conditions of Earth below.
He may be compared to Heaven and Earth in their supporting and containing all things,
and in their overshadowing and covering all things.
He may be compared to the four seasons in their alternating progress,
All things are nurtured together without harming one another,
and all ways proceed in parallel without conflicting with one another.
The lesser virtues flow like rivers,
while the great virtues deeply transform.
This is why Heaven and Earth are so great.
Only the most sagely under heaven
can possess the intelligence, discernment, wisdom, and knowledge
sufficient to oversee.
Broad, generous, gentle, and mild,
they are sufficient to embrace all.
Energetic, strong, firm, and resolute,
they are sufficient to persevere.
Dignified, solemn, centered, and upright,
they are sufficient to command respect.
Cultured, orderly, meticulous, and discerning,
they are sufficient to make distinctions.
Vast and deep like an abundant spring,
they manifest in due time.
Vast as the heavens,
deep as the abyss.
When they appear, none among the people fail to respect them;
when they speak, none fail to trust them;
when they act, none fail to be pleased.
Thus, their fame overflows throughout the Middle Kingdom,
extending to the barbarian tribes;
wherever boats and carriages can reach,
wherever human strength can penetrate,
whatever Heaven covers,
whatever Earth supports,
wherever the sun and moon shine,
wherever frost and dew fall,
all beings with blood and breath
honor and cherish them;
therefore, it is said they match Heaven.
Only the most sincere under heaven
can manage the great principles of the world,
establish the great foundation of the world,
and understand the transformative nurturing of Heaven and Earth.
How could they rely on anything else?
Sincere is their benevolence,
profound is their depth,
vast is their heavenliness.
If not one who is truly intelligent, sagely, wise, and comprehending the virtue of Heaven,
who else can understand this?
The Book of Songs says:
'She wore an embroidered robe over a plain one,
disliking the ostentation of its pattern.'
Thus, the way of the noble person
is subtle yet becomes more evident daily.
The way of the petty person
is glaring yet fades daily.
The way of the noble person
is plain yet never tiresome,
simple yet elegant,
gentle yet principled.
Knowing the near in the distant,
knowing the source in the wind,
knowing the manifest in the subtle,
one can enter into virtue.
The Book of Songs says:
'Though hidden and submerged,
it is still very clear.'
Thus, the noble person introspects without guilt,
and has nothing to be ashamed of in their aspirations.
What makes the noble person unattainable
is precisely what others do not see!
The Book of Songs says:
'Looked at in your chamber,
you should still be blameless even in the darkest corner,'
thus the noble person is revered without moving,
trusted without speaking.
The Book of Songs says:
'In silence the offering is made,
and at that time there is no contention,'
thus the noble person encourages the people without rewards,
and the people stand in awe of the axe and executioner without anger.
The Book of Songs says:
'How illustrious is his virtue!
All the princes emulate him.'
Thus, the noble person, through sincere reverence, brings peace to the world.
The Book of Songs says:
'I cherish your bright virtue,
which does not raise its voice or show its countenance.'
32.31 The Master said:
"Using voice and countenance to transform the people
is the lowest means."
The Book of Songs says:
"Virtue is as light as a hair."
Yet a hair still has substance.
"The workings of high Heaven
are without sound or smell,"
this is the ultimate!
33.1 The Master said:
"Ah, return!
The noble person is obscure yet illustrious,
without arrogance yet dignified,
without severity yet awe-inspiring,
without speaking yet trustworthy."
33.2 The Master said:
"The noble person does not commit faults in demeanor before others,
does not err in expression before others,
does not misspeak before others.
Therefore, the noble person's appearance is enough to inspire awe,
their expression enough to evoke respect,
their words enough to be trusted.
The Punishments of Fú say:
"Be reverent and cautious,
so that no inappropriate words come from your person."' "
33.3 The Master said:
"The informal and formal robes are not worn together,
to teach the people not to be disrespectful."
The Master said:
"In sacrifice, utmost reverence is shown,
not followed by revelry;
in court, utmost clarity is maintained,
not followed by weariness."
33.4 The Master said:
"The noble person is cautious to avoid calamity,
sincere to avoid being overwhelmed,
reverent to stay far from disgrace."
33.5 The Master said:
"The noble person grows stronger daily through dignity and reverence,
while with ease and indulgence, they deteriorate daily.
The noble person does not for a single day allow themselves to be careless,
as if they could not last the day."
The Master said:
"Observe purification to serve ghosts and spirits,
choose the day and month to see the ruler,
for fear the people might not be reverent."
The Master said:
"Those who are frivolous and insulting
may face death without fear."
33.6 The Master said:
"Without words of introduction, one does not receive guests;
without the proper rituals, one does not meet them;
to teach the people not to be disrespectful.
The Yì Jīng says:
'The first divination informs,
repeating it is disrespectful,'
and disrespect means it will not inform."
33.7 The Master said:
"Benevolence is
the standard of the world;
righteousness is
the measure of the world;
reciprocity is
the benefit of the world."
The Master said:
"When goodness is repaid with goodness,
the people are encouraged;
when enmity is repaid with enmity,
the people are warned.
The Book of Songs says:
'No word goes without response,
no virtue without repayment.'
The Tài Jiǎ says:
'Without the sovereign,
the people cannot live in peace;
without the people,
the sovereign cannot rule the four quarters.' "
The Master said:
"Repaying enmity with goodness
is the benevolence of self-preservation;
repaying goodness with enmity
is the behavior of those deserving punishment."
The Master said:
"Those who love benevolence without desire,
and hate what is not benevolent without fear,
are but one in the world.
Therefore, the noble person deliberates on the Way starting from themselves,
and establishes laws based on the people."
The Master said:
"There are three kinds of benevolence,
which achieve the same results but with different motivations.
Achieving the same results as benevolence,
their benevolence may not be known;
but when they share the same faults as benevolence,
then their benevolence can be known.
The benevolent are at ease with benevolence,
the wise pursue benevolence for its benefits,
and those fearing punishment practice benevolence by force.
Benevolence is like the right hand,
the Way is like the left hand.
Benevolence is about humanity,
the Way is about righteousness.
Those thick in benevolence but thin in righteousness
are affectionate but not revered;
those thick in righteousness but thin in benevolence
are revered but not affectionate.
The Way has its utmost,
righteousness has its examination.
The utmost Way leads to kingship,
the righteous Way leads to hegemony,
and the examined Way ensures no mistakes."
33.8 The Master said:
"Benevolence has its measures,
righteousness its degrees of length and brevity, greatness and smallness.
Grief and pain in the heart,
constitute the benevolence of loving others;
the constrained accordance with the law
is that of the benevolence which is a resource.
It is said in the Book of Poetry,
'Though the Feng stream presents its millet,
did king Wǔ not remain at his work?
He laid his plans for the succession,
and secured the repose of his son.
Oh! king Wǔ was the one man.'
This describes the benevolence which extends over many generations.
In the Odes of the States it is said,
'I am now not approved;
how should I think of anything beyond my own person?'
This describes the benevolence which is confined to a lifetime."
33.9 The Master said,
"Benevolence is a heavy vessel to carry,
and a long road to travel.
None can lift the vessel,
or complete the journey.
He who takes the largest number (of steps in it) may be pronounced benevolent;
is not the effort to be benevolence
a difficult thing?
Therefore, when the superior man measures men by the standard of righteousness,
it is difficult to be a man;
when he measures them by the standard of man,
it may be known who is worthy."
The Master said,
"He whose heart is naturally at rest under the requirement of benevolence,
is but one under heaven."
It is said in the Major Odes,
'The virtue is light as a hair,
but the people seldom can bear it.
I think upon it;
only Zhòng Shānfǔ could bear it,
but though we love him, we cannot help him.'"
In the Minor Odes it is said,
'The high hill I look up to;
the great road I travel on.'"
The Master said,
"Such is the love of benevolence in the Book of Poetry.
(The poet) was pursuing the way,
and stopped when he had gone half way,
forgetting the decay of his body,
and not knowing that the number of his years was insufficient.
Daily he was diligent and laborious,
till he died and then he rested."
The Master said,
"For long has it been difficult to be perfectly benevolent.
Every one fails in what he loves;
and therefore the errors of the benevolent man are easily described."
The Master said,[57"Gravity is near to propriety;
economy is near to benevolence;
good faith is near to (genuine) feeling.
If a man conduct himself with reverence and deference,
though he may transgress,
the error will not be great.
Gravity with few errors,
genuine feeling that may be believed in,
and economy that is easily carried out;
to fail in these things
is seldom the case, is it not?
It is said in the Book of Poetry,
'The grave and courteous man
is the foundation of virtue.'"
The Master said,
"For long has it been difficult to be perfectly benevolent;
it is only the superior man who can attain to it.
Therefore the superior man does not require from others the utmost of their ability,
nor does he put them to shame because of their inability.
Thus, in framing his rules of conduct,
he does not lay them down in accordance with himself,
in order to give the people the stimulus of something to strive for and the shame of falling short,
and so to carry out his words.
He regulates them by the rules of propriety,
binds them by good faith,
manifests them in his demeanor,
clothes them with his dress,
and gives them their fullest development in the intercourse of friends.
(All this) he desires, that the people may have this one aim.
It is said in the Minor Odes,
'How can you not be ashamed before men,
and stand in awe of Heaven?'
Therefore the superior man, wearing his square-cut robes and the cap on his head,
produces the deportment of the superior man;
with that deportment,
he produces the speech of the superior man;
with that speech perfected,
he produces the virtue of the superior man.
Therefore the superior man is ashamed to wear the robes and not have the deportment,
ashamed to have the deportment and not have the speech,
ashamed to have the speech and not have the virtue,
ashamed to have the virtue and not have the conduct.
Therefore, when the superior man wears the mourning crape and hempen girdle, he has a sad countenance;
when he wears the square-cut robes and the cap on his head, he has a reverent countenance;
when he wears his coat of mail and helmet, he has an unyielding countenance.
It is said in the Book of Poetry,
'How does the pelican stand on the dam,
and yet does not wet its wings?
So that man there,
is not equal to his clothes!'"
33.10 The Master said,
"What the superior man calls righteousness
is that all, in their several positions, should have their services for the kingdom.
The son of Heaven himself ploughs,
to provide the grain for the vessels with millet and the fragrant spirits for the service of God;
and hence the feudal princes are diligent in assisting at his services."
The Master said,
"In the service of their superiors by inferiors,
though the latter have the great virtue of protecting the people,
they do not presume to have the mind of being lords over them,
such is the richness of their benevolence.
Therefore the superior man is grave and economical,
seeking thereby to be serviceable in the exercise of benevolence;
he is faithful and self-yielding,
seeking thereby to be serviceable in the exercise of propriety;
he does not exalt his services,
nor hold his person in high honor;
he is sparing of his place, and has few desires;
he gives the honor to the worthy,
and humbles himself in honouring others;
he is careful and stands in awe of righteousness;
seeking thus to serve his ruler.
If he obtain his object, he is still the same;
if he do not obtain it, he is still the same.
He follows the appointment of Heaven.
It is said in the Book of Poetry,
'Luxuriant and dense are the dolichos and other creepers,
extending to the branches and tips.
Mild and gentle, the superior man,
seeks for happiness, not by crooked ways.'
Was it not thus with Shun, Yǔ, king Wén,
and the duke of Zhōu?
They had the great virtue of being lords of the people,
and the careful mind in the service of their superiors.
It is said in the Book of Poetry,
'This king Wén,
with watchful and reverent mind,
illustrated his service to God,
and secured the great blessing.
His virtue was without deflection,
and so he received the allegiance of all the states.'"
The Master said,
"The ancient kings gave the (honorary) name according to the (real) nobility (of the person),
and regulated it by the consideration of one excellence,
being ashamed if the name went beyond the practice.
Therefore the superior man did not magnify his doings,
nor exalt his achievements,
seeking to be in accordance with the real feeling;
he did not follow the example of extraordinary conduct,
seeking to be in accordance with generous feeling;
he proclaimed the good qualities of others,
and celebrated their achievements,
seeking to honor the worthy.
Therefore, though the superior man might humble himself,
the people honored and revered him."
The Master said,
"Hòujì carried on the work (of agriculture) for all under heaven.
Was it by the strength of one hand and one foot?
He only wished that his doings might go beyond his name,
and therefore he called himself a convenient man."
33.11 The Master said,
"What the superior man calls benevolence
is very difficult!"
It is said in the Book of Poetry,
'Mild and gentle, the superior man,
is the parent of the people.'
Mild, he uses them strongly in teaching;
gentle, he uses them pleasantly in giving rest.
Happy and not abandoned;
having the rules of propriety, and yet affectionate;
majestic and yet placid;
showing filial piety and reverence.
He causes the people to have the reverence of a father,
and the affection of a mother.
When he is thus, he may be the parent of the people.
But without the highest virtue, who can attain to this?
Now, in the affection of a father for his son,
he loves the worthy among them, and places below the incompetent;
in that of a mother for her son,
she loves the worthy, and pities the incompetent.
The mother
is affectionate, but not reverent;
the father
is reverent, but not affectionate.
Water
is affectionate to men, but not reverent;
fire
is reverent, but not affectionate.
Earth
is affectionate to men, but not reverent;
Heaven
is reverent, but not affectionate.
Commands among the people,
are intimate but not revered,
while spirits
are revered but not intimate."
33.12 The Master said:
"The Way of the Xià dynasty revered commands,
serving ghosts and honoring spirits yet keeping them at a distance,
drawing near to people and being loyal to them,
prioritizing emoluments before authority,
rewards before punishments,
thus intimate but not revered;
the flaws of their people:
simple-minded and foolish,
arrogant and uncouth,
plain and unrefined."
33.13 "The Yīn people revered spirits,
leading the people to serve them,
prioritizing ghosts before rituals,
punishments before rewards,
thus revered but not intimate;
the flaws of their people:
unrestrained and unsettled,
contentious and shameless.
The Zhōu people revered rituals and esteemed bestowals,
serving ghosts and honoring spirits yet keeping them at a distance,
drawing near to people and being loyal to them,
their rewards and punishments were based on rank and hierarchy,
thus intimate but not revered;
the flaws of their people:
profit-seeking and crafty,
refined yet unashamed,
harmful and obscured."
33.14 The Master said:
"The Way of the Xià did not profane words,
did not demand perfection,
had no great expectations of the people,
the people did not tire of their intimacy;
the Yīn people did not profane rituals,
yet demanded perfection from the people;
the Zhōu people compelled the people,
did not profane spirits,
yet rewards, ranks, and punishments were exhausted."
33.15 The Master said:
"The Ways of Yú and Xià
aroused little resentment among the people;
the Ways of Yīn and Zhōu
were overwhelmed by their flaws."
The Master said:
"The substance of Yú and Xià,
the refinement of Yīn and Zhōu,
reached their peak.
The refinement of Yú and Xià did not surpass their substance;
the substance of Yīn and Zhōu did not surpass their refinement."
The Master said:
"Even if there are creators in later ages,
they cannot reach the level of Emperor Yú;
he ruled the world,
lived without selfishness,
did not enrich his son upon death;
treated the people as parents would,
had compassionate love,
and taught loyalty and benefit;
intimate yet revered,
peaceful yet respectful,
authoritative yet loving,
wealthy yet ritual-minded,
generous yet able to distribute;
his noblemen revered benevolence and stood in awe of righteousness,
were ashamed of waste and valued substance,
loyal without offense,
righteous and obedient,
refined and calm,
broad-minded yet discerning.
The 'Punishments of Fǔ' says:
'The awe of virtue is true awe,
the clarity of virtue is true clarity.'
Who but Emperor Yú could be like this?"
33.16 The Master said:
"In serving a ruler, first substantiate your words,
then offer yourself in service,
to fulfill your trustworthiness.
Thus, the ruler may hold his minister accountable,
and the minister may die for his words.
Therefore, he receives emoluments without deceit,
and incurs fewer faults."
33.17 The Master said:
"In serving a ruler, grand words bring expectations of great profit,
minor words bring expectations of small profit;
thus, a nobleman does not accept great emoluments for minor words,
nor small emoluments for grand words.
The 'Yì' says:
'Not eating at home
is auspicious.'"
33.18 The Master said:
"In serving a ruler, do not pursue personal gains,
do not overvalue rhetoric,
do not attach yourself to the unworthy.
The 'Xiǎo Yǎ' says:
'Quietly fulfill your position,
associate with the upright,
the spirits will heed this,
and bestow good fortune upon you.'"
33.19 The Master said:
"Advising a ruler from a distance is flattery;
being close yet not advising is self-serving profit."
The Master said:
"Close ministers maintain harmony,
the prime minister rectifies the百官,
great ministers deliberate on the four directions."
The Master said:
"In serving a ruler, desire to advise, not to display.
The 'Shī' says:
'In heart, I love him,
why not speak of it?
Keeping it hidden in my heart,
how can I forget it day by day?'"
33.20 The Master said:
"In serving a ruler, difficult to advance but easy to retreat,
then positions are orderly;
easy to advance but hard to retreat,
then there is chaos.
Thus, a nobleman advances after three bows,
retires after one farewell,
to avoid chaos."
The Master said:
"If one leaves the ruler three times yet does not depart the state,
it is for profit and emolument:
even if others say he is not seeking it,
I do not believe it."
The Master said:
"In serving a ruler, be cautious at the start and respectful till the end."
The Master said:
"In serving a ruler, one may be honored or humiliated,
enriched or impoverished,
spared or killed,
but must not be made to cause disorder."
33.21 The Master said:
"In serving a ruler,
in the army, do not avoid hardship,
at court, do not decline lowly tasks;
to hold a position without fulfilling its duties
is disorder.
Thus, when a ruler employs his minister, if he achieves his aim,
he should cautiously deliberate and follow;
if not,
he should thoroughly deliberate and follow,
retiring after the matter ends,
this is the minister's generosity.
The 'Yì' says:
'Not serving kings and lords,
but elevating one's own affairs.'"
33.22 The Master said:
"Only the Son of Heaven receives the mandate from Heaven,
scholars receive their mandate from the ruler.
Thus, if the ruler's command is proper, the minister follows properly;
if the ruler's command is improper, the minister resists it.
The 'Shī' says:
'The magpie clamors,
the quail flutters;
the man without goodness,
I take as my ruler.'"
33.23 The Master said:
"A nobleman does not judge a person solely by words.
Thus, when the world has the Way,
actions have branches and leaves;
when the world lacks the Way,
words have branches and leaves.
Therefore, a nobleman beside one in mourning,
if unable to contribute to the funeral expenses,
does not ask about the cost;
beside one who is ill,
if unable to offer food,
does not ask about their desires;
with a guest,
if unable to provide lodging,
does not ask where they stay.
Thus, the interaction of a nobleman is like water;
that of a petty person is like sweet wine.
The nobleman, through plainness, achieves;
the petty person, through sweetness, ruins.
The 'Xiǎo Yǎ' says:
'Slanderous words are very sweet,
disorder is thus increased.'"
33.24 The Master said:
"If a nobleman does not praise people with empty words,
the people will practice loyalty.
Thus, a nobleman, upon asking if someone is cold,
clothes them;
upon asking if someone is hungry,
feeds them;
upon praising someone's excellence,
enfeoffs them.
The 'Guó Fēng' says:
'The sorrow in my heart,
where shall I find rest?'"
33.25 The Master said:
"To make promises lightly and fail to keep them
will bring disaster upon oneself.
Therefore, a gentleman would rather incur resentment by refusing
than have the reproach of breaking his word.
The 'Guó Fēng' says:
'How we smiled and talked,
How clear our誓言 dǎn dàn were;
But we did not think they would be broken.
That they would be broken was not thought of,
But it is all over now.'"
33.26 The Master said:
"A gentleman does not seek to please others with his countenance;
if one is inwardly distant but outwardly familiar,
isn't that like the thief who bores through the wall?"
The Master said:
"In feelings, one should be sincere;
in speech, one should be skillful."
33.27 The Master said:
"The wise kings of the three dynasties of old
all served the spirits of heaven and earth,
never failing to use divination by tortoise-shell and milfoil,
not daring to serve God
with their private feelings.
Therefore, they did not violate the appointed days,
nor go against the divinations.
Divination by tortoise-shell and by milfoil were not used for the same purpose.
For great affairs there were fixed days;
for small affairs there were no fixed days,
but only milfoil divination.
External affairs used strong days;
internal affairs used weak days.
They did not go against the tortoise and milfoil."
The Master said:
"With the victims, music, and offerings complete,
there is no harm done to the spirits,
and no resentment among the people."
33.28 The Master said:
"The sacrifices of Hòu Jì were easily rich;
his words were respectful,
his desires moderate,
and his blessings extended to his descendants.
The 'Shī' says:
'Since Hòu Jì inaugurated the sacrifices,
there has been no crime or regret,
and so it has continued till now.'"
33.29 The Master said:
"The vessels of the great man are威严 wēi yán and respectful.
The Son of Heaven does not use milfoil divination;
the feudal lords have their own diviners.
The Son of Heaven uses milfoil on the road;
the feudal lords do not use milfoil outside their states.
They divine about their dwellings and sleeping apartments.
The Son of Heaven does not divine about the great temple."
The Master said:
"A gentleman, when respectful, uses sacrificial vessels.
Therefore, he does not neglect the days,
nor go against the tortoise and milfoil,
in respectfully serving his ruler and elders.
Thus, those above do not act recklessly towards the people,
and those below do not show disrespect towards their superiors."
34.1 The Master said:
"When the superior is easy to serve,
and the inferior is easy to understand,
then punishments will not be numerous."
34.2 The Master said:
"If one loves the worthy as in the 'Zī Yī',
and hates the wicked as in the 'Xiàng Bó',
then ranks will not be misused and the people will become honest,
punishments will not be employed and the people will all submit.
The 'Dà Yǎ' says:
'Pattern after King Wén,
and all states will trust you.'"
34.3 The Master said:
"The people,
if taught by virtue,
and uniformed by the rites,
will have a sense of shame and become good;
if taught by government,
and uniformed by punishments,
will try to avoid them but have no sense of shame.
Therefore, he who rules the people,
loving them as his children,
will be loved by them;
binding them by good faith,
they will not betray him;
presiding over them with respect,
they will be obedient.
The 'Fǔ Xíng' says:
'The Miáo people did not use commands,
but restrained by punishments,
they made the five oppressive punishments called laws.'
Thus, the people had bad virtue,
and in the end their line was cut off."
34.4 The Master said:
"Inferiors serving superiors
do not follow their orders,
but their actions.
If the superior likes something,
the inferiors are sure to like it even more.
Therefore, what the superior likes and dislikes
must be carefully considered,
for it is the model for the people."
34.5 The Master said:
"When Yǔ had been on the throne three years,
the people became benevolent—
was it necessarily that all were benevolent?
The 'Shī' says:
'Illustrious is Minister Yǐn,
the people all look to you.'
The 'Fǔ Xíng' says:
'When one man is virtuous,
the myriad people rely on him.'
The 'Dà Yǎ' says:
'The faith of King Chéng
is the pattern for the lower world.'"
34.6 The Master said:
"If the superior loves benevolence,
then the inferiors will strive to be benevolent before others.
Therefore, he who rules the people
manifests his will, corrects his teaching, and honors benevolence,
loving the people as his children;
then the people will exert themselves to please their superior.
The 'Shī' says:
'With virtuous conduct upright,
all states will follow you.'"
34.7 The Master said:
"The king's words are like threads,
but when issued are like cords;
the king's words are like cords,
but when issued are like ropes.
Therefore, the great man does not promote idle words.
What can be said
but cannot be done,
the gentleman does not say;
what can be done
but cannot be said,
the gentleman does not do.
Then the people will not say what is dangerous to do,
nor do what is dangerous to say.
The 'Shī' says:
'Be careful in your behavior,
and not err in demeanor.'"
34.8 The Master said:
"The gentleman guides men by his words,
and restrains them by his actions.
Therefore, in speaking he must consider the end,
and in acting he must examine the possible defects;
then the people will be cautious in speech and careful in action.
The 'Shī' says:
'Be careful in your speech,
and respectful in your demeanor.'
The 'Dà Yǎ' says:
'Profound was King Wén,
oh! continuously bright and respectful.'"
34.9 The Master said:
"He who rules the people,
if his dress is not changed,
and his demeanor is constant,
to uniform his people,
then the virtue of the people will be unified.
The 'Shī' says:
'Those metropolitan men,
in their yellow fox-furs,
their demeanor unchanged,
their words full of pattern,
their actions returning to Zhōu,
are the hope of the myriad people.'"
34.10 The Master said:
"If the superior can be known by being looked at,
and the inferior can be described and remembered,
then the ruler will not doubt his ministers,
and the ministers will not be perplexed by their ruler.
Yǐn Jì said:
'Only I and Tāng
had one virtue.'
The 'Shī' says:
'The good man, the gentleman,
his demeanor is without error.'"
34.11 The Master said:
"He who possesses a state,
manifesting the right and the hateful,
to show the people sincerity,
then the feelings of the people will not be divided.
The 'Shī' says:
'Quietly fulfill your duties,
and love this correctness and straightness.'"
34.12 The Master said:
"If the superior is doubtful, the people will be perplexed;
if the inferior is hard to know, the ruler will be troubled.
Therefore, he who rules the people,
manifesting what he likes to show the people customs,
and being careful about what he hates to control the people's excesses,
then the people will not be perplexed.
Ministers should model their actions,
not emphasize words,
not drag in what is beyond their reach,
nor trouble with what they do not know,
then the ruler will not be troubled."
The Book of Songs says:
"When God acts perversely,
the common people suffer greatly."
The Minor Odes state:
"Not only do they fail in their duties,
but they become a burden to the king."
34.13 The Master said:
"When governance fails to be implemented,
and education fails to be accomplished,
it is because ranks and emoluments are insufficient to encourage,
and punishments are insufficient to instill shame.
Therefore, those in authority must not treat punishments lightly nor bestow ranks carelessly.
The Announcement of Kānggào says:
"Reverently and clearly apply your punishments."
The Punishments of Fǔxíng states:
"Promulgate punishments where the Way is not followed."
34.14 The Master said:
"When high ministers are not close,
and the common people are not at peace,
it is because loyalty and reverence are insufficient,
while wealth and honor are already excessive.
When high ministers are not properly managed, then courtiers become cliquish.
Therefore, high ministers must be treated with respect,
for they are the models for the people.
Courtiers must be chosen with caution,
for they are the guides for the people.
The ruler should not use the small to plan for the great,
not use the distant to speak of the near,
not use the internal to scheme for the external.
Then high ministers will not resent,
courtiers will not be jealous,
and distant ministers will not be obscured.
Duke Yè's deathbed charge said:
"Do not use small plans to ruin great undertakings,
do not let favored consorts resent the dignified queen,
do not let favored courtiers resent the dignified scholars,
great officers, ministers, and officials."
The Master said:
"When the great man does not befriend the worthy,
but trusts the base;
the people thereby lose their proper affections,
and governance becomes vexatious.
The Book of Songs says:
"When he sought me,
it was as if he could not get me;
having obtained me, he treats me with disdain,
and does not employ my strength."
The Jūnchén says:
"Before seeing the sage,
he felt as if unable to meet him;
after seeing the sage,
he still could not follow the sage."
34.15 The Master said:
"The petty man drowns in water,
the gentleman drowns in speech,
the great man drowns in the people—
all drown in what they treat lightly.
Water is close to people and drowns them;
virtue is easily familiarized but difficult to truly approach,
thus easily causing drowning.
Speech is wasteful and vexatious,
easily uttered but hard to regret,
thus easily causing drowning.
The people are constrained by others,
and possess vulgar minds;
they should be revered, not treated with contempt,
thus easily causing drowning.
Therefore, the gentleman must be cautious.
The Tàijiǎ says:
"Do not transgress his mandate to overthrow yourself."
"Like drawing a bow,
go and examine the arrowhead against its measure before releasing."
The Yuèmìng says:
"From the mouth arise shames,
from armor and helmet arise conflicts,
robes and garments are stored in boxes,
shield and spear should be examined in one's own person."
The Tàijiǎ says:
"Heaven-sent calamities
can be avoided;
self-made calamities
cannot be escaped."
The Yǐn Jí says:
"Only Yǐn's person was heavenly,
appearing in the western city
Xià; from Zhōu there was an end,
and the ministers also had their end."
34.16 The Master said:
"The people take the ruler as their heart,
the ruler takes the people as his body.
When the heart is dignified, the body is at ease;
when the heart is solemn, the countenance is respectful.
What the heart loves,
the body will surely find peace in;
what the ruler loves,
the people will surely desire.
The heart is preserved through the body,
but can also be harmed by the body;
the ruler exists through the people,
but can also perish because of the people.
The Book of Songs says:
"Of old we had a former worthy,
whose words were clear and pure;
the state and family were thereby tranquil,
cities and towns were thereby built,
the multitude of people thereby lived.
Who can uphold the state's achievements,
without making himself correct,
yet ultimately toiling the common people?"
The Jūn Yǎ says:
"In summer's heat and rain,
the common people only complain;
in winter's severe cold,
the common people also only complain."
34.17 The Master said:
"When inferiors serve superiors,
if their persons are not correct,
and their words are not trustworthy,
then their righteousness is not unified,
and their conduct lacks pattern."
The Master said:
"Speech should have substance and conduct should have pattern.
Thus in life, one's will cannot be taken away,
and in death, one's name cannot be taken away.
Therefore, the gentleman hears much,
evaluates it and holds to it;
remembers much,
evaluates it and draws near to it;
knows precisely,
and acts upon the essentials.
The Jūnchén says:
"In going out and coming in,
take counsel from your multitude,
until all opinions agree."
The Book of Songs says:
"The good man, the gentleman,
his demeanor is uniform."
34.18 The Master said:
"Only the gentleman can love what is correct,
while the petty man hates what is correct.
Therefore, the gentleman's friendships have their direction,
and his dislikes have their principle.
Thus those nearby are not confused,
and those far away have no doubts.
The Book of Songs says:
"The gentleman has a good mate."
34.19 The Master said:
"To easily cut off from the poor and humble,
but reluctantly cut off from the rich and noble,
shows that love for the worthy is not firm,
and hatred for the wicked is not clear.
Even if people say such a person is not self-interested,
I would not believe it.
The Book of Songs says:
"Friends assist each other,
assisting with dignity and decorum."
34.20 The Master said:
"Private favors that do not accord with virtue
are not retained by the gentleman.
The Book of Songs says:
"Those who are good to me
show me the great way."
34.21 The Master said:
"If there is a carriage,
one must see its crossbar;
if there is clothing,
one must see its wear;
if a person speaks,
one must hear the sound;
if a person acts,
one must see the result.
The Gé Tán says:
"Wear it without tiring."
34.22 The Master said:
"When speech is followed by action,
then speech cannot be embellished;
when action is followed by speech,
then action cannot be embellished.
Therefore, the gentleman speaks little
and acts to establish his trustworthiness,
so that the people cannot exaggerate their virtues and minimize their faults.
The Book of Songs says:
"A flaw in a white scepter
can still be ground away;
a flaw in these words
cannot be undone."
The Minor Odes state:
"Truly, the gentleman,
sincerely achieves great accomplishment."
The Jūnshì says:
"Of old, God
completely observed King Wén's virtue,
and laid the great mandate upon his person."
34.23 The Master said:
"The people of the south have a saying:
'A person without constancy
cannot be employed as a diviner
by tortoise shell or milfoil stalks.'
Is this an ancient transmitted saying?
Even the tortoise and milfoil cannot know such a person,
how much less can humans?
The Book of Songs says:
'Our tortoise shells are weary,
they no longer tell us the plans.'
The Announcement of Yuè says:
'Do not confer rank on those with vicious virtue,
lest the people establish this as proper conduct.'
'To offer sacrifice with impurity
is to show irreverence;
when affairs become troublesome, they become chaotic;
serving the spirits then becomes difficult.'
The Yì Jīng says:
'Not maintaining virtue consistently,
one may incur shame.'
'Maintaining virtue persistently in divination,
for a woman is auspicious,
for a man is inauspicious.'"
35.1 The rites for hastening to a funeral:
Upon first hearing of a parent's death,
one should weep in response to the messenger,
expressing full grief;
after inquiring about the circumstances,
weep again expressing full grief.
35.2 Then depart,
traveling one hundred lǐ per day,
not traveling at night.
Only for the funeral of parents
may one travel when stars are visible
and stop when stars are visible.
If unable to depart immediately,
then don mourning garments before departing.
When passing through states and reaching borders,
weep expressing full grief then stop.
Weep avoiding markets and courts.
Upon seeing the state's border, weep.
Upon reaching home,
enter through the left gate,
ascend by the western steps,
sit facing west east of the coffin,
weep expressing full grief,
bind the hair, bare the shoulders,
descend from the hall, take position to the east,
face west and weep,
perform the leaping ceremony,
don the upper garment and hempen girdle east of the wall,
and the twisted girdle.
Return to position,
bow to guests, perform the leaping ceremony,
escort guests out,
return to position;
if there are guests who arrive later,
then bow to them,
perform the leaping ceremony and escort them out as before.
All the masters and brothers go outside the gate,
cease weeping when outside the gate;
close the gate,
the assistant announces to take positions.
At the second weeping,
bind the hair, bare the shoulders, perform the leaping ceremony;
at the third weeping,
still bind the hair, bare the shoulders, perform the leaping ceremony.
On the third day,
don full mourning garments,
bowing to and escorting guests out as before.
35.3 If the one hastening to the funeral is not the chief mourner,
then the chief mourner performs the bowing to and escorting of guests.
Those hastening to funerals in lesser mourning than full attire
enter through the left gate, stand in the central courtyard facing north, weep expressing full grief,
don the mourning cap and hempen girdle east of the wall,
take position and bare the shoulders,
weep with the chief mourner, perform the leaping ceremony.
At the second and third weepings, all don the mourning cap and bare the shoulders,
if there are guests,
then the chief mourner bows to and escorts the guests.
The manner in which men and women await them
is all like their positions at morning and evening weepings,
with no changes.
35.4 Hastening to a mother's funeral:
face west and weep expressing full grief,
bind the hair, bare the shoulders,
descend from the hall, take position to the east,
face west and weep,
perform the leaping ceremony,
don the upper garment, mourning cap, and hempen girdle east of the wall,
bow to and escort guests out,
all like the rites for hastening to a father's funeral,
except at the second weeping, do not bind the hair.
35.5 When women hasten to funerals,
ascend by the eastern steps,
sit facing west east of the coffin,
weep expressing full grief;
arrange the hair eastward,
take position,
and alternate leaping with the chief mourner.
35.6 If those hastening to the funeral miss the encoffining,
first go to the tomb,
sit facing north,
weep expressing full grief.
The way the chief mourner receives them:
take position to the left of the tomb,
women to the right of the tomb,
perform the leaping ceremony,
express full grief,
bind the hair,
take position to the east with the chief mourner,
don the hempen girdle and twisted girdle,
weep and perform the leaping ceremony,
bow to guests,
return to position,
perform the leaping ceremony,
the assistant announces the completion of affairs.
Then don the cap, return home,
enter through the left gate,
face north, weep expressing full grief,
bind the hair, bare the shoulders, perform the leaping ceremony,
take position to the east,
bow to guests and perform the leaping ceremony.
When guests depart,
the chief mourner bows in sending them off;
if there are guests who arrive later,
then bow to them, perform the leaping ceremony,
escort guests out as before.
All the masters and brothers go outside the gate,
cease weeping when outside the gate,
the assistant announces to take positions.
At the second weeping,
bind the hair, perform the leaping ceremony;
at the third weeping,
still bind the hair, perform the leaping ceremony.
On the third day don full mourning garments,
at the fifth weeping,
the assistant announces the completion of affairs.
What differs for a mother compared to a father:
only once bind the hair,
for the remainder wear the mourning cap until affairs conclude,
otherwise like the rites for hastening to a father's funeral.
35.7 For those in lesser mourning than full attire who miss the encoffining:
first go to the tomb,
face west and weep expressing full grief,
don the mourning cap and hempen girdle to the east,
take position,
weep with the chief mourner and perform the leaping ceremony,
don the upper garment.
If there are guests,
then the chief mourner bows to and escorts the guests;
if there are guests who arrive later,
bow to them as before.
The assistant announces the completion of affairs.
Then don the cap, return home,
enter through the left gate,
face north, weep expressing full grief,
don the mourning cap, bare the shoulders, perform the leaping ceremony,
take position to the east,
bow to guests and perform the leaping ceremony,
when guests depart,
the chief mourner bows in sending them off.
At the second weeping,
don the mourning cap, bare the shoulders, perform the leaping ceremony;
at the third weeping,
still don the mourning cap, bare the shoulders, perform the leaping ceremony.
On the third day don full mourning garments,
at the fifth weeping,
the assistant announces the completion of affairs.
35.8 Hearing of a death but being unable to hasten to the funeral:
weep expressing full grief;
after inquiring about the circumstances,
weep again expressing full grief.
Then set up a position,
bind the hair, bare the shoulders, perform the leaping ceremony,
don the upper garment, hempen girdle, twisted girdle, take position,
bow to guests, return to position, perform the leaping ceremony.
When guests depart,
the chief mourner bows in sending them off outside the gate,
returns to position;
if there are guests who arrive later,
bow to them, perform the leaping ceremony,
escort guests out as before.
At the second weeping,
bind the hair, bare the shoulders, perform the leaping ceremony,
at the third weeping,
still bind the hair, bare the shoulders, perform the leaping ceremony,
on the third day don full mourning garments,
at the fifth weeping,
bowing to and escorting guests out as before.
35.9 If one returns after the mourning period has been removed,
then goes to the tomb,
weeps, performs the full jumping ritual,
ties hair to the east, bares the shoulders, and wears the mourning headband,
bows to the guests and completes the jumping,
sees off the guests and returns to position,
weeps again to exhaust grief,
then removes the mourning attire,
and does not weep at home.
The way the host receives him,
does not change in attire,
weeps with him,
but does not jump.
35.10 From the level of zīcuī downward,
what differs
is the use of the mourning cap and hemp.
35.11 Whenever assuming a position for mourning,
if it is not for the death of a parent,
for zīcuī and below
all take their positions, weep to exhaust grief,
then go east to don the mourning cap and headband,
take their positions,
bare shoulders, complete the jumping, and cover up,
bow to the guests and return to position,
weep and complete the jumping,
see off the guests and return to position,
the usher announces to proceed to the temporary shelter.
Over three days,
weep five times, when finished,
the host goes out to see off the guests;
the other family members and brothers all go out the door,
weeping stops.
The usher announces the matters are concluded.
Don the full mourning attire and bow to the guests.
If the home for which the position is assumed is distant,
then don the full mourning attire and go.
35.12 For zīcuī,
weep upon seeing the hometown;
for dàgōng,
weep upon seeing the gate;
for xiǎogōng,
weep upon reaching the gate;
for sīmá,
weep upon taking the position.
35.13 Weep for the father's kin in the temple;
for the mother's or wife's kin in the inner chamber;
for a teacher outside the temple gate;
for a friend outside the inner chamber gate;
for acquaintances, set up a curtain in the open field.
Whenever assuming a position, do not make offerings.
Weep for the Son of Heaven nine times,
for feudal lords seven times,
for ministers and high officials five times,
for shì three times.
A minister weeping for a feudal lord,
does not dare to bow to guests.
Officials in another state,
assume a position and weep,
do not dare to bow to guests.
Being brothers with a feudal lord,
also assume a position and weep.
Whenever assuming a position, bare the shoulders once.
35.14 When an acquaintance comes to condole,
first weep at home and then go to the tomb,
all perform the full jumping ritual for them,
follow the host facing north and jump.
In all mourning,
if the father is alive, the father presides;
if the father is deceased,
and brothers live together,
each presides over their own mourning.
If the kinship is the same,
the eldest presides;
if different,
the closer relative presides.
35.15 Hearing of the death of a distant brother,
after the mourning period has been removed and then hearing of the death,
don the mourning cap, bare shoulders, complete the jumping,
when bowing to guests, still use the left hand.
35.16 Those who assume a position without wearing mourning attire,
are only for sister-in-law and brother-in-law, and for women whose mourning is reduced
and have no attire, use hemp.
35.17 Whenever rushing to a funeral,
if a dàfū arrives,
bare shoulders,
bow to him,
complete the jumping and then cover up;
for a shì,
cover up and then bow to him.
When a parent first dies,
remove the cap, go barefoot,
tuck up the upper garment,
cross hands and weep.
The heart of sorrow,
the intent of pain and distress,
injure the kidneys, dry the liver, scorch the lungs,
not allowing water or gruel to enter the mouth,
for three days not lighting a fire,
so neighbors make congee for them to eat and drink.
With grief and sorrow inside,
thus the form changes outwardly,
with pain and distress in the heart,
thus the mouth finds no sweetness in flavor,
the body finds no comfort in finery.
After three days, the body is encoffined,
on the bed it is called the corpse,
in the coffin it is called the bier,
moving the corpse or lifting the bier,
weeping and jumping are countless.
The heart of sorrow,
the intent of pain and distress,
grief, stifled will, and abundant qi,
thus bare shoulders and jump,
to move the body, calm the heart, and lower the qi.
Women should not bare shoulders,
thus bare the chest, strike the heart, and jump like a sparrow,
with a thumping and pattering sound,
like a collapsing wall,
such is the extremity of grief, sorrow, pain, and distress.
Thus it is said:
"Beating the breast, jumping, and weeping, mournfully send it off.
Send the form away,
and welcome the essence back."
When going to send it off,
gazing anxiously, eagerly,
as if chasing but unable to catch up;
when returning to weep,
restlessly
as if seeking but unable to find.
Thus going to send it off is like yearning,
returning is like doubt.
Seeking but finding nothing,
entering the gate and not seeing,
going up the hall and still not seeing,
entering the room and still not seeing.
Gone!
Lost!
Never to be seen again!
Thus weeping, beating the breast, and jumping,
exhaust grief and then stop.
The heart is怅怅, 怆怆,
惚惚, 愾愾,
the heart is severed, the will sorrowful, that is all.
Sacrificing in the ancestral temple,
offering it as a ghost to feast,
hoping for a chance to return.
After completing the burial and returning,
dare not enter and dwell in the room,
reside in the lean-to hut,
grieving that the parent is outside;
sleep on straw mats and pillow on clods,
grieving that the parent is in the earth.
Thus weeping without fixed times,
performing laborious service for three years,
the heart of longing and remembrance,
is the filial son's will,
the reality of human emotion.
Someone asked:
"Why wait three days after death before encoffining?"
The answer:
"When a filial son's parent dies,
grief and sorrow stifle the will,
thus he crawls and weeps for them,
as if they might come back to life,
how could one forcibly take and encoffin them?
Thus it is said:
Waiting three days before encoffining,
is to await their revival;
if after three days they do not revive,
they will not revive anymore.
The filial son's heart also gradually declines;
the household's preparations,
the clothing and necessities,
can also be completed;
distant relatives,
can also arrive.
Therefore, the sage made the decision, setting three days as the ritual rule."
Someone asked:
"Why does one wearing a cap not bare the flesh?"
The answer:
"The cap
is the most honored,
it should not be on a bared body,
thus use the mourning cap to replace it."
"Then a bald person does not wear the mourning cap,
a hunchback does not bare shoulders,
a lame person does not jump,
not because they are not sad;
the body has incurable ailments,
and cannot fully perform the rites.
Thus it is said:
'In mourning rites, grief is the main thing.'
When women weep and are sorrowful,
they beat their chests and grieve their hearts;
when men weep and are sorrowful,
they kowtow touching the ground without regard for appearance,
such is the extremity of grief."
Someone asked:
"What is the purpose of the mourning cap (miǎn)?"
The reply was:
"It is worn by those who do not yet wear the formal cap.
The Rites state:
'A youth does not wear the fine hemp mourning (sī),
except when he is the head of the household, then he wears sī.'
Those who wear sī also wear the mourning cap (miǎn),
so when heading the household, he wears the mourning cap and uses the staff."
Someone asked:
"What is the staff?"
The reply was:
"Both bamboo and paulownia are used.
Thus for the father, the rough staff is used,
the rough staff,
is of bamboo;
for the mother, the trimmed staff,
the trimmed staff,
is of paulownia."
Someone asked:
"What is the purpose of the staff?"
The reply was:
"When a filial child loses a parent,
they weep incessantly,
observe mourning duties for three years,
their body ailing and weakened,
so they use the staff to support their infirmity.
But if the father is alive, they dare not use the staff,
because the honored one is present;
they do not use the staff in the main hall,
to avoid the place of the honored one;
they do not hurry in the main hall,
showing they are not rushed.
This is the intent of the filial child,
the reality of human emotion,
the constant principle of ritual and righteousness,
not something descended from heaven,
nor emerged from earth,
but simply human emotion."
The Tradition says:
"There are cases of following light mourning with heavy,"
as when the wife of a lord's son mourns for her mother-in-law.
"There are cases of following heavy mourning with light,"
as when mourning for one's wife's parents.
"There are cases of following no mourning with mourning,"
as when the wife of a lord's son mourns for the lord's son's external brothers.
"There are cases of following mourning with no mourning,"
as when a lord's son does not mourn for his wife's parents.
The Tradition says:
"If the mother has been repudiated,
then one mourns for the kin of the stepmother;
if the mother has died,
then one mourns for the kin of one's own mother."
When mourning for the kin of one's own mother,
one does not mourn for the kin of the stepmother.
In the three-year mourning,
after the sacrifice at the end of the first year (liàn),
if a one-year mourning occurs,
after the burial,
then one wears the old girdle of dolichos cloth,
the headband of the one-year mourning,
and the coarse garment of the seven-month mourning.
If there is a nine-month mourning,
it is also like this.
For the five-month mourning,
there is no change.
Hemp with roots,
changes the dolichos cloth of the three-year mourning.
After the liàn sacrifice,
if encountering hemp without roots,
for the mourning cap (miǎn),
one wears the headband;
after removing the mourning cap,
one removes the headband.
Whenever possible to wear the headband, one must wear it;
after wearing it,
then remove it.
The five-month mourning does not change the liàn cap of the mourning;
if wearing the mourning cap,
then wear the headband of the fine or five-month mourning,
following the original dolichos girdle.
The hemp of the fine mourning,
does not change the dolichos of the five-month mourning;
the hemp of the five-month mourning,
does not change the dolichos of the nine-month mourning.
That with roots is considered for change.
For premature deaths:
the older and middle categories,
change the dolichos of the three-year mourning.
Complete the months calculated for the premature death,
then return to the dolichos of the three-year mourning.
This is not because hemp is heavy,
but because there is no change after the end-of-wailing sacrifice for them.
For the lower category of premature death, it is not so.
A feudal lord mourns for the Son of Heaven for three years,
his lady like the external clan mourning for the lord.
The heir does not mourn for the Son of Heaven.
Those for whom the lord presides:
his lady wife, the heir, and the principal wife of the heir.
The principal son of a minister mourns for the lord, his lady, and the heir,
as the officers do.
If the lord's mother
is not the principal lady,
then the officials do not mourn.
Only the close attendants and the charioteers follow in mourning,
only what the lord mourns,
they mourn.
The duke, for his ministers, wears hemmed sackcloth while at home,
and when going out also does so.
When attending to affairs, he wears the ceremonial cap with headband.
Ministers do for each other,
also like this.
For one's wife,
when going to her, one wears it,
but when going out, not.
In general, when seeing others, one does not remove the headband,
even when attending the lord's court
one does not remove the headband.
Only at the duke's gate does one remove the even-hemmed sackcloth.
The Tradition says:
"A gentleman does not deprive others of their mourning,
nor should his mourning be deprived."
The Tradition says:
"Crimes are many but punishments are five,
mournings are many but garments are five,
attaching above and attaching below,
is the ranking."
38.1 Why is the unhemmed sackcloth (cuī) worn with coarse hemp?
Coarse hemp,
has an ugly appearance,
so it expresses the inner feelings and displays them outwardly.
The appearance for unhemmed sackcloth is like coarse hemp,
for even-hemmed sackcloth like finer hemp,
for nine-month mourning as if restrained,
for five-month and fine hempen mourning, the countenance may be normal,
this is how grief is expressed in the face and body.
The weeping for unhemmed sackcloth,
is as if going without return;
for even-hemmed sackcloth,
as if going and returning;
for nine-month mourning,
with three turns and a drawn-out sound;
for five-month and fine hempen mourning,
a sorrowful countenance is acceptable.
This is how grief is expressed in the voice.
For unhemmed sackcloth,
one responds but does not answer;
for even-hemmed sackcloth,
one answers but does not speak;
for nine-month mourning,
one speaks but does not discuss;
for five-month and fine hempen mourning,
one discusses but does not reach to music.
This is how grief is expressed in speech.
For unhemmed sackcloth,
one does not eat for three days;
for even-hemmed sackcloth,
for two days;
for nine-month mourning,
three meals not eaten;
for five-month and fine hempen mourning,
two meals not eaten;
if an officer participates in the enshrouding,
then one meal not eaten.
Thus for parents' mourning,
after the encoffining, one eats porridge,
in the morning one yì of rice,
in the evening one yì of rice;
for even-hemmed sackcloth mourning,
coarse food and plain water,
not eating vegetables or fruits;
for nine-month mourning,
not eating pickles or sauces;
for five-month and fine hempen mourning,
not drinking sweet wine.
This is how grief is expressed in drinking and eating.
For parents' mourning,
after the sacrifice at the burial and the end-of-wailing sacrifice,
coarse food and plain water,
not eating vegetables or fruits;
at one year, the small auspicious sacrifice,
then eat vegetables and fruits;
at another year, the great auspicious sacrifice,
then have pickles and sauces;
in the intervening month, the removal sacrifice,
after which drink sweet wine.
When beginning to drink wine, first drink sweet wine.
When beginning to eat meat, first eat dried meat.
For parents' mourning,
dwell in a lean-to,
sleep on straw and pillow on clods,
not removing the headband and girdle;
for even-hemmed sackcloth mourning,
dwell in a plain room,
with cut rush mats but not hemmed;
For the mourning of dàgōng,
one sleeps on a mat;
for xiǎogōng and sīmá,
a bed is permissible.
This is how grief is expressed in one's dwelling.
For the mourning of parents,
after the yú and zúkū sacrifices,
the pillar and lintel are set up, the screen is trimmed,
the rush mat is cut and not tucked in;
at the first anniversary, the xiǎoxiáng,
one resides in the èshì,
sleeping on a mat;
at the second anniversary, the dàxiáng,
one returns to the normal bedroom;
in the intervening month, the dàn sacrifice,
after which one may use a bed.
Zhǎncuī uses three shēng of hemp,
zīcuī uses four, five, or six shēng,
dàgōng uses seven, eight, or nine shēng,
xiǎogōng uses ten, eleven, or twelve shēng,
sīmá uses fifteen shēng minus half,
with the threads worked but the cloth left untreated, it is called sī.
This is how grief is expressed in clothing.
Zhǎncuī uses three shēng,
after the yú and zúkū sacrifices,
it is replaced by finished cloth of six shēng for the robe and seven for the cap;
for the mother, shūcuī uses four shēng,
replaced by finished cloth of seven shēng for the robe and eight for the cap.
Hemp is discarded and replaced by gé,
the gé belt is threefold.
At the first anniversary, xiǎoxiáng,
a liàn cap with quán trim,
the waist dié is not removed,
men remove it from the head,
women from the belt,
—why do men remove it from the head?
Why do women remove it from the belt?
Because men emphasize the head,
women emphasize the belt.
When removing mourning attire, the more important part is removed first;
when changing attire, the lighter part is changed.
At the second anniversary, dàxiáng,
plain gǎo and máyī are worn.
In the intervening month, the dàn sacrifice,
after which fine fabrics are worn,
and all ornaments may be carried.
What does changing attire mean?
It means changing the lighter parts.
In zhǎncuī mourning,
after the yú and zúkū sacrifices,
if zīcuī mourning occurs,
the lighter parts are wrapped,
the heavier parts remain distinct.
After the liàn ceremony,
if dàgōng mourning occurs,
hemp and gé are worn together.
38.2 In zīcuī mourning,
after the yú and zúkū sacrifices,
if dàgōng mourning occurs,
hemp and gé are worn together.
38.3 The gé for zhǎncuī
is the same as the hemp for zīcuī;
the gé for zīcuī
is the same as the hemp for dàgōng;
the gé for dàgōng
is the same as the hemp for xiǎogōng;
the gé for xiǎogōng
is the same as the hemp for sī,
if the hemp is the same, they are worn together.
When wearing both, if the heavier part is present,
then the lighter part is changed.
39.1 Why is there a three-year mourning period?
It is said:
To match the emotions and establish the rules,
thereby adorning the community,
distinguishing the degrees of kinship and social status,
which cannot be reduced or increased.
Hence it is said:
"It is an unchangeable way."
Great wounds take long to heal,
severe pain delays recovery;
the three-year period
matches the emotions and establishes the rules,
serving as the ultimate expression of grief.
Wearing zhǎncuī, holding the jūzhàng,
living in the yǐlú,
eating congee,
sleeping on straw with a clod as pillow,
these are the adornments of extreme grief.
The three-year mourning
ends in twenty-five months;
though sorrow is not fully spent,
and longing not forgotten,
yet mourning attire ends here—
is it not that sending off the dead has its limit,
and returning to life its measure?
39.2 All beings between heaven and earth,
those with blood and qi,
necessarily have awareness;
those with awareness
all know to love their kind.
Even great birds and beasts,
when they lose their companions,
after months or seasons pass,
will surely return to patrol,
pass their old haunts,
circle in flight,
cry out,
pace hesitantly,
linger aimlessly,
before they can leave;
smaller ones like swallows and sparrows
still have moments of chirping mournfully,
before they can leave;
thus among creatures with blood and qi,
none are more knowing than humans,
so humans for their kin
grieve until death without end.
39.3 If following those corrupt and wayward people,
they would forget by evening what was lost in the morning,
yet if we comply with that,
then we would be inferior even to birds and beasts—
how could we live together in groups without chaos?
39.4 If following the cultivated gentlemen,
then the three-year mourning,
ending in twenty-five months,
seems as brief as a steed passing a crack,
yet if extended indefinitely,
it would be endless.
39.5 Thus the ancient kings established a moderate regulation,
uniformly ensuring it suffices to complete the pattern of propriety,
then it is relinquished.
39.6 Then why does it extend to one year?
It is said:
For the closest kin, it ends at one year.
Why is this?
It is said:
Heaven and earth have already changed,
the four seasons have transformed,
and all within heaven and earth
undergo renewal,
thus mirroring this.
39.7 Then why three years?
It is said:
To add emphasis,
thus doubling it,
hence two years.
39.8 Why are there periods below nine months?
It is said:
To make them less.
Thus three years is considered emphasized,
sī and xiǎogōng as reduced,
one year and nine months as intermediate.
Above, it takes symbols from heaven,
below, models from earth,
in between, principles from humans,
exhaustively covering the reasons for harmonious group living.
Therefore, the three-year mourning
is the ultimate expression of human propriety,
this is called the utmost emphasis.
It is what all kings share,
uniform across ancient and modern times,
though none know its origin.
Confucius said:
"A child is held in the parents' arms for three years
before leaving their embrace;
thus the three-year mourning
is the universal mourning of the world."
In ancient times, the shēnyī
had its regulations,
to correspond to the compass, square, plumb line, weight, and balance.
Short, it should not expose the skin;
long, it should not drag on the ground.
The jin is continuous,
the edge hooked.
The waist seam is half the lower width;
the height of the gē
allows elbow movement;
the sleeve length,
when folded back, reaches the elbow.
The belt below should not press on the thigh,
above not press on the ribs,
but rest where there is no bone.
The design:
twelve panels correspond to the twelve months;
round sleeves correspond to the compass;
curved collar like a square corresponds to the square;
the back seam reaching the ankle corresponds to straightness;
the even hem corresponds to balance and level.
Thus, the compass,
signifies raising the hand to form the posture;
bearing the plumb line and embracing the square,
is to straighten one's governance,
and square one's righteousness.
Therefore, the "Yì" says:
"The movement of the second six of the Kūn hexagram,
is straight and square."
The lower part being even like a steelyard,
is to calm the will and pacify the heart.
Once the five methods are applied,
the sage dons it.
Thus, the compass and square are chosen for their impartiality,
the plumb line for its straightness,
the steelyard for its balance,
hence the ancient kings valued them.
Therefore, it can be worn for civil affairs,
for military affairs,
for receiving guests,
for assisting,
for managing the army,
complete yet not wasteful,
it is the next best to fine garments.
If both parents and grandparents are present,
the garment's trim is embroidered;
if only parents are present,
the trim is blue.
If an orphan,
the trim is plain.
The cuffs, edges, and borders,
are each one and a half inches wide.
41.1 The ritual of pitch-pot:
the host presents the arrows,
the director of archery presents the tally-holder,
and has someone hold the pot.
The host requests:
"I have crooked arrows and a whistling pot,
may I entertain the guests with them."
The guest says:
"You have fine wine and delicious food,
I have already been treated,
and now with this entertainment,
I dare decline."
The host says:
"The crooked arrows and whistling pot,
are not worth declining,
I insist on requesting."
The guest says:
"I have already been treated,
and now with this entertainment,
I firmly decline."
The host says:
"The crooked arrows and whistling pot,
are not worth declining,
I insist on requesting."
The guest says:
"Since my firm refusal is not accepted,
I dare not but respectfully comply."
41.2 The guest bows twice and accepts,
the host turns around and says:
"I avoid the honor."
The host bows from the eastern steps to send off,
the guest turns around and says:
"I avoid the honor."
41.3 After bowing,
receiving the arrows,
advancing to between the two pillars,
retreating back to position,
he invites the guest to the mat.
41.4 The director of archery advances to measure the pot's distance,
set at two and a half arrows apart,
returns to position,
sets up the tally-holder,
faces east,
and holds eight tallies, standing.
41.5 He announces to the guest:
"A smooth throw counts as in,
consecutive throws without release do not count,
the winner drinks, the loser is drunk,
after the proper cup is served,
please set up a horse for the winner,
one horse follows two horses,
when three horses are set,
congratulate the one with more horses."
The same is announced to the host.
41.6 He orders the musician:
"Please play 'Lí Shǒu',
evenly and consistently."
The grand musician says:
"Yes."
41.7 When both sides announce arrows are ready,
they take turns to throw.
If someone gets one in,
the director sits and places one tally.
The guest's party is on the right,
the host's party on the left.
41.8 After all have thrown,
the director holds the tallies and says:
"Both sides have finished throwing,
please count."
Two tallies make a pair,
take them in pairs,
one tally is an odd.
Then he announces with the odd tally:
"So-and-so leads so-and-so by so many pairs."
If there's an odd, he says
"and an odd",
if equal, he says
"both sides are even".
41.9 He orders the pourer:
"Please serve the cup."
The pourer says:
"Yes."
Those who should drink all kneel and hold the cup,
saying:
"I am granted the drink";
the winner kneels and says:
"I respectfully nourish."
41.10 After the proper cup is served,
please set up the horses.
Each horse corresponds to its tally.
One horse follows two horses,
for congratulation.
The congratulatory ritual says:
"Three horses are ready,
please congratulate the one with more horses."
Both guest and host say:
"Yes."
After the proper cup is served,
please remove the horses.
41.11 The number of tallies depends on the seating.
The arrow's length:
in the room, five fist-widths,
in the hall, seven fist-widths,
in the courtyard, nine fist-widths.
The tally is one foot two inches long.
The pot:
neck length seven inches,
belly length five inches,
mouth diameter two and a half inches;
capacity one dou five sheng.
The pot is filled with small beans,
to prevent the arrows from bouncing out.
The pot is two and a half arrows away from the mat.
Arrows are made of mulberry or thorn,
without removing the bark.
41.12 In Lǔ, the disciples' admonition says:
"No covering,
no arrogance,
no standing with back turned,
no excessive talk;
standing with back turned or excessive talk,
incurs a fixed penalty."
In Xuē, the disciples' admonition says:
"No covering,
no arrogance,
no standing with back turned,
no excessive talk;
such offenders are fined to drink."
41.13 The drum: half Lǔ drum;
half Xuē drum.
Using half or less is for pitch-pot ritual,
using all is for archery ritual.
The director of archery,
the court elder,
and standing capped officers,
all belong to the guest's party;
musicians, messengers, and youths,
all belong to the host's party.
Lǔ drum:
half
Xuē drum:
half.
42.1 Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Confucius:
"Master, your attire,
is it the attire of a scholar?"
Confucius replied:
"I lived in Lǔ in my youth,
wearing wide-sleeved clothes,
lived in Sòng in my adulthood,
wearing a Zhāngfǔ cap.
I have heard:
a gentleman's learning is broad,
his attire is that of his homeland;
I do not know of a scholar's attire."
Duke Āi said:
"May I ask about the conduct of a scholar?"
Confucius replied:
"To recount it hastily
cannot cover all matters,
to detail it fully would take long,
even with changed attendants, it could not be finished."
Duke Āi ordered a mat.
Confucius attended.
It is said:
"The scholar possesses treasures on the mat awaiting employment,
studies diligently day and night awaiting inquiries,
holds loyalty and trustworthiness awaiting recommendation,
exerts effort in action awaiting selection,
such is their self-reliance.
"The scholar dresses appropriately,
acts with caution,
in great yielding appears indifferent,
in small yielding seems insincere,
in major matters appears awe-inspiring,
in minor matters appears ashamed,
they are hard to advance but easy to retreat,
humble as if incapable,
such is their demeanor.
"The scholar lives with disciplined diligence,
sits and rises with respect,
speaks with trustworthiness first,
acts with integrity always,
does not contend for advantages on dangerous or easy roads,
nor for comfort in winter or summer's shade,
cherishes life to await opportunities,
nurtures the body to accomplish deeds.
Such is their preparedness.
"The scholar does not treasure gold and jade,
but considers loyalty and trustworthiness as treasures;
does not pray for land,
but establishes righteousness as their land;
does not pray for abundant accumulation,
but considers broad learning as wealth.
Hard to obtain but easy to support,
easy to support but hard to retain,
they do not appear out of season,
is that not hard to obtain?
They do not unite without righteousness,
is that not hard to retain?
Labor first and receive support later,
is that not easy to support?
Such is their approachability.
"The scholar, when entrusted with wealth,
or immersed in pleasures,
does not compromise righteousness for gain;
when threatened by crowds,
or deterred by weapons,
does not change their principles facing death;
confronts fierce beasts without measuring courage,
lifts heavy tripods without measuring strength;
does not regret the past,
nor anticipate the future;
does not repeat mistaken words,
nor pursue rumors;
maintains dignity constantly,
does not rehearse schemes.
Such is their independence. "
42.2 "The scholar can be befriended but not coerced;
can be approached but not pressured;
can be killed but not humiliated.
Their dwelling is not extravagant,
their diet not rich;
their faults can be subtly noted but not confronted directly.
Such is their fortitude. "
42.3 "The scholar considers loyalty and trustworthiness as armor,
ritual and righteousness as shield;
practices benevolence in actions,
upholds righteousness in dwelling,
even under tyranny,
does not change their principles.
Such is their self-reliance. "
42.4 "The scholar may have a small house,
surrounded by narrow walls,
a wicker gate and small opening,
thatched door and window like a jar;
changes clothes to go out,
eats once in two days,
when employed dares not doubt,
when not employed dares not flatter.
Such is their service. "
42.5 "The scholar lives with contemporaries,
emulates ancients;
acts in present times,
becomes model for future generations;
if encountering an unpropitious age,
without support from above,
or push from below,
with slanderous people
forming cliques to endanger them,
their body may be endangered,
but their will cannot be taken,
though in danger, in daily life
ultimately faithful to their will,
still not forgetting the people's sufferings.
Such is their concern. "
42.6 "The scholar learns broadly without end,
practices earnestly without weariness:
lives in seclusion without dissipation,
communicates with superiors without distress:
values harmony in rituals,
the beauty of loyalty and trustworthiness;
the method of ease and leisure,
recommends the worthy and accommodates the multitude,
rounds edges to fit like tiles.
Such is their magnanimity. "
42.7 "The scholar recommends internally without avoiding kin,
recommends externally without avoiding enemies,
assesses achievements and accumulated deeds,
promotes the worthy to advance them,
without expecting reward;
when the ruler achieves their aim,
if it benefits the state,
seeks no wealth or honor.
Such is their recommendation of the worthy. "
42.8 "The scholar upon hearing goodness informs others,
upon seeing goodness shows others;
yields precedence in rank,
faces death together in hardship;
waits long for friends,
summons from afar.
Such is their responsibility in recommendation. "
42.9 "The scholar cleanses the body and bathes in virtue,
presents views and retires,
quietly corrects matters,
without the superior's knowledge;
if roughly prompted,
is not hasty to act;
does not act superior overlooking depths,
nor claim more with little added;
in orderly times not lightweight,
in chaotic times not despondent;
does not side with similars,
nor blame differents.
Such is their independent conduct. "
42.10 "The scholar above does not serve the Son of Heaven as minister,
below does not serve feudal lords;
cautious and calm,崇尚 broad-minded,
firm and resolute with others,
learned and knowing service;
near culture to sharpen integrity;
even if offered a state, as if mere trifles,
neither serves as minister nor official.
Such is their principle. "
42.11 "The scholar unites in will and direction,
pursues the Way with same method:
delights in standing together,
not weary of deferring to each other;
long unseen,
hears rumors but不相信;
their conduct is based on principle and established righteousness,
advances with agreement,
retreats with disagreement.
Such is their friendship. "
42.12 "Gentleness and goodness
are the root of benevolence;
reverence and caution
are the ground of benevolence;
magnanimity
