is the action of benevolence;
humble interaction
is the ability of benevolence;
ritual and moderation
are the appearance of benevolence;
speech and conversation
are the pattern of benevolence;
song and music
are the harmony of benevolence;
distribution
is the bestowal of benevolence;
the scholar possesses all these,
yet still dares not claim benevolence.
Such is their reverence and yielding. "
42.13 "The scholar is not discouraged by poverty and low status,
nor elated by wealth and honor,
not shamed by rulers,
not burdened by elders,
not distressed by officials,
hence called scholar.
Now people name scholars recklessly,
often using 'scholar' as a term of reproach. "
Confucius arrived at his lodging,
Duke Āi housed him,
hearing these words,
his speech became more trustworthy,
his actions more righteous:
"Until the end of my days,
I dare not mock scholars. "
43.1 The Way of the Great Learning
lies in illustrating illustrious virtue,
in renovating the people,
in resting in the highest good.
Knowing where to rest, then there is determination,
determination then calmness,
calmness then tranquility,
tranquility then deliberation,
deliberation then attainment.
Things have roots and branches,
affairs have beginnings and ends,
knowing what comes first and last,
then one is near the Way.
The ancients who wished to illustrate illustrious virtue throughout the kingdom
first ordered well their own states.
Wishing to order well their states,
they first regulated their families.
Wishing to regulate their families,
they first cultivated their persons.
Wishing to cultivate their persons,
they first rectified their hearts.
Wishing to rectify their hearts,
they first sought to be sincere in their thoughts.
Wishing to be sincere in their thoughts,
they first extended to the utmost their knowledge.
Such extension of knowledge lay in the investigation of things.
Things being investigated,
knowledge became complete.
Their knowledge being complete,
their thoughts were sincere.
Their thoughts being sincere,
their hearts were then rectified.
Their hearts being rectified,
their persons were cultivated.
Their persons being cultivated,
their families were regulated.
Their families being regulated,
their states were rightly governed.
Their states being rightly governed,
the whole kingdom was made tranquil and happy.
From the son of Heaven down to the mass of the people,
all must consider the cultivation of the person the root of everything besides.
It cannot be, when the root is neglected,
that what should spring from it will be well ordered.
It never has been the case that what was of great importance has been slightly cared for,
and, at the same time, that what was of slight importance has been greatly cared for.
This is called knowing the root.
This is called the perfection of knowledge.
What is meant by "making the thoughts sincere"
is the allowing no self-deception,
as when we hate a bad smell,
and as when we love what is beautiful.
This is called self-enjoyment.
Therefore, the superior man must be watchful over himself when he is alone.
There is no evil to which the mean man, dwelling retired, will not proceed,
but when he sees a superior man,
he instantly tries to disguise himself,
concealing his evil,
and displaying what is good.
The other beholds him,
as if he saw his heart and reins;-of what use is his disguise?
This is an instance of the saying-
"What truly is within will be manifested without."
Therefore, the superior man must be watchful over himself when he is alone.
The disciple Zēng said,
"What ten eyes behold,
what ten hands point to,
is to be regarded with reverence!"
Riches adorn a house,
and virtue adorns the person.
The mind is expanded,
and the body is at ease.
Therefore, the superior man must make his thoughts sincere.
In the Book of Poetry, it is said,
"Look at that winding course of the Qí,
With the green bamboos so luxuriant!
Here is our elegant and accomplished prince!
As we cut and then file;
As we chisel and then grind.
So has he cultivated himself.
How grave is he and dignified!
How majestic and distinguished!
Our elegant and accomplished prince
Never can be forgotten."
That expression-"As we cut and then file,"
indicates the work of learning.
"As we chisel and then grind,"
indicates that of self-culture.
"How grave is he and dignified!"
indicates the feeling of cautious reverence.
"How majestic and distinguished!"
indicates an awe-inspiring deportment.
"Our elegant and accomplished prince never can be forgotten,"
indicates how, when virtue is complete and excellence extreme,
the people cannot forget them.
In the Book of Poetry, it is said,
"Ah! the former kings are not forgotten."
Future princes deem worthy what they deemed worthy,
and love what they loved.
The common people delight in what delighted them,
and are benefited by their beneficial arrangements.
It is on this account that the former kings, after they have quitted the world, are not forgotten.
In the Announcement to Kāng, it is said,
"He was able to make his virtue illustrious."
In the Tàijiǎ, it is said,
"He contemplated and studied the illustrious decrees of Heaven."
In the Canon of the Emperor Yáo, it is said,
"He was able to make illustrious his lofty virtue."
These passages all show how those sovereigns made themselves illustrious.
On the bathing tub of Tāng, the following words were engraved:
"If you can one day renovate yourself,
do so from day to day.
Yea, let there be daily renovation."
In the Announcement to Kāng, it is said,
"To stir up the new people."
In the Book of Poetry, it is said,
"Although Zhōu was an ancient state,
the ordinance which lighted on it was new."
Therefore, the superior man in everything uses his utmost endeavors.
In the Book of Poetry, it is said,
"The royal domain of a thousand lǐ
Is where the people rest."
In the Book of Poetry, it is said,
"The twittering yellow bird
Lights on a thickly-wooded mound."
The Master said,
"When it rests, it knows where to rest.
Is it possible that a man should not be equal to this bird?"
In the Book of Poetry, it is said,
"Profound was King Wén.
With how bright and unceasing a feeling of reverence
Did he regard his resting places!"
As a sovereign, he rested in benevolence.
As a minister, he rested in reverence.
As a son, he rested in filial piety.
As a father, he rested in kindness.
In communication with his subjects, he rested in good faith.
The Master said,
"In hearing litigations,
I am like any other body.
What is necessary
is to cause the people to have no litigations?"
So, those who are devoid of principle find it impossible to carry out their speeches,
and a great awe would be struck into men's minds;-this is called knowing the root.
What is meant by "The cultivation of the person depends on rectifying the mind"
may be thus illustrated:-If a man be under the influence of passion,
he will be incorrect in his conduct.
If he be under the influence of terror,
he will be incorrect in his conduct.
If he be under the influence of fond regard,
he will be incorrect in his conduct.
If he be under the influence of sorrow and distress,
he will be incorrect in his conduct.
When the mind is not present,
we look and do not see;
we hear and do not understand;
we eat and do not know the taste of what we eat.
This is what is meant by saying that the cultivation of the person depends on the rectifying of the mind.
What is meant by "The regulation of one's family depends on the cultivation of his person"
is this:-Men are partial where they feel affection and love;
partial where they despise and dislike;
partial where they stand in awe and reverence;
partial where they feel sorrow and compassion;
partial where they are arrogant and rude.
Thus it is that there are few men in the world
who love and at the same time know the bad qualities of the object of their love,
or who hate and yet know the excellences of the object of their hatred.
Hence it is said, in the common adage,
"A man does not know the wickedness of his son;
he does not know the richness of his growing corn."
This is what is meant by saying that if the person be not cultivated, a man cannot regulate his family.
What is meant by "In order rightly to govern the state, it is necessary first to regulate the family"
is this:-It is not possible for one to teach others,
while he cannot teach his own family.
Therefore, the ruler, without going beyond his family,
completes the lessons for the state.
There is filial piety:-therewith the sovereign should be served.
There is fraternal submission:-therewith elders and superiors should be served.
There is kindness:-therewith the multitude should be treated.
In the Announcement to Kāng, it is said,
"Act as if you were watching over an infant."
If a mother is really anxious about it,
though she may not hit exactly the wants of her infant,
she will not be far from doing so.
There never has been a girl who learned to bring up a child,
that she might afterwards marry.
When the one man is benevolent,
his whole family will be aroused to benevolence.
When the one man is urbane,
his whole family will be aroused to urbanity.
On the other hand, if the one man be greedy and perverse,
his whole family will be thrown into disorder.
Such is the influence of one man;-truly, it may be feared.
Therefore it is said, "One word may ruin an affair;
one man may settle a country."
Yáo and Shùn led on the kingdom with benevolence,
and the people followed them.
Jié and Zhòu led on the kingdom with violence,
and the people followed them.
The orders which these issued were contrary to the practices which they loved,
and so the people did not follow them.
On this account, the ruler must himself be possessed of the good qualities,
and then he may require them in the people.
He must not have the bad qualities in himself,
and then he may require that they shall not be in the people.
Never has there been a man, who, not having reference to his own character and wishes in dealing with others,
was able effectually to instruct them.
Therefore, the order of the state depends on the regulation of the family.
In the Book of Poetry, it is said,
"That peach tree, so delicate and elegant!
How luxuriant is its foliage!
This girl is going to her husband's house.
She will rightly order her household."
The Book of Songs says:
"He can be a worthy elder brother and a compliant younger brother."
Only when one can be a worthy elder brother and a compliant younger brother
can he then teach the people of the state.
The Book of Songs says:
"His deportment is without fault,
and he rectifies the four quarters of the state."
Only when he is sufficient as a model for father and son, elder and younger brothers
will the people then take him as their model.
This is what is meant by "governing the state lies in regulating the family."
What is meant by "bringing peace to the world lies in governing the state" is this:
When the ruler respects the aged, the people will be stimulated to filial piety;
when the ruler honors elders, the people will be stimulated to fraternal duty;
when the ruler shows compassion to the orphaned, the people will not act contrary.
Therefore, the noble person possesses the way of the measuring square.
What one dislikes in superiors
should not be used to treat subordinates;
what one dislikes in subordinates
should not be used to serve superiors;
what one dislikes in those before
should not be used to precede those after;
what one dislikes in those after
should not be used to follow those before;
what one dislikes in those on the right
should not be used to interact with those on the left;
what one dislikes in those on the left
should not be used to interact with those on the right:
This is what is called the way of the measuring square.
The Book of Songs says:
"How joyful is the noble person,
the parent of the people."
What the people like, he likes;
what the people dislike, he dislikes:
This is what is meant by "parent of the people."
The Book of Songs says:
"Lofty is that Southern Mountain,
with its rugged rocks;
majestic is the Grand Tutor Yǐn,
whom the people all look up to."
Those who possess a state cannot but be cautious,
for if they deviate, they will be punished by the world.
The Book of Songs says:
"Before the Yīn dynasty lost the multitude,
it could match the Lord on High;
take warning from the Yīn:
the great mandate is not easily preserved."
The Way is this: gain the multitude and you gain the state;
lose the multitude and you lose the state.
Therefore, the noble person first cultivates virtue with caution.
With virtue, there will be the people;
with the people, there will be the land;
with the land, there will be wealth;
with wealth, there will be resources for use.
Virtue is the root,
wealth is the branch.
To treat the root as external and the branch as internal
is to contend with the people and practice plunder.
Therefore, when wealth is gathered, the people are scattered;
when wealth is scattered, the people are gathered.
Therefore, what goes out contrary to the Way
will also come in contrary to the Way;
what comes in contrary to the Way
will also go out contrary to the Way.
The "Kāng Gào" says:
"The mandate is not constant!"
If one follows the good Way, one gains it;
if one does not follow the good Way, one loses it.
The Chǔ Shū says:
"The state of Chǔ does not consider anything as treasure,
only goodness as treasure."
Jiù Fàn said:
"The exiled man has nothing to consider as treasure,
only regarding kinship with benevolence as treasure."
The "Qín Shì" says:
"If there be a minister,
sincere and without other skills,
his mind is at ease,
and he is capable of tolerance.
When others have skills,
it is as if he has them himself;
when others are wise and sage,
his heart loves them,
not merely as if it came from his own mouth;
he truly can tolerate them.
He can protect my descendants and the black-haired people;
is this not indeed beneficial!
When others have skills,
he is jealous and hates them;
when others are wise and sage,
he obstructs them so they cannot advance;
he truly cannot tolerate them.
He cannot protect my descendants and the black-haired people;
is this not indeed dangerous!"
Only the benevolent person can banish such men,
driving them to the four barbarian tribes,
not allowing them to dwell in the Middle Kingdom.
This is what is meant by "only the benevolent person can love others,
and can hate others."
To see the worthy and not be able to promote them,
or to promote them but not give them precedence,
is negligence;
to see the unworthy and not be able to dismiss them,
or to dismiss them but not keep them at a distance,
is a fault.
To love what others hate,
and to hate what others love,
is to go against human nature,
and disaster is sure to reach one's person.
Therefore, the noble person has a great Way:
he must be loyal and trustworthy to attain it,
and he will lose it through arrogance and extravagance.
There is a great Way to produce wealth:
let the producers be many,
the consumers few;
let there be haste in production,
and slowness in expenditure:
then wealth will always be sufficient.
The benevolent use wealth to develop their character;
the non-benevolent sacrifice their character to amass wealth.
There has never been a case where the superiors loved benevolence
and the subordinates did not love righteousness;
there has never been a case where those who loved righteousness
did not bring their affairs to completion;
there has never been a case where the wealth in the treasury
did not belong to the ruler.
Mèng Xiànzǐ said:
"He who keeps a carriage and horses
does not look after chickens and pigs;
a family that uses ice in sacrifices
does not keep cattle and sheep;
a family that possesses a hundred chariots
does not keep ministers who amass wealth.
Rather than have ministers who amass wealth,
it is better to have ministers who steal."
This means that the state does not take profit as its benefit,
but takes righteousness as its benefit.
He who heads a state and is devoted to wealth and expenditure
must be influenced by petty men.
If he considers them good,
and employs petty men to govern the state,
calamities and injuries will come together.
Even if there be good men,
what can they do
about it?
This means that the state does not take profit as its benefit,
but takes righteousness as its benefit.
What makes a human being human
is ritual and righteousness.
The beginning of ritual and righteousness
lies in correcting the bodily demeanor, harmonizing the facial expression, and smoothing the speech.
When the bodily demeanor is correct,
the facial expression harmonious,
and the speech smooth,
then ritual and righteousness are complete.
They are used to rectify the relationship between ruler and minister, to make father and son intimate, and to harmonize elder and younger.
When ruler and minister are rectified,
father and son intimate,
and elder and younger harmonious,
then ritual and righteousness are established.
Therefore, after the capping, the ceremonial attire is complete;
after the ceremonial attire is complete, the bodily demeanor is correct, the facial expression harmonious, and the speech smooth.
Hence it is said:
"The capping
is the beginning of ritual."
Therefore, the ancient sage kings valued the capping.
In ancient times, for the capping ceremony, they divined for the day and the guests,
in order to show reverence for the capping affair.
Reverencing the capping affair
is how they valued ritual;
valuing ritual is how they made it the foundation of the state.
Therefore, the capping took place at the eastern steps,
to mark the succession;
the libation was offered at the guest's position,
and the three additions of caps increased in dignity,
to signify the achievement of maturity;
after being capped, he was given a style-name,
which is the way of the adult.
He visited his mother,
and his mother bowed to him;
he visited his elder and younger brothers,
and his elder and younger brothers bowed to him:
this is because, as an adult, he was treated with ritual.
Wearing a black cap and black robes,
he presented his gift to the ruler,
and then with his gift visited the local officers and elders:
this was to present himself as an adult.
To make someone an adult
is to demand of him the ritual of an adult.
To demand the ritual of an adult
is to demand that he practice the ritual of being a son,
a younger brother, a minister,
and a junior.
To demand these four kinds of conduct from a person,
must not the ritual be weighty?
Therefore, when the practices of filial piety, fraternal duty, loyalty, and obedience are established,
then one can be considered a proper person;
being able to be a proper person,
then one can govern others.
Hence, the sage kings valued ritual.
Thus it is said:
"The capping ceremony
is the beginning of ritual,
and the most important of auspicious events."
For this reason, the ancients valued the capping ceremony;
valuing it, they performed it in the ancestral temple;
performing it in the ancestral temple
was to show respect for the significant event;
respecting the significant event and not daring to assume such importance lightly;
not daring to assume such importance lightly,
was to humble oneself and honor the ancestors.
45.1 The wedding ceremony
is to join the harmony of two surnames,
above to serve the ancestral temple,
and below to continue the posterity.
Therefore, the gentleman values it.
Thus, in the wedding ceremony, the procedures of nàcǎi,
wèn míng,
nà jí,
nà zhēng,
and qǐng qī,
all involve the host setting out mats and a small table in the temple,
and going outside the gate to bow and welcome the guests,
who then enter,
bow and yield to each other as they ascend,
and receive instructions in the temple,
all to show reverence, caution, and the proper solemnity of the wedding ceremony.
45.2 The father personally toasts his son,
and commands him to go and meet the bride,
showing that the man takes the initiative over the woman.
The son, receiving the command, goes to meet her,
while the host sets out mats and a small table in the temple,
and goes outside the gate to bow and welcome him.
The groom enters holding a wild goose,
bows and yields as he ascends to the hall,
bows twice and presents the goose,
for he is personally receiving her from her parents.
He descends,
goes out,
drives the bride's carriage,
and the groom hands her the mounting cord,
then drives the wheel three circles.
He first waits outside the gate,
and when the bride arrives,
the groom bows to her and they enter together,
share the same animal for the meal,
and drink from the same split gourd cup,
all to unite them as one body,
equalize their status, and make them intimate.
45.3 Through reverence, caution, and proper solemnity, they then become intimate;
this is the essence of ritual,
and how the distinction between men and women is established,
and the righteousness of husband and wife is set.
When men and women are distinct,
then husband and wife have righteousness;
when husband and wife have righteousness,
then father and son have affection;
when father and son have affection,
then ruler and minister have correctness.
Therefore it is said:
"The wedding ceremony
is the foundation of ritual."
45.4 Ritual begins with the capping ceremony,
is founded on the wedding,
emphasized in mourning and sacrifice,
honored in court audiences and diplomatic missions,
and harmonized in archery
and village ceremonies—this is the essence of ritual.
45.5 Rising early,
the bride bathes and awaits to meet her in-laws;
at dawn,
the assistant presents the bride to her parents-in-law,
holding a basket with dates, chestnuts, and dried meat to present,
the assistant offers sweet wine to the bride,
the bride offers dried meat and paste in sacrifice,
and offers the sweet wine,
completing the rites of a wife.
The parents-in-law enter the room,
and the bride offers a special pig as a gift,
demonstrating her obedience as a wife.
The next morning,
the parents-in-law together entertain the bride with a one-round toast ceremony,
and set down the return toast.
The parents-in-law first descend by the western steps,
and the bride descends by the eastern steps,
to mark her succession.
45.6 Completing the rites of a wife,
demonstrating her obedience,
and further emphasizing her succession,
all serve to heavily charge her with the duty of wifely obedience.
Wifely obedience means
obedience to parents-in-law,
harmony with the household members;
then being suitable to her husband,
managing the work of silk, hemp, cloth, and silk fabrics,
and carefully guarding the stores and reserves.
Thus, when wifely obedience is complete, the household is harmonious and well-ordered;
when the household is harmonious and well-ordered, the family can long endure;
therefore, the sage kings valued it.
45.7 Thus, in ancient times, three months before a woman married,
if her ancestral temple had not been dismantled,
she was taught in the ducal palace;
if the ancestral temple had been dismantled,
she was taught in the clan hall,
instructed in wifely virtue, speech, appearance, and work.
After her education was complete, a sacrifice was held,
using fish as the victim,
flavored with duckweed and algae,
to complete her training in wifely obedience.
45.8 In ancient times, the queen established six palaces,
with three consorts, nine concubines, twenty-seven wives,
and eighty-one attendants,
to oversee the internal governance of the realm,
and to illuminate and display wifely obedience;
thus, the realm was internally harmonious and families well-ordered.
The emperor established six ministries,
with three dukes, nine ministers, twenty-seven senior officials,
and eighty-one scholars,
to oversee the external governance of the realm,
and to illuminate and display the male teachings of the realm;
thus, externally there was harmony and the state was well-governed.
Therefore it is said:
"The emperor oversees male teachings,
the queen oversees female obedience;
the emperor governs the way of yang,
the queen governs the virtue of yin;
the emperor handles external governance,
the queen handles internal duties.
When teachings and obedience become customs,
external and internal are harmonious and compliant,
the state and families are well-ordered and governed,
this is called great virtue."
45.9 Therefore, if male teachings are not cultivated,
yang affairs are not proper,
it is reflected in heaven,
and the sun is eclipsed;
if wifely obedience is not cultivated,
yin affairs are not proper,
it is reflected in heaven,
and the moon is eclipsed.
Thus, when a solar eclipse occurs, the emperor dons plain robes and rectifies the duties of the six ministries,
to cleanse the yang affairs of the realm;
when a lunar eclipse occurs, the queen dons plain robes and rectifies the duties of the six palaces,
to cleanse the yin affairs of the realm.
Thus, the emperor and the queen
are like the sun and the moon,
yin and yang,
mutually dependent to achieve completion.
The emperor cultivates male teachings,
which is the way of the father;
the queen cultivates female obedience,
which is the way of the mother.
Therefore it is said:
"The emperor and the queen
are like the father and the mother."
Thus, for the heavenly king, one wears the unhemmed mourning dress,
as for a father;
for the queen, one wears the hemmed mourning dress,
as for a mother.
46.1 The meaning of the village drinking ceremony:
the host bows and welcomes the guest outside the school gate,
they enter,
bow three times before reaching the steps,
yield three times before ascending,
all to express respect and deference.
Washing hands, rinsing the cup, and raising the vessel
are to express cleanliness.
Bowing upon arrival,
bowing for the rinsing,
bowing to receive,
bowing to send off,
bowing after completion,
are to express reverence.
Respect, deference, cleanliness, and reverence
are how gentlemen interact with each other.
When gentlemen are respectful and deferential, they do not contend;
clean and reverent, they are not negligent;
not negligent and not contentious,
they stay far from fights and disputes;
without fights and disputes,
there are no calamities of violence and disorder;
this is how gentlemen avoid human calamities,
thus the sages established it with the Way.
46.2 The villagers, scholars, and gentlemen,
honor the ceremony in the room,
shared by host and guest.
The honored vessel contains plain water,
valuing its simplicity.
Delicacies come from the eastern room,
provided by the host.
The washing station is opposite the eastern eaves,
where the host cleanses himself,
to serve the guest.
46.3 The guest and host represent Heaven and Earth;
the intermediary and assistant represent yin and yang;
the three guests represent the three luminaries;
the three deferrals
symbolize the moon forming its brightness on the third day;
the seating on four sides
symbolizes the four seasons.
The stern and congealing qi of Heaven and Earth
begins in the southwest
and peaks in the northwest;
this is the qi of dignity and reverence of Heaven and Earth,
the qi of righteousness of Heaven and Earth.
The warm and generous qi of Heaven and Earth
begins in the northeast
and peaks in the southeast;
this is the qi of abundant virtue of Heaven and Earth,
the qi of benevolence of Heaven and Earth.
The host honors the guest,
thus seating the guest in the northwest,
and seating the intermediary in the southwest to assist the guest.
The guest
receives others with righteousness,
hence seated in the northwest.
The host,
receives others with virtue and generosity,
hence seated in the southeast.
And the assistant is seated in the northeast
to assist the host.
With benevolence and righteousness in interaction,
and duties fulfilled by guest and host,
having regulated numbers of sacrificial vessels and offerings is called sageliness;
establishing sageliness and guiding it with reverence is called ritual;
ritual embodying the care for elders and young is called virtue.
Virtue
is what is attained in oneself.
Hence it is said:
"Those in ancient times who learned the arts of the Way
did so to attain it in themselves.
Therefore, the sages devoted themselves to it."
46.4 Offering sacrifices to the recommended dishes
and to the wine
is to show reverence in ritual.
Tasting the lung
is to experience the ritual.
Sipping the wine
completes the ritual.
At the end of the mat,
it signifies that this mat's purpose
is not solely for eating and drinking,
but for performing rituals,
which is why ritual is valued over wealth.
Finishing the goblet,
and presenting the substance on the western steps,
indicates that this mat's setting
is not exclusively for eating and drinking,
embodying the principle of prioritizing ritual over wealth.
Prioritizing ritual over wealth
then leads the people to practice reverence and deference without contention.
46.5 In the Xiāng Yǐn Jiǔ ritual,
those aged sixty sit,
those aged fifty stand in attendance,
to listen to administrative duties,
thereby clarifying respect for elders.
Those aged sixty have three dishes,
seventy have four dishes,
eighty have five dishes,
ninety have six dishes,
thereby clarifying the care for the aged.
When the people know to respect elders and care for the aged,
then they can practice filial and fraternal devotion at home.
The people practicing filial and fraternal devotion at home,
and respecting elders and caring for the aged outside,
then education is accomplished,
and with education accomplished, the state can be secure.
What the noble person calls filial piety
is not something enforced daily in every household;
rather, by integrating it with the Xiāng Shè ritual,
and teaching through the Xiāng Yǐn Jiǔ ritual,
the practice of filial and fraternal devotion is established.
46.6 Confucius said:
"I observe the Xiāng Yǐn Jiǔ ritual,
and understand how the Kingly Way can be easily achieved."
46.7 The host personally invites the guest and intermediary,
and the other guests follow on their own.
Arriving outside the gate,
the host bows to the guest and intermediary,
and the other guests enter by themselves;
the distinction between noble and humble is thus made clear.
46.8 After three bows reaching the steps,
with three deferrals the guest ascends;
the rituals of bowing upon arrival, offering, toasting,
and the nuances of declining and yielding are elaborate.
With the intermediary, they are simplified.
As for the other guests, they ascend to receive,
sit to make offerings,
stand to drink,
and descend without reciprocal toasting;
the distinction between elaborate and simple is thus made clear.
46.9 The musicians enter,
ascend and sing three pieces,
and the host offers them drink;
the flutists enter and play three pieces,
and the host offers them drink;
alternating singing and playing for three pieces each,
combined music for three pieces,
the musicians announce the completion of the music,
and then depart.
One person raises a goblet,
and a supervisor is established,
showing that they know how to harmonize joy without excess.
46.10 The guest toasts the host,
the host toasts the intermediary,
the intermediary toasts the other guests,
with order by age,
ending with those who pour and wash;
showing that they know to respect elders without omission.
46.11 Descending,
they remove their shoes and ascend to sit,
with unlimited rounds of drinking.
The moderation in drinking
ensures that morning duties are not neglected,
and evening duties are not abandoned.
When the guest leaves,
the host bows in farewell,
and the ceremonial procedures are fully completed.
Showing that they can enjoy repose without disorder.
46.12 With nobility and humility clarified,
elaboration and simplicity distinguished,
harmony and joy without excess,
respect for elders without omission,
repose without disorder—
these five practices
are sufficient to rectify oneself and secure the state.
That state being secure, the world is secure.
Hence it is said:
"I observe the Xiāng Yǐn Jiǔ ritual,
and understand how the Kingly Way can be easily achieved."
46.13 The meaning of the Xiāng Yǐn Jiǔ ritual:
establishing the guest to symbolize Heaven,
establishing the host to symbolize Earth,
setting the intermediary and assistant to symbolize the sun and moon,
and the three guests to symbolize the three luminaries.
In ancient times, when creating rituals,
they took Heaven and Earth as the warp,
the sun and moon as the woof,
and correlated them with the three luminaries,
forming the foundation of governance and education.
46.14 A dog is cooked in the east,
honoring the emergence of yang qi in the east.
The washing station is at the eastern steps,
with water placed east of it,
honoring the eastern sea of Heaven and Earth.
The vessel contains dark wine,
teaching the people not to forget their origins.
46.15 The guest must face south.
The east represents spring;
spring signifies stirring,
and producing all things is sagely.
The south represents summer;
summer signifies growth,
nurturing, developing, and fostering—
that is benevolence.
The west represents autumn;
autumn signifies gathering,
gathering in due time, examining
and upholding righteousness.
The north represents winter;
winter signifies centrality,
and centrality means storing.
Therefore, when the Son of Heaven stands,
he faces sageliness to the left and benevolence to the front,
with righteousness to the right and storage behind.
The intermediary must face east,
intermediating between guest and host.
The host must reside in the east;
the east represents spring,
spring signifies stirring,
producing all things;
the host initiates,
producing all things.
The moon forms its brightness on the third day,
and three months complete a season;
hence the ritual has three deferrals,
and establishing a state must appoint three ministers.
The three guests
are the foundation of governance and education,
the great correlation of ritual.
47.1 In ancient times, when feudal lords performed the archery ritual,
they necessarily first conducted the Yàn礼;
when ministers, great officers,
and scholars performed the archery ritual,
they necessarily first conducted the Xiāng Yǐn Jiǔ ritual.
Thus, the Yàn礼
serves to clarify the righteousness between ruler and minister;
the Xiāng Yǐn Jiǔ ritual
serves to clarify the order of elders and young.
47.2 Therefore, in archery,
advancing, retreating, and circling must accord with ritual,
the inner will must be upright,
the outer posture must be straight,
and only then can one grasp the bow and arrows steadily and firmly;
grasping the bow and arrows steadily and firmly,
only then can one speak of hitting the target,
and through this, virtuous conduct can be observed.
47.3 Its rhythms:
the Son of Heaven uses the "Zōu Yú" as the rhythm;
feudal lords use the "Lí Shǒu" as the rhythm;
high ministers and grandees use the "Cǎi Pín" as the rhythm;
officers use the "Cǎi Fán" as the rhythm.
The "Zōu Yú"
celebrates the completeness of officials;
the "Lí Shǒu"
celebrates the timely assembly;
the "Cǎi Pín"
celebrates following the laws;
the "Cǎi Fán"
celebrates not neglecting duties.
Hence, the Son of Heaven takes the completeness of officials as the rhythm;
feudal lords take timely assembly with the Son of Heaven as the rhythm;
high ministers and grandees take following the laws as the rhythm;
officers take not neglecting duties as the rhythm.
Thus, understanding the intent of these rhythms,
and not failing in their duties,
then achievements are completed and virtuous conduct is established;
when virtuous conduct is established, there will be no calamities of violence and disorder.
When achievements are completed, the state is secure.
Therefore, it is said:
"Archery
is a means to observe great virtue."
47.4 Therefore, in ancient times, the Son of Heaven used archery to select feudal lords, high ministers, grandees, and officers.
Archery
is the affair of men,
and thus it is adorned with ritual and music.
Hence, among affairs that fully embody ritual and music,
and can be frequently practiced,
to establish virtuous conduct,
none compares to archery,
and thus the sage kings devoted themselves to it.
47.5 Therefore, according to the system of the ancient Son of Heaven:
feudal lords annually presented tribute scholars to the Son of Heaven,
and the Son of Heaven tested them in the archery palace.
Those whose demeanor and posture matched ritual,
whose rhythm matched music,
and who hit the target frequently,
were allowed to participate in the sacrifices.
Those whose demeanor and posture did not match ritual,
whose rhythm did not match music,
and who hit the target infrequently,
were not allowed to participate in the sacrifices.
Frequent participation in sacrifices brought rewards to the lord;
frequent non-participation brought reprimands to the lord.
Frequent rewards led to increased territory;
frequent reprimands led to reduced territory.
Therefore, it is said:
"Archery
is shooting to become a feudal lord."
Thus, feudal lords, rulers, and ministers devoted themselves to archery
to practice ritual and music.
For rulers and ministers who practice ritual and music to end up in exile and ruin,
has never happened.
47.6 Therefore, the "Shī" says:
"The descendant, the lord of the clan,
the four correct positions all raised;
grandees and gentlemen,
all the various officers,
great and small, none staying behind,
attend at the ruler's place,
to feast and to shoot,
then feasting then praise."
This means that rulers and ministers together devote themselves to archery
to practice ritual and music,
then there is peace and praise.
Thus, the Son of Heaven established this system,
and feudal lords devoted themselves to it.
This is how the Son of Heaven nurtured feudal lords,
without using military force,
and how feudal lords rectified themselves.
47.7 Confucius shot in the garden of Jué Xiàng,
and the spectators were like a wall.
When the shooting reached the point of the marshal,
he had Zǐlù hold a bow and arrows
and come out to invite shooters, saying:
"Generals who have lost armies,
grandees of ruined states,
and those who become heirs to others, do not enter;
all others may enter."
Then about half left,
and half entered.
He also had Gōngwǎng Zhī Qiú and Xù Diǎn
raise their cups and speak:
Gōngwǎng Zhī Qiú raised his cup and said:
"Those who in youth are filial and brotherly,
in old age love ritual,
do not follow vulgar customs,
cultivate themselves to await death—are there not
such
in this position?"
Then about half left,
and half remained.
Xù Diǎn again raised his cup and said:
"Those who love learning without weariness,
love ritual without change,
and in advanced age still uphold the Way without disorder—are there not
such
in this position?"
Then barely any remained.
47.8 Archery (shè) means to express (yì),
or to say to release (shě).
To express
means each expresses their own will.
Thus, with a calm heart and correct posture,
grasping the bow and arrows steadily and firmly,
grasping the bow and arrows steadily and firmly,
then the shot hits the target.
Therefore, it is said:
"For those who are fathers,
take the father as the target;
for those who are sons,
take the son as the target;
for those who are rulers,
take the ruler as the target;
for those who are ministers,
take the minister as the target."
Thus, archers each shoot at their own target.
Therefore, the great archery of the Son of Heaven
is called shooting at the feudal lords;
shooting at the feudal lords
means shooting to become a feudal lord.
Hitting the target allows one to become a feudal lord;
missing the target prevents one from becoming a feudal lord.
47.9 When the Son of Heaven was to sacrifice,
he first practiced shooting at the marsh.
The marsh
was where scholars were selected.
After shooting at the marsh,
they then shot at the archery palace.
Those who hit the target were allowed to participate in the sacrifice;
those who missed were not allowed to participate.
Those not allowed to participate were reprimanded,
and their territory was reduced;
those allowed to participate were rewarded,
and their territory was increased.
This means advancing in rank or reducing territory.
47.10 Therefore, when a boy is born,
a mulberry bow and six arrowweed arrows
are used to shoot toward heaven, earth, and the four directions.
Heaven, earth, and the four directions
are where a man's affairs lie.
Thus, he must first have the will for all his affairs,
and only then dare to use grain,
meaning to eat.
47.11 Archery
is the way of benevolence.
Archery seeks to rectify oneself;
when one is rectified, then one shoots;
if the shot misses the target,
one does not resent those who surpass oneself,
but turns to seek the cause in oneself.
Confucius said:
"The gentleman has no contentiousness,
except perhaps in archery!
Bowing and yielding, they ascend;
descending, they drink—
their contention is that of a gentleman."
47.12 Confucius said:
"How does the archer shoot? How does he listen?
Following the sound, he releases;
releasing without missing the target—
is this not only the worthy?
As for the unworthy person,
how could he hit the target?"
The "Shī" says:
"Shoot that target,
to pray for your cup."
Pray
means to seek;
to seek to hit the target and decline the cup.
Wine
is for nurturing the aged,
and for nurturing the sick;
to seek to hit the target and decline the cup
is to decline such nurture.
48.1 In ancient times, among the officials of the Zhōu Son of Heaven,
there was the office of the shùzǐ official.
The shùzǐ official was in charge of the groups
of the secondary sons of feudal lords,
high ministers, grandees, and officers,
overseeing their commands and prohibitions,
and their instruction and governance,
distinguishing their ranks,
and correcting their positions.
When the state has major affairs,
the director leads the state's sons and presents them to the crown prince,
to be used as needed.
If there are matters of armor and weapons,
then they are provided with chariots and armor,
their units are assembled,
their officers are appointed,
and they are governed by military law,
with the Minister of War not interfering.
In all state administrative affairs,
the state's sons who remain as roving recruits
are made to cultivate virtue and study the Way.
In spring, they gather at various schools,
in autumn, they gather at various archery grounds,
to examine their skills and promote or demote them accordingly.
48.2 The meaning of the feudal lords' banquet ritual:
The ruler stands southeast of the eastern steps,
facing south toward the ministers
and grand masters, who all advance slightly,
to establish their positions;
the ruler's mat is placed above the eastern steps,
occupying the host's position;
the ruler alone ascends and stands on the mat,
facing west in solitary stance,
signifying that none dare oppose him.
48.3 Setting up host and guest
is the ritual of drinking;
having the steward act as the host for toasts
means no minister dares to match rituals with the ruler;
not using a high minister or minister as the guest of honor,
but instead a grand master,
is to avoid suspicion,
clarifying the principle of resolving doubt;
when the guest enters the central courtyard,
the ruler descends one step and bows to him,
showing him ritual respect.
48.4 When the ruler proposes a toast to the guest,
and when the guest receives the cup bestowed by the ruler,
he descends, bows twice and touches his head to the ground,
then ascends to complete the bow,
clarifying the ritual of ministers;
the ruler returns the bow,
for in ritual there is no lack of response,
clarifying the ritual of the ruler.
Ministers exert their strength and ability to achieve merit for the state,
and the ruler must reward them with ranks and emoluments,
therefore ministers all strive to exert their strength and ability to achieve merit,
thus the state is secure and the ruler tranquil.
In ritual, there is no lack of response,
meaning the superior does not take from below without return.
The superior must clarify the correct way to guide the people,
the people follow it and achieve results,
then one-tenth is taken from them,
thus the ruler's needs are met and the people do not lack;
therefore, superior and inferior are harmonious and close without resentment toward each other.
Harmony and tranquility,
these are the application of ritual;
this is the great meaning between ruler and minister, superior and inferior.
Hence it is said:
"The banquet ritual
serves to clarify the meaning between ruler and minister."
48.5 Seating:
junior ministers follow senior ministers,
grand masters follow junior ministers,
officers and common sons take their positions below in order.
When a toast is made to the ruler,
the ruler proposes a toast and the drinking proceeds;
then a toast is made to the ministers,
the ministers propose a toast and the drinking proceeds;
then a toast is made to the grand masters,
the grand masters propose a toast and the drinking proceeds;
then a toast is made to the officers,
the officers propose a toast and the drinking proceeds;
then a toast is made to the common sons.
The sacrificial stands, vessels, animal offerings, presentations, and delicacies
all have distinctions of rank,
serving to clarify nobility and baseness.
49.1 In the courtesy of embassy,
a duke has seven attendants,
a marquis or earl five,
a viscount or baron three,
serving to clarify nobility and baseness.
Attendants relay the messages,
for the nobleman dares not be informal with those he respects,
showing the utmost reverence.
49.2 Three deferrals before relaying the message,
three deferrals before entering the temple gate,
three bows before reaching the steps,
three deferrals before ascending,
serving to express honor and deference.
49.3 The ruler sends officers to meet at the border,
grand masters to greet in the suburbs,
the ruler personally goes to welcome within the great gate and receives in the temple,
facing north bows for the gift,
bows for the honor of the ruler's command,
serving to express respect.
49.4 Respect and deference
are how noblemen interact with each other.
Therefore, when feudal lords interact with respect and deference,
they do not invade or oppress each other.
49.5 A minister acts as chief usher,
a grand master as assistant usher,
an officer as introducing usher.
The ruler personally treats the guest with ritual,
the guest has private audience,
private presentation,
provisions are sent,
the jade tablets are returned,
gifts are presented,
there are banquets, feasts, and entertainments,
serving to clarify the meaning of guest and host, ruler and minister.
49.6 Thus the Son of Heaven regulates the feudal lords,
with minor embassies every year,
major embassies every three years,
urging each other with ritual.
If an envoy errs in his embassy,
the host ruler does not personally feast him.
This is to shame and urge him.
When feudal lords urge each other with ritual,
externally they do not invade each other,
internally they do not oppress each other.
This is how the Son of Heaven nurtures the feudal lords,
without using military force
yet the feudal lords rectify themselves.
49.7 Using jade tablets for embassy
emphasizes ritual;
after the embassy returning the jade tablets
signifies esteeming ritual over wealth.
When feudal lords urge each other to value ritual over wealth,
then the people practice deference.
49.8 The host state treats the guest,
with three supplies on arrival and departure,
provisions for the guest at his lodging,
five sets of sacrificial animals displayed inside,
thirty cartloads of rice,
thirty cartloads of grain,
fodder and firewood twice the grain,
all displayed outside,
five pairs of birds daily,
all attendants have provision animals,
one meal, two banquets,
entertainments and timely gifts without number,
serving to honor the weighty ritual.
49.9 The ancients did not always use wealth like this,
yet they used wealth so generously
to show completeness in ritual.
Being complete in ritual,
then internally ruler and minister do not oppress each other,
and externally they do not invade each other.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven institutes this,
and the feudal lords devote themselves to it.
49.10 The rituals of embassy and archery
are the greatest rituals.
They begin at dawn
and are completed near midday,
none but the strong and capable can perform them.
Therefore, the strong and capable
are to perform the rituals.
Though the wine is clear,
and one thirsty, one dares not drink;
though the meat is dry,
and one hungry, one dares not eat;
though the day wanes and one weary,
solemn and reverent,
correct and orderly,
one dares not be remiss.
Thus completing the ritual节度,
rectifying ruler and minister,
making father and son close,
harmonizing elder and younger.
This is difficult for most people,
but the nobleman practices it,
therefore he is called one who has conduct;
having conduct means having righteousness,
having righteousness means being brave and strong.
Therefore, what is valued in bravery and strength
is the ability to establish righteousness;
what is valued in establishing righteousness
is having conduct;
what is valued in having conduct
is practicing ritual.
Therefore, what is valued in bravery and strength
is the daring to practice ritual and righteousness.
Thus the brave, strong, and capable,
when the world is at peace,
use it for ritual and righteousness;
when the world has affairs,
use it for victory in battle.
Used for victory in battle, they are invincible;
used for ritual and righteousness, there is orderly governance,
externally invincible,
internally orderly governance,
this is called abundant virtue.
Thus, the sage kings valued courage and strength
in this way.
If courage and strength
are not applied to ritual righteousness and victorious warfare,
but are used for contention and strife,
then such a person is called a troublemaker.
When punishments are implemented in the state,
those executed are troublemakers.
In this manner,
the people follow order and the state is secure.
49.11 Zǐgòng asked Confucius:
"May I ask why the nobleman values jade and disparages mín-stone?
Is it because jade is rare and mín-stone is abundant?"
Confucius said:
"It is not because mín-stone is abundant
that we disparage it,
nor because jade is rare
that we value it.
The noblemen of old compared virtue to jade.
Warm, smooth, and lustrous -
this is benevolence;
fine-textured and solid -
this is wisdom;
sharp-edged but not cutting -
this is righteousness;
hanging as if descending -
this is propriety;
when struck, its sound is clear and prolonged,
then abruptly ends -
this is music;
flaws don't conceal beauty, beauty doesn't conceal flaws -
this is loyalty;
its brilliance radiates all around -
this is faithfulness;
its aura like a white rainbow -
this is heaven;
its essence manifests in mountains and rivers -
this is earth;
guī and zhāng tablets presented directly -
this is virtue;
all under heaven valuing it -
this is the Way.
The Book of Songs says:
'I think of my nobleman,
so warm like jade.'
Therefore the nobleman values it."
50.1 The main principles of ritual
embody heaven and earth,
follow the four seasons,
model yin and yang,
and accord with human feelings -
therefore it is called ritual.
Those who criticize it
do not understand how ritual arises.
50.2 Ritual
has different ways for auspicious and inauspicious occasions,
which should not interfere with each other -
this derives from yin and yang.
Mourning has four regulations,
changing according to appropriateness -
this derives from the four seasons.
There is affection and principle,
there is moderation and flexibility -
this derives from human feelings.
Affection is benevolence,
principle is righteousness,
moderation is propriety,
flexibility is wisdom.
With benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom,
the way of humanity is complete.
50.3 For those with deep affection,
their mourning garments are heavy;
thus for the father, one wears the cuī mourning for three years -
this is regulated by affection.
50.4 Within the household,
affection covers righteousness;
outside the household,
righteousness cuts off affection.
Serving the ruler based on serving the father,
the respect is the same;
honoring the honorable and respecting the respected
is the great meaning of righteousness.
Therefore for the ruler one also wears cuī mourning for three years -
this is regulated by righteousness.
50.5 Eating after three days,
bathing after three months,
wearing plain silk after one year,
grieving without destroying one's nature -
this means not injuring the living because of the dead.
Mourning doesn't exceed three years,
hemp garments aren't mended,
graves aren't maintained;
on the auspicious day,
playing the plain qin,
announcing to the people there is an end -
this is regulated by moderation.
Serving the mother based on serving the father,
the love is the same.
Heaven has no two suns,
earth no two kings,
state no two rulers,
family no two superiors -
it is governed by unity.
Therefore when the father is alive
one wears qīcuī mourning for the mother for one year -
this shows there are no two superiors.
50.6 What is the staff for?
It indicates rank.
On the third day, the son receives a staff;
on the fifth day, high officials receive staffs;
on the seventh day, lower officials receive staffs.
Some say it's "to support the chief mourner";
some say it's "to assist the ill";
women and children don't use staffs -
they cannot be considered ill.
When all officials are available,
all things are prepared,
and affairs proceed without speaking,
one rises with support;
when affairs proceed after speaking,
one rises with a staff;
when one must handle affairs personally,
one merely shows a dirty face.
The bald don't untie their hair,
the hunchbacked don't bare their shoulders,
the lame don't jump,
the old and sick don't abstain from wine and meat.
All these eight cases
are regulated by flexibility.
50.7 At death,
three days without negligence,
three months without relaxation,
one year of sorrow,
three years of grief -
this is the gradation of affection.
The sages established moderation according to this gradation,
hence the three-year mourning period.
The worthy cannot exceed it,
the unworthy cannot fall short -
this is the mean in mourning;
this is what kings constantly practice.
The Book of Documents says:
"Gāozōng in the mourning hut,
did not speak for three years" -
this praises him;
all kings practice this ritual.
Why single him out for praise?
The answer:
Gāozōng was Wǔdīng.
Wǔdīng
was a worthy king of Yīn.
Succeeding to the throne, he was devoted to mourning;
at that time,
Yīn declined and revived,
rituals were abandoned and restored -
therefore he was praised.
Being praised,
he was recorded in the Book of Documents and elevated,
hence called Gāozōng.
During the three-year mourning,
the ruler does not speak;
the Book of Documents says:
"Gāozōng in the mourning hut,
did not speak for three years" -
this refers to this.
However, when it is said:
"Speech should not be ornate",
this refers to ministers.
According to ritual:
for cuī mourning,
one responds but doesn't answer;
for qīcuī mourning,
one answers but doesn't speak;
for dàgōng mourning,
one speaks but doesn't discuss;
for sī and xiǎogōng mourning,
one discusses but doesn't reach music.
For parents' mourning,
wearing mourning clothes, hemp caps, rope ties, and rush shoes,
eating porridge after three days,
bathing after three months,
wearing plain silk cap after thirteen months,
completing the mourning after three years.
50.8 Through these three stages,
the benevolent can observe one's love,
the wise can observe one's principles,
the strong can observe one's will.
Governed by ritual,
rectified by righteousness,
filial sons, respectful younger brothers, and chaste wives
can all be discerned.
